## Dīgha Nikāya
## Mahāvagga-aṭṭhakathā
## Namo Tassa Bhagavato Arahato Sammāsambuddhassa
## 1. Commentary on the Mahāpadāna Sutta
## Discourse Connected with the Continuity of Aggregates Lived in the Past

This discourse, beginning with "Evaṃ me sutaṃ" and ending with "Karerikuṭikāyaṃ," is the Mahāpadāna Sutta. In this Mahāpadāna Sutta, the following is the explanation of the new terms. In the phrase "Karerikuṭikāyaṃ," "Karerī" is the name of the Karerī tree (Varuṇa tree). Because a Karerī tree in the form of a pavilion stood near the door of that dwelling, it is called "Karerikuṭikā" (Karerī Hut). This is similar to how a dwelling is called "Kosambakuṭikā" because it stood near the door of a Kosamba tree.

It is heard that within the Jetavana Monastery, there were four great dwellings: Karerikuṭikā, Kosambakuṭikā, Gandha-kuṭikā, and Salaḷāgāra (a dwelling made of pine wood). Each of these dwellings was constructed by sacrificing one hundred thousand in wealth. Among these four dwellings, the Salaḷāgāra was commissioned by King Pasenadi, while the remaining dwellings were commissioned by the merchant Anāthapiṇḍika. Thus, the Blessed One dwelt in the Karerikuṭikā, which was built upon pillars by the householder Anāthapiṇḍika and resembled a celestial mansion.

"Pacchābhattaṃ" (after the meal) means that for monks who observe the dhutaṅga practices of being a one-session eater (ekāsanika) and refusing later food (khalupacchābhattika), having eaten early in the morning, even the period within midday is considered "after the meal." However, in this context, "after the meal" is intended to mean after the regular meal. "Piṇḍapātapaṭikkantānaṃ" means those who have returned from the alms-round, having finished the business of the meal and risen from their seats.

"Karerimaṇḍalamāဠေ" means in the sitting hall (pavilion) constructed not far from that Karerī pavilion. That Karerī pavilion was situated between the Gandha-kuṭikā and the hall...
2:
It was also between those buildings; therefore, the Gandha-kuṭikā, the Karerikuṭikā, and the hall are collectively called "Karerimaṇḍalamāḷa." "Pubbenivāsapaṭisaṃyuttā" refers to talk connected with the knowledge of recollecting past lives (pubbenivāsa-abhiññā), which is the continuity of aggregates lived in the past, analyzed as "one birth, two births," and so on. "Dhammī" means talk connected with the Dhamma.

"Udapādi" refers to the question that arose: "Oh, how wonderful is the knowledge of past lives of the Ten-Powered Blessed One! Who can recollect the continuity of aggregates lived in the past, and who cannot?" Sectarians (titthiyas) can recollect, and disciples (sāvakas), Paccekabuddhas, and the Buddhas can also recollect. What kind of sectarians can recollect? Even those Kammavādī sectarians who have reached the peak can only recollect forty aeons (kappas), and not beyond that. Disciples can recollect one hundred thousand aeons. The two Chief Disciples can recollect one incalculable (asaṅkheyya) and one hundred thousand aeons. Paccekabuddhas can recollect two incalculables and one hundred thousand aeons. For the Buddhas, however, there is no such limitation; they can recollect as much as they desire.

Sectarians recollect according to the succession of aggregates; they are unable to recollect by skipping the succession. Even while recollecting in succession, when they reach the realm of non-percipient beings (Asaññasatta), they cannot see the occurrence of aggregates. They become like a bird fallen into a net or a lame person fallen into a pit. Staying there in that Asaññasatta realm, they hold the wrong view: "There is only this much; there is nothing beyond this." Thus, the sectarians' recollection of past lives is like a blind man walking by the tip of a staff. Indeed, blind people can only walk when there is someone holding the tip of the staff; without it, they must sit right there. In the same way, sectarians can only recollect according to the succession of aggregates; they are unable to recollect by abandoning the succession.

Disciples also recollect only according to the succession of aggregates; when they reach the Asaññasatta realm, they do not see the occurrence of aggregates. This being so, for those disciples, there is no such time when there are no aggregates for beings wandering in Saṃsāra. In the Asaññasatta realm, however, they exist for five hundred aeons; therefore, having bypassed that much time and standing on the method given by the Buddhas, they can continue to recollect further, like the Elder Sobhita. The two Chief Disciples and Paccekabuddhas, however, can recollect by observing death (cuti) and rebirth (paṭisandhi). For the Buddhas, there is no need to observe death and rebirth; whatever place they wish to see, they see that very thing.
3:
When the wanderers (titthiyas) recollect the continuity of aggregates lived in past lives, they can only recollect what they themselves have seen, done, or heard. The same is true for the disciples (sāvakas) and the Pacceka Buddhas. The Buddhas, however, can recollect everything that was seen, done, or heard, whether by themselves or by others.

The knowledge of past lives (pubbenivāsañāṇa) of the wanderers is like the light of a firefly. The knowledge of past lives of the disciples is like the light of a lamp. The knowledge of past lives of the chief disciples (aggasāvakas) is like the light of the morning star. The knowledge of past lives of the Pacceka Buddhas is like the light of the moon. The knowledge of past lives of the Buddhas is like the light of the sun's orb shining in the autumn month of Tazaungmon. For the Buddha's knowledge of past lives, there is no limit such as hundreds, thousands, or hundreds of thousands of births, nor hundreds, thousands, or hundreds of thousands of aeons (kappas). For the Blessed One who recollects everything, there is neither error nor obstruction in the object; it is connected merely with reflection (āvajjana) and with the arising of the thought of attention (manasikāra) as desired. It proceeds without attachment, like an arrow shot with great speed through a weak bundle of leaves, or like the thunderbolt (vajira) of Sakka released on the peak of Mount Sineru. "Oh, how great is the Blessed One's knowledge of past lives!"—this is the meaning of the conversation that arose concerning the Blessed One. To show all this in brief, it is said in the Pali: "Thus also is the past life, thus also is the past life" (Itipi pubbenivāso). In that Pali, "itipi" means "it is also of such a nature."

2-3. Regarding the passage "Assosi kho...pe... atha bhagavā anuppatto" (The Blessed One heard... the Blessed One arrived), what should be said has already been stated in the commentary on the Brahmajāla Sutta. This is the distinction: in that Brahmajāla Sutta, he heard through the knowledge of omniscience (sabbaññutañāṇa); in this Mahāpadāna Sutta, he heard through the divine ear (dibbasota). In that Brahmajāla Sutta, the talk concerning praise and dispraise was not yet finished (when the Blessed One arrived); in this Sutta, the talk concerning the continuity of aggregates lived in past lives was not yet finished (when he arrived). Therefore, the Blessed One thought: "These monks are praising my virtue by focusing on my knowledge of past lives, but they do not know the fulfillment of my knowledge of past lives. Now, I will show them the fulfillment of that knowledge by teaching it." Thus, he approached and sat on the noble Buddha-seat, which is naturally prepared for the Buddhas to sit and teach the Dhamma, and which the monks had dusted and offered at that moment. After the question "What was the subject of your talk, monks?" and the reply "Here, Bhante..." and so on, he said "Do you wish [to hear]?" and so forth, desiring to give a Dhamma talk related to past lives. In that passage, "iccheyyātha no" means "do you wish?". Then the monks, with joyful minds, requested him, saying "Blessed One, [give] this Dhamma talk..." and so on. In that passage, "etassa" means "of the making of this Dhamma talk."
4:
Then the Blessed One, accepting their request and wishing to teach, said: "Monks, if that is so, listen." He directed them toward listening and proper attention (sādhuka-manasikāra). Wishing to reveal the recollection of those who have cut the path of the round of existence (chinnavaṭuma), which is not shared by others, he said: "From here, monks (ninety-one aeons ago)..." and so on. In that passage, "yaṃ Vipassī" means "the aeon in which the Buddha Vipassī [appeared]." This word "yaṃ" is seen in the nominative case (paccattavacana) in such places as: "Bhante, whatever (yaṃ) I have heard and received in the presence of the Tāvatiṃsa devas, I report that to the Blessed One." It is seen in the accusative case (upayogavacana) in: "That which (yaṃ) we asked, you have told us; we ask another, please tell us that." It is seen in the instrumental case (karaṇavacana) in: "Monks, it is impossible, it cannot happen, that (yaṃ) in a single world system..." and so on. Here, however, it should be understood as being in the locative sense (bummattha). Therefore, it is said: "In which aeon." "Udapādi" means he was born, causing the ten-thousandfold world system to resound.

"Bhaddakappa" (Auspicious Aeon) means a beautiful aeon or a worthy aeon, because it is adorned by the appearance of five Buddhas. The Blessed One said this while wishing to praise this aeon. To speak in detail, since our Blessed One made his initial aspiration (abhinīhāra) [at the feet of Dīpaṅkara], there has never been another single aeon in this interval where five Buddhas were born. Before our Blessed One's aspiration, four Buddhas—Taṇhaṅkara, Medhaṅkara, Saraṇaṅkara, and Dīpaṅkara—were born in a single aeon. After those four Buddhas, there was one incalculable period (asankheyya) that was entirely empty of Buddhas (buddhasuñña).

At the end of that incalculable aeon, a single Buddha named Koṇḍañña arose in one aeon. After him, there was again an incalculable period empty of Buddhas. At the end of that incalculable aeon, four Buddhas—Maṅgala, Sumana, Revata, and Sobhita—arose in one aeon. After them, there was again an incalculable period empty of Buddhas. At the end of that incalculable aeon, more than a hundred thousand aeons plus one incalculable period above this [current aeon], three Buddhas—Anomadassī, Paduma, and Nārada—arose in one aeon. After them, there was again an incalculable period empty of Buddhas. At the end of that incalculable aeon, a hundred thousand aeons above this aeon, a single Blessed One named Padumuttara arose in one aeon. After that Buddha, thirty thousand aeons above this aeon, two Buddhas—Sumေdha and Sujāta—arose in one aeon. After that, eighteen thousand aeons above this aeon, three Buddhas—Piyadassī, Atthadassī, and Dhammadassī...
5:
Buddhas appear in a certain aeon. Apart from that, ninety-four aeons before this Bhadda-kappa, a single Buddha named Siddhattha appeared in one aeon. Ninety-two aeons before this, two Buddhas named Tissa and Phussa appeared in one aeon. Ninety-one aeons before this, the Blessed One Vipassī appeared. Thirty-one aeons before this, two Buddhas named Sikhī and Vessabhū appeared. In this Bhadda-kappa, four Buddhas have appeared: the Blessed One Kakusandha, the Blessed One Koṇāgamana, the Blessed One Kassapa, and our Blessed One, Gotama; and the Blessed One Metteyya will also appear. Thus, because this aeon is adorned with the appearance of five Buddhas, the Blessed One praised this aeon, saying it is a 'Sundara-kappa' (Beautiful Aeon) and a 'Sāra-kappa' (Essential Aeon).

Is the knowledge that 'so many Buddhas have appeared or will appear in this aeon' evident only to the Buddhas, or is it evident to others as well? It is evident to others too. To whom is it evident? It is evident to the Suddhāvāsa Brahmās. To explain in detail: during the time of the world's formation, when the world-system exists as a single vast expanse of space for one incalculable period (asaṅkhyeyya), rain begins to fall for the sake of the world's establishment. At first, it is like a fall of frost during the eight intermediate days (the last four days of the month of Tabodwe and the first four days of Tabaung). After that, the torrents of rain become the size of a sesame seed, then a broken grain of rice, then a whole grain of rice, then a kidney bean, a cowpea, a jujube fruit, a myrobalan fruit, a cucumber, a pumpkin, and a gourd. Gradually, they become the size of one usabha, two usabhas, half a gāvuta, one gāvuta, two gāvutas, half a yojana, one yojana, two yojanas... and so on, up to a hundred yojanas, a thousand yojanas, and a hundred thousand yojanas. These fill the interior of the hundred billion world-systems up to the Brahma worlds that were not destroyed and remain there. Afterwards, that water gradually recedes. When the water recedes, the celestial realms are established in their natural places. The method of the establishment of those celestial realms has already been described in the 'Talk on the Recollection of Past Lives' (Pubbenivāsakathā) in the Visuddhimagga.

Particularly, when the water reaches the place where the human world is to be established, the water stays firm by the power of the wind, as if the mouth of a water-filter (dhammakaraṇa) were closed. The earth forms on the surface of the water like a lotus leaf. The site of the Mahābodhi-pallaṅka is the last to be destroyed when the world perishes and the first to be established when the world forms. At that spot, a single lotus plant arises as a preliminary sign. If a Buddha is to appear in that aeon, a flower blooms. If not, it does not bloom. If flowers do bloom, and if one Buddha is to appear, one flower blooms. If two, three, four, or five Buddhas are to appear, five flowers bloom. These flowers bloom as a cluster (kaṇṇikā) on a single stalk. The Suddhāvāsa Brahmās...
6:
"saying, 'Come, friends, let us look at the preliminary sign,' and they come to the site of the Mahābodhi-pallaṅka. In an aeon where no Buddhas appear, no flower blooms. Seeing the plant without flowers, those Brahmās become displeased, thinking, 'Alas, friends, the world will be in darkness; beings who die will fill the four lower realms; the six celestial realms and the nine Brahma realms will be empty.' However, in an aeon where flowers bloom, seeing the flowers, they joyfully utter an exclamation (udāna), saying, 'We shall behold the miracles such as the shaking of the ten thousand world-systems when the Omniscient Bodhisattas descend into their mother's womb, when they are born, when they realize the Four Noble Truths, when they turn the Wheel of Dhamma, when they perform the Twin Miracle (Yamaka-pāṭihāriya), when they descend from the Tāvatiṃsa heaven, when they relinquish the life-force (āyusaṅkhāra), and when they attain Parinibbāna.' They also think, 'The four lower realms will diminish, and the six celestial realms and the nine Brahma realms will be filled,' and then they return to their respective Brahma worlds. In this Bhadda-kappa, five lotuses have bloomed. By the power of those signs, four Buddhas have appeared, and the fifth Buddha will also appear. The Suddhāvāsa Brahmās also knew this matter by seeing those lotuses. Therefore, I said, 'It is evident to others as well.'

## Description of the Life Span (Āyupariccheda-vaṇṇanā)

5–7. Thus, the Blessed One, having shown the recollection of past lives by way of defining the aeons in the manner beginning with 'Monks, from this [aeon] backwards...', now spoke the words beginning with 'Monks, the Buddha Vipassī...' in order to show them by way of defining the birth and so forth of those Buddhas. In that section on the life span, both the terms 'parittaṃ' and 'lahukaṃ' are synonyms for the word 'appaka' (small/brief), meaning having a small extent. That life span which is small is both limited (paritta) and brief (lahuka).

The phrase 'appakaṃ vā bhiyyo' (a little or more) means living a little more than a hundred years, or living for twenty, thirty, forty, fifty, or sixty years without reaching another hundred years. Such a long-lived person is extremely rare; one must go here and there to see them, saying, 'It is said that such a person lives this long.' Among them, the laywoman Visākhā lived for one hundred and twenty years. Likewise, the brahmin Pokkharasāti, the brahmin Brahmāyu, the brahmin Sela, the brahmin Bāvariya, the Elder Ānanda, and the Elder Mahākassapa [lived for the same duration]. The Elder Anuruddha lived for one hundred and fifty years, and the Elder Bākula lived for one hundred and sixty years. This Elder Bākula was the longest-lived of all. Even he did not live up to two hundred years."
7:
All Bodhisattvas, beginning with Vipassī, take conception in their mother's womb with a consciousness that is unprompted (asaṅkhārika), associated with knowledge (ñāṇa-sampayutta), accompanied by joy (somanassa), and preceded by loving-kindness (metta). Because they take conception with such a consciousness, their lifespan could last for an incalculable (asaṅkheyya) aeon; thus, all Buddhas are of incalculable lifespan. Why then do they not remain for an incalculable period? It is because of the ruin of climate and food (utu-bhojana). Indeed, by the power of climate and food, lifespan both decreases and increases.

Among those decreases and increases, when kings are unrighteous, then the sub-kings, generals, wealthy merchants, the entire city, and the entire country also become unrighteous. At that time, their guardian deities, the earth-dwelling deities (bhumma-deva) who are friends of those deities, and further, the sky-dwelling deities, the deities of heat (uṇha-valāhaka), the deities of clouds (abbha-valāhaka), the deities of cold (sīta-valāhaka), the deities of rain (vassa-valāhaka), the deities of the Four Great Kings (Cātumahārājikā), the Tāvatiṃsā deities, and the Yāmā deities, and so forth, also become unrighteous. In this manner, up to the highest point of existence (bhavagga), excluding the noble disciples (ariya-sāvaka), the entire assembly of deities and Brahmas becomes unrighteous.

Because those deities are unrighteous, the moon and the sun move irregularly. The wind also does not blow according to its regular course but blows off-course, causing the celestial mansions in the sky to shake and tremble. When the mansions shake, the deities' minds do not incline toward pleasure and play. When the deities' minds do not incline toward play, the seasons, characterized by cold and heat, do not occur correctly or perfectly according to the time. When the seasons are irregular, the rain does not fall well; sometimes it rains, sometimes it does not; it rains in some places and not in others. Even when it rains, it falls or ceases in a manner that does not benefit the crops during the times of sowing, sprouting, stalking, flowering, or the formation of the milky grain. For that reason, the crops ripen unevenly and are deficient in fragrance, appearance, and taste. Even rice cooked in a single pot may remain as hard grains in one part, be overcooked and mushy in another, and be well-cooked in only one part. When such food is consumed, it is digested within the stomach in those same three ways. For that reason, beings suffer from many diseases and have short lifespans. Thus, first of all, by the power of climate and food, the lifespan decreases.
8:
When, however, the kings are righteous, then the sub-kings are also righteous. In this manner, following the method previously mentioned, all beings up to the Brahma realm become righteous. Because they are righteous, the moon and the sun move regularly. The wind blows according to its regular course. The wind blowing on its regular course does not shake the celestial mansions in the sky. Because those mansions are not shaken, the deities' minds incline toward pleasure and play. Thus, at the proper time, the seasons are perfect and the rain falls well. From the time of sowing, the rain falls at the proper time and ceases at the proper time, benefiting the crops. Therefore, the crops ripen evenly, are fragrant, beautiful in appearance, excellent in taste, and full of nutrients. Even when the food prepared from those crops is consumed, it reaches proper digestion. For that reason, beings are free from disease and are long-lived. Thus, by the power of climate and food, the lifespan increases.

Among those lifespans, the Blessed One Vipassī was born during the period of an 80,000-year lifespan. The Blessed One Sikhī was born during the period of a 70,000-year lifespan. This is presented as if it decreased successively; however, it did not decrease only in such a successive manner. It should be understood that it decreased only after increasing and increasing. How? In this auspicious aeon (Bhadda-kappa), first, the Blessed One Kakusandha was born during the period of a 40,000-year lifespan. Dividing the lifespan into five parts, he remained for four parts and attained Parinibbāna while the fifth part still remained. When that lifespan decreased and reached the ten-year period, it increased again to become an incalculable (asaṅkheyya) lifespan. From there, it decreased again and stood at the 30,000-year period; at that time, the Blessed One Koṇāgamana was born. When he likewise attained Parinibbāna, that lifespan reached the ten-year period, increased again to become incalculable, and after decreasing again, stood at the 20,000-year period; at that time, the Blessed One Kassapa was born. When he likewise attained Parinibbāna, that lifespan reached the ten-year period, increased again to become incalculable, and after decreasing again, reached the 100-year period; then our Fully Enlightened Buddha was born. Thus, it should be understood that it decreased and decreased, increased and increased, and then decreased. Among those lifespans, in whatever lifespan humans exist when the Buddhas are born, the lifespan of those Buddhas is also exactly that same lifespan of those humans.

## The Explanation of the Lifespan is Finished.

## Commentary on the Section on the Bodhi Tree

In the section on the Bodhi tree, "at the foot of the Pāṭali" means beneath the Pāṭali tree. On the day the Bodhisatta Vipassī attained Buddhahood, the trunk of that Pāṭali tree grew to a height of fifty cubits, and the branches were also fifty cubits, making the total height one hundred cubits. On that day, the Pāṭali tree was entirely covered from its roots with flowers as if they were arranged in clusters, and a divine fragrance wafted abroad. At that time, not only did this single Pāṭali tree bloom, but all the Pāṭali trees in the ten thousand world systems also bloomed.

Not only the Pāṭali trees, but on the trunks of all trees in the ten thousand world systems, trunk-lotuses bloomed; on the branches, branch-lotuses; on the vines, vine-lotuses; and in the sky, sky-lotuses. Great lotuses also rose up, breaking through the surface of the earth. The great ocean was also covered with five-colored lotuses, blue lotuses, and red lotuses. The entire ten thousand world systems were filled with rows of banners and garlands, and were brilliant with various colored flowers scattered about like suspended floral tassels and clusters, resembling the Nandana Grove, the Cittalatā Grove, the Missaka Grove, and the Phārusaka Grove. Banners hoisted at the edge of the eastern world system touched the edge of the western world system. Banners hoisted at the edges of the western, southern, and northern world systems also touched the edge of the southern world system. In this way, the world systems were connected by their mutual splendor. "Abhisambuddho" means having penetrated and realized all the glory and power of a Buddha's qualities, and having fully realized the Four Noble Truths.

In the Pali texts such as, "Monks, the Blessed One Sikhī, the Worthy One, the Perfectly Enlightened One, attained full enlightenment at the foot of a Puṇḍarīka tree," the explanation of the terms should be understood in this same manner. Here, "Puṇḍarīka" refers to a white mango tree. The dimensions of that white mango tree were also the same as previously mentioned. On the day the Bodhisatta Sikhī attained Buddhahood, that white mango tree was also well-covered with flowers of divine fragrance. It was covered not only with flowers but also with fruits. On one side of the tree, there were young fruits; on another side, medium-sized fruits; on another side, semi-ripe fruits; and on another side, fruits that were fully ripe and delicious as if infused with divine essence, hanging in clusters. Just like that white mango tree, all flowering trees in the entire ten thousand world systems were adorned with flowers, and all fruiting trees were adorned with fruits.

"Sālo" refers to the Sāla tree. Its dimensions were the same as the Pāṭali tree, and its splendor of flowers should be understood in the same way. The same applies to the Sirīsa tree. Regarding the Udumbara tree...
10:
On the Udumbara tree, flowers did not bloom; however, its splendor of fruits should be understood in the same way as described for the mango tree. The same should be understood for the Nigrodha tree and the Assattha tree. Thus, the seat (pallaṅka) of all Buddhas is one and the same, but the trees under which they attain enlightenment are different. Among those trees, whichever tree's foot the Buddhas penetrate and realize the Bodhi, known as the Knowledge of the Four Paths, that specific tree is called the Bodhi tree. This is known as the Section on the Bodhi Tree.

## Commentary on the Section on the Pairs of Disciples

In the section on the pairs of disciples, "Khaṇډatissa" refers to the Elder Khaṇḍa and the Elder Tissa. Between these two, the Elder Khaṇḍa was the younger brother of the same father, and the Elder Tissa was the son of the court chaplain (purohita). The Elder Khaṇḍa reached the summit of the perfection of wisdom (paññā-pāramī), while the Elder Tissa reached the summit of the perfection of concentration (samādhi-pāramī). "Agga" (Chief) means he is noble because of his incomparable qualities compared to the remaining disciples, excluding the Blessed One Vipassī. "Bhaddayugaṃ" (Auspicious Pair) is so called because of their excellence. "Abhibhūsambhava" refers to the Elder Abhibhū and the Elder Sambhava. Between these two, the Elder Abhibhū reached the summit of the perfection of wisdom. Together with the Blessed One Sikhī, he went from the city of Aruṇavatī to the Brahma world and, while performing various miracles before the assembly of Brahmas, he preached the Dhamma. He then filled the ten thousand world systems with darkness, and for the Brahmas who were struck with awe, wondering "What is this?", he diffused radiance. He made the resolution, "Let all Brahmas see my form and hear my voice," and while reciting the two verses beginning with "Ārambhatha" (Exert yourselves), he made his voice heard. The Elder Sambhava reached the summit of the perfection of concentration.

"Soṇuttara" refers to the Elder Soṇa and the Elder Uttara. Between these two, the Elder Soṇa reached the perfection of wisdom, and the Elder Uttara reached the perfection of concentration. "Vidhurasañjīva" refers to the Elder Vidhura and the Elder Sañjīva. Between these two, the Elder Vidhura reached the perfection of wisdom, and the Elder Sañjīva reached the perfection of concentration. The Elder Sañjīva, who frequently entered meditative attainments, dwelt in meditation through the power of attainment in night-quarters, day-quarters, monasteries, caves, pavilions, and so on. One day, while he was in the forest in the attainment of cessation (nirodha-samāpatti), forest workers and others, thinking "He is dead," cremated him. That Elder Sañjīva, having emerged from the attainment at the predetermined time, shook his robes and entered the village for alms. Because of that event, people came to know him well as "Sañjīva" (The Living One). "Bhiyyosuttara" refers to the Elder Bhiyyosa and the Elder Uttara. Between these two, the Elder Bhiyyosa was superior in wisdom, and the Elder Uttara was chief in concentration. "Tissabhāradvāja" refers to the Elder Tissa and the Elder Bhāradvāja. Between these two, the Elder Tissa reached the perfection of wisdom, and the Elder Bhāradvāja reached the perfection of concentration...
11:
(It) happened. "Sāriputtamoggallāna" refers to the Venerable Sāriputta and the Venerable Moggallāna. Among these two elders, the Venerable Sāriputta was foremost in the sphere of wisdom, and the Venerable Moggallāna was foremost in the sphere of concentration. This is called the Classification of the Pair of Disciples (Sāvaka-yuga-pariccheda).

## Explanation of the Classification of the Assembly of Disciples

In the Classification of the Assembly of Disciples, the first assembly of the Blessed One Vipassī was fourfold. (These four factors were:) all the monks were "Ehi Bhikkhu" monks; all the monks possessed robes and bowls created by psychic power; all the monks arrived of their own accord without being invited; and they gathered on the fifteenth-day Uposatha. Then the Teacher, holding a fan, sat down and recited the Ovāda Pātimokkha. The same method applies to the second and third assemblies. Likewise, it should be understood for all assemblies of the remaining Buddhas. However, for our Blessed One, there was only one assembly during the early period of Enlightenment (Paṭhama-bodhi). This Sutta was also spoken at a later time. Therefore, without concluding, "Monks, now there is only one assembly of my disciples," he said, "(It) happened."

In that text, "twelve hundred and fifty monks" refers to the one thousand former matted-hair ascetics and the two hundred and fifty followers of the two chief disciples, totaling twelve hundred and fifty monks. Among that group, the story should be told starting from the aspiration of the two chief disciples to show their entry into the monkhood. Among those who had ordained, the Venerable Mahāmoggallāna reached Arahantship on the seventh day. The General of the Dhamma, Venerable Sāriputta, on the fifteenth day, while the Vedanāpariggaha Sutta was being preached to his nephew, the wandering ascetic Dīghanakha, in the Sūkarakhata (Boar's) Cave on the slopes of Mount Gijjhakūṭa, sent forth his knowledge following the discourse and attained the Knowledge of a Disciple's Perfection (Sāvaka-pāramī-ñāṇa). The Blessed One, knowing the Elder's attainment of Arahantship, rose into the air and stayed at the Veluvana monastery itself. The Elder, reflecting "Where has the Blessed One gone?", knew he was at Veluvana and he himself rose into the air and stayed at the Veluvana monastery. Then the Blessed One recited the Ovāda Pātimokkha. Referring to that assembly, the Blessed One said, "twelve hundred and fifty monks." This is called the Classification of the Assembly of Disciples (Sāvaka-sannipāta-pariccheda).

In the Classification of Attendants (Upaṭṭhāka-pariccheda), the discourse "Monks, Ānanda is the foremost" was spoken referring to his being a permanent attendant. To elaborate on that: during the early period of Enlightenment, the Blessed One did not have a permanent attendant. At one time, the Venerable Nāgasamāla took the bowl and robes and followed him. At other times, the Venerable Nāgita, the Venerable Upavāna, the Venerable Sunakkhatta, the novice named Rādha, the Venerable Sāgata, and the Venerable Meghiya took the bowl and robes and followed him. Once, while the Blessed One was traveling a long distance with the Venerable Nāgasamāla, they reached a fork in the road. The Elder turned away from the path and said, "Blessed One, I will go by this way." Then the Blessed One said, "Come, monk, let us go by this way." However, that Venerable Nāgasamāla said, "Blessed One, please take your bowl and robes; I will go by this way," and [was about to] place the bowl and robes on the ground...
12:
## Explanation of the Classification of Attendants

In the Classification of Attendants, the statement "Monks, Ānanda is the foremost" was spoken referring to his status as a permanent attendant (nibaddhupaṭṭhāka). For the Blessed One, during the early period of Enlightenment, there were no permanent attendants. At one time, the Venerable Nāgasamāla took the bowl and robes and wandered [with him]. At other times, the Venerable Nāgita, the Venerable Upavāna, the Venerable Sunakkhatta, the novice Cunda, the Venerable Sāgata, and the Venerable Meghiya took the bowl and robes and wandered [with him].

Among those attendants, once, while the Blessed One was traveling a long distance with the Venerable Nāgasamāla, they reached a fork in the road. Then the Elder turned away from the path and said, "Blessed One, I will go by this way." Then the Blessed One said, "Come, monk, let us go by this way." That Elder said, "Blessed One, please take your bowl and robes; I will go by this way," and attempted to place the bowl and robes on the ground. Then the Blessed One said, "Monk, bring them," and taking the bowl and robes, he proceeded. Robbers took the bowl and robes of that monk who went by the other path and also split his head. That Elder thought, "Now the Blessed One alone is my refuge, no one else," and with blood flowing, he went to the Blessed One. When asked, "Monk, why is there this flow of blood?", he reported the matter. Then the Blessed One comforted him, saying, "Monk, do not worry; it was because I foresaw this reason that I forbade your going."

At another time, the Blessed One went to Jantugāma village in the Pācinavaṃsa Deer Park with the Venerable Meghiya. In that village, after the Venerable Meghiya had wandered for alms, he saw a pleasant mango grove by the riverbank and said, "Blessed One, please take your bowl and robes; I will practice the Dhamma of a recluse in that mango grove." Although the Blessed One forbade him three times, he went there and was beset and overwhelmed by unwholesome thoughts. He returned and reported the matter. The Blessed One also said, "Monk, it was because I foresaw this reason that I forbade your going," and in due course, he went to the city of Sāvatthī.

While staying at the noble Buddha-seat prepared in the precinct of the Gandhakuṭi in Sāvatthī, surrounded by the assembly of monks, he addressed the monks: "Monks, I am now old. When I say, 'Let us go by this path,' some monks go by another path. Some monks drop my bowl and robes on the ground. Choose a monk who will be my permanent attendant." Spiritual urgency (dhamma-saṃvega) arose in the monks. Then the Venerable Sāriputta rose from his seat, paid homage to the Blessed One, and...
13:
"Venerable Sir, aspiring for You alone, I have fulfilled the perfections for an incalculable period and a hundred thousand aeons. A person of great wisdom like me is truly fit to be an attendant; I will serve You," he submitted. Then the Blessed One declined, saying, "Enough, Sāriputta. In whichever direction you reside, that direction is not empty for Me. Your instruction is like the instruction of the Buddhas. I have no need for an attendant's service from you." In this manner, starting with the Venerable Mahāmoggallāna, the eighty great disciples stood up and made their requests, but the Blessed One declined them all.

The Venerable Ānanda, however, remained silent. Then the monks said to him, "Friend Ānanda, the Saṅgha of monks is requesting the position of attendant; you should also make a request." Ānanda replied, "Friends, what kind of thing is an attendantship obtained by begging? Does the Teacher not see me? If He is pleased, He will say, 'Let Ānanda serve Me.'" Then the Blessed One said, "Monks, Ānanda does not need to be urged by others. He will know by himself and serve Me." Thereafter, the monks urged him again, saying, "Rise, friend Ānanda! Rise, friend Ānanda! Request the position of attendant from the One of Ten Powers (Dasabala)." The Elder stood up and requested eight boons, consisting of four refusals and four requests.

The four refusals were: "Venerable Sir, if the Blessed One will not give me the fine robes He Himself receives; if He will not give me the fine alms-food; if He will not allow me to stay in the same Fragrant Chamber (Gandhakuṭī); if He will not take me along when He goes to an invitation—if so, I will serve the Blessed One." When asked, "Ānanda, what disadvantage do you see in this?" he replied, "Venerable Sir, if I were to receive these things, there would be those who say, 'Ānanda enjoys the fine robes received by the One of Ten Powers, he enjoys the alms-food, he stays in the same Fragrant Chamber, he goes to invitations together; he serves the Tathāgata because he receives such gains. What burden is there in serving like this?'" Thus he requested these four refusals.

The four requests were: "Venerable Sir, if the Blessed One will go to an invitation accepted by me; if I may be allowed to bring the audience who have come from other countries and other districts to see the Blessed One at the very moment they arrive; if I may be allowed to approach the Blessed One at the very moment a doubt arises in me; if the Blessed One will repeat to me the Dhamma He has taught in my absence—if so, I..."
14:
"...will serve the Blessed One." When asked, "Ānanda, what benefit do you see in this?" he replied, "Venerable Sir, in this Dispensation, faithful clansmen who do not get an opportunity with the Blessed One might say to me, 'Venerable Ānanda, please come to our house for alms tomorrow together with the Blessed One.' Venerable Sir, if the Blessed One does not go to that invitation, I would not have the opportunity to let the audience see Him at the moment they arrive, nor to dispel their doubts. Then there would be those who say, 'Why does Ānanda serve the One of Ten Powers? The Blessed One does not even grant him this much favor.' Also, in the Blessed One's absence, people will ask me, 'Friend Ānanda, where was this verse, this sutta, this Jātaka taught?' If I cannot fulfill that question, there would be those who say, 'Friend, do you not even know this much? Why do you follow the Blessed One for so long without parting, like a shadow?' Therefore, I desire the repeating of the Dhamma taught in my absence." Thus he requested these four requests. The Blessed One granted those boons to him.

Thus, having taken these eight boons, he became the permanent attendant. For that very position of attendant, he reached the fruit of the perfections fulfilled for a hundred thousand aeons. Referring to this state of being the permanent attendant, the Buddha said, "Monks, now the monk Ānanda is my attendant, the foremost attendant (aggupaṭṭhāka)." This is called the Upaṭṭhākapariccheda (Section on the Attendant).

The Pitipariccheda (Section on the Father) is quite clear in its meaning.

Regarding the phrase "He entered the monastery," why did He enter the monastery? It is said that after speaking this much, the Blessed One thought: "I have not yet taught the lineage of the seven Buddhas continuously to the end. Today, while I am inside the monastery, these monks will speak in praise of the knowledge of past lives (pubbenivāsañāṇa) to a great extent. Then I will come and teach the Buddhavamsa (Lineage of the Buddhas) continuously to the end." Thus, giving the monks an opportunity for discussion, He rose from His seat and entered the monastery.

In that sequence of the Pali text taught by the Blessed One, these nine sections (vāra) are included: the section on the aeon, the section on the birth, the section on the clan, the section on the lifespan, the section on the Bodhi, the section on the pair of disciples, the section on the assembly of disciples, the section on the attendant, and the section on the father. As for the Sambahulavāra (Section on the Many), although it is not yet included, it should be brought forth and shown (from the Commentaries).
15:
## Commentary on the Chapter of the Many (Sambahulavāra)

For all Bodhisattas, it is the lineage and tradition to renounce the world and go forth into homelessness only after a son, worthy of the family line, is born. Why is this? From the moment an Omniscient Bodhisatta enters his mother’s womb, many previously described miracles occur. In such circumstances, if the Bodhisatta’s birthplace, father, mother, wife, and son were not known, people would think: "His birthplace is unknown, and his father, wife, and son are also unknown. He must be a deity, Sakka, Māra, or Brahmā. Such miracles are not surprising for deities." Thinking thus, they would neither listen to what should be heard nor believe what should be believed. Without listening and faith, the realization of the Four Noble Truths (abhisamaya) would not occur. Without realization, the arising of a Buddha would be fruitless, and the Dispensation (Sāsana) would not be a means of deliverance from Saṃsāra. Therefore, for all Bodhisattas, this lineage and tradition—"to renounce and go forth when a son worthy of the family line is born"—is constant. Thus, the various sections should be presented through the influence of the sons and others.

## Commentary on the Specification of the Many (Sambahulapariccheda)

Among those (Sambahulavāra):
Samavattakkhandha and Atula,
Suppabuddha and Uttara,
Satthavāha, Vijitasena, and
the seventh, Rāhula.

These should be known as the seven sons of the seven Bodhisattas in order. Among those sons, when Prince Rāhula was born, a birth record was first brought and placed in the Bodhisatta’s hand. At that moment, paternal love for the son arose, causing his entire body to tremble. The Bodhisatta thought: "When one son is born, such love for a son arises. I might have more than a thousand sons. If this bond of love increases with the birth of each one, it will be difficult to break. Rāhu (an eclipse/shackle) is born; a bond is born." On that very day, he renounced the kingship and went forth. This is the method to be understood regarding the birth of sons for all Bodhisattas. This is the specification of sons.
16:
Sumanā (Sutanā), Sabbakāmā, Sucittā, and also Rocinī, Rucaggatī, Sunandā, and Bimbā was the seventh [among the queens].

These were the mothers of those seven Bodhisatta sons. Queen Bimbā, however, became known as Rāhulamātā (Mother of Rāhula) when Prince Rāhula was born. This is the specification of wives (Bhariyapariccheda).

Vipassī Buddha and Kakusandha Buddha, these two Bodhisattas, departed for the Great Renunciation riding in chariots drawn by thoroughbred horses. The two, Sikhī Buddha and Koṇāgamana Buddha, departed riding on the backs of noble elephants. Vessabhū Buddha departed sitting in a golden palanquin. Kassapa Buddha, while remaining on the upper floor of his palace, attained the fourth jhāna of mindfulness of breathing (ānāpāna). Emerging from that jhāna and using it as a basis, he resolved: "May the palace fly up and descend at the site of enlightenment (Bodhimanda)." The palace traveled through the air and descended at the Bodhimanda. The Great Being (Mahāpurisa) also descended from the palace, stood on the ground, and thought: "May the palace return to its original place." The palace then stood in its original place. The Great Being practiced striving (padhāna) for seven days, and sitting upon the Bodhi-throne, he penetrated Omniscience. Our Bodhisatta, however, departed for the Great Renunciation riding the noble horse Kanthaka. This is the specification of vehicles (Yānapariccheda).

The monastery of the Blessed One Vipassī was established on a site measuring one yojana. The monastery of Sikhī was on a site of three gāvutas; Vessabhū’s on half a yojana; Kakusandha’s on one gāvuta; Koṇāgamana’s on half a gāvuta; and Kassapa’s on twenty usabhas. The monastery of our Blessed One was established on a site measuring sixteen karīsas by the standard cubit, or eight karīsas by the royal cubit. This is the specification of monasteries (Vihārapariccheda).

The ground for the monastery of the Blessed One Vipassī was purchased by laying out gold bricks one cubit long, one span wide, and eight finger-breadths thick, placed on their edges (cūḷaṃsa). The ground for Sikhī’s monastery was purchased by covering it with gold bars the size of plowshares. The ground for Vessabhū’s monastery was purchased by making gold pieces the size of elephant feet and covering the ground with them on their edges. The ground for Kakusandha’s monastery was purchased by covering it with gold bricks in the manner already described. The ground for Koṇāgamana’s monastery was purchased by covering it with gold tortoise-figures in the manner already described.
17:
The site for the monastery of the Buddha Kassapa was purchased by covering it with gold pieces. However, the site for the monastery of our Buddha was purchased by covering it completely with marked coins (kahāpaṇas). This is the distinction regarding the wealth used for purchasing the monastery site.

Among the donors who purchased those monastery sites, the attendant donor who purchased the land and built the monastery for the Buddha Vipassī was named Punabbasu-mitta. For the Buddha Sikhī, he was named Sirivaḍḍhana. For the Buddha Vessabhū, he was named Sotthiya. For the Buddha Kakusandha, he was named Accuta. For the Buddha Koṇāgamana, he was named Ugga. For the Buddha Kassapa, he was named Sumana. For our Buddha, he was named Sudatta. All these individuals were great wealthy merchants known as gahapati-mahāsālas. This is known as the distinction regarding the attendant donors.

Furthermore, there are four kinds of 'unforsaken places' (avijahitaṭṭhāna) common to all Buddhas. The place where the Bodhi throne (Bodhi-pallaṅka) of all Buddhas is situated is an unforsaken place and occurs in the same location. The place where the Wheel of Dhamma was turned (Dhammacakkappavattana) in the Isipatana Migadāya is also an unforsaken place. The place where the Buddha first set foot at the gate of the city of Saṅkassa upon descending from the Tāvatiṃsa heaven is also an unforsaken place. The locations of the four bed-legs in the Gandhakuti of the Jetavana monastery are also unforsaken places.

As for the monastery, it can be small or large. Although the Jetavana monastery is also an unforsaken place, the city itself is forsaken (changes location). When the city is in the east, the monastery is in the west. When the city is in the south, the monastery is in the north. When the city is in the west, the monastery is in the east. When the city is in the north, the monastery is in the south. At the present time, the city is in the north and the monastery is in the south.

Among all Buddhas, there are five kinds of variations (vematta): variation in lifespan, variation in height, variation in caste, variation in exertion, and variation in radiance. Variation in lifespan means that some Buddhas have a long lifespan, while others have a short lifespan. Indeed, the lifespan of the Buddha Dīpaṅkara was one hundred thousand years, whereas the lifespan of our Buddha was one hundred years.

Variation in height means that some Buddhas are tall, while others are short. Indeed, the Buddha Dīpaṅkara was eighty cubits tall, the Buddha Sumana was ninety cubits tall, and our Buddha was eighteen cubits tall.
18:
Variation in caste (kula-vematta) means that some Buddhas are born into the Khattiya (warrior-noble) caste, while others are born into the Brāhmaṇa (priestly) caste. Variation in exertion (padhāna-vematta) means that the practice of austerities (dukkara-cariyā) for some Buddhas lasts for only a short period, as in the case of the Buddha Kassapa. For other Buddhas, the practice lasts for a long period, as in the case of our Buddha.

Variation in radiance (rasmi-vematta) means that the bodily radiance of the Buddha Maṅgala extended throughout ten thousand world systems. The bodily radiance of our Buddha extended to a distance of one fathom (byāma) all around. This variation in radiance is connected to their wish; whatever extent a Buddha wishes to pervade with his radiance, his bodily radiance pervades that much. For the Buddha Maṅgala, however, his wish was: "May it always pervade ten thousand world systems." Regarding the qualities of a Buddha attained through penetration, there is no variation among any of the Buddhas.

As another point, the distinction of the co-borns and the distinction of the constellations are shown only for our Buddha. It is said that together with the Bodhisatta, the mother of Rāhula, the Elder Ānanda, Channa, the horse Kaṇṭaka, the four great pots of treasure, the Great Bodhi tree, and the minister Kāḷudāyī—these seven are the co-borns (sahajāta). The Great Man (Bodhisatta) descended into his mother's womb, renounced the world, turned the Wheel of Dhamma, and performed the Twin Miracle (Yamaka-pāṭihāriya) under the constellation of Uttarāsāḷha. He was born, attained enlightenment, and entered Parinibbāna under the constellation of Visākhā. The assembly of his disciples and the relinquishing of his life-force factor (āyusaṅkhāra-ossajjana) occurred under the constellation of Māgha. His descent from the celestial realm occurred under the constellation of Assayuja. This much should be brought forth and shown. This is called the distinction of various matters (sambahula-pariccheda).

Now, regarding the words beginning with "Atha kho tesaṃ bhikkhūnaṃ," those monks said: "Friends, the progression of the knowledge of past lives (pubbenivāsa-ñāṇa) from the moment of death to the moment of rebirth is the usual course. However, to send the knowledge backward from the moment of rebirth to reach the moment of death is extremely difficult. The Blessed One has preached this as if showing footprints in the sky." Being filled with great wonder, they said, "Friends, it is marvelous!" and so on. Then, wishing to show another reason, they said, "Yatra hi nāma Tathāgato," and so forth. In that context, "Yatra hi nāma" is a particle used in the sense of wonder, meaning "The Blessed One who..." In the term "chinnapapañca," the three defilements of craving (taṇhā), conceit (māna), and views (diṭṭhi) are called papañca. In the term "chinnavaṭuma," vaṭuma refers to the cycle of wholesome and unwholesome kamma. "Pariyādinnavaṭṭa" is a synonym for that same term, meaning one who has exhausted the entire cycle of kamma. "Sabbadukkhavītivatta" means [one who has transcended] all suffering known as the cycle of results (vipākavaṭṭa)...
19:
Having transcended all suffering known as the round of resultants (vipākavaṭṭa). Regarding the word "anussarissati" (he will remember), although this is a future tense form due to the influence of the particle "yatra," its meaning here should be understood in the past tense. This is because the Blessed One has already recollected those Buddhas, and it is not that he will only now recollect them. "Evaṃsīlā" (of such virtue) means they possessed such virtue through the virtue of the path, the virtue of the fruition, and both mundane and supramundane virtue. In the phrase "evaṃဓမ္မာ" (of such qualities), the qualities associated with concentration (samādhi) are intended; it means they possessed such concentration through the concentration of the path, the concentration of the fruition, and both mundane and supramundane concentration. "Evaṃpaññā" (of such wisdom) means they possessed such wisdom specifically through the power of the wisdom of the path and so forth. Regarding the phrase "evaṃvihārī" (of such abiding), since the qualities associated with concentration have already been mentioned above, "abiding" (vihāra) would already be included. If one asks why that which is already included is mentioned again, it is not a mere repetition; this is spoken to indicate the attainment of cessation (nirodhasamāpatti). Therefore, the meaning here should be understood as: those Blessed Ones were accustomed to abiding in such an attainment of cessation.

Regarding the phrase "evaṃvimuttā" (of such liberation), there are five kinds of liberation: liberation by suppression (vikkhamphanavimutti), liberation by substitution of opposites (tadaṅgavimutti), liberation by eradication (samucchedavimutti), liberation by tranquilization (paṭippassaddhivimutti), and liberation by escape (nissaraṇavimutti). Among these five, the eight attainments (samāpatti) are called "liberation by suppression" because they are liberated from the hindrances (nīvaraṇa) and so forth, which they themselves have suppressed. The seven types of contemplation, such as the contemplation of impermanence (aniccānupassanā), are called "liberation by substitution of opposites" because they are liberated from the perception of permanence (niccasaññā) and so forth, which are abandoned by the power of their respective opposing factors. The four noble paths are called "liberation by eradication" because they are liberated from the defilements (kilesa) which they themselves have completely cut off. The four fruits of recluseship (sāmaññaphala) are called "liberation by tranquilization" because they arise at the end of the subsiding of defilements through the power of the path. Nibbāna is called "liberation by escape" because it is the escape from all defilements, being free from them and standing far off. Thus, the meaning of the phrase "evaṃ vimuttā" should be understood by way of these five kinds of liberation.

"Paṭisallānā vuṭṭhito" means having arisen from solitary seclusion.

What is the connection (anusandhi) here: "Monks, this Dhamma-element (dhammadhātu) has been well-penetrated by the Tathāgata alone"? This sutta is connected to these two statements: "Monks, this Dhamma-element has been well-penetrated by the Tathāgata alone" and "The deities also informed the Blessed One of this matter." Among these two, the statement about the deities informing him will be examined at the end of the sutta, showing the commotion in the celestial realms during his journey to the heavens. However, by way of the connection to the term "Dhamma-element," this teaching...
20:
...the teaching was begun. In that teaching, the eleven terms beginning with "khattiyo jātiyā" (a kshatriya by birth) should be understood exactly as explained in the Nidānakhaṇḍa.

## Description of the Nature of a Bodhisatta

Furthermore, in the phrases beginning with "Atha kho, bhikkhave, vipassī bodhisatto" (Then, monks, the Bodhisatta Vipassī), the name "Vipassī" was the name of that Bodhisatta. He received that name because of his skill in seeing (passana) diverse (vividha) meanings. "Bodhisatta" means a wise being (paṇḍitasatta) or a being who understands causes and effects. Alternatively, he is called "Bodhisatta" because his mind is attached to or fixed upon the four paths known as Bodhi. In the phrase "sato sampajāno" (mindful and clearly comprehending), "sato" refers to mindfulness (sati) itself. "Sampajāno" refers to wisdom (ñāṇa). The meaning is that he descended into his mother's womb after well-establishing mindfulness and discerning with wisdom. By the word "okkamī" (he descended), the Pali text only shows the fact of his descent, not the sequence of the descent. However, since that sequence is presented in the Commentary (Aṭṭhakathā), it should be understood as follows:

Indeed, all Bodhisattas, after fulfilling the thirty perfections (pāramīs), making the five great sacrifices (mahāpariccāga), reaching the pinnacle of the three modes of conduct—conduct for the benefit of relatives (ñātattha-cariyā), conduct for the benefit of the world (lokattha-cariyā), and conduct for the attainment of Buddhahood (buddhattha-cariyā)—and while existing in the third existence similar to King Vessantara, having given the seven great gifts and shaken the earth seven times, they pass away and are reborn in the Tusita heaven in the second thought-moment. The Bodhisatta Vipassī also did the same and, having been reborn in the city of Tusita, remained there for fifty-seven koṭis and six million years (576,000,000 years). At other times when perfections are not yet complete, Bodhisattas reborn in long-lived celestial realms do not remain for the full lifespan. Why? Because it is difficult to fulfill the perfections there. Those Bodhisattas perform "adhimuttikālakiriya" (determined death) and are reborn only in the human realm. However, just as one is now able to achieve omniscience in a single existence when fulfilling perfections, the Bodhisatta Vipassī, because his perfections were entirely fulfilled, remained in that Tusita heaven for his full lifespan.

For the deities, five great preliminary omens (pubbanimittāni) appear, indicating: "According to human calculation, he will pass away within seven days from now." These are: the flowers he wears wither, his clothes become soiled, sweat is released from his armpits, physical discoloration occurs in his body, and the deity does not remain steady on his celestial throne. Among those five omens, "mālā" (flowers) refers to those worn on the day of taking conception...
21:
The flowers worn [by the deities] remained unwithered for a period exceeding five hundred and seventy-six million years, yet they wither at that time [of death]. The same applies to the garments worn. For such a long time, the deities experienced neither cold nor heat, but at that time of death, sweat drops like strings of pearls exude from their bodies. For such a long duration, no disfigurement such as broken teeth or gray hair appeared on their bodies. The goddesses appeared as if they were sixteen years old, and the gods as if they were twenty. However, at the time of death, their physical forms appeared exhausted. For such a long time, there was no such thing as boredom in the celestial realm, but at the time of death, they sigh, stretch their limbs, and find no delight in their seats.

These preliminary signs (pubbanimitta) appear only to deities of great power, just as omens like falling meteors, earthquakes, and lunar eclipses appear only for great kings and ministers of great merit in the world, and not for everyone. Just as among humans, only those skilled in astrology know the omens and not everyone, so too, not all deities know these signs; only the wise ones know. Among them, those gods born of meager wholesome kamma become afraid when these signs appear, thinking, 'Who knows now? Where will we be reborn?' Those of great merit, however, do not fear, reflecting, 'Based on the generosity (dāna) we have given, the virtue (sīla) we have guarded, and the meditation (bhāvanā) we have developed, we shall enjoy prosperity in the higher celestial realms.' The Bodhisatta Vipassī also, seeing those preliminary signs, did not fear, knowing, 'Now, in the existence immediately following this, I shall become a Buddha.' Then, when those signs appeared, the deities from the ten thousand world systems assembled and entreated him: 'O Great Being, when you fulfilled the ten perfections (pāramīs), you did not fulfill them aspiring for the prosperity of Sakka, Māra, Brahmā, or a Universal Monarch. You fulfilled them aspiring for Buddhahood for the sake of delivering the world. Now is the time, O Great Being, for Buddhahood; now is the opportune moment, O Great Being, for Buddhahood.'

Then the Great Being, without yet giving his consent to those deities, made the Five Great Observations (pañcamahāvilokana) regarding the time, the continent, the region, the family, and the lifespan of the mother. Among those five, he first observed the time, [thinking], 'Is it now the time or not?' In that observation, a period when the lifespan is increased beyond one hundred thousand years is not considered the [right] time. Why? Because at that time, birth, aging, and death of beings...
22:
...are not apparent. The Dhamma teaching of the Buddhas is never free from the three characteristics [of existence]. When they [the Buddhas] preach 'Impermanence, Suffering, and Non-self' (anicca, dukkha, anattā), those beings do not think to listen or believe, [wondering], 'What is this they are saying?' Because they cannot reflect thus, the realization of the Four Noble Truths (abhisamaya) cannot occur. Without that realization, the Dispensation (sāsana) cannot be emancipating (niyyānika). Therefore, that is the wrong time (akāla). A period when the lifespan is less than one hundred years is also not the [right] time. Why? Because at that time, beings have excessive defilements. The advice given to beings with excessive defilements does not remain in the place of advice; it disappears quickly like a line drawn on water with a stick. Therefore, that too is indeed the wrong time. The period when the lifespan is below one hundred thousand years and above one hundred years is called the [right] time. At that time, humans had a lifespan of eighty thousand years. Then the Great Being saw the time, [thinking], 'This is the time for me to be conceived.'

Then, observing the continent, he looked at the four great continents along with their surrounding islands and saw the continent, [thinking], 'Buddhas are not born in the [other] three continents; they are born only in Jambudīpa.'

Then, [thinking], 'Jambudīpa is large, measuring ten thousand yojanas; in which region are Buddhas born?' he observed the region and saw the Majjhimadesa (Middle Country). The Majjhimadesa is the region described in the Vinaya texts in this manner: 'To the east is the market town named Gajaṅgala,' and so on. That Majjhimadesa is three hundred yojanas in length, two hundred and fifty in width, and nine hundred in circumference. In this very region, Buddhas, Paccekabuddhas, Chief Disciples, the eighty Great Disciples, Universal Monarchs, and other powerful Khattiyas, Brāhmaṇas, and wealthy householders (gahapati-mahāsāla) are born. 'In this Majjhimadesa is the city named Bandhumatī; I should be born there,' he reached a conclusion.

Then, observing the family, [he thought], 'Buddhas are born only in a noble family esteemed by the world. At present, the Khattiya (warrior-noble) family is the one esteemed by the world. I shall be born in that Khattiya family; King Bandhumā shall be my father.' Thus he saw the family.

Then, observing the mother, [he thought], 'The mother of a Bodhisatta is not frivolous or flighty, nor is she a drunkard. She is one who has fulfilled the perfections for a hundred thousand aeons and has kept the five precepts unbroken since birth. This Queen named Bandhumatī is of such a nature; she shall be my mother.' Thus he saw [the mother].
23:
When he observed the lifespan of the one who would become his mother, he saw, "It will last for ten months and seven days." Having thus made these Five Great Observations (Mahāvilokana), he gave his word to the deities, intending to favor them, saying, "Friends, now is the time for me to become a Buddha." After dismissing those deities with the words, "You may go," he entered the Nandavana Garden in the Tusita heaven, surrounded by the Tusita deities. Indeed, the Nandavana Garden exists in all celestial realms. There, the deities wandered about, reminding the Bodhisatta of his previously performed meritorious deeds, saying, "When you pass away from this Tusita heaven, may you go to a happy destination (sugati)." While wandering in that garden, surrounded by the deities who were thus reminding him of his merits, he passed away.

Even when passing away in this manner, he knew, "I am about to pass away," but he did not know the death-consciousness (cuti-citta) itself. Even after taking rebirth-linking, he knew it, but he did not know the rebirth-linking consciousness (paṭisandhi-citta) itself. However, he did know, "I have taken rebirth-linking in this place." Some elders, however, say, "Since he is entitled to the process of adverting (āvajjana), he will know it in the second or third thought-moment."

But the Elder Tipiṭaka Mahāsīva said: "The rebirth-linking of Bodhisattas is not like the rebirth-linking of others; their mindfulness and clear comprehension (sati-sampajañña) reach the highest point. However, because that consciousness cannot be known by that same consciousness, he does not know the death-consciousness. Even at the moment of death, he knows, 'I am about to pass away.' Although he does not know the rebirth-linking consciousness, he knows, 'I have taken rebirth-linking in such a place.' At that time, the ten-thousandfold world system trembles." Thus, entering the mother's womb with mindfulness and clear comprehension, he took rebirth-linking with a Great Resultant consciousness (Mahāvipāka-citta) similar to the unprompted wholesome consciousness accompanied by joy and associated with knowledge (somanassa-sahagata ñāṇa-sampayutta asaṅkhārika kusala-citta) preceded by loving-kindness, out of the nineteen types of rebirth-linking consciousness. Elder Mahāsīva, however, said it was with a consciousness accompanied by equanimity (upekkhā-sahagata). Just as our Blessed One took rebirth-linking on the full moon day of Āsāḷha under the Uttarāsāḷha constellation, so too did that (Vipassī) Bodhisatta take rebirth-linking on the full moon day of Āsāḷha under the Uttarāsāḷha constellation.

At that time, starting from the seventh day before the full moon of Āsāḷha, the Bodhisatta's mother, who was celebrating the constellation festival (nakkhatta-kīḷā) adorned with flowers, scents, and such, and abstaining from intoxicants, rose early on the seventh day. She bathed with scented water, adorned herself with all ornaments, ate excellent food, undertook the eight-fold uposatha precepts, entered the magnificent state-chamber, and while lying down on the magnificent couch and falling asleep, she saw this dream: "The four...
24:
...it is said that the Great Kings lifted her up together with the couch, took her to Lake Anotatta, bathed her, clothed her in divine garments, anointed her with divine scents, and adorned her with divine flowers. Not far from that Lake Anotatta was a Silver Mountain, inside of which was a Golden Mansion; there they laid her down with her head towards the east. Then the Bodhisatta, having become a noble white elephant, wandered on a Golden Mountain not far from that Silver Mountain, and descending from that Golden Mountain, he ascended the Silver Mountain, entered the Golden Mansion, circumambulated his mother three times to the right, and appeared to enter her womb after piercing her right side.

Then the Queen, having awakened, reported the dream to the King. When the night had turned into dawn, the King summoned about sixty-four eminent Brahmins. He had magnificent seats prepared on a ground smeared with fresh cow-dung and adorned with auspicious offerings such as parched rice. To the Brahmins seated there, he gave excellent milk-rice (pāyāsa) prepared with ghee, honey, and sugar, filling gold and silver bowls and covering them with gold and silver bowls. He also satisfied them with other gifts such as new clothes and tawny cows. Having thus satisfied them with all desirable sensual objects, he reported the dream and asked, "What will happen?" The Brahmins said, "Great King, do not worry. A pregnancy has been established in the Queen's womb, and it is a male pregnancy, not a female one. You will have a noble son. If he lives the household life, he will become a Universal Monarch (Cakkavatti). If he goes forth from the household life and ordains, he will surely become a Buddha in the world, one who has removed the veil of defilements." This is the sequence of explanation for the phrase "He descended into the mother's womb."

"This is the natural order (dhammatā) here" means that in this descent into the mother's womb, it is the natural order, the nature, the fixed law (niyāma). This fixed law is fivefold: the law of kamma (kamma-niyāma), the law of seasons (utu-niyāma), the law of seeds (bīja-niyāma), the law of mind (citta-niyāma), and the law of nature (dhamma-niyāma).

Among those five, the law of kamma (kamma-niyāma) is the giving of desired results by wholesome kamma and undesired results by unwholesome kamma. To illustrate that kamma-niyāma, stories should be told using the verse beginning with "Na antalikkhe." Furthermore, to say it in another way: a woman, having quarreled with her husband and wishing to hang herself, put a noose around her neck. A man, while sharpening a billhook, saw the woman's action and, wishing to cut the rope, shouted, "Do not be afraid, do not be afraid!" and ran to help her. At that moment, the rope turned into a venomous snake and remained there. That man fled in terror. The woman, however, died right there. Thus, the kamma-niyāma is shown by such stories. The simultaneous blooming and fruiting of trees in various regions during various seasons like spring, the blowing or not blowing of the wind, the intensity or lack of heat from the sun, the falling or not falling of rain, the blooming of lotuses...
25:
A woman wishing to die put a noose around her neck. A man who was sharpening a billhook saw her action and, wishing to cut the rope, ran towards her comforting her, "Do not be afraid, do not be afraid!" At that moment, the rope turned into a venomous snake and remained there. The man fled in fear. The woman, however, died right there. Such stories should be shown here.

The simultaneous blooming and fruiting of trees in various regions at various times, the blowing or not blowing of the wind, the intensity or mildness of the sun's heat, the falling or not falling of rain, the blooming of lotuses by day and their wilting by night—these are called Utuniyāma (the order of seasons/physical law).

The fact that only rice fruit comes from rice seed, sweet taste from sweet seeds, and bitter fruit from bitter seeds—this is called Bījaniyāma (the order of seeds/biological law).

The fact that preceding mental states (citta and cetasika) assist succeeding mental states through the condition of strong dependence (upanissaya-paccaya), such as the arising of receiving consciousness (sampaṭicchana) immediately after eye-consciousness (cakkhu-viññāṇa)—this is called Cittaniyāma (the order of mind/psychic law).

The occurrence of events such as the shaking of the ten thousand world-systems during the Bodhisatta's descent into his mother's womb—this is called Dhammaniyāma (the order of phenomena/natural law). In this context, Dhammaniyāma is intended. Therefore, to show that very meaning, the Buddha said, "Monks, this is the nature (dhammatā)," and so forth.

In that context, "descends into the womb" means he has already descended into the womb. This is because this happens only when the Bodhisatta has already descended, not while he is in the process of descending. "Appamāṇa" means having a great magnitude; "vipula" means extensive. "Uḷāra" is also a synonym for that very appamāṇa. In passages such as "they eat magnificent (uḷāra) foods," uḷāra refers to something delicious. In passages such as "The Venerable Vacchāyana praises the Ascetic Gotama with magnificent (uḷāra) praise," uḷāra refers to something noble. Here, however, it means extensive. In the phrase "the divine majesty (devānubhāva) of the devas," the radiance of the devas' clothing, bodies, ornaments, and mansions spreads for twelve yojanas; the meaning is that [the light] surpasses that majesty.

Lokantarika refers to the three world-systems'...
26:
Lokantarika refers to the individual Lokantarika hells located between every three world-systems (cakkavāḷa), like the space in the middle of three cartwheels or three alms-bowls placed touching each other. This Lokantarika hell is eight thousand yojanas in extent. Agha means an eternally open void. Asaṃvuta means having no supporting ground below. Andhakāra means a realm of darkness. Andhakāra-timisa means being endowed with intense darkness that causes blindness because it prevents the arising of eye-consciousness. It is said that eye-consciousness does not arise in that Lokantarika hell.

Evaṃ-mahiddhika means that the moon and sun appear simultaneously in three continents; thus they have great psychic power. In each direction, they can dispel darkness and show light up to a distance of nine hundred thousand yojanas; thus they have great majesty (mahānubhāva). Ābhāya nānubhonti means they are unable to shine with their own radiance [there]. It is said that those moons and suns travel around the middle of the Cakkavāḷa mountains, while the Lokantarika hells are situated beyond the Cakkavāḷa mountains. Therefore, those moons and suns are unable to shine with their radiance in those Lokantarika hells.

Ye pi tattha sattā refers to whatever beings are born in that great Lokantarika hell. What kind of kamma do they perform to be born there? They are born there after committing heavy and cruel offenses against their parents or against righteous recluses and brahmins, or after committing acts of violence such as killing living beings day after day, like the thieves Abhaya and Nāga in the island of Tambapaṇṇi. The bodies (attabhāva) of those hell-beings are three gāvutas in height, and they have long claws like bats. They cling to the Cakkavāḷa mountains with their claws like bats on a tree. When they move and come within reach of each other's hands, they think, "We have found food," and while struggling for those beings, they tumble and fall into the water that supports the world. Just as madhuka fruits are severed from their stalks and fall when the wind blows, they lose their grip and fall into the water. As soon as they fall, they dissolve like a ball of flour in extremely salty water.

"Friends, just as we experience great suffering, so too other beings are born here to experience this suffering," they see [each other] on that day. This radiance, however, does not last even for the duration of a single sip of rice gruel; it flashes like lightning for only a moment (the snap of a finger) and disappears even while they are saying, "What is this?" Saṅkampati means it shakes all around. The other two terms are merely synonyms of the preceding word. Again, the words beginning with "appamāṇo ca" are spoken for the purpose of conclusion.
27:
In the statement 'The four Great Kings approach from the four directions to protect the Bodhisatta,' the word 'four' (cattāro) refers to the four Great Kings (Cātumahārājā). However, in the ten thousand world-systems, if four are counted for each, there are forty thousand kings. Among them, the Great Kings of this world-system, holding swords in their hands, approach and enter the state chamber (siri-gabbha) to protect the Bodhisatta. The remaining kings, starting from the chamber door, clear away the groups of demons such as earth-dwelling spirits (pamsupisāca) who might cause disturbance, and maintain a guard as far as the edge of the world-system.

What is the purpose of this protection? From the moment of conception, starting from the stage of the clear embryo (kalala), even if a hundred thousand Māras were to lift a hundred thousand Mount Sinerus and come to harm the Bodhisatta or the Bodhisatta’s mother, would they not all vanish in the interim? This was also stated by the Blessed One in the Ruhiruppāda case: 'It is impossible, monks, it is out of the question, that a Tathāgata should be deprived of life by the effort of another. Monks, Tathāgatas attain Parinibbāna without the effort of others. Go, monks, to your respective dwellings; Tathāgatas, monks, are beyond the need for protection' (Cūḷavagga 341). Thus, although their lives cannot be endangered by the effort of others, there are non-human beings (amanussa) of deformed, unsightly, and terrifying appearance, as well as wild animals and birds. Upon seeing their forms or hearing their sounds, fear or terror might arise in the Bodhisatta’s mother. The protection is undertaken for the purpose of warding them off. Furthermore, out of reverence born from the power of the Bodhisatta’s merit, and prompted by their own respectful minds, those Great Kings acted in this way.

Do those four Great Kings, who have entered and remain within the chamber, show themselves to the Bodhisatta’s mother or not? They do not show themselves during times of bodily care such as bathing, adorning, or eating. However, when she enters the state chamber and lies down on the noble bed, they do show themselves. In that regard, although the sight of non-human beings is generally terrifying to humans, the Bodhisatta’s mother, through the power of her own merit and that of her son, is not afraid upon seeing them. Her mind regards them just like ordinary palace guards.

'Naturally virtuous' (pakatiyā sīlavatī) means she was endowed with virtue by her very nature. It is said that when a Buddha has not yet arisen, people approach ascetics and wanderers, bow, sit in a crouching position, and take the precepts. The Bodhisatta’s mother also took the precepts from the ascetic Kāladevila. However, in truth, while the Bodhisatta is residing in the womb, it is not fitting to sit at the feet of another. Sitting on a seat equal in height and taking the precepts is merely an act of reflection. Therefore, it means she undertook the precepts of her own accord.
28:
(The mother) undertook the precepts in the presence of the ascetic. In truth, however, while the Bodhisatta is residing in the womb, she is unable to sit at the feet of another; even the precepts taken while sitting on an equal seat are merely an act of reflection. Therefore, it means she undertook the precepts of her own accord.

'Regarding men' (purisesu) means that, starting with the Bodhisatta’s father and including all other men, no thought of desire for a man arose in her. Indeed, even highly skilled artists are unable to depict the form of the Bodhisatta’s mother in paintings or sculptures. While it cannot be said that passion would not arise in a man upon seeing her, if a man should wish to approach her with a lustful mind, his feet would fail to carry him, as if bound by divine shackles (dibba-saṅkhalikā). Therefore, it is said, 'She could not be transgressed,' and so forth.

By the phrase 'of the five cords of sensual pleasure' (pañcannaṃ kāmaguṇānaṃ), the rejection of the base practice through desire for men was previously mentioned; here, the acquisition of the objects of sensual pleasure is shown. At that time, it is said that upon hearing that such a son had been conceived in the Queen’s womb, kings from all around sent gifts consisting of precious ornaments, musical instruments, and other objects of the five senses. Because of the abundance of the past deeds of the Bodhisatta and the Bodhisatta’s mother, there was no limit to the amount of gains and honors.

'Unwearied body' (akilanta-kāya) means that while other women become weary due to the weight of the womb and suffer from swelling of the hands and feet, she experienced no such weariness. 'The one within the womb' (tirokucchigataṃ) refers to seeing the one who is inside the belly. She sees him only after the stage of the clear embryo (kalala) has passed, when the major and minor limbs have formed and the sense faculties are complete. For what purpose does she look? Only for the sake of his comfortable dwelling. Just as a mother, whether lying or sitting with her young son, would lift and adjust his hand or foot if it were hanging down, to ensure his comfort, so too the Bodhisatta’s mother looks toward the comfort of her son during her own rising, walking, sitting, and turning, as well as when consuming hot, cold, salty, bitter, or pungent food, thinking, 'Is there any suffering for my son?' As she looks, she sees the Bodhisatta sitting cross-legged (pallaṅkaṃ ābhujitvā). While other beings in the womb remain crouched, pressing against the place of digested food, carrying the place of undigested food, with the abdominal membrane behind them, leaning against the backbone, and resting their chin on their two fists...
29:
