When it rains, monkeys sit in the hollow of a tree; the Bodhisatta does not sit like that. Indeed, the Bodhisatta sits cross-legged, keeping his back straight like a Dhamma preacher on a Dhamma seat, facing the front of his mother. The merit performed by the mother of the Bodhisatta in previous lives purifies the womb, the place where the son resides. When the womb is pure, the sign of delicate skin arises. Then, the skin of the belly cannot conceal the Bodhisatta; when the mother looks, he is clearly visible as if he were outside. To clarify this meaning with a simile, the Blessed One spoke the words beginning with 'Seyyathāpi'. Furthermore, the Bodhisatta within the womb does not see his mother. This is because eye-consciousness does not arise within the womb.

'Kālaṅkaroti' (passes away) means she dies not because of the cause of childbirth, but only because her lifespan has ended. This is because the place where a Bodhisatta has resided is like a shrine-room (cetiya-kuṭi), and is not fit for others to use. Since it is impossible to remove the Bodhisatta’s mother from the position of Chief Queen and place another in that position, the lifespan of a Bodhisatta’s mother is only that much. Therefore, she passes away seven days after giving birth. At what age does she pass away? She passes away in middle age. In the first stage of life, the desire and lust (chandarāga) for the self-identity of beings is strong. Therefore, a woman who becomes pregnant in that first stage cannot protect the fetus, and the fetus is prone to many illnesses. However, after passing two parts of middle age, in the third part, the womb is clear. When the womb is clear, the children born are healthy. Therefore, the Bodhisatta’s mother also enjoys prosperity in the first stage of life, gives birth in the third part of middle age, and then passes away. This is the natural law (dhammatā) in this matter.

In the phrase 'nine or ten months', by the power of the word 'vā' (or) expressing variation, it should be understood that seven, eight, eleven, or twelve months, etc., are also included. Among them, a child born at seven months survives but cannot withstand cold and heat. A child born at eight months does not survive. Children born in the remaining nine, ten, eleven months, etc., survive.

'The devas first receive him' means the Suddhāvāsa Brahmas, who are Arahants, receive him. How do they receive him? Some say, 'Taking the appearance of midwives.' Rejecting that statement, it is said in the Great Commentary (Mahā-aṭṭhakathā): At that time, the Bodhisatta’s mother stood wearing a garment woven with gold thread and covered down to her toes with a dukūla cloth resembling fish-eyes. Then, her light delivery from the womb occurred, like water flowing out of a water-strainer (dhammakaraka). Then, those Suddhāvāsa Arahant Brahmas approached in their natural Brahma form and first received him with a golden net. From the hands of those Brahmas, the four Great Kings received him with a rug of antelope skin. From them, humans received him with a roll of fine cloth (dukūla). In that way...
30:
The Suddhāvāsa Brahmas received [the Bodhisatta] with a golden net. From the hands of those Brahmas, the four Great Kings received him with a rug of antelope skin. From them, humans received him with a roll of fine cloth. Because they received him thus, it is said, 'The devas first receive him, then humans.'

'Cattāro naṃ devaputtā' refers to the four Great Kings. 'Paṭiggahetvā' means having received him with a rug of antelope skin. 'Mahesakkho' means one who possesses great power, great glory, and is endowed with the [auspicious] marks.

'Visadova nikkhamati' means that unlike other beings who emerge struggling and stuck in the birth canal, he is born without being stuck anywhere. 'Udena' means [without being smeared] by the liquid [of the womb]. 'Kenaci asucinā' means that while other beings, due to kamma-born winds, are turned upside down with feet up and head down, thrust into the birth canal as if falling into a hundred-fathom deep hell-abyss, and suffer great pain like an elephant being pulled through a keyhole, emerging smeared with various impurities—the Bodhisatta is not like that. Indeed, the kamma-born winds cannot turn the Bodhisatta upside down with feet up and head down. Like a Dhamma preacher descending from a Dhamma seat, or like a man descending a ladder, he emerges stretching out both hands and both feet, standing, without being smeared by any impurity originating in the mother's womb.

'Udakassa dhārā' refers to streams of water. Among those streams, the cold water falls into a golden vessel, and the warm water falls into a silver vessel. This was spoken to show the drinking and usable water for the Bodhisatta and his mother, which was unmixed with any impurity on the ground, and the water for playing, which was not shared with others. However, there is no limit to the water brought in other gold and silver jars, or the water in lotus ponds where hamsa birds and water-cocks sport.

'Sampatijāto' refers to one born at that very moment. Although in the Pali it is shown as if he had just emerged from the mother's womb, it should not be understood only in that way. In truth, the Brahmas first received the newly born Bodhisatta with a golden net; from the hands of those Brahmas, the four Great Kings with a rug of antelope skin; from them, humans with a roll of fine cloth. Having been released from the hands of humans, he stood upon the earth. While the white parasol of the devas was held over him—here, the attendants of the parasol...
31:
The five royal regalia, such as the sword and others, also arrived. However, in the Pali text, only the parasol is mentioned as being present when a king travels. Among those royal regalia, only the parasol was visible, but the one holding the parasol was not seen. Similarly, only the sword, the palm-leaf fan, the peacock-feather fan, the yak-tail whisk, and the turban were visible, but those holding these items were not seen. It is said that deities with invisible forms held all those royal regalia. Thus it was also said:

“Deities held in the sky a parasol made of jewels, with many branches and a thousand circles. Yak-tail whisks with golden handles waved to and fro, yet those holding the whisks and the parasol were not seen.” (Sn. 693)

The phrase “all directions” refers to the looking at all directions while standing after taking the seven steps. However, it should not be understood in this way. For when the Great Being was released from the hands of humans and stood upon the earth, he looked towards the eastern direction. Many thousands of world-systems became like a single open space. There, deities and humans, making offerings with perfumes, flowers, and so on, said: “O Great Man, there is no one even equal to you in this world, how could there be anyone superior?” In this manner, having surveyed the ten directions—the four cardinal directions, the four intermediate directions, below, and above—and seeing no one equal to himself, he thought, “This is the northern direction,” and facing north, he took seven steps. This is how the meaning should be understood.

'Āsabhi' means supreme. 'Aggo' means the very first (foremost) in terms of qualities. The remaining two terms (jeṭṭho and seṭṭho) are synonyms of this term 'aggo'. With the two phrases “This is the last birth” and “Now there is no further rebirth,” he declared the Arahantship to be attained in this very existence.

Furthermore, standing on the earth with even feet is the premonitory sign of the attainment of the four bases of power (iddhipāda). Facing the north is the premonitory sign of proceeding by overwhelming and overcoming the multitude of people. Taking seven steps is the premonitory sign of the attainment of the seven factors of enlightenment (bojjhaṅga). The carrying of the divine white parasol is the premonitory sign of the attainment of the noble white parasol of liberation (vimutti). The acquisition of the five royal regalia is the premonitory sign of liberation through the five kinds of liberation. Surveying all directions is the premonitory sign of the attainment of unobstructed knowledge (anāvaraṇañāṇa). Uttering the bold speech is the premonitory sign of the setting in motion of the Wheel of Dhamma (dhammacakka) which cannot be turned back by others. The lion-like bold declaration, “This is the last birth,” is the premonitory sign of the final passing away into the Nibbāna element without remainder (anupādisesa-nibbānadhātu).
32: This should be understood. These sections appear in the Pali text, but the 'manifold section' (sambahulavāra) does not; it is brought and shown from other scriptures. Indeed, on the day the Great Being was born, the ten-thousandfold world-system shook. Deities living in the ten-thousandfold world-system gathered in a single world-system. First the deities received him, then the humans. Lutes strung with strings and drums covered with skin sounded by themselves without anyone playing them. The shackles and bonds of humans broke into pieces. All diseases were calmed, becoming as clean as copper tarnished with green rust washed with acid. Those blind from birth saw forms. Those deaf from birth heard sounds. The lame became endowed with speed. Mindfulness was established even in those who were foolish or driveling from birth. Ships sailing to other lands reached a good port. Jewels situated in the sky and jewels situated on the ground shone with their own radiance. Enemies attained a mind of loving-kindness. The fire in the Avīci hell was extinguished. Light appeared in the inter-world hells. Water in the rivers ceased to flow. The water in the great ocean became sweet in taste. The wind stopped blowing. Birds in the sky, on mountains, and in trees fell and descended to the ground. The moon shone exceedingly beautifully. The sun was neither hot nor cold; it was stainless and endowed with temperate weather. Deities, standing at the doors of their respective celestial mansions, engaged in great festivities by clapping their hands, shouting, and tossing their garments. A great cloud rained over all four continents. The multitude of people was not oppressed by hunger or thirst. Door-leaves opened by themselves. Trees that bear flowers and fruits took on flowers and fruits. The ten-thousandfold world-system became like a single mass of banners and garlands. In those events such as the earthquake, the nature of being a premonitory sign should also be understood. The shaking of the ten-thousandfold world-system is the premonitory sign of the attainment of omniscience (sabbaññutañāṇa). The gathering of deities in a single world-system is the premonitory sign of their gathering all at once to listen to the Dhamma when the Wheel of Dhamma is set in motion. The deities receiving him first is the premonitory sign of the attainment of the four fine-material sphere jhānas (rūpāvacara-jhāna). The humans receiving him afterwards is the premonitory sign of the attainment of the four immaterial sphere jhānas (arūpāvacara-jhāna). The self-sounding of stringed lutes is the premonitory sign of the attainment of the successive abidings (anupubbavihāra). The sounding of skin-covered drums is the premonitory sign of the proclamation of the great drum of Dhamma. The breaking of bonds and shackles is the premonitory sign of the total cutting off of the conceit 'I am' (asmimāna). The disappearance of diseases among the multitude is the premonitory sign of the attainment of the Four Noble Truths. The seeing of forms by those blind from birth is the premonitory sign of the attainment of the divine eye (dibba-cakkhu).
33:
Precursory Omens. The hearing of sounds by the deaf is the precursory omen for the attainment of the divine ear element (dibba-sota-dhātu). The ability of the lame to move swiftly is the precursory omen for the attainment of the four bases of power (iddhipāda). The establishment of mindfulness in the mute is the precursory omen for the attainment of the four foundations of mindfulness (satipaṭṭhāna). The arrival of ships sailing to other lands at a good port is the precursory omen for the attainment of the four analytical knowledges (paṭisambhidā). The shining of jewels with their own power and radiance is the precursory omen for the showing of the light of Dhamma to the world. The arising of loving-kindness in enemies is the precursory omen for the attainment of the four divine abodes (brahmavihāra). The extinguishing of the fires in the Avīci hell is the precursory omen for the extinguishing of the eleven fires. The appearance of light in the Lokantarika hell is the precursory omen for seeing the light of knowledge after dispelling the darkness of ignorance. The sweetness of the water of the great ocean is the precursory omen for the single taste of the essence of Nibbāna. The stillness of the winds without blowing is the precursory omen for the destruction of the sixty-two types of wrong views. The descent of birds to the ground is the precursory omen for the many people taking refuge for life after hearing the instruction. The moon shining exceedingly is the precursory omen for being beloved by many people. The sun avoiding heat and cold to provide a comfortable season is the precursory omen for the attainment of physical and mental happiness. The devas standing at the doors of their celestial mansions and playing by clapping their hands and so forth is the precursory omen for the uttering of inspired verses (udāna) upon reaching Buddhahood. The falling of great rain over the four continents is the precursory omen for the falling of the great rain of Dhamma. The absence of oppression by hunger is the precursory omen for the attainment of the Deathless (amata), which is mindfulness directed to the body (kāyagatāsati). The absence of oppression by thirst is the precursory omen for being happy with the bliss of liberation (vimuttisukha). The opening of door-leaves by themselves is the precursory omen for the opening of the door of the Noble Eightfold Path. The abundance of flowers and fruits on trees is the precursory omen for blooming with the flowers of liberation and being filled with the burden of the fruits of recluseship (sāmaññaphala). The ten thousand world-systems being decorated as if with a single banner is to be understood as the precursory omen for being decorated with a succession of Noble banners. This is called the Section of Many (Sambahulavāra).

Here, they ask a question: "When the Great Man, standing on the earth and facing north, walked with strides and spoke noble words, did he go by way of the ground or by way of the sky? Did he go visibly or invisibly? Did he go naked or adorned and prepared? As a youth..."
34:
...The absence [of hunger] is the precursory omen for the attainment of the Deathless, which is mindfulness directed to the body. The absence of oppression by thirst is the precursory omen for the attainment of happiness through the fruit of Arahantship (arahattaphala). The opening of door-leaves by themselves is the precursory omen for the opening of the door of the Noble Eightfold Path. The taking of flowers and fruits by trees is the precursory omen for blooming with the flowers of liberation and for being endowed with the burden of the fruits of recluseship. The appearance of a single banner in the ten thousand world-systems is to be understood as the precursory omen for being adorned with a succession of Noble banners. This previously mentioned view is called the Section of Many (Sambahulavāra).

Here, they ask a question. How so? "When the Great Man, standing on the earth and facing north, walked and spoke noble words, did he go by way of the ground or by way of the sky? Did he go visibly or invisibly? Did he go naked or adorned and prepared? Did he go as a youth or as an adult? Was he like that afterwards as well, or did he become an infant again?" This question arose at the Lower Lohapāsāda and was answered by the Elder Tipiṭaka Cūḷābhaya. The Elder, having spoken many words there by way of the fixed nature of things (niyata), past deeds (pubbekata-kamma), and the creation by a Lord (issara-nimmāna), finally answered thus: "Although the Great Man walked on the ground, to the multitude it appeared as if he were walking in the sky. Although he walked visibly, to the multitude it appeared as if he were invisible. Although he walked naked, to the multitude it appeared as if he were adorned and prepared. Although he walked as a youth, to the multitude it appeared as if he were a sixteen-year-old. Afterwards, however, he was just an infant, not like that (sixteen-year-old)." And the assembly was delighted, saying, "Friends, the Elder has explained the question as if he were the Buddha." The Section on the Lokantarika (Lokantarikavāra) is the same as the method already mentioned.

It should be understood that all these natural phenomena (dhammatā) described from the beginning occur for all Bodhisattas.

## Description of the Thirty-Two Marks of a Great Man

"Addasa kho" means he saw the son who was brought and laid in a silk wrap (dukūla-cumbaṭaka). "Mahāpurisassa" means of the man who is great by way of birth, lineage, family, region, and so forth. "Dwe gatiyo" means two destinies, two outcomes. Indeed, this word "gati"—in the passage, "Sāriputta, there are these five destinies" (M. Ni. 1.153)—refers to the destiny (gati) to be gone to by beings, distinguished by hell and so forth. In the passage, "I do not know the coming (āgati) or the going (gati) of these virtuous monks of good character" (M. Ni. 1.508), it refers to inclination (ajjhāsaya). In the passage, "Nibbāna is the destiny (gati) of the Arahant" (Pari. 339), it refers to refuge (pattissaraṇa). In the passage, "O Brahma, I know your destiny (gati) and I know your radiance (juti); such is the great power of Baka Brahma" (M. Ni. 1.503), it refers to accomplishment (nipphatti). It should be understood that here also, this word "gati" refers to accomplishment (nipphatti). "Anaññā" means there is no other destiny (accomplishment).

"Dhammiko" means one endowed with the ten wholesome courses of action, free from going to the four wrong paths (agati). "Dhammarājā" is a synonym for the preceding term. Or, he is called "Dhammarājā" because he obtained kingship through Dhamma.
35:
Cāturanto means the ruler of the entire earth bounded by the four oceans, such as the Eastern Ocean. Vijitāvī means one who has won battles (a conqueror). In the time of this prince, the people of the realm reach a state of permanent stability; therefore, he is called Janapadatthāvariyappatta. When a harsh king oppresses the people with taxes, punishments, and so on, people abandon the central realm and take refuge in peripheral areas such as the foot of mountains or the seashore. In the time of an excessively soft king, people who are oppressed by the violent looting of robbers abandon the peripheral areas and gather to live in the center of the realm. If such kings exist, the realm cannot reach stability. However, when this prince rules, to show that his realm will be as firm as if placed on a stone slab and surrounded by iron plates, they said 'Janapadatthāvariyappatta.'

In the term 'Sattaratanasamannāgato,' it is called a treasure (ratana) because of its nature of producing delight and joy. Alternatively: 'It is called a treasure because it is honored, highly valuable, incomparable, rare to see, and used only by noble beings.' From the time the Wheel Treasure appears, there are no other shrines or celestial abodes; all people perform offerings of scents, flowers, etc., and pay homage only to that Wheel Treasure. Thus, it is a treasure in the sense of being honored (cittīkata). Because it is impossible to determine that the Wheel Treasure is worth this much wealth, it is also a treasure in the sense of being highly valuable (mahaggha). Because the Wheel Treasure is incomparable to any other treasures existing in the world, it is also a treasure in the sense of being peerless (atula). Furthermore, because Cakkavatti kings appear only in the aeons when Buddhas appear, and Buddhas appear only very rarely, it is also a treasure in the sense of being rare to see (dullabhadassana). That Wheel Treasure appears only to a noble being who is perfect in birth, appearance, lineage, and power, and not to anyone else. Therefore, it is also a treasure in the sense of being used by noble beings (anomasattaparibhogga). Just like the Wheel Treasure, the remaining treasures are also called treasures in the same way. Because he is endowed with these seven treasures as a retinue and as the basis for all enjoyments, he is called 'Sattaratanasamannāgato.'

Now, to show those treasures in detail, the words beginning with 'Tassimāni' are spoken. Among those words beginning with 'Cakkaratanaṃ,' the brief meaning is: the Wheel Treasure appears, which is capable of bringing and bestowing the glory and wealth of the four great islands surrounded by two thousand small islands. Likewise, the Elephant Treasure appears, which is capable of traveling around the entire earth bounded by the four oceans within just the morning time, and is capable of traveling through the sky. Similarly, the Horse Treasure appears. Endowed with the four factors...
36:
...the Gem Treasure appears, which is capable of dispelling darkness for about one league (yojana) and allowing light to be seen; the Queen Treasure appears, who is free from the six faults and is pleasing to the heart; the Householder Treasure appears, who is capable of seeing treasure pots buried within the earth for about one league; and the Counselor Treasure appears, known as the eldest son, born from the womb of the chief queen, who is capable of advising and governing the entire kingdom.

'Parosahassaṃ' means more than a thousand. 'Sūrā' means those who are fearless. 'Vīraṅgarūpā' means those who possess the factor of the brave, which is energy (vīriya); they are of energetic nature, energetic character, made of energy, and are tireless. It means they do not become weary even if they fight all day long. 'Sāgarapariyantaṃ' means the earth bounded by the ocean, with Mount Cakkavāḷa as its limit. 'Adaṇḁena' means that unlike kings who rule by imposing wealth-fines of a hundred or a thousand on guilty beings, or kings who govern by the punishment of weapons such as cutting and breaking, this prince abandons both types of punishment and dwells ruling without punishment. 'Asatthena' means that it is not ruling by oppressing others with weapons such as single-edged swords; without even causing the blood of a small fly to flow, he conquers the earth in the aforementioned manner by righteousness (dhamma) alone, being welcomed and accepted by rival kings saying, 'Come, Great King,' and dwells having overcome and become the lord.

Having thus spoken of one accomplishment, the words beginning with 'Sace kho pana' are spoken to describe the second accomplishment. Therein, he is called 'Vivaṭacchado' because the covering or veil known as lust, hatred, delusion, pride, wrong view, defilements, and craving has been destroyed and opened. Although there is a reading 'Vivaṭṭacchadā,' the meaning is the same.

Having thus spoken of the second accomplishment, the words beginning with 'Ayañhi deva kumāro' are spoken to show the marks (lakkhaṇa) that are the signs of those accomplishments. Therein, 'Suppatiṭṭhitapādo' means that unlike others whose toes, heels, or one side of the foot touches first when placing the foot on the ground, or who have a gap in the middle, or whose one part of the foot lifts first when raising the foot, it is not so for him. For him, like the surface of a golden sandal, the entire sole of the foot touches the ground all at once and lifts from the ground all at once. Therefore, he is one with well-placed feet.
37:
Cakkāni means having two wheels on both soles. The spokes, rims, and hubs of these wheels have already been taught in the Pali. This distinction should be understood by the term 'Sabbākāraparippūrāni' (complete in every aspect). In the center of those wheels on the soles, the hub (nābi) is seen; the circular lines defining the hub are seen; the rim-face encircling the hub is seen; the opening of the hub is seen; the spokes are seen; the circular lines on the spokes are seen; the rims and the circular beads on the rims are seen. These are points directly mentioned in the Pali. Although not directly mentioned in the Pali, the numerous accompanying marks should be understood as follows: a spear, srivatsa, nandi (jasmine flower), three neck lines, a crest-flower, a food tray (vaddhamānaka), a pair of fish, a bhaddapīṭha (auspicious seat), a goad, a palace, a gateway, a white umbrella, a sword, a palm-leaf fan, a peacock-tail fan, a yak-tail whisk, a turban, a gem, an alms-bowl, a jasmine garland, a blue lotus, a red lotus, a white lotus, a paduma lotus, a puṇḍarīka lotus, a jar filled with mustard seeds etc., a bowl filled with white mustard seeds etc., the ocean, the world-system (Cakkavāḷa), the Himavanta mountains, Mount Sineru, the moon and the sun, the constellations, the four great islands, and the two thousand small islands. At the very least, the entire retinue of a Universal Monarch is merely an accompaniment to the wheel-mark.

Āyatapaṇhi means having long heels and full heels. While for others the forefoot is long and the leg bone (ankle) stands on top of the heel as if the heel were shifted back, it is not so for the Great Man. If the foot of the Great Man is divided into four parts, two parts are the forefoot, the leg stands on the third part, and the fourth part is the heel, which is like a red woolen ball turned round with a lathe.

Dīghangulī means that unlike others whose fingers are some long and some short, the fingers and toes of the Great Man are long like those of a monkey. They are thick at the base and gradually taper to the tip, resembling sticks of realgar (haritāla) kneaded with resinous oil and rolled. Thus it is called "Dīghangulī".

Mudutalunahatthapādo means being soft like a layer of cotton wool that has been carded a hundred times and dipped in clarified butter. Just as they are soft at the time of birth, the hands and feet will remain soft and tender even in old age. Because of having such soft and tender hands and feet, he is called Mudutalunahatthapādo.

Jālahatthapādo does not mean the spaces between the fingers are connected by skin. Such a hand, where the fingers are joined by skin, is called phaṇahatthaka (cobra-hood hand), which is a human defect and such a person cannot receive ordination. For the Great Man...
38:
...four fingers and five toes are of equal length. Because the fingers and toes are of equal length, the barley-grain marks (yavalakkhaṇa) on the finger joints are aligned with one another. Then, the hands and feet of that Great Man are like a lattice window well-crafted by a skilled carpenter. Therefore, he is called 'jālahatthapādo' (one with net-like hands and feet).

Because of having ankles set high, the Great Man has feet with high-set ankles; therefore, he is called 'ussaṅkhapādo' (one with high ankles). Indeed, in other people, the ankles are on the sides of the feet, and thus their feet are as if fixed by a pin and cannot turn easily; when they walk, the soles of their feet are not visible. But the Great Man's ankles are set high above the top of the foot; therefore, from the navel upward, his upper body remains as steady as a golden statue placed on a boat, and only the lower body moves. The feet turn easily, and the soles are clearly visible to those standing and watching from the front, the back, or from both sides, unlike elephants whose soles are seen only from behind.

'Eṇijaṅgho' means having calves like those of the antelope called Eṇī. His calves are full and rounded due to the abundance of flesh. The flesh is not bunched on one side, but he is endowed with calves that are surrounded by evenly distributed flesh, well-rounded, and resembling the belly of a grain of hill-paddy or barley.

'Anonamanto' means without bending. By this term, the Great Man's state of being neither hunchbacked nor dwarfed is shown. Indeed, other people are either hunchbacked or dwarfed. The upper body of the hunchbacked is incomplete, and the lower body of the dwarfed is incomplete. Because their bodies are incomplete, they are unable to touch their knees without bending. The Great Man, however, because both his upper and lower body are complete, is able to touch his knees without bending.

'Kosohitavatthaguyho' means having the male organ covered by a sheath, like that of a bull or a noble elephant, resembling the calyx of a golden lotus. 'Vatthaguyha' refers to the organ that should be concealed by cloth.

'Suvaṇṇavaṇṇo' means having a body like a solid gold statue that has been cleaned with vermilion, polished with a tusker's tooth, and finished with gold paint. By this term, the Great Man's solid, smooth, and fine body is shown, and to describe the complexion of his skin, it is said 'kañcanasannibhattaca' (one whose skin is like gold). Or else, it is a synonym for the previous term.
39:
"Rajojalla" means fine dust or coarse dirt. Just as a drop of water does not stick to a lotus leaf but rolls off, so this dirt does not stick [to the Buddha's body]. However, the Buddhas perform [acts such as] washing their hands for the sake of the season and for the merit of the donors. Alternatively, they do so out of duty. It is said: "A monk entering the monastery should wash his feet before entering."

"Uddhaggaloma" means having body hairs that, at the end of their clockwise curl, point upwards as if looking up at the beauty of the face.

"Brahmujugatta" means having a body as straight as a Brahma's. He will have a body that is straight and tall. Generally, beings bend in three places: the nape of the neck, the waist, and the knees. Those who bend at the waist bend backwards. Those who bend at the other two places bend forwards. Some tall people are crooked at the sides. Some walk with their faces turned upwards as if counting the stars. Some, having little flesh and blood, are like a spit. Some lean forward and walk trembling. But this Great Man will be straight and tall, like a golden gatepost erected in a celestial city. Just as this mark of being straight like Brahma is spoken of with reference to how it will become in the future, so too, any mark of a Great Man that is not fully complete at birth should be understood as being spoken of with reference to its future completion.

"Sattussada" means having full fleshy protuberances in seven places: the backs of the two hands, the backs of the two feet, the two shoulders, and the nape of the neck. In others, the network of veins is visible on the backs of hands and feet, and the joints of bones are visible on the shoulders and neck. Such people look like hungry ghosts (petas) to others. The Great Man is not like that. Because he has full fleshy protuberances in the seven places, his hands and feet, where the network of veins is hidden, are prominent. With a neck like a small, well-rounded golden drum, he appears to others like a stone statue or a painted image.

"Sīhapubbaddhakāya" means having a body like the front half of a lion. A lion's front body is full, but its hind body is not. For the Great Man, however, the whole body is full like the front half of a lion. Like a lion's body, in various parts, by way of bending or rising...
40:
...[the Great Man's body] is not ill-formed or distorted. It is long in parts that should be long. In parts where it is appropriate to be short, thick, thin, wide, or rounded, it is exactly so. For this was said by the Blessed One:

“Monks, when the result of a pleasing wholesome kamma appears, those limbs that are beautiful when long, remain long. Those limbs that are beautiful when short, remain short. Those limbs that are beautiful when thick, remain thick. Those limbs that are beautiful when thin, remain thin. Those limbs that are beautiful when wide, remain wide. Those limbs that are beautiful when rounded, remain rounded.”

Thus, the physical body of the Great Man, fashioned by various meritorious thoughts and adorned with the ten perfections (pāramīs), cannot be replicated even by all the artists or all the powerful beings in the world.

“Citantaraṃsa” means: the space between the two shoulder blades is called “antaraṃsa”; because that space is filled, it is called “citantaraṃsa.” In others, that place is hollow, and the two shoulder blades appear separately. For the Great Man, however, a layer of flesh rises from the waist to the shoulders, covering the back like a well-erected golden slab.

“Nigrodhaparimaṇḍala” means: having a body as proportionate as a banyan tree. Just as a banyan tree of fifty or a hundred cubits is equal in height and spread (the span of its branches), so too [the Great Man] is equal in height and wingspan. It means that unlike others whose bodies are unequal, being either taller or wider, his proportions are equal. Therefore, it was said: “yāvatakvassa kāyo” and so on. There, “yāvatakvassa” means “yāvatako assa.”

“Samavaṭṭakkhandha” means: having a well-rounded neck. Just as some people have long necks, crooked necks, or thick necks like cranes, herons, or pigs...
41:
Some people have long necks, crooked necks, or thick necks like those of cranes, herons, or pigs. When they speak, the network of their veins becomes visible, and their voice comes out faintly. This is not so for the Great Man. The Great Man, however, has a neck that is well-rounded like a golden drum. When he speaks, the network of his veins is not visible. He has a powerful voice like the roar of a thundercloud.

In the term "rasaggasaggī," they are called "rasaggasā" because they carry or receive taste. This is a designation for the taste-nerves (rasaharaṇī). Because that prince possesses excellent taste-nerves, he is called "rasaggasaggī." It is said that the Great Man has seven thousand taste-nerves that point upwards and meet at the throat. Even if a piece of food the size of a sesame seed is placed on the tip of his tongue, the essence pervades his entire body. For this reason, while he was practicing the great exertion (dukkara-cariyā), he was able to sustain his body with just one grain of rice or a single spoonful of bean soup. For others, however, because they do not have such nerves, the nutrients cannot pervade the entire body. Therefore, those people are prone to many illnesses.

He is called "sīhahanu" because he has a jaw like that of a lion king. In that regard, only the lower jaw of a lion king is full, not the upper one. For the Great Man, however, both jaws are full like the lower jaw of a lion, resembling the moon on the twelfth day of the waxing fortnight. At that time, the prognosticators, observing the edges of his jaws, noted: "In these jaws, there will be twenty teeth below and twenty above, forty teeth in total, which will be even and without gaps." They then reported, "Your Majesty, this prince will have forty teeth," and so on. The meaning of this is: even among others who have a full set of teeth, there are only thirty-two. For this prince, however, there will be forty. The teeth of others are uneven, some being high and some low. For this prince, however, they will be even like a conch shell slice cut with a saw. The teeth of others are gapped like those of crocodiles; when they eat fish or meat, the gaps become filled. For this prince, however, his teeth will be without gaps, like a row of diamonds set on a golden pedestal, or like the distinct divisions shown on a painter's brush-stroke. Others may develop decayed teeth, causing some canines to be black or discolored. This prince, however, has very pure white canines, and he will be one whose canines possess a radiance that surpasses even the morning star (Osadhī).

"Pahūtajivho" means having a broad tongue. The tongues of others may be thick, thin, short, stiff, or uneven. The tongue of the Great Man, however, is soft, long, broad, and beautiful in color. To dispel the doubts of those who come to search for this mark, because it is soft, he can roll that tongue like a needle and touch both nostrils; because it is long, he can touch both ear-holes.
42:
He touches (the nostrils, etc.); because it is broad, he can cover his entire forehead up to the hairline. Thus, by demonstrating the softness, length, and breadth of his tongue, he dispels their doubts. Referring to the tongue endowed with these three characteristics, it is said, "pahūtajivho."

"Brahmassaro" means that while others may have broken voices, cracked voices, or voices like a crow, this Great Man will be endowed with a voice like that of Mahābrahmā. The voice of Mahābrahmā is clear because it is not obstructed by bile or phlegm. The meritorious deeds performed by the Great Man also purify the physical source of his voice. Because the source is pure, the voice that arises from the navel is exceptionally clear and emerges endowed with the eight qualities. Because he speaks like a Karavīka bird, he is called "karavīka-bhāṇī." It means he has a sweet voice like the song of an intoxicated Karavīka bird.

"Abhinīlanetto" does not mean the entire eye is blue. In the parts that should be blue, his eyes are endowed with an extremely pure blue color like the flax flower (ummapuppha). In the parts that should be yellow, they are yellow like the Kaṇikāra flower; in the parts that should be red, they are red like the Bandhujīvaka flower; in the parts that should be white, they are white like the morning star (Osadhī); and in the parts that should be black, they are black like black beads (addāriṭṭhaka). They appear like jeweled lion-windows opened in a golden mansion.

In the term "gopakhumo," "pakhuma" refers to the entire eye-complex. That eye has a dark quality like that of a black calf, and is especially clear like that of a red calf. It means he has eyes like those of a tender red calf born that very moment. The eyes of others are incomplete. They may be endowed with protruding eyes or deep-set eyes like those of elephants, mice, and so on. For the Great Man, however, his eyes are like polished and burnished jewel-spheres, surrounded by eyelashes that are soft, smooth, blue, and delicate.

"Uṇṇā" refers to the auspicious hair (Urna). "Bhamukantare" means it is born between the two eyebrows, just above the nose, and rising upwards, it stays in the middle of the forehead. "Odātā" means it is pure, with a color like the morning star. "Mudū" means it is like a layer of cotton-wool that has been washed a hundred times and placed in clarified butter. "Tūlasannibhā" means it has a color like silk-cotton or vine-cotton. This is a metaphor for its whiteness. If that auspicious hair is held by the tip and pulled, it extends to half the length of an arm. When released, it curls to the right and its tip points upwards. It is beautiful with a splendor that greatly attracts the heart, like a silver star placed in the middle of a golden pedestal, or like a stream of milk flowing from a golden pot, or like the morning star in the sky at dawn. The term "uṇhīsasīso" is spoken in reference to two benefits: having a full forehead and having a well-shaped head. Starting from the clockwise hair-fringe of the Great Man...
43:
When released, it [the uṇṇā hair] turns clockwise and stands with its tip pointing upwards. It shines with an exceedingly delightful splendor, like a silver bubble placed in the middle of a golden plate, like a stream of milk flowing from a golden pot, and like the morning star in the sky tinged with the glow of dawn.

The term "uṇhīsasīsa" is used in reference to two meanings: having a full forehead and having a full head. In detail, a layer of flesh rises from the edge of the Great Man's right ear, covers and fills the entire forehead, and rests at the edge of the left ear. That layer of flesh is as beautiful as a royal turban-band. Having seen this mark on the Great Man, kings created the turban-band. This is the first meaning. Other people have incomplete heads; some have heads like monkeys, some like fruits, some like bones, some like elephants, some like gourds, and some like mountain slopes. The Great Man's head, however, is perfectly full like a water bubble, as if it were well-rounded by a lathe. Between these two, according to the first method, he is called "uṇhīsasīsa" because he has a head that appears as if wrapped with a turban. According to the second method, he is called "uṇhīsasīsa" because he has a head that is circular in all parts like a turban-band.

## Explanation of the Name Vipassī

Regarding the word "sabbakāmehi", although it is spoken as if it were done after having the marks examined, it should not be understood in that way. It should be understood that first they satisfied the fortune-tellers, and only then was the examination of the marks performed. The details of this were already mentioned in the section on descending into the womb. "Pāyenti" means they provide milk. For that prince, sixty nurses provided with faultless and sweet milk were made to attend. Likewise, sixty nurses each, skilled in various other tasks, were also made to attend. To command those nurses, sixty men were appointed, and sixty ministers were appointed to observe whether each task was completed or not. Thus, there were four groups of sixty women and two groups of sixty men, making six groups of sixty attendants in total. "Setacchattaṃ" refers to a divine white parasol. The white parasol given by relatives, however, remains only in the auspicious inner chamber. In the phrases beginning with "mā naṃ sītaṃ vā", the meaning should be understood as "let it not oppress him". "Svāssudaṃ" should be broken down into "so assudaṃ". From the lap of one to the lap of another, from the arm of one to the arm of another, from another's...
44:
...from the shoulder of one person only to the shoulder of another; it means he is carried or brought.

"Mañjussara" means having a voice that is not harsh. "Vaggussara" means having a voice that is skilled and refined. "Madhurassara" means having a voice that is sweet. "Pemaniyassara" means having a voice that generates love.

In that illustration, regarding the sweetness of the Karavīka birds' voice: it is said that when a Karavīka bird pecks a ripe mango of delicious flavor with the tip of its beak, drinks the flowing juice, flaps its wings, and sings, four-legged creatures begin to frolic like those who are intoxicated. Even four-legged creatures engaged in seeking food spit out the grass in their mouths and listen to that sound. Wild beasts such as lions and tigers, while chasing small deer, stand still without lowering their raised feet to the ground. The hunted deer also stand still, forgetting the fear of death. Even birds flying in the sky stand still with their wings spread out while listening to that sound. Even fish in the water flap their ear-flaps and remain still while listening to that sound. In this way, Karavīka birds have an extremely sweet voice.

Queen Asandhimittā, the queen of King Dhammāsoka, also asked the Saṅgha, "Venerable sirs, is there anyone whose voice is like the voice of the Buddha?" When they replied, "The voice of the Karavīka bird is similar," she asked, "Venerable sirs, where are those birds?" They replied, "They are in the Himālaya mountains." She said to the King, "Great King, I wish to see a Karavīka bird." The King issued an order, "Let the Karavīka bird come and sit in this cage," and released a golden cage.

The cage went and stood before a Karavīka bird. The bird reflected, "This cage has come by royal command; it is impossible not to go," and sat in it. The cage returned and stood before the King, but no one could make the Karavīka bird produce a sound. Then the King asked, "Friends, why does this bird not make a sound?" They replied, "Great King, it is because it does not see its kin." Then the King had the bird surrounded with mirrors.

When the bird saw its own reflection in the mirrors, it thought, "My kin have come," flapped its wings, and sang with a sweet voice as if blowing a jeweled flute. All the people in the whole city frolicked with joy like those who are intoxicated. Queen Asandhimittā thought, "If even the voice of this animal is so sweet, how sweet must have been the voice of the Blessed One who attained the splendor of Omniscience?" She generated joy (pīti) directed towards the Buddha. Without letting go of that joy, she, along with seven hundred female attendants who followed on foot, was established in the Fruit of Stream-entry. In this way, the voice of the Karavīka bird is very sweet.
45:
It should be understood that Prince Vipassī possessed a voice that was a hundred or even a thousand times sweeter than the sound of a Karavīka bird. The term 'kamma-vipākaja' (born of the fruit of karma) refers not to a meditative divine eye, but to a fleshly eye (maṃsacakkhu) similar to that of the devas, produced by the power of the fruit of wholesome karma. With that eye, he was able to identify and pick out even a single sesame seed that had been marked and thrown into a cartload of sesame, saying, "This is that very seed."

Regarding the term "Vipassī", the meaning is as follows: He is called Vipassī because he sees clearly, free from the darkness caused by blinking from time to time, and because he sees with open eyes. According to the second method, he is called Vipassī because he sees after investigating and scrutinizing (viceyya viceyya); the meaning is that he sees after careful examination. "Atthe panāyati" means he knows, sees, or promotes welfare and meanings.

One day, while King Bandhuma was sitting in the place of judgment, they brought the Great Being (Prince Vipassī), adorned and prepared, and placed him in the King's arms while the King was advising on matters of welfare in the court. While the King was fondling his son on his lap, the ministers made the rightful owner lose and the non-owner win (a wrongful judgment). Then the Bodhisatta uttered a sound of displeasure. The King said, "What is this sound? Investigate!" Upon investigation, finding no other cause, they thought, "This must have happened because the case was poorly decided," and they decided in favor of the rightful owner again. Wanting to test whether the Prince did this knowingly, they again made the rightful owner lose. The Bodhisatta uttered the same sound again. From then on, the King realized, "The Great Being knows," and became heedful. With reference to this, it is said: "The Prince, having investigated again and again, understands the meanings" (viceyya viceyya kumāro atthe panāyati).

In the terms "Vassika" and so on: a palace that is comfortable for living in during the rainy season is called Vassika. The same principle applies to the other seasons. The etymological meaning here is: living during the rains is "vassa"; a palace suitable for that rainy season is "Vassika". The same principle applies to the Hemantika (winter) and other terms.

Among them, the Vassika palace is neither too high nor too low. Its doors and windows are neither too many nor too few. In this rainy season palace, floor coverings, beddings, and various kinds of food are provided in a mixed and suitable manner. In the Hemantika (winter) palace, the pillars and walls are low. The doors and windows are small with only tiny openings. Wall-projections are extended to let in heat. In that palace, floor coverings, beddings, robes, and blankets...
46:
...warm blankets and such are suitable. The food is smooth, spicy, and prepared without water. In the summer (Gimhika), the pillars and walls are high. In that summer palace, the main doors and windows are numerous and large. Floor coverings made of fine silk (dukūla) are suitable. The food is full of sweet flavors. Near the windows of that palace, nine new pots are placed, filled with water and covered with blue lotuses and such. In various places, water machines are constructed from which streams of water come out like falling rain.

"Without men" (nippurisehi) means devoid of males. Not only were the musical instruments played without men, but all places were devoid of men; even the gatekeepers were women, and those who performed services like bathing were women. It is said that the King thought, "Let my son, while enjoying such sovereign bliss and success, not have any suspicion regarding men upon seeing a man," and thus he stationed only women for all tasks.

## The Commentary on the First Recitation Section is Finished.

## Explanation of the Old Man

43-4. In the second recitation section, "gopānasivaṅkaṃ" means crooked like a roof-rafter. "Bhoggaṃ" means bent in three places: the neck, the waist, and the knees. "Daṇḍaparāyanaṃ" means one whose gait depends on a staff, or who takes a staff as a support. "Āturaṃ" means oppressed by old age. "Gatayobbanaṃ" means one whose youth has passed and who stands in the final stage of life. "Having seen" means: although he was surrounded by an army for half a yojana and well-guarded, as he was going, the chariot was in front and the army was behind; in such an opening, he saw that old man manifested right in front of the chariot by the Arahant Brahmas of the Pure Abodes (Suddhāvāsa) through their own power. It is said that the Pure Abode devas thought, "The Great Being is stuck in the five cords of sensual pleasure like an elephant in the mud; we shall arouse mindfulness in him," and so they showed him. Both the Bodhisatta and the charioteer saw him as he was thus shown. The Brahmas showed him for the sake of the Bodhisatta’s heedfulness and for the sake of a conversation with the charioteer. "What is this?" (kiṃ paneso) means he asked, "What is meant by this 'old man'? Friend, I have never seen such a person before this."
47:
"Tena hi" means: "If I too am to have such hair and such a body, then, friend charioteer, there is no benefit in going to the park today." Having set out with the thought "Today I will see the park," he then said, "Enough of that parkland," because his heart was agitated, speaking words appropriate to his sense of spiritual urgency (saṃvega). Upon reaching the inner palace, he dismissed the women and sat alone in the auspicious chamber. He sat there digging at the root of birth (jāti), thinking, "Woe to this birth, for when there is birth, old age is manifest; this birth is loathsome," as if his heart had been pierced by the first arrow.

"Having sent for the charioteer" means: The King had been keeping a watchful ear ever since the time the fortune-telling brahmins had spoken. Hearing that "the Prince turned back halfway while going to the park," he sent for the charioteer. The meaning is that he thought, "Let him only rule the kingdom, let him not renounce; let the words of the brahmins not be true."

## Description of the Sick Man (Vyādhipurisa-vaṇṇanā)
"He saw" means he saw the one shown by the Suddhāvāsa Brahmas, as previously mentioned. "Ābādhika" (afflicted) refers to one who is ill with an unnatural ailment that disrupts the bodily postures. "Dukkhita" (suffering) refers to one who has come to suffering due to the pain of disease. "Bāḷhagilāna" (severely ill) refers to one who is in intense pain. "Palipanna" (sunk) refers to one who is overwhelmed. In this instance too, thinking, "When there is birth, these two—old age and sickness—are manifest; woe to that birth, only the unborn (ajata) is secure (khema)," he sat digging at the root of birth, as if pierced by a second arrow.

## Description of the Dead Man (Kālaṅkatapurisa-vaṇṇanā)
"Vilāta" refers to a palanquin (bier). "Peta" refers to one who has departed from this life. "Kālaṅkata" refers to one who has completed his time; the meaning is one who has died after finishing the entire duration of life he was meant to live. The Brahmas showed this dead man as well, in the same manner as before. In this instance too, thinking, "When there is birth, these three—old age, sickness, and death—are manifest; woe to that birth, only the unborn is secure," he sat digging at the root of birth, as if pierced by a third arrow.
48:
## Description of the Renunciant (Pabbajita-vaṇṇanā)
"Bhaṇḍu" means shaven-headed. The Brahmas showed this monk to the Prince in the same manner as before. In the phrases beginning with "Sādhu dhammacariyā" (Good is the practice of Dhamma), the connection of the meaning of each word should be understood as: "O Prince, practicing the Dhamma in this way is excellent," and thus he renounced. All these terms are synonyms for the ten wholesome courses of action (dasa-kusalakamma-patha). "Avihiṃsā" (non-violence) at the end is the preliminary stage of compassion (karuṇā). "Anukampā" (sympathy) is the preliminary stage of loving-kindness (mettā). The phrase "Tena hi" is a particle used in the sense of urging. Having seen the monk, the Prince's mind inclined toward renunciation. Then, wishing to speak with that monk and wanting to urge the charioteer, he spoke the words beginning with "Tena hi."

## Description of the Bodhisatta's Renunciation (Bodhisatta-pabbajjā-vaṇṇanā)
"Atha kho, bhikkhave" (Then, O monks) means: Having heard the words beginning with "Good is the practice of Dhamma as a monk," as well as many other discourses concerning the disadvantages of living in a house crowded with wife and children protected by a great multitude, and the benefits of seclusion for a monk living happily in the forest with a mind like a deer, he desired to renounce. Thus it is said, "Then, O monks, Prince Vipassī addressed the charioteer."

Seeing these four omens and renouncing is the lineage (vaṃsa), the thread (tanti), and the tradition (paveṇī) of all Bodhisattas. Other Bodhisattas, like Prince Vipassī, see these omens only after long intervals. Our Bodhisatta, however, saw all four omens on the very same day, went forth in the Great Renunciation (Mahābhinikkhamana), and renounced on the banks of the Anomā River. Therefore, when he reached Rājagaha and was asked by King Bimbisāra, "O Wise One, for what reason have you renounced?", he replied:

'Having seen the aged, the suffering, and the sick,
And having seen the dead whose life-span was exhausted,
And having seen the monk wearing the saffron-dyed robes,
Therefore, O King, I have renounced.'

## Description of the Multitude Following in Renunciation (Mahājanakāya-anupabbajjā-vaṇṇanā)
"Sutvāna tesaṃ" means: Having heard the words of those eighty-four thousand beings, such a thought occurred. "Orako" means inferior or lesser. "Anupabbajjiṃsu" means they followed in renunciation.
49:
They followed his example and went forth into homelessness. However, regarding the renunciation of these eighty-four thousand beings following the Bodhisatta, why is it not stated here, as it is later mentioned in the renunciation of Khaṇḍa and Tissa, that they "departed from the royal city of Bandhumatī"? It is not stated because they heard the news only after they had already left the city. It is said that all these eighty-four thousand men were the attendants of Prince Vipassī. They went to serve him early in the morning, but not seeing the prince, they went to have their breakfast. After eating, they returned and asked, "Where has the prince gone?" Hearing that he had gone to the park, they thought, "We shall see him right there," and set out. On their way, they met the charioteer returning and heard his words, "The prince has gone forth as a monk." Right at the place where they heard this, they took off all their ornaments, ordered dyed robes from the market, shaved off their hair and beards, and went forth. Thus, because they heard the news outside the city after having already departed, it is not stated here that they "departed from the royal city of Bandhumatī."

"Cārikaṃ carati" (He wanders on a journey) means that in every place he reached, a large pavilion was prepared and offerings were arranged. Being invited for the next day, he accepted only the alms-food requested by the people and wandered for four months.

"Ākiṇṇo" means being surrounded by this group of monks. When did this thought of wanting to live alone, withdrawing from the group, occur to the Bodhisatta Vipassī? It occurred on the fourteenth day, thinking, "Tomorrow will be the full moon day of Visākha." It is said that at that time, the Bodhisatta Vipassī thought, "Just as these people surrounded and followed me in the past when I was a layman, they do the same now that I have gone forth. What is the use of this group?" Being weary of associating with the group, he thought, "I will go this very day." Then he thought again, "Today is not the right time. If I go now, all these monks will know I am leaving. I will go only tomorrow."

On the day he had that thought, the villagers living in a village similar to Uruvelā invited him for the next day. They prepared only milk-rice for all those eighty-four thousand monks and the Bodhisatta. Then, on the following day, after finishing the meal with those monks in that village, the Bodhisatta returned to his dwelling place. There, those monks performed their duties toward the Bodhisatta and then entered their respective places for the night and day. The Bodhisatta also entered his leaf hut and sat down.

"When it is the time of midday,
And the birds rest quietly,
The great forest seems to rustle;
That fear appears to me."
50:
At such a time, which is fearful for all beings who do not delight in solitude and is a time of distress, he thought, "This is the time (for me to depart)," and leaving the leaf hut, he closed the door and headed toward the Bodhimanda. At other times, while wandering in that area, he had seen the Bodhimanda, but his mind had never before inclined toward sitting there. On that day, however, the Bodhisatta Vipassī's knowledge had reached maturity. Therefore, seeing the adorned Bodhimanda, the thought arose to ascend it. The Bodhisatta approached from the southern direction, made a circumambulation to the right, and after preparing a fourteen-cubit seat on the eastern side, he sat down, making a resolution with fourfold effort: "As long as I have not become a Buddha, I shall not rise from this seat."

With reference to his living in seclusion, it is said: "He lived alone, withdrawn from the group."

"Anyeneva tāni" means that those eighty-four thousand monks came to the Bodhisatta in the evening and sat surrounding the leaf hut. When it became very late, they said, "Let us investigate," and opened the door of the hut, but they did not see the Bodhisatta. However, they did not follow him, asking, "Where has he gone?" Instead, they said, "The Great Being seems weary of living with a group and wishes to live alone. We shall see him only when he has become a Buddha," and they departed on a journey toward the interior of Jambudīpa.

## Description of the Bodhisatta's Reflection

"Vāsūpagatassa" means having come to stay for one night at the Bodhimanda. "Rahogatassa" means having gone into seclusion. "Paṭisallīnassa" means dwelling in seclusion by way of one-pointedness of mind. "Kicchaṃ" means suffering. "Cavati ca upapajjati ca"—these two terms are spoken with reference to the repeated process of death and rebirth. In this context, "jarāmaraṇassa" is mentioned because the Bodhisatta had gone forth after seeing only the aged, the sick, and the dead; thus, only aging and death became apparent to him. Therefore, it is said: "jarāmaraṇassa." Thus, the reflection of the Bodhisatta, who took aging and death as the root and applied his mind, was like one descending from the highest point of existence (bhavagga). Then, O monks, this thought occurred to the Bodhisatta Vipassī:

"Yonisomanasikārā" means reflection by way of proper means, or primary reflection. Indeed, reflecting on impermanence and so forth in the manner of impermanence is called wise attention (yonisomanasikāra). This reflection, which proceeds by way of contemplating arising and passing away, such as "When what exists do birth and so forth come to be? When what does not exist do they not come to be?", is that very wise attention.
51:
For the person who attends, wise attention (yoniso manasikāra) through proper means occurs. Because of a certain kind of attention through the power of observing the arising and passing away, the Bodhisatta Vipassī attained penetration through wisdom due to wise attention. Through the Bodhisatta's wisdom, [he realized] that when a certain thing exists, aging and death occur; there was a meeting with the cause of aging and death. What is that cause? It is birth. Therefore, it is said: "When there is birth, aging and death come to be." The meaning here is that there was a meeting (insight) of the Bodhisatta with the wisdom that grasps birth as the cause of aging and death. In this way, all terms should be understood.

In the phrase "When there is name-and-form, consciousness comes to be," it should also be said, "When there are volitional formations, consciousness comes to be," and "When there is ignorance, volitional formations come to be." However, both were not taken. Why? Because ignorance and volitional formations belong to the past life, and this insight (vipassanā) does not connect with those ignorance and volitional formations. This is because the Great Being (Mahāpurisa) attended only by way of present phenomena. If one objects, "Is it not impossible to become a Buddha without seeing the unseen ignorance and volitional formations?"—it is true that it is impossible. However, the Bodhisatta saw those ignorance and volitional formations only through the power of seeing existence (bhava), clinging (upādāna), and craving (taṇhā). At this point, the discourse on Dependent Origination (paṭiccasamuppāda) should be explained in detail. However, that discourse has already been explained in the Visuddhimagga.

"Paccudāvattati" means "it turns back" or "it recoils." Which consciousness turns back here? Both rebirth-linking consciousness (paṭisandhi-viññāṇa) and insight-knowledge (vipassanā-ñāṇa) turn back. Therein, rebirth-linking consciousness turns back from its cause (volitional formations), and insight-knowledge turns back from its object. Both do not transcend name-and-form; they do not go beyond name-and-form. To this extent, in the phrases such as "it may be born," when consciousness is the condition for name-and-form, and name-and-form is the condition for consciousness, both being mutual conditions, by just this much mutual assistance of consciousness and name-and-form, a being "may be born" or "may be born repeatedly." Apart from this consciousness and name-and-form, what other thing will be born? Is it not this collection of consciousness and name-and-form alone that is born? Thus, having shown the five terms along with successive death and rebirth, and wishing to assign the meaning stated as "by this much," he said, "With name-and-form as condition, consciousness comes to be; with consciousness as condition, name-and-form comes to be." After that, by way of the forward order of Dependent Origination, to show birth, aging, and death in the future which have name-and-form conditioned by consciousness as their root, he said, "With name-and-form as condition, the six sense bases come to be," and so on. Therein, "the origin of this whole mass of suffering" means the arising of the entire mass of suffering consisting of birth, aging, death, sorrow, lamentation, pain, grief, and despair. Thus, the Great Being saw the arising of the entire suffering of the round of rebirths.
52:
'Samudaya, samudaya' means arising, arising. 'In things unheard of before' refers to dhammas that have not been heard before, not previously heard. In phrases such as 'the eye arose,' it refers to this insight-wisdom (vipassanā-paññā) that perceives the arising. It is called 'eye' (cakkhu) in the sense of seeing, 'knowledge' (ñāṇa) in the sense of causing to know, 'wisdom' (paññā) in the sense of knowing distinctly, 'vision' (vijjā) in the sense of knowing by penetrating and piercing through, and 'light' (āloka) in the sense of illuminating.

Regarding this, it was taught: "The eye arose in the sense of seeing. Knowledge arose in the sense of knowing. Wisdom arose in the sense of knowing distinctly. Vision arose in the sense of penetration. Light arose in the sense of illumination. The eye-dhamma has the nature of seeing. The knowledge-dhamma has the nature of knowing. The wisdom-dhamma has the nature of knowing distinctly. The vision-dhamma has the nature of penetration. The light-dhamma has the nature of illumination" (in the Paṭisambhidāmagga). What is meant by these terms? It means merely recognizing the causal relationship: "When this exists, that comes to be." Alternatively, it refers to tender insight (taruna-vipassanā) that has just entered the path of insight.

'Adhigato kho myāyaṃ' should be analyzed as 'adhigato kho me ayaṃ' (I have attained this). 'Magga' refers to the path of insight (vipassanā-magga). 'Bodhyāya' means for the sake of knowing the Four Truths or for the sake of knowing Nibbāna. Furthermore, it is called 'Bodhi' because it knows; this is a name for the Noble Path (ariya-magga), and it is said to be for that purpose. This is because the Noble Path has the path of insight as its foundation. Now, wishing to bestow that path, he said, "Because of the cessation of this mind-and-matter," and so on. Here, by terms in the nominative case such as 'the cessation of consciousness,' only Nibbāna is meant. In this way, the Great Man, the Bodhisatta, saw the non-arising cessation of the entire suffering of the round of rebirths.

'Nirodha, nirodha' means non-arising, non-arising. The terms 'eye' and so on have the same meanings as previously stated. In this context of cessation (nirodha), however, all these terms mean merely recognizing the cessation: "When this does not exist, that does not come to be." Alternatively, it refers to powerful insight leading to emergence (vuṭṭhānagāminī-vipassanā).

'At another time' means in the period after having thus known the cause and the cessation of the cause. 'In the aggregates of clinging' means in the aggregates that serve as the cause for clinging. 'Contemplating arising and falling' means repeatedly contemplating that very arising and falling which was first seen. 'He dwelt' means he lived while carrying on the insight leading to emergence that had reached its peak. Why was this said? Because all Bodhisattas who have fulfilled the perfections, in their final existence, when their son...
53:
Bodhisattas who have fulfilled the perfections, in their final existence, depart on the very day of their son's birth through the Great Renunciation and become monks. Then, applying themselves to meditation, they ascend the Throne of Enlightenment, defeat the forces of Māra, and in the first watch of the night, they recollect their former existences. In the second watch, they purify the divine eye. In the third watch, they contemplate Dependent Origination, and after emerging from the fourth jhāna of mindfulness of breathing, they direct their minds to the five aggregates of clinging. Observing the fifty characteristics by way of rise and fall, they develop insight up to the knowledge of change-of-lineage (gotrabhū-ñāṇa) and, through the Noble Path, penetrate all the qualities of a Buddha. This Bodhisatta Vipassī was also a Great Being (Mahāpurisa) who had fulfilled the perfections. Having performed everything in the aforementioned sequence, that Bodhisatta emerged from the fourth jhāna of mindfulness of breathing in the final watch and directed his mind to the five aggregates of clinging, beginning the insight that observes rise and fall in the manner described. To show that observation of rise and fall, this statement was made.

In that context, "Thus is form" means: this is form, form is only this much, and there is no form beyond this. This refers to the comprehensive grasping of form without remainder by way of its characteristic, function, manifestation, and proximate cause, beginning with its nature of being deformed (ruppana) and the distinction between the great essentials and derived matter. By the phrase "Thus is the arising of form," the observation of the cause of form thus grasped is stated. Therein, "thus" means "in this way the arising occurs." The detail of that meaning should be understood as follows: "With the arising of ignorance, form arises; with the arising of craving, form arises; with the arising of kamma, form arises; with the arising of nutriment, form arises." One who sees the characteristic of birth also sees the arising of the aggregate of form. Regarding cessation: "With the cessation of ignorance, form ceases... one who sees the characteristic of change also sees the cessation of the aggregate of form." This is the detailed explanation of that.

In the phrases "Thus is feeling," etc., it means: this is feeling, feeling is only this much, and there is no feeling beyond this. This is perception, these are mental formations, this is consciousness, consciousness is only this much, and there is no consciousness beyond this. This refers to the comprehensive grasping of feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness without remainder by way of their characteristics, functions, manifestations, and proximate causes, beginning with the natures of experiencing, perceiving, constructing, and cognizing, as well as the distinctions such as pleasure, etc., perception of forms, etc., contact, etc., and eye-consciousness, etc. By the phrases "Thus is the arising of feeling," etc., the observation of the cause of feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness thus grasped is stated. Therein also, "thus" means "in this way the arising occurs." The detail of those should be understood in the same manner as stated for form: "With the arising of ignorance, feeling arises." However, there is this distinction: for the three [mental] aggregates, instead of saying "with the arising of nutriment," one should say "with the arising of contact." For the aggregate of consciousness...
54:
...just as the phrase "with the arising of name-and-form" is used, the phrase for cessation should also be applied by way of that contact and name-and-form. This is the summary here; the detailed determination of rise and fall (udayabbaya-viniścaya) in all its aspects has been stated in the Visuddhimagga. For that Bodhisatta Vipassī, as he dwelt observing the rise and fall in those five aggregates of clinging by way of the fifty characteristics, his insight knowledge gradually developed. Through the cessation that is non-arising, his mind was liberated from the defilements known as taints (āsavas) without clinging or grasping. That mind is said to be "being liberated" at the path moment and "liberated" at the fruit moment. Alternatively, at the path moment, it is both "liberated" and "being liberated," while at the fruit moment, it is simply "liberated."

By this much, the Great Being was well-liberated from all bonds. With a mind-continuity as fully blossomed as a lotus touched by the sun's rays, he attained the four path knowledges, the four fruit knowledges, the four analytical knowledges, the knowledge that distinguishes the four modes of birth, the knowledge that distinguishes the five destinations, and the six uncommon knowledges. Having all the qualities of a Buddha in his hand, and with his purpose fulfilled, while still seated on the Throne of Enlightenment, he reflected:

"Through many a birth in saṃsāra have I wandered, seeking but not finding the builder of this house. Sorrowful is birth again and again.
O house-builder! You are seen. You shall build no house again. All your rafters are broken, your ridge-pole is shattered. My mind has attained the unconditioned; it has attained the end of craving."

And also:
"Just as the destination of a spark struck by a smith's hammer, which glows and then gradually goes out, cannot be known;
Even so, for those who are well-liberated, who have crossed the flood of the bond of sensuality, and who have reached the unshakable happiness of Nibbāna, there is no destination that can be described."

Reflecting in this way, he shone like the sun in autumn or like the full moon.

## The explanation of the second recital section is finished.
55:
## Commentary on the Request by Brahmā

In the third recitation section, the phrase "Should I teach the Dhamma?" means "If I were to teach the Dhamma." When did this thought arise? It arose in the eighth week after he had attained Buddhahood. After becoming the Buddha, he sat for seven days on the Bodhi-throne; for seven days he stood gazing at the Bodhi-throne; for seven days he walked on the jeweled walkway; for seven days he sat in the Ratanaghara (Jeweled House) contemplating the Dhamma; for seven days he sat at the foot of the Ajapāla Banyan tree; for seven days he sat at the foot of the Mucalinda tree; for seven days he sat at the foot of the Rājāyatana tree. Rising from there, in the eighth week, as soon as he returned and sat at the foot of the Ajapāla Banyan tree, this thought—which is the custom of all Buddhas—and the thought immediately following it, arose.

Among those terms, "adhigato" means realized through penetration. "Dhammo" refers to the Dhamma of the Four Noble Truths. "Gambhīro" is a term that rejects the nature of shallowness. "Duddaso" means difficult to see because of its depth; it is to be seen with difficulty and cannot be seen easily. Because it is difficult to see, "duranubodho" means it is to be understood with difficulty and cannot be understood easily. "Santo" means the calming of defilements. "Paṇīto" means that which does not cause satiety (extremely sublime). These two terms are spoken with reference only to the supramundane (lokuttara) Dhamma. "Atakkāvacaro" means a Dhamma that cannot be entered into by reasoning, but must be entered into only by wisdom. "Nipuṇo" means subtle. "Paṇḍitavedanīyo" means a Dhamma to be known only by the wise who have practiced the right path. "Ālayarāmā" means that beings are attached to the five cords of sensual pleasure; therefore, those sensual pleasures are called "ālaya" (attachments). The 108 types of craving are also called "ālaya". Because they delight in these attachments, they are called "ālayarāmā". Because they enjoy these attachments, they are called "ālayaratā". Because they greatly rejoice in these attachments, they are called "ālayasammuditā".

For example, just as a king who enters a garden well-prepared and filled with trees laden with flowers and fruits delights in those various perfections, rejoices, and being happy, does not grow weary and has no desire to leave even at night; in the same way, beings delight in these attachments to sensual pleasure and attachments to craving, and they live in the round of rebirth (saṃsāra) rejoicing without weariness. Therefore, the Blessed One, wishing to show those beings the two kinds of attachments as if they were garden grounds, spoke the words beginning with "ālayarāmā".

"Yadidaṃ" is a particle; with reference to its place, it should be understood as "yaṃ idaṃ" (which is this), and with reference to dependent origination (paṭiccasamuppāda), it should be understood as "yo ayaṃ" (which is this). "Idappaccayatā-paṭiccasamuppādo" means: the causes of these effects (such as formations) are called "idappaccaya" (having this as condition); the state of having these conditions is "idappaccayatā"; and because it is both that conditionality and dependent origination, it is called "idappaccayatā-paṭiccasamuppādo".
56:
This name (idappaccayatā-paṭiccasamuppādo) is the name for ignorance (avijjā) and so on, which are the causes of the effects such as formations (saṅkhāra). The entire meaning of "sabbasaṅkhārasamatha" and so on refers only to Nibbāna. Indeed, because all the fluctuations of formations are calmed and specifically stilled depending on that Nibbāna, it is called "sabbasaṅkhārasamatha" (the stilling of all formations). And because all acquisitions (upadhi) are relinquished, all cravings are exhausted, all lust of defilements fades away, and all suffering of the round ceases depending on that Nibbāna, it is called "sabbūpadhipaṭinissagga" (the relinquishment of all acquisitions), "taṇhākkhaya" (the destruction of craving), "virāga" (the fading of lust), and "nirodha" (cessation). That craving is called "vāna" because it weaves or binds together one existence to another, or action (kamma) with its fruit. Because it is the exit from that craving called "vāna", it is called "Nibbāna". "That teaching would be a weariness to me" means that teaching the Dhamma to those who do not know or understand would be a weariness of the body and a distress to the body for me. In the minds of the Buddhas, however, both these kinds of weariness and distress do not exist.

The word "apissu" is a particle meaning "furthermore" or "repeatedly". It shows: "Not only did this thought occur, but these verses (gāthā) also appeared in my knowledge." In the words beginning with "Vipassiṃ", it means "to the Blessed One, the Arahant, the Fully Enlightened One, Vipassī". "Anacchariyā" means repeatedly wonderful. "Paṭibhaṃsu" means they became the objects of the knowledge known as intuition (paṭibhāna); they reached the state of being contemplated.

"Kicchena" means obtained with difficulty; it does not mean obtained through painful practice (dukkha-paṭipadā). This is because all four paths of the Buddhas are only pleasant practice (sukha-paṭipadā). However, this was said with reference to the practice leading to the attainment [of Buddhahood], such as when fulfilling the perfections (pāramīs), while still possessing lust, hatred, and delusion, he cut off his decorated head and gave it to any beggars who came, or drew out his throat-blood, or uprooted his eyes, or gave away his children and wife, and underwent cutting and breaking in existences such as that of Khantivādī the hermit. The word "halaṃ"—here the letter "ha" is merely a particle—means "alaṃ" (enough/capable). "Pakāsituṃ" means to teach. It means: "I am capable of teaching the Dhamma thus obtained with difficulty; what benefit would there be in teaching it [to those who cannot understand]?" "Rāgadosaparetehi" means by those overwhelmed by lust and hatred, or those followed by lust and hatred.

"Paṭisotagāmiṃ" refers to the Dhamma of the Four Noble Truths which proceeds in the manner of impermanence (anicca), suffering (dukkha), non-self (anatta), and foulness (asubha), which are the opposites of permanence (nicca) and so on. "Rāgarattā" refers to beings who are dyed with sensual lust, lust for existence, and lust for views. "Na dakkhanti" means they will not see [the Dhamma] through its true nature as impermanence, suffering, non-self, and foulness...
57:
(Beings) will not see (the Four Noble Truths). Who would be able to make such beings, who do not see, accept and believe in the nature of impermanence and so forth? "Obscured by a mass of darkness" means being overwhelmed by the mass of ignorance (*avijjā*). "Inaction" (*appossukkatā*) means the state of being without effort, the desire not to teach the Dhamma.

Why did the Blessed One's mind incline in this way (towards not teaching)? Did he not attain omniscience (*sabbaññutaññāṇa*) after making an aspiration and fulfilling the perfections (*pāramīs*), saying: "When I am liberated, I will liberate others; when I have crossed over, I will help others cross over," and "What is the use of realizing the Dhamma in an obscure form in this life?
