Only after attaining omniscience will I save the world including the devas"? It is true that he made such an aspiration. However, his mind inclined this way due to the power of reflection (*paccavekkhaṇa*). After attaining omniscience, as he reflected on the thickness of beings' defilements and the depth of the Dhamma, the thickness of beings' defilements and the depth of the Dhamma became clear to him in every aspect. Then, as he thought, "These beings are filled with defilements (*kilesa*), like a gourd full of sour gruel, like a pot full of buttermilk, like a worn cloth soaked in fat, or like hands smeared with collyrium; they are extremely defiled, stained by greed (*rāga*), corrupted by hatred (*dosa*), and deluded by ignorance (*moha*). How could they possibly penetrate (the Dhamma)?"—his mind inclined this way due to the power of reflecting on the thickness of defilements.

"This Dhamma is as deep as the body of water supporting the earth, as hard to see as a mustard seed hidden by a mountain, and as difficult to understand as aligning the ends of a hair split into a hundred parts. While I was striving to penetrate this Dhamma, there was no gift I had not given, no virtue (*sīla*) I had not guarded, and no perfection (*pāramī*) I had not fulfilled. Even for someone like me, the earth did not shake when I was crushing the army of Māra, nor did it shake when I was recollecting past lives (*pubbenivāsanussati*) in the first watch of the night, nor when I was purifying the divine eye (*dibbacakkhu*) in the middle watch. It was only when I penetrated Dependent Origination (*paṭiccasamuppāda*) in the last watch that the ten-thousandfold world system shook. How then will the common people of the world penetrate this Dhamma, which was realized with such difficulty even by one with sharp wisdom like me?" It should be understood that his mind inclined this way also due to the power of reflecting on the depth of the Dhamma.
58:
Furthermore, his mind inclined this way because he wished to teach only when requested by a Brahma. Indeed, the Blessed One knew: "If my mind inclines toward inaction, Mahābrahmā will request me to teach the Dhamma. These beings respect Brahma; they will listen well, thinking, 'The Teacher, it is said, did not wish to teach the Dhamma, but Mahābrahmā requested him to do so. The Dhamma is indeed peaceful! The Dhamma is indeed sublime!'" It should be understood that his mind inclined toward inaction for this reason, and not because he truly did not wish to teach the Dhamma.

In the phrase "*aññatarassa*" (of a certain one), although it says "a certain one," it should be understood as the Great Brahma (*Mahābrahmā*) who is the chief of this universe. "Alas, the world is perishing!"—it is said that he uttered this sound so loudly that the Brahmas of the ten-thousandfold world system heard it and all assembled. "*Yatra hi nāma*" means in whichever world. "*Purato pāturahosi*" means he appeared together with those ten thousand Brahmas. "*Apparajakkhajātika*" refers to those who have little dust of greed, hatred, and delusion in their eye of wisdom. "*Assavanatā*" means because of not hearing. By the word "*bhavissanti*," he shows that there will be many—not just one or two, but hundreds of thousands—who will understand the Dhamma; those who have performed merits through the ten bases of meritorious action (*puññakiriyavatthu*) under previous Buddhas, whose faculties are mature, and who, like lotuses waiting for sunlight, long for the Dhamma and are worthy of entering the stage of the Noble Ones (*ariya*) at the end of a four-line verse.

"*Ajjhesanaṃ*" means requesting in this way three times. "*Buddha-eye*" (*buddhacakkhu*) refers to the knowledge of the degrees of faculties of beings (*indriyaparopariyattañāṇa*) and the knowledge of their latent tendencies (*āsayānusayañāṇa*). These two knowledges are called the "Buddha-eye," while omniscience (*sabbaññutaññāṇa*) is called the "All-seeing eye" (*samantacakkhu*), and the three path knowledges (*maggañāṇa*) are called the "Dhamma-eye" (*dhammacakkhu*). In the terms "*apparajakkha*" and so forth, those who have little dust of greed and so on in their eye of wisdom, as previously explained, are called *apparajakkha* (those with little dust). Those who have much dust are called *mahārajakkha*. Those whose faculties such as faith are sharp are called *tikkhindriya*. Those whose faculties are dull are called *mudindriya*. Those whose dispositions such as faith are good are called *svākāra*. Those who can note the reasons taught and are easy to make understand are called *suviññāpaya*. Those who see the next world and faults as danger are called *paralokavajjabhayadassāvī*.

In clarifying the meaning of these terms like *apparajakkha*, the Pāḷi text states: A person with faith is called *apparajakkha*; a person without faith is called *mahārajakkha*. A person with energetic effort and established mindfulness is called *apparajakkha*; a person who lacks mindfulness is called *mahārajakkha*. A person who is composed is called *apparajakkha*; one who is not composed is called *mahārajakkha*. A person with wisdom is called *apparajakkha*; one with little wisdom is called *mahārajakkha*. Similarly, a person with faith is called *tikkhindriya*. A person with wisdom who habitually sees the next world and the faults of defilements as danger is called *paralokavajjabhayadassāvī*; one with little wisdom does not habitually see them so. The "world" (*loka*) refers to the world of aggregates (*khandha*), the world of elements (*dhātu*), the world of bases (*āyatana*), the world of prosperous existence (*sampattibhava*), the world of ruinous existence (*vipattibhava*), the world of the origin of prosperity (*sampattisambhava*), and the world of the origin of ruin (*vipattisambhava*).
59:
The Pali text in this matter is: "A person with faith is one with little dust (apparajakkha); a person without faith is one with much dust (mahārajakkha). ... A person with energetic effort ... a person who is lazy ... a person with established mindfulness ... a person with confused mindfulness ... a person with concentration ... a person without concentration ... a person with wisdom ... a person with little wisdom is one with much dust. Likewise, a person with faith is one with keen faculties ... a person with wisdom is one who sees the danger in faults and the hereafter; a person with little wisdom is one who does not see the danger in faults and the hereafter. The 'world' (loka) refers to the world of aggregates (khandha-loka), the world of elements (dhātu-loka), the world of sense bases (āyatana-loka), the world of prosperous existence (sampatti-bhava-loka), the world of ruinous existence (vipatti-bhava-loka), the world of prosperous origin (sampatti-sambhava-loka), and the world of ruinous origin (vipatti-sambhava-loka). The world as one: all beings subsist on nutriment. The world as two: mind and matter (nāma and rūpa). The world as three: the three feelings (vedanā). The world as four: the four nutriments (āhāra). The world as five: the five aggregates of clinging (upādānakkhandha). The world as six: the six internal sense bases (ajjhattika-āyatana). The world as seven: the seven stations of consciousness (viññāṇaṭṭhiti). The world as eight: the eight worldly conditions (lokadhamma). The world as nine: the nine abodes of beings (sattāvāsa). The world as ten: the ten sense bases (āyatana). The world as twelve: the twelve sense bases (āyatana). The world as eighteen: the eighteen elements (dhātu). 'Fault' (vajja) means all defilements are faults, all misconducts are faults, all volitional formations (abhisaṅkhāra) are faults, and all kammas leading to rebirth are faults. Thus, in this world and in this fault, a keen perception of danger is established, just as the perception of danger arises towards an executioner with a raised sword. Through these fifty modes, He knows, sees, understands, and penetrates with wisdom these five faculties; this is the Tathāgata's knowledge of the maturity of the faculties of others (indriyaparopariyatta-ñāṇa)."

'Uppalinī' means in a lotus pond. The same method applies to the other terms. 'Anto-nimugga-posīnī' refers to other paduma lotuses that grow while remaining submerged within the water. 'Udakaṃ accuggamma ṭhitāni' refers to lotuses that stand having emerged above the water. Among them, those that stand having emerged above the water, awaiting the touch of the sun's rays, will bloom today. Those that stand level with the water will bloom tomorrow. Those that have not yet emerged from the water but are growing within the water will bloom on the third day. However, there are also other water-born lotuses (saroja) and the like that do not emerge from the water and will never bloom, but will only become food for fish and tortoises; these are not included in the Pali text but are brought forth in the commentary for clarification. Just like these four types of lotuses, there are four types of persons: the one of quick understanding (ugghaṭitaññū), the one who understands through expansion (vipañcitaññū), the one who needs guidance (neyya), and the one for whom the word is the maximum (padaparama). Among those four:
60:
A person who realizes the Four Noble Truths at the very time a teaching is briefly uttered is called an 'ugghaṭitaññū' person. A person who realizes the Four Noble Truths only when the meaning of a briefly uttered Pali text is analyzed in detail is called a 'vipañcitaññū' person. A person who realizes the Four Noble Truths gradually through studying the Pali text, questioning and discussing the meaning, wise reflection, and associating with, following, and attending upon good friends is called a 'neyya' person. A person who, though hearing much of the Dhamma, reciting it much, learning and memorizing it much, and teaching it much, cannot realize the Four Noble Truths in that lifetime is called a 'padaparama' person. (Puggalapaññatti 148, 149, 150, 151)

Among those four types of persons, when the Blessed One surveyed the ten-thousandfold world system, which is like a lotus pond, He saw: "the ugghaṭitaññū like the lotuses blooming today, the vipañcitaññū like the lotuses blooming tomorrow, the neyya like the lotuses blooming on the third day, and the padaparama like the lotuses that are food for fish and turtles." Having seen thus, He saw in every aspect: "This many beings have the eye of wisdom with little dust of defilement, this many beings have the eye of wisdom with much dust of defilement; and among them, this many persons are ugghaṭitaññū."

Among these four types of persons, the Buddha's teaching fulfills the benefit for the first three types of persons in this very life; for the padaparama persons, it serves as a habitual tendency (vāsanā) for the future.

Then, the Blessed One, having known the teaching that brings benefit to these four types of persons and having generated the desire to teach, again divided all beings in all three realms of existence into two groups: the capable (bhabba) and the incapable (abhabba). With reference to this division, it was said: "Those beings who are possessed of the obstruction of kamma (pañcānantariya-kamma), possessed of the obstruction of resultant (ahetuka or dvihetuka rebirth), possessed of the obstruction of defilement (niyata-micchādiṭṭhi), who lack faith, lack desire for merit, and are ignorant—these beings are incapable of entering the path of assurance (niyāma), the rightness in wholesome states; these are called 'incapable' (abhabba) beings. Which beings are 'capable' (bhabba)? Those beings who are not possessed of the obstruction of kamma... these are called 'capable' (bhabba) beings." (Vibhaṅga 827; Paṭisambhidāmagga 1.114)

In that classification, setting aside all incapable persons and taking up only the capable persons with His knowledge, He made six divisions: "This many persons have a lustful temperament (rāga-carita), this many have temperaments of hatred, delusion, speculation, faith, and wisdom (dosa, moha, vitakka, saddhā, buddhi-carita)." Having done so, He thought, "I shall teach the Dhamma."
61:
The Blessed One thought thus. Knowing that thought of teaching the Dhamma, Brahma Sahampati, filled with joy, addressed the Blessed One with verses. With reference to this joy upon knowing the intent to teach, it was said: "Then, monks, the Great Brahma..." and so on.

In that text, "Ajjhabhāsi" means addressing excessively, or addressing specifically regarding a particular matter.

"Sela yathā pabbatamuddhaniṭṭhito" means as if standing on a solid rocky mountain peak. Indeed, for one standing on such a mountain peak, there is no need for actions such as raising or stretching the neck to see. "Tathūpamaṃ" means similar to that solid rock mountain, or using the rock mountain as a simile. The summary meaning of this verse is: Just as a man with sight standing on a rocky mountain peak would see the people all around, so too, O Sumedha (Wise One), the Blessed One, the All-Knowing One with the eye that sees all around, having ascended the palace made of Dhamma and wisdom, being yourself free from sorrow, look upon the people immersed in sorrow and overwhelmed by birth and aging; observe and examine them.

The meaning here is: Suppose a large field was made around the foot of a mountain, and small huts were built on the ridges of the fields, and fires were lit at night. There would be darkness characterized by four factors. Then, for a man with sight standing on the mountain top looking down at the ground, neither the field, nor the ridges, nor the huts, nor the people sleeping there would be visible; only the flames of the fires in the huts would be seen. Similarly, for the Tathāgata who has ascended the Palace of Dhamma and looks upon the assembly of beings, those beings who have not performed meritorious deeds do not come into the range of the Buddha-eye, even if they are sitting near his right knee in the same monastery; they are like arrows shot at night. However, those veneyya persons (tractable beings) who have performed meritorious deeds come into the range of the Buddha-eye even if they are far away. They are prominent like a flame or like Mount Himavanta. Regarding this, it was said:
"The good shine from afar like Mount Himavanta;
The wicked are not seen here, like arrows shot at night."
(Dhp. 304).

With the word "Uṭṭhehi" (Arise), he speaks requesting the Blessed One to wander for the purpose of teaching the Dhamma. In the words "Vīra" and so on: the Blessed One is called "Vīra" (Hero) because of his energy. He is called "Vijitasaṅgāma" (Victor in Battle) because he has conquered the Maras of the devas, death, and defilements. He is called "Satthavāha" (Caravan Leader) because he is capable of leading veneyya beings from the difficult journey of saṃsāra, such as the wilderness of birth, to Nibbāna. He is known as "Aṇaṇa" (Debtless) because he has no debt of sensual desire. Apari...
62:
Because of being victorious, he is "Vijitasaṅgāma" (Victor in Battle). Because of his ability to lead veneyya beings across the wilderness of birth and so on, he is "Satthavāha" (Caravan Leader). He should be known as "Aṇaṇa" (Debtless) because of the absence of the debt of sensual desire.

"Apārutā" means opened. "Amatassa dvārā" (Doors to the Deathless) refers to the Noble Path. For that is the door to Nibbāna, which is called the Deathless. He shows that "it has been opened and set by me." "Pamuñcantu saddhaṃ" means let all beings release or send forth their faith. In the last two phrases, the meaning is: "I, being conscious of the weariness of body and speech, did not speak this profound and supreme Dhamma, though it was well-mastered and well-rehearsed by me. But now, let all people bring the vessel of faith; I shall fulfill their aspirations."

## Description of the Pair of Chief Disciples

"Bodhirukkhamūle" means disappeared at the Ajapāla Banyan tree not far from the Bodhi tree. "Kheme Migadāye" refers to Isipatana. At that time, it was a park named Khema. It is called Migadāya (Deer Park) because it was given as a safe dwelling for deer. With reference to that, it was said: "In the Khema Deer Park." Just as the Blessed One Vipassī, so too other Buddhas, when going for the first teaching of the Dhamma, travel through the air and descend right there. But our Blessed One, seeing the underlying tendency (upanissaya) of the Ajivaka named Upaka, thought: "Upaka has set out on this long journey; he will see me, converse with me, and then go. Later, becoming disenchanted, he will come back and realize Arahantship." Knowing this, he traveled the eighteen-yojana journey on foot. "Dāyapālaṃ āmantesi" means that upon seeing him, looking again and again, the park-keeper approached saying, "Venerable sir, our master has arrived," and the Buddha addressed him.

75-6. "Anupubbī kathaṃ" (Progressive talk) means he gave a discourse in sequence: talk on giving (dāna), followed by virtue (sīla), followed by heaven (sagga), followed by the path (magga). Among those, "Dānakathā" means: this thing called giving is the source of happiness, the root of prosperity, the foundation of wealth. It is the protection, the shelter, the destination, and the refuge for one who has fallen into distress. In this world and the world beyond, there is no support, foundation, object, protection, shelter, destination, or refuge equal to giving. This giving is like a jeweled lion throne in the sense of being a support; it is like the great earth in the sense of being a foundation.
63:
(Giving) is like a rope for grasping because of its nature as an object of focus. Indeed, this giving is like a boat because it crosses over suffering; it is like a brave warrior on the battlefield because it provides relief; it is like a well-fortified city because it protects from danger; it is like a lotus because it is unstained by the filth of stinginess; it is like fire because it consumes those impurities; it is like a cobra because it is difficult to approach; it is like a lion because it is fearless; it is like an elephant because it is powerful; it is like a white noble bull because it is regarded as highly auspicious; it is like Valāhaka, the king of horses, because it brings one to the land of safety. Giving can grant the splendor of Sakka, the splendor of Māra, the splendor of Brahmā, the splendor of a Cakkavatti (Universal Monarch), the knowledge of a disciple's perfection, the knowledge of a Paccekabuddha, and the knowledge of Omniscience. Thus, He spoke words connected to the virtues of giving.

Because one who gives is able to undertake virtue, He taught the discourse on virtue (sīlakathā) immediately after the discourse on giving. Virtue is a support, a foundation, an object, a protection, a shelter, a destination, and a final resort. For the splendors of this world and the world beyond, there is no support, foundation, object, protection, shelter, destination, or final resort equal to virtue. There is no ornament like virtue, no flower like the flower of virtue, and no scent like the scent of virtue. The world, including the devas, never tires of looking at one adorned with the ornament of virtue, wearing the flower of virtue, and anointed with the scent of virtue. Thus, He spoke words connected to the virtues of virtue.

To show that this heaven is obtained by relying on this virtue, He taught the discourse on heaven (saggakathā) immediately after virtue. Heaven is desirable, lovely, and pleasing to the heart. Here, one constantly obtains play and splendors. The devas of the Realm of the Four Great Kings enjoy divine happiness and splendor for nine million years. The Tāvatiṃsa devas (enjoy divine happiness and splendor) for thirty-six million years. Thus, He spoke words connected to the virtues of heaven. Even the mouths of the Buddhas are not sufficient to describe the splendor of heaven. As it was said: 'Monks, I could speak the discourse on heaven in many ways,' and so on.

After enticing them with the discourse on heaven, just as one might adorn an elephant and then cut off its trunk, He showed that 'this heaven is also impermanent and unstable; one should not have desire or lust for it.' He spoke of the drawbacks of sensual pleasures in this way: 'Sensual pleasures provide little satisfaction, much suffering, and much despair; the danger in them is great,' and so on.
64:
He taught the danger, the vileness, and the defilement (of sensual pleasures). In that context, 'ādīnava' means fault. 'Okāra' means 'avakāra,' the state of being low or vile. 'Saṃkilesa' means the defilement of beings in saṃsāra by those (pleasures). As it was said: 'Alas, friends, beings are defiled.' Thus, having made them weary through the danger of sensual pleasures, He revealed the benefits of renunciation (nekkhamma), meaning He revealed the virtues of monkhood. The remaining words are as explained in the commentary on the Ambaṭṭha Sutta and are clear in meaning.

'They obtained'—how did they obtain it? They obtained it through the 'Ehi Bhikkhu' (Come, Monk) ordination. It is said that the Blessed One, seeing the supporting conditions (upanissaya) for them to obtain miraculous bowls and robes, and seeing their past deeds such as giving robes in many previous lives, said, 'Come, monks,' and so on. At that very moment, they appeared with shaven heads, wearing saffron robes, equipped with the eight requisites of a monk upon their bodies, and sat down paying homage to the Blessed One like elders of a hundred years.

In the words 'He showed' (sandassesi) and so on, He showed the benefit of this life (idhalokattha) and the benefit of the life hereafter (paralokattha). In showing the benefit of this life, He showed it as impermanent, suffering, and non-self; He showed the aggregates, the elements, the sense bases, and dependent origination. In showing the arising of the aggregate of form, He showed five characteristics; likewise for the aggregate of feeling and so on. Similarly, in showing the passing away, He showed fifty characteristics by way of arising and passing away (udayabbaya). In showing the benefit of the life hereafter, He showed hell, the animal realm, the peta realm, the asura realm, and the splendor of the six deva worlds and nine Brahma worlds, which are the results of the three types of merit.

'He exhorted' (samādapesi) means He made them undertake wholesome qualities such as the fourfold purification of virtue, the thirteen dhutaṅga practices, and the ten subjects of discourse.

'He inspired' (samuttejesi) means He made them well-sharpened and greatly encouraged. He spoke by making them feel terror regarding the benefits of this life and the life hereafter, as if they had already attained (the goal). Indeed, when the Blessed One spoke, causing terror regarding the benefits of this life through the thirty-two types of torture and the twenty-five varieties of great fear, (the listener) feels agitated and stirred, like one whose hands are tied behind his back, bound tightly, beaten with a hundred blows at a crossroads, and led out through the south gate; or like one whose head is placed on an execution block; or like one impaled on a stake; or like one being trampled by an elephant in rut.
65:
When He speaks for the benefit of the world beyond, it is as if [the listeners] are being born in hell and the like, or as if they are experiencing celestial bliss.

"Sampahamsesi" means He taught by making the attained qualities appear as a great benefit.

"Saṅkhārānaṃ ādīnavaṃ" means that previously, He taught the danger of sensual pleasures (kāmaguṇa) to enable the attainment of the path of Stream-entry (Sotāpatti-magga). In this context, however, to enable the attainment of the higher paths, He showed the danger and the lowliness of formations (saṅkhāra), as well as the weariness caused by those formations, in this manner: "Monks, formations are impermanent, they are unstable, they provide no solace. Monks, this is enough to become weary of all formations, enough to become dispassionate toward them, enough to be liberated from them."

Just as He showed the benefits of renunciation (nekkhamma) when teaching to enable the attainment of the first path, so too, in teaching to enable the attainment of the higher paths, He showed the benefits of Nibbāna in this manner: "Monks, this Nibbāna is peaceful, it is sublime, it is a protection, it is a refuge for those weary of the dangers of saṃsāra."

## Description of the Renunciation of the Great Multitude

"Mahājanakāya" (The Great Multitude) refers to the group of attendants of those two princes, Khaṇḍa and Tissa.

In the phrase "We go to the Blessed One and the Dhamma as refuge," they took only the two-word refuge because the Saṅgha was not yet complete.

"Alatthuṃ" means they received [ordination] through the "Come, bhikkhu" (ehi bhikkhu) method, just as described previously. This same method should be understood for the subsequent instances of renunciation.

## Description of the Allowance for Wandering

"The thought arose"—when did it arise? It arose after seven years, seven months, and seven days had passed since He realized the Four Noble Truths. The Blessed One remained while providing support to His father. King Bandhuma also thought: "My eldest son has renounced and become a Buddha. My second son has renounced and become the Chief Disciple. The Chaplain's son is the second Chief Disciple. All these other monks used to surround my son even when they were laymen. All these monks..."
66:
"Now too, they are my responsibility alone. I alone will support them with the four requisites; I will not give others the opportunity." Thinking thus, the King had acacia (khadira) posts erected on both sides of the road from the monastery gate to the palace gate. He had the path covered with mats on the outside and cloth on the inside, with a roof above. He had various flower-garland canopies made, decorated with gold stars and as thick as palm trunks. On the ground below, he had ornate rugs spread. Inside, on both sides, he placed full jars (puṇṇaghaṭa) shaped like flowering plants. To make the entire path fragrant, he placed flowers between perfumes and perfumes between flowers. Then he sent word to the Blessed One that it was time.

Surrounded by the Saṅgha of monks, the Blessed One went to the palace only within the screens, and after finishing His meal, He returned to the monastery. No one else got even a glimpse of Him, let alone the chance to offer food, pay homage, or hear the Dhamma. The citizens thought: "It has been over seven years and seven months since the Teacher appeared in the world. We do not even get to see Him, let alone offer food, pay homage, or hear the Dhamma. The King thinks 'My Buddha, my Dhamma, my Saṅgha' and supports them alone. When the Teacher arises, He arises for the welfare and benefit of the whole world, including the devas. Hell is not hot only for the King, nor is it like a blue lotus forest for others. Therefore, let us speak to the King. If he gives us [access to] the Teacher, that is good. If not, we will fight the King, take the Saṅgha, and perform meritorious deeds like giving. However, it is not possible to do this with only the citizens; let us also take a leading man as an ally."

They approached the General (Senāpati) and, after informing him of the matter, asked, "Lord, will you be on our side or the King's?" He said, "I am on your side, but I must be given the first day [to offer]." They agreed. The General approached the King and said, "Great King, the citizens are angry with you." When asked, "Dear man, why are they angry?", he replied, "It is because you alone support the Teacher and we do not get the chance. If they get the chance now, they will not be angry; if they do not, they wish to fight you, O King." The King said, "Dear man, I will fight; I will not give up the Saṅgha of monks." The General replied, "Great King, they say they will fight you even though they are your servants. On whom will you rely to fight?" The King asked, "Are you not the General?" The General replied, "Without the citizens..."
67:
“Great King, I am not able,” he replied. Then the King, realizing that “the citizens are powerful, and the General is also on their side,” said, “Let them grant me the opportunity to serve the Saṅgha of monks for another seven years and seven months.” The citizens did not agree. The King reduced his request to “six years, five, four, three, two, one year,” but even as he reduced it, they did not agree. He then pleaded for another seven days. The citizens, thinking, “It is no longer proper to be so extremely stubborn with the King,” granted him permission.

The King distributed the offerings he had prepared for seven years and seven months within just seven days. For six days, he gave alms without letting certain people see, and on the seventh day, he summoned the citizens and asked, “Friends, will you be able to give such an alms as this?” They replied, “Is it not because of us that this alms-giving has become possible for Your Majesty? We are able.” The King, wiping away his tears with the back of his hand, paid homage to the Blessed One and said, “Venerable Sir, I intended to serve six million eight hundred thousand monks with the four requisites for the rest of my life without giving a turn to anyone else. Now the citizens do not permit me; they are angry, saying, ‘We do not get the chance to give alms.’ May the Blessed One show favor to those citizens starting from tomorrow.”

Then, on the second day, the General prepared a great alms-giving and stationed men all around, saying, “Today, guard so that no one else can give even a single meal’s worth of alms.” On that day, the merchant’s wife, weeping, said to her daughter, “Dear daughter, if your father were alive today, I would have been the first to offer alms to the Buddha.” The daughter said to her mother, “Mother, do not worry; I will arrange it so that the Saṅgha of monks headed by the Buddha will partake of our alms first.”

Then, she filled a golden bowl worth a hundred thousand with pure milk-rice, prepared it with ghee, honey, and sugar, covered it with another golden bowl, and wrapped it with jasmine garlands until it looked like a ball of flowers. At the time the Blessed One was entering the village, she lifted it herself and, surrounded by a group of maidservants, departed from the city. Along the way, the General’s attendants forbade her, saying, “Mother, do not come this way.” Those with great merit possess pleasant speech, and it is not easy to reject the words of such people even when they speak repeatedly. She asked, “Uncles and elders, why do you not allow me to pass?” They said, “The General has stationed us here, saying, ‘Do not let anyone else give food or offerings.’” She asked, “What then, do you see food or offerings in my hand?” They replied, “We see only a ball of flowers.”
68:
“We see it,” they replied. She asked, “Does your General not even allow the offering of a flower garland?” They answered, “He allows it, mother.” “In that case, move aside, move aside!” she said, and approaching the Blessed One, she said, “Venerable Sir, please accept this ball of flowers.” The Blessed One, looking at one of the General’s attendants, had him receive the ball of flowers. The merchant’s daughter paid homage to the Blessed One and made an aspiration: “Venerable Sir, wherever I may be reborn in the round of births, may I never live a life of hardship. Like this jasmine flower, may I be loved and cherished by others wherever I am born, and may my name be Sumana.” The Teacher said, “May you be happy.” She paid homage, circumambulated him, and departed.

The Blessed One went to the General’s house and sat on the prepared seat. When the General approached with gruel, the Teacher covered his bowl. “Venerable Sir, the Saṅgha of monks is seated in full,” he said. “Lay follower, we have already received one portion of alms on the way,” the Teacher replied. The General removed the flowers and saw the alms-food. The young attendant said, “Master, that woman deceived me by saying it was flowers.” That milk-rice was sufficient for all the monks headed by the Buddha. The General also gave his own offerings. After the Teacher had finished his meal and spoken words of blessing, he departed. The General asked, “Who was that woman who gave the alms?” “Master, she is the merchant’s daughter,” they replied. “That woman is wise; if such a woman lives in a house, it is not difficult for a man to attain the bliss of heaven,” he said, and having her brought to him, he placed her in the position of his chief wife.

The next day, the citizens gave alms; the day after that, the King gave alms. Thus, they began to give alms on alternate days. The King stationed spies and gave alms that were superior to those given by the citizens. The citizens did the same, giving alms superior to those given by the King. The palace dancers said to the young novices, “Take this, dear ones; this was not made by hands that wiped the clothes of householders or washed the saliva and snot of children; it is prepared purely and exquisitely.” The next day, the citizens, while giving, said, “Take this, dear ones; this was not made from rice, milk, curd, or ghee collected from towns and villages, nor was it brought by breaking the legs, heads, or backs of others; it is made only from the ghee and milk of cows raised in our own homes.” In this way, seven years, seven months, and seven days passed, and then this thought arose in the Blessed One. Therefore, it is said: “Seven years, seven months, and seven days after the Great Enlightenment, this thought arose.”
69:
"A certain Great Brahmā" refers to the very Brahmā who requested the preaching of the Dhamma.

"Eighty-four thousand dwellings" refers to eighty-four thousand monasteries. All of them were great monasteries capable of accommodating twelve hundred thousand monks, similar to the Abhayagiri, Cetiyapabbata, Cittalapabbata, and Mahāvihāra monasteries.

"Patience is the highest austerity" means that the patience known as endurance (adhivāsana-khanti) is the supreme practice of austerity (tapo). 'Titikkhā' is simply a synonym for 'khanti'. The meaning is that endurance, which is called patience, is the highest austerity. "Nibbāna is supreme" means the Buddhas say that Nibbāna is supreme in every way. "One who strikes another is not a renunciant" means that one who, due to being devoid of endurance, harms, oppresses, or hurts another is not truly called a renunciant (pabbajita). The fourth line of the verse is a synonym for that very statement. The synonym for "not a renunciant" (na hi pabbajito) is "is not a recluse" (na samaṇo hoti), and the synonym for "one who strikes another" (parūpaghātī) is "one who harasses another" (paraṃ viheṭhayanto). Alternatively, 'parūpaghātī' means a destroyer of virtue (sīlūpaghātī). Virtue is called 'para' (supreme) because of its noble meaning. The meaning is that a recluse who harasses any being whatsoever is a destroyer of virtue, a destroyer of his own virtue, and thus is not truly called a renunciant. Alternatively, one who, due to the absence of endurance, becomes a killer of others, even intentionally taking the life of a gadfly or mosquito, is not a renunciant. Why? Because he has not yet cast out his defilements. "One casts out one's own defilements, therefore one is called a renunciant (pabbajita)"—this is the characteristic of a renunciant. One who does not kill but harms or oppresses with sticks and so on, harassing others, is not a recluse (samaṇa). Why? Because his cruelty has not been stilled. "Because of the stilling of evils, one is called a recluse (samaṇa)"—this is the characteristic of a recluse.

In the second verse, 'sabbapāpassa' means of all unwholesome deeds. 'Akaraṇaṃ' means not producing. 'Kusalassa' means of wholesome deeds belonging to the four planes. 'Upasampadā' means attainment (fulfillment). 'Sacittapariyodapanaṃ' means purifying one's own mind; that purification of the mind occurs through the fruit of Arahantship. Thus, having abandoned all evil through the restraint of virtue (sīla-saṃvara), and having fulfilled wholesome deeds through tranquility and insight (samatha-vipassanā), one should purify the mind through the fruit of Arahantship; this is the instruction, the advice, and the teaching (sāsana, ovāda, anusisṭhi) of the Buddhas.
70:
In the third verse, 'anūpavādo' means not disparaging anyone with speech. 'Anūpaghāto' means not committing harm with the body. 'Pātimokkhe' refers to the most noble and especially supreme virtue. It is called 'Pātimokkha' because it protects from the specific bad destinations (agati), because it liberates from the fear of miserable states (duggati), or because it liberates the one who protects it. Restraint in that Pātimokkha virtue; 'mattaññutā' means knowing the measure in receiving and using requisites; 'pantañca sayanāsanaṃ' means a lodging that is secluded and free from the disturbance of people. It should be understood that by mentioning two requisites (alms-food and lodging), contentment with the four requisites is indicated. "This is the teaching of the Buddhas" means that not disparaging others, not harming, restraint in the Pātimokkha virtue, knowing the measure in receiving and using requisites, and resorting to a secluded lodging to master the eight attainments (samāpatti) are the instruction, the advice, and the teaching of the Buddhas. These verses should be known as the verses of the Pātimokkha exhortation (Ovāda-pātimokkha) of all the Buddhas.

## Explanation of the Deities' Announcement

Having shown the state of the Dhamma-element being well-penetrated through the detailed explanation following the life-story (apadāna) of the Blessed One Vipassī, saying "Monks, this Dhamma-element has been well-penetrated by the Tathāgata," now, to show the announcement by the deities, saying "The deities also announced this matter to the Tathāgata," the words beginning with "Ekamidāhaṃ" are spoken.

In that Pali, 'Subhagavane' means in the forest of that name. 'Sālarājamūle' means at the foot of the king of trees, a great Sal tree. 'Kāmacchandaṃ virājetvā' means having abandoned and removed sensual desire by the Path of Non-returning (anāgāmi-magga) through uprooting. Just as the deities who had lived the holy life in the dispensation of the Blessed One Vipassī announced it, so too did the deities who had lived the holy life in the dispensations of the remaining Buddhas. However, the Pali text comes only by way of the Blessed One Vipassī and our Blessed One.

Among those deities and Brahmās, they are called 'Avihā' because they do not fall away from their own prosperity. They are called 'Atappā' because they do not cause distress to any being. They are called 'Sudassā' because they are beautiful and inspiring. They are called 'Sudassī' because they see well or because their vision is excellent. They are called 'Akaniṭṭhā' because they are all great in their virtues and the perfection of their existence, and there are no juniors among them. At this point, the recitations (bhāṇavāra) should be combined. To speak in detail, in this Mahāpadāna Sutta, three recitations are taught by way of the life-story of the Blessed One Vipassī. Just as three recitations are taught by way of the life-story of the Blessed One Vipassī, so too by way of the life-story of the Buddhas beginning with Sikhī, three...
71:
At this point, the recitation sections (bhāṇavāras) should be summarized. In this Mahāpadāna Sutta, three bhāṇavāras are spoken by virtue of the life story (apadāna) of the Blessed One Vipassī. Just as they are spoken by virtue of the life story of Vipassī, they are likewise spoken by virtue of the life stories of Sikhī and the others. However, the Pali text is abbreviated. Thus, by virtue of the seven Buddhas, our Blessed One has preached twenty-one bhāṇavāras. Likewise, with the Aviha Brahmas, the Atappa Brahmas, the Sudassa Brahmas, the Sudassī Brahmas, and the Akaniṭṭha Brahmas (each group accounting for 21 bhāṇavāras), the total becomes one hundred and twenty-six bhāṇavāras. In the Word of the Buddha within the Three Pitakas, there is no other sutta that measures one hundred and twenty-six bhāṇavāras in length; therefore, this sutta should be known as the King of Suttas (Suttantarājā). Following this, desiring to conclude the two sequences (anusandhi), He said the words beginning with "Thus, O bhikkhus." All those words are quite clear in meaning.

## Thus ends the explanation of the Mahāpadāna Sutta
## in the Commentary of the Dīgha Nikāya named Sumangalavilāsinī.
72:
## 2. Mahānidāna Sutta Vaṇṇanā
## Nidāna Vaṇṇanā
This sutta, beginning with "Evaṃ me sutaṃ" and ending with "Kurūsu," is the Mahānidāna Sutta. Within this Mahānidāna Sutta, the following is the explanation of terms that are not clear. In the phrase "Kurūsu viharati," the term Kuru refers to the princes of the Kuru country. A single district which is the dwelling place of those princes is also called "Kuru" by way of conventional usage (ruḷhī). (The Blessed One was staying) in that Kuru district.

However, the teachers of the Commentary say this: In the time of King Mandhātā, the people of the three great continents heard that "Jambudīpa is the birthplace of noble beings such as Buddhas, Paccekabuddhas, Great Disciples, and Wheel-turning Monarchs. It is a noble island and is exceedingly delightful." Therefore, placing the Wheel Treasure (Cakkaratana) at the front, they followed King Mandhātā, the Wheel-turning Monarch, as he traveled through the four great continents. Thereafter, King Mandhātā asked his Counselor Treasure (Pariṇāyakaratana), "Dear son, is there any place more delightful than the human world?" (The Counselor Treasure) replied, "Great King, why do you speak thus? Do you not see the majesty of the moon and the sun? Is the place where those moons and suns abide not more delightful than this human world?"

The King, placing the Wheel Treasure at the front, went to that region (of the Four Great Kings). When the Four Great Kings heard that "The Great King Mandhātā has arrived," they reflected, "This king possesses great psychic power and majesty; it is not possible to resist him by war," and they surrendered their own celestial realm (Cātumahārājikā). After King Mandhātā took possession of that celestial realm, he again asked the Counselor Treasure, "Dear son, is there any place more delightful than this?"

Then, (the assembly headed by the Counselor Treasure) informed him about the Tāvatiṃsa celestial realm. "Great King, the Tāvatiṃsa realm is more delightful than this Cātumahārājikā realm. In that Tāvatiṃsa realm, these Four Great Kings stand in the position of gatekeepers as attendants to Sakka, the King of Devas. Sakka, the King of Devas, possesses great psychic power and majesty. These are his places of enjoyment: the Vejayanta Palace, which is a thousand leagues high; the Sudhammā celestial assembly hall, which is five hundred leagues high; the Vejayanta chariot, which is one hundred and fifty leagues long, as well as the Erāvaṇa elephant; the Nandana Garden, Cittalatā Garden, Phārusaka Garden, and Missaka Garden, which are adorned with thousands of celestial trees; and there is also the Pāricchattaka coral tree, which is a hundred leagues high. Beneath that tree, there is the Paṇḍukambala stone seat, which is sixty leagues long, fifty leagues wide, and fifteen leagues thick, having a color like that of the Jayakusuma flower. Due to the softness of that stone seat, when Sakka sits down, half of his body sinks into it."
73:
Upon hearing those words, King Mandhātu, wishing to go to the Tāvatiṃsa heaven, raised the Wheel Treasure. The Wheel Treasure, together with the fourfold army, stood in the sky. Then, the Wheel Treasure descended from the midst of the two deva worlds and stood on the earth along with the fourfold army led by the Counselor Treasure. King Mandhātu went to the Tāvatiṃsa realm alone. As soon as Sakka heard that "Mandhātu has arrived," he went out to welcome him and said, "Welcome, Great King! This heaven is your own, Great King; please rule over it." Dividing the sovereignty of the deva realm into two parts, including the celestial dancers, he gave one part to him. As soon as he was established in the Tāvatiṃsa realm, Mandhātu’s human state disappeared and his divine state became manifest. It is said that the difference between Mandhātu and Sakka, as they sat together on the Paṇḍukambala stone throne, could only be discerned in the blink of an eye. Devas who did not notice this detail were confused by the difference between Sakka and Mandhātu. While enjoying divine bliss in that deva realm, he ruled until thirty-six Sakkas had arisen and passed away; yet, being unsatisfied with sensual pleasures, he passed away from that realm, fell into his own park, and died with a body afflicted by hot winds.

When the Wheel Treasure stood again on the earth, the Counselor Treasure had King Mandhātu’s sandals engraved on a gold plate and ruled the country, saying, "This is the kingdom of King Mandhātu." The people who had come from the three great continents, being unable to return to their own places, approached the Counselor Treasure and pleaded, "Lord, we came by the power of the King; now we are unable to return. Please grant us a place to live." The Counselor Treasure gave each of them a province. Among those places, the region inhabited by people from Pubbavideha became known as "Videharaṭṭha" according to their former designation. The region inhabited by people from Aparagoyāna became known as "Aparantajanapada." The region inhabited by people from Uttarakuru became known as "Kururaṭṭha." Because it is referred to in the plural based on the many villages and market towns, it is said, "He was dwelling among the Kurus."

In the phrase "the market town of the Kurus named Kammāsadhamma," some teachers explain the meaning by replacing the letter "dh" with "d." It is called "Kammāsadamma" because Kammāsa was tamed (damita) there. "Kammāsa" refers to the man-eater Kammāsapāda Porisāda. It is said that when the wound on his foot, pierced by a stump, healed, it looked like variegated wood; thus he was known as "Kammāsapāda." He was tamed in that place.
74:
That Porisāda was restrained from his state of being a man-eater. Who tamed him? The Bodhisatta tamed him. In which Jātaka was he tamed? Some teachers say it was in the Mahāsutasoma Jātaka. However, the elders who preserve this Majjhima Nikāya say he was tamed in the Jayaddisa Jātaka. Indeed, at that time, the Bodhisatta tamed Kammāsapāda. As the Blessed One said:

"When I was the son of Jayaddisa,
The offspring of the ruler of the Pañcāla kingdom,
Renouncing my life, I freed my father Jayaddisa from danger,
And I also inspired faith in Kammāsapāda of the variegated feet."

Some teachers explain the meaning using the letter "dh" itself. It is said that the practice of the Five Precepts (Kuru-vatta-dhamma) of the inhabitants of the Kuru kingdom became "spotted" (kammāsa) or corrupted in that place; therefore, because the Dhamma became spotted there, it is called "Kammāsadhamma." The name of the market town established there is also the same. Why is it not spoken of with the locative case (indicating a specific dwelling)? Because there was no monastery for residence. It is said that in that market town, there was no monastery (vihāra) for the Blessed One to reside in. Departing from the market town, there was a large forest grove in a pleasant area well-supplied with water; the Blessed One dwelt in that forest grove, making that market town his alms-resort. Therefore, the meaning here should be understood as: "He dwells among the Kurus; there is a market town of the Kuru people named Kammāsadhamma, and he dwelt there making it his alms-resort."

The word "Āyasmā" (Venerable) is a term of endearment and a term of respect. "Ānanda" is the name of that Elder. "Ekamantaṃ" (to one side) is a neuter singular adverbial usage (bhāvanapuṃsakaniddesa), as in "visamaṃ candimasūriyā parivattanti" (the moon and sun revolve unevenly). Therefore, it should be understood here that he sat in such a way that his sitting was appropriate and suitable. Alternatively, this word "ekamantaṃ" uses the accusative case in the sense of the locative; "nisīdi" means he approached and sat down. Wise people, having approached a person worthy of respect, are skillful in seating and usually sit in a suitable place. This Venerable Ānanda was also one among those wise people; therefore, he sat down to one side.

How does one sit so that it is called "sitting to one side"? It is by sitting while avoiding the six faults of sitting. Those six faults are: sitting too far, too near, upwind, on high ground, directly in front, and directly behind. If one sits too far away, one must speak in a loud voice when wishing to speak. If one sits too near, it causes physical contact. If one sits upwind, one disturbs the other with body odor. If one sits on high ground...
75:
Sitting in a high place displays a lack of respect. If one sits directly in front, one might have to look eye-to-eye when wishing to see. If one sits too far behind, one might have to turn the neck to look. Therefore, this Venerable Ānanda, after circumambulating the Blessed One three times and paying respects with great reverence, avoided these six faults of sitting and sat in front of the right knee-cap. He entered within the six-colored Buddha-rays, like entering into clear lac-dye, like being wrapped in a golden cloth, or like entering the middle of a canopy of red lotuses. Thus, the Treasurer of the Dhamma, Venerable Ānanda, sat down. Therefore, it is said, "He sat on one side."

At what time and for what reason did this Venerable approach the Blessed One? He approached in the evening for the purpose of asking a question regarding Dependent Origination (paṭiccasamuppāda). It is heard that on that day, Venerable Ānanda, as if placing a bag of a thousand coins at every door to support the lay devotees, wandered for alms in the village of Kammāsadhamma. After returning from the alms round, he performed the major and minor duties for the Blessed One. When the Blessed One entered the Fragrant Chamber (gandhakuṭi), he paid respects to the Blessed One, went to his own place for the day's rest, and had his disciples perform their duties. When the disciples had left, he swept the place of rest again, spread out a piece of leather, cooled his hands and feet with water from a water-pot, and sat down cross-legged, entering the attainment of the fruition of stream-entry (sotāpattiphala-samāpatti). Then, emerging from the attainment at the designated time, he applied his knowledge to Dependent Origination. He contemplated the twelve factors of Dependent Origination three times, proceeding from the beginning to the end starting with "with ignorance as condition, volitional formations" (avijjāpaccayā saṅkhārā), from the end to the beginning, from both ends to the middle, and from the middle to both ends. As he contemplated thus, Dependent Origination became exceedingly clear and manifest to him.

Then, Venerable Ānanda thought: "All Buddhas have taught that this Dependent Origination is both deep and appears deep. However, to me, a disciple established in limited knowledge (padesañāṇa), it appears exceedingly clear and manifest. Does it appear clear only to me, or to others as well?" Then he thought: "Now, I shall take this question and ask the Blessed One. Surely, the Blessed One, taking this matter as a basis, will preach a unique discourse (suttanta), as if lifting Mount Sineru along with its core. Indeed, when the Buddhas reach these four topics—the Vinaya regulations, the specific planes of existence, Dependent Origination, and the specific philosophical views—their preaching is very grand, their knowledge penetrates, the greatness of the Buddha-knowledge is manifest, the teaching is profound, and it is connected with the three characteristics and with emptiness (suññatā)." Although he usually approached the Blessed One a hundred or a thousand times a day, he would not approach without a reason. But on that day, he thought: "I shall take this question and approach the Elephant King, the Buddha, to hear the elephant-trumpet of his knowledge; I shall approach the Lion, the Buddha, to hear the lion's roar of his knowledge; I shall approach the Thoroughbred Horse, the Buddha, to see the gait of his knowledge." Thus, rising from his place of rest, taking his leather mat and shaking it out, he approached the Blessed One in the evening. Therefore, I said, "He approached in the evening for the purpose of asking a question regarding Dependent Origination." In the phrase "gambhīro" (deep), the meaning is...
76:
(The four topics: Vinaya regulations, specific planes of existence, Dependent Origination, and specific philosophical views.) The teaching delivered upon reaching these four matters is grand. (Because it is so grand,) the greatness of the Blessed One's knowledge is manifest, the teaching is profound, and it is connected with the three characteristics and with emptiness (suññatā). (Such was the thought of Venerable Ānanda.) Although Venerable Ānanda normally approached the Blessed One a hundred or a thousand times a day, he never did so without a reason. But on that day, he thought: "I shall approach this Elephant King, the Buddha, to hear the elephant-trumpet of his knowledge; I shall approach the Lion, the Buddha, to hear the lion's roar of his knowledge; I shall approach the Thoroughbred Horse, the Buddha, to see the speed of his gait." Thus, rising from his place of rest, shaking out and taking his leather mat, he approached the Blessed One in the evening. Therefore, I said, "He approached in the evening for the purpose of asking a question regarding the mode of conditions (paccayākāra/paṭiccasamuppāda)."

In the phrase "yāva gambhīro," the word "yāva" is used in the sense of exceeding a measure. Because it is deep beyond measure, it means "exceedingly deep." "Gambhīrāvabhāso" means that it is deep and also appears so. Indeed, some things, like old water blackened by rotten leaves, appear deep even though they are shallow. Such water may be only knee-deep, yet it appears as deep as a hundred fathoms. Some things, like the clear water of the River Gaṅgā with the color of gems, appear shallow even though they are deep. Such water may be a hundred fathoms deep, yet it appears only knee-deep. Some things, like water in a pot, are shallow and appear shallow. Some things, like the water of the great ocean at the foot of Mount Sineru, are deep and appear deep. Thus, water receives four names. In Dependent Origination, however, those (four types) do not exist. This Dependent Origination receives only one name: it is both deep and appears deep. "Even though it is of such a nature, yet to me it appears exceedingly shallow. It is wonderful, Bhante! It is marvelous, Bhante!" Thus, manifesting his amazement, he asked the question and sat down in silence.

The Blessed One, hearing the words of Venerable Ānanda, thought: "Ānanda speaks of the subject that is the domain of the Buddhas as being shallow to him, as if he were stretching out his hand to grasp the peak of existence (bhavagga), as if he were striving to split Mount Sineru to extract its marrow, as if he wished to cross the great ocean without a boat, or as if he were striving to turn the earth over to take its essence. Now, I shall tell this Ānanda about the profound nature (of this Dhamma)." Thinking thus, he spoke the words beginning with "Mā hevaṃ." In the phrase "Mā hevaṃ," the letter "ha" is merely an expletive (nipāta). It means "Do not say so." The Blessed One said "Mā hevaṃ" to Venerable Ānanda both to encourage him and to restrain him.
77:
## Explanation of Exaltation (Ussādanāvaṇṇanā)

Between those two (exaltation and suppression), the Blessed One, wishing to exalt [Ānanda], said: "Ānanda, you possess great wisdom; you possess clear insight. Because of such great and clear wisdom, this profound Dependent Origination appears shallow to you." He continued, "However, this Dependent Origination should not be regarded as shallow by others; in truth, it is both deep and has a profound appearance." Regarding the fact that Dependent Origination appears shallow to the Venerable Ānanda, the commentators provide four similes.

Suppose a great wrestler, who has been nourished by the essence of fine food for six months and has trained constantly, is going to the place of a festival where wrestling matches are held. On the way, he sees a great stone that other wrestlers cannot lift and asks, "What is this?" When told, "It is a stone for wrestlers to lift," he says, "Bring it here." When they say, "We cannot lift it," he goes there himself, asks, "Where is the heavy part of this stone?" and lifting two stones with both hands, he tosses them about like play-dice and goes on his way. In this simile, though the stone is light to the great wrestler, it should not be said to be light for others. Just like the great wrestler nourished by fine food for six months, the Venerable Ānanda is one who has fulfilled his aspirations and perfections for a hundred thousand aeons. Just as the stone is light to the wrestler because of his great strength, so too is Dependent Origination shallow to the Elder because of his great wisdom. However, it should not be said that Dependent Origination is shallow for others.

In the great ocean, the fish named Timi is two hundred yojanas long, the Timingala is three hundred yojanas, the Timipiṅgala is four hundred yojanas, and the Timirapiṅgala is five hundred yojanas long. The four great fish called Ānanda, Timinanda, Ajjhāroha, and Mahātimi are each one thousand yojanas long. Among these great fish, let us illustrate with the simile of the Timirapiṅgala fish. When that Timirapiṅgala fish moves its right ear, the water for five hundred yojanas around it becomes turbulent. It is the same when it moves its left ear, its tail, or its head. When it begins to play by moving both ears, striking the water with its tail, and tossing its head to and fro, the water for seven hundred or eight hundred yojanas around it boils and bubbles up like water placed in a pot on a stove. In a place where the water is about three hundred yojanas deep, it is not even enough to cover the back of that great fish. That great fish might say, "They say this great ocean is deep, very deep; where is its depth? We do not even have enough water to cover our backs." In this simile, though the great ocean is shallow to the Timirapiṅgala fish with its massive body, it should not be said to be shallow for other small fish. In the same way, though Dependent Origination is shallow to the Elder who is endowed with great wisdom, it should not be said to be shallow for others.
78:
The King of Garuḍas (Supaṇṇarājā) is also eight hundred and fifty (850) yojanas in size. The right wing of that King of Garuḍas is fifty yojanas, and likewise, the left wing is fifty yojanas. The tail-spread is sixty yojanas. The neck is thirty yojanas. The mouth is nine yojanas. The feet are twelve yojanas. When that King of Garuḍas strives to show the force of the wind from its wings, a space of seven hundred or eight hundred yojanas is not sufficient. That King of Garuḍas might say, "They say this sky is infinite, infinite; where is its infinity? We do not even have enough space to spread our wings." In this simile, the sky is said to be small for the King of Garuḍas who is endowed with a great body, but it should not be said to be small for other small birds. In the same way, Dependent Origination is said to be shallow for the Elder who is endowed with great wisdom, but it should not be said to be shallow for others.

Rāhu, the Lord of Asuras (Asurinda), is four thousand eight hundred yojanas tall from the tips of his toes to the tips of his hair. The span between his two arms is one thousand two hundred yojanas. In thickness, he is six hundred yojanas. The palms of his hands and the soles of his feet are three hundred yojanas; likewise, his mouth is three hundred yojanas. Each finger joint is fifty yojanas; likewise, the space between his eyebrows is fifty yojanas. The forehead is three hundred yojanas. The head is nine hundred yojanas. For that Lord of Asuras who has descended into the great ocean, the deep water only reaches the height of his knees. That Lord of Asuras might say, "They say this great ocean is deep, deep; where is its depth? We do not even have enough water to cover our knees." In this simile, the great ocean is said to be shallow for Rāhu who is endowed with a great body, but it should not be said to be shallow for others. In the same way, Dependent Origination is said to be shallow for the Elder who is endowed with great wisdom, but it should not be said to be shallow for others. With reference to this meaning, the Blessed One said, "Say not so, Ānanda; say not so."

Indeed, for four reasons, Dependent Origination, though profound, appears shallow to the Elder. What are the four reasons? They are: the achievement of past sufficing conditions (pubbūpanissayasampatti), having resided at the source [with the Teacher] (titthavāsa), being a Stream-enterer (sotāpannatā), and being of great learning (bahussutabhāva).

## Account of Past Perfections (Pubbūpanissayasampattikathā)
One hundred thousand aeons ago from this present age, a Teacher named Padumuttara appeared in the world. He had a city named Haṃsāvatī, and a king named Ānanda was his father.
79:
His father was King Ānanda, and his mother was Queen Sumedhā. The Bodhisatta was known as Prince Uttara. On the very day his son was born, Prince Uttara departed in the Great Renunciation and became a monk. Practicing austerities, he gradually attained Omniscience and uttered the solemn utterance beginning with "Aneka-jāti-saṃsāraṃ". After spending seven days on the Bodhi-throne, he thought, "I shall step upon the earth," and extended his foot. At that moment, a great lotus flower burst through the earth and emerged. The outer petals of that lotus were ninety cubits, the filaments were thirty cubits, and the pericarp was twelve cubits, with pollen in a quantity as if contained in nine jars.

The Blessed One was fifty-eight cubits in height. The span between his two shoulders was eighteen cubits, his forehead was five cubits, and his hands and feet were eleven cubits. As soon as the Blessed One stepped on the twelve-cubit pericarp with his eleven-cubit foot, the pollen, in a quantity of nine jars, rose up to a height of fifty-eight cubits and fell all around like scattered red arsenic powder. Because a lotus (paduma) emerged by breaking the earth where he stepped, the Blessed One became known only as "Padumuttara". He had two chief male disciples, Devala and Sujāta, and two chief female disciples, Amitā and Asamā. His attendant was named Sumana. The Blessed One Padumuttara, while showing favor to his father, resided in the royal city of Haṃsāvatī, surrounded by one hundred thousand monks.

The Blessed One had a younger brother named Prince Sumana. To this younger brother, the Great King gave a revenue village in a place one hundred and twenty yojanas away from the city of Haṃsāvatī. That prince used to come occasionally to visit his father and the Teacher. Then one day, an uprising occurred in the border region. Prince Sumana sent word to the Great King, saying, "An uprising has occurred in the border region." The King sent back a message, saying, "Why did I station you there?" The prince went out, suppressed the rebels, and sent word to the King, saying, "Great King, the province is now peaceful." The King was delighted and said, "Let my son come quickly." The prince had about a thousand ministers. Along the way, he consulted with his ministers, saying, "My father is delighted; if he grants me a boon, what should I take?" Then some ministers said, "Take elephants, take horses, take chariots, take a province, or take the seven kinds of jewels." Other ministers, however, said, "You are the sons of a king who rules the land; wealth is not difficult for you to obtain. Even if obtained, all this must be left behind when one goes. Only merit can be taken along. Therefore, when the King grants a boon, take the boon to serve the Blessed One Padumuttara for the three months of the rainy season." The prince said, "You are my good friends; I did not have such a thought, but you have inspired it. I shall do exactly that," and went to his father...
80:
The prince paid homage to his father, and the father embraced and kissed his son on the head, saying, "Dear son, I grant you a boon." The prince replied, "Great King, very well. I wish to serve the Blessed One with the four requisites for the three months of the rainy season to make my life fruitful. Please grant me this boon." The father said, "Dear son, that is not possible. Choose another boon." But the prince replied, "Great King, for Khattiyas, there are no two words. Please grant me only this; I desire no other." The father said, "Dear son, the minds of the Buddhas are difficult to know. If the Blessed One does not wish it, what can be done even if I grant permission?" The prince said, "Very well, Great King, I shall find out the Blessed One's intention," and went to the monastery.

At that time, the Blessed One had finished his meal and entered the Gandhakuṭi. The prince went to the monks who were assembled in the pavilion, and the monks asked, "Prince, why have you come?" "I have come to see the Blessed One. Please allow me to see Him," he replied. The monks said, "Prince, we do not get to see the Teacher at every moment we desire." "Venerable sirs, who then is allowed to see Him?" he asked. "The Elder named Sumana is allowed," they replied. He asked, "Venerable sirs, where is that Elder?" and having asked for the Elder's location, he went there, paid homage, and said, "Venerable sir, I wish to see the Blessed One. Please allow me to see Him."

The Elder said, "Come, Prince," and taking him along, he left him in the precinct of the Gandhakuṭi and went up into the Gandhakuṭi. Then the Blessed One asked, "Sumana, why have you come?" "Venerable sir, the prince has come to see the Blessed One," he replied. "Monk, if that is so, prepare a seat," the Blessed One said. The Elder prepared the seat, and the Blessed One sat on the prepared seat. The prince paid homage to the Blessed One and exchanged polite greetings. The Blessed One asked, "Prince, when did you arrive?" "Venerable sir, I have been here since You entered the Gandhakuṭi. However, the monks said they do not get to see the Blessed One whenever they wish and sent me to the Elder Sumana. The Elder, however, allowed me to see You with just a single word. Venerable sir, I think this Elder must be very intimate in Your Dispensation."

"Prince, it is so. This monk is indeed intimate in My Dispensation," the Blessed One said. "Venerable sir, by doing what does one become intimate in the Dispensation of the Buddhas?" the prince asked. "Prince, by giving alms, undertaking virtue, and observing the Uposatha, one becomes intimate," He replied.

"Blessed One, I too wish to be intimate in the Dispensation like the Elder. Please consent to spend the Rains Retreat at my monastery for the three months of the rainy season," the prince requested. The Blessed One, reflecting on whether there would be benefit in going there and seeing that there would be, said, "Prince, the Tathāgatas delight in seclusion."
81:
The Blessed One said, "The Tathāgatas delight in seclusion." The prince replied, "I understand, Blessed One; I understand, Sugata." He then said, "Venerable sir, I shall go ahead and build a monastery. When I send word, please come together with a hundred thousand monks." Having received the promise, he went to his father and said, "Great King, the Blessed One has given me His promise. When I send word, please escort the Blessed One." He paid homage to his father and departed. He had a resting-place built at every league (yojana) along the journey of one hundred and twenty leagues. Upon reaching his city, while searching for a site for the monastery, he saw the garden of a householder named Sobhana. He bought it for a hundred thousand and spent another hundred thousand to build the monastery.

In that monastery, he had a Gandhakuṭi built for the Blessed One, and for the other monks, he had huts (kuṭi), caves (leṇa), and pavilions (maṇဍapa) built for their use during the night and day. He also constructed the surrounding walls and completed the gatehouse, then sent word to his father: "My task is finished. Please escort the Teacher."

The Great King offered a meal to the Blessed One and said, "Exalted Blessed One, Prince Sumana's task is finished. He awaits Your arrival." The Blessed One set out, surrounded by a hundred thousand monks, staying at the monasteries built at every league. Hearing that the Teacher had arrived, the prince went out for one league to welcome Him. Honoring Him with flowers and other offerings, he escorted Him into the monastery and said:

"This garden named Sobhana, which I bought for a hundred thousand,
And built for another hundred thousand, O Great Sage, please accept it."

With these words, he donated the monastery by pouring the water of dedication. On the day of entering the Rains Retreat, he gave alms and summoned his wife, children, and ministers, saying, "This Blessed One has come to us from afar. Buddhas are those who honor the Dhamma, not material things (āmisa). Therefore, for the three months of the rainy season, I shall wear only two cloths, undertake the ten precepts, and stay right here in the presence of the Blessed One. You all should provide alms to the hundred thousand Arahants in this same manner for the three months."

That Prince Sumana stayed in a place similar to the dwelling of the Elder Sumana. Seeing all the duties, large and small, that the Elder performed for the Blessed One, he thought, "This Elder is truly intimate in this place. It is fitting that I too should make an aspiration for such a position." As the day of Pavāraṇā approached, he entered the village and gave great alms for seven days. On the seventh day, he placed triple robes (ticīvara) at the feet of the hundred thousand monks, paid homage to the Blessed One, and said, "Venerable sir, starting from the building of monasteries at every league along the way, I have performed meritorious deeds. I do not desire the bliss of the devas through this merit, but..."
82:
Having paid homage to the Blessed One, he said, “Venerable Sir, whatever merit I have performed, starting from the building and offering of monasteries at intervals of one league (yojana) along the road, was not done by me aspiring for the prosperity of devas, the prosperity of Māra, or the prosperity of Brahmās, but was done solely aspiring for the position of an attendant to a Buddha. Therefore, O Blessed One, may I also become an attendant to a Buddha in the future, just like the Elder Sumana.” Having said this, he paid homage by prostrating with the fivefold touch.

The Blessed One, reflecting, “The intention of this clansman is great; will it be fulfilled?” and knowing, “In the future, one hundred thousand aeons from now, a Buddha named Gotama will arise, and he will indeed be the attendant of that Buddha,” spoke thus:

“May all that you wish for and aspire to be fulfilled.
May all your intentions be fulfilled, like the full moon on the fifteenth day.”

Upon hearing those words, the prince thought, “There is no ambiguity in the words of the Buddhas,” and on the very next day, he acted as if he were following closely behind that Blessed One, carrying his bowl and robes. Having given alms for a hundred thousand years during that Buddha’s dispensation, he was reborn in the celestial realm. During the time of Kassapa Buddha, he offered his upper garment to an Elder who was wandering for alms so that the Elder might receive a bowl, and thus performed an act of worship. Again, he was reborn in the celestial realm, and after passing away from there, he became the King of Bārāṇasī. He built leaf-roofed hermitages for eight Paccekabuddhas, offered them gem-studded bowl-rests, and served them with the four requisites for ten thousand years. These are the well-known accounts.

That future Ānanda, who had given alms for a hundred thousand aeons, was reborn in the Tusita heaven together with our Bodhisatta. After passing away from there, he took rebirth in the house of the Sakyan King Amitodana. When the Blessed One, having in due course renounced the world and attained Supreme Enlightenment, first arrived at Kapilavatthu, and when the princes renounced the world to become the Blessed One’s retinue, he left together with Prince Bhaddiya and others. He was ordained in the presence of the Blessed One and, before long, after hearing a Dhamma discourse from the Venerable Puṇṇa Mantāṇiputta, he was established in the fruit of stream-entry (sotāpatti-phala). Thus, this venerable one was endowed with past supporting conditions (upanissaya). Because of that perfection of past supporting conditions, even the profound Dependent Origination (paṭiccasamuppāda) appeared to him as if it were clear and plain.
83:
## Titthavāsādivaṇṇanā
Titthavāsa refers to the repeated learning of the Pāḷi, hearing the meaning of the Pāḷi, discussing and questioning difficult points, and retaining the meaning of the Pāḷi in the presence of noble teachers. This residence under teachers (titthavāsa) was exceedingly pure for the Elder Ānanda. For this reason, even though this Dependent Origination is profound, it appeared to the Elder Ānanda as if it were clear.

Indeed, for stream-enterers (sotāpanna), the structure of conditions (paccayākāra) appears only as something clear; and this venerable one was a stream-enterer. Furthermore, for those of great learning (bahussuta), the distinction between mind and matter (nāmarūpa-pariccheda) becomes as evident as a bed and stool when a lamp is lit in a room of four cubits; and this venerable one was the foremost among those of great learning. Through the power of that great learning, even though the structure of conditions is profound, it appeared to him as if it were clear.

## Paṭiccasamuppādagambhīratā
In that context, Dependent Origination is called profound in four ways: profundity of meaning (attha-gambhīratā), profundity of the Dhamma (dhamma-gambhīratā), profundity of the teaching (desanā-gambhīratā), and profundity of penetration (paṭivedha-gambhīratā).

Among those four, the nature of aging and death arising and repeatedly coming into being due to the condition of birth is profound. ...pe... The nature of mental formations arising and repeatedly coming into being due to the condition of ignorance is profound. This is called the profundity of meaning (attha-gambhīratā).

The nature of ignorance being a condition for mental formations is profound. ...pe... The nature of birth being a condition for aging and death is profound. This is called the profundity of the Dhamma (dhamma-gambhīratā).

In some suttas, Dependent Origination is taught in forward order (anuloma); in some, in reverse order (paṭiloma); in some, in both forward and reverse order; in some, starting from the middle in forward order, or reverse order, or both forward and reverse order. In some, it is taught with three connections and four groups; in some, with two connections and three groups; in some, with one connection and two groups. This is called the profundity of the teaching (desanā-gambhīratā).

Furthermore, the nature of ignorance as non-knowing, non-seeing by way of realization, and the non-penetration of the Four Noble Truths is profound. The nature of mental formations as constructing, accumulating, being with lust, and being without lust is profound. The nature of consciousness as being void, without agency, without transmigrating, and the manifestation of rebirth-linking is profound. The nature of mind-and-matter as arising together, being distinct, being inseparable, bending towards an object, and being transformed by contrary conditions is profound. The nature of the six sense bases as having predominance, being the world that is subject to rise and fall, being the doors for the enjoyment of states such as contact, being the field where states such as contact arise, and the state of being a subject that takes an object is profound.
84:
Contact (phassa) is profound due to the meaning of touching, striking, meeting, and coinciding. Feeling (vedanā) is profound due to the meaning of experiencing the flavor of the object, existing as pleasant, painful, or neutral (equanimity), and having the nature of experiencing without a soul or life. Craving (taṇhā) is profound due to the meaning of great delight, attachment to objects, flowing like a river, entangling like a creeper, and being difficult to fill like the river of craving or the ocean of craving. Clinging (upādāna) is profound due to the meaning of adhering, grasping, wrong attention, wrong misapprehension, and being difficult to overcome. Becoming (bhava) is profound due to the meaning of accumulating and conditioning (in kammabhava), and casting into the four births (yoni), five destinations (gati), seven stations of consciousness (viññāṇatthiti), and nine abodes of beings (sattāvāsa) (in upapattibhava). Birth (jāti) is profound due to the meaning of arising, repeated arising, descending, appearing, and manifesting. Aging and death (jarāmaraṇa) are profound due to the meaning of exhaustion, decay, breaking up, and transformation. In this way, the nature of ignorance (avijjā) and so on is profound. The penetration by which ignorance and so on are penetrated according to their own characteristics is profound; this is to be known as paṭivedhagambhīratā (profundity of penetration). All that profundity appeared to the Venerable Ānanda as if it were shallow (clear). Therefore, the Blessed One, wishing to encourage Ānanda's wisdom, said "Do not say so" (mā hevaṃ) and so on. The meaning here is: Ānanda, you possess great wisdom and clear knowledge; therefore, the profound Dependent Origination appears to you as if it were shallow. Thus, do not say, "Does this appear shallow only to me, or to others as well?"

## Apasādanāvaṇṇanā
Regarding the word "apasādento" (rebuking), this is the meaning: Ānanda, do not say, "Indeed, it appears very, very shallow to me." If this Dependent Origination appears very shallow to you, why did you not become a Stream-enterer (Sotāpanna) by your own nature? Why did you penetrate the Path of Stream-entry only by standing on the method given by me? Ānanda, is only Nibbāna profound, while Dependent Origination has become shallow to you? If Dependent Origination is shallow, why do you not realize the fruit of Once-returning (Sakadāgāmiphala) by utterly uprooting these four defilements: the coarse fetter of sensual lust, the fetter of ill-will, the coarse underlying tendency to sensual lust, and the underlying tendency to ill-will? Why do you not realize the fruit of Non-returning (Anāgāmiphala) by uprooting those same four defilements in their subtle form? Why do you not realize Arahantship by utterly uprooting these eight defilements: the five fetters such as lust for form, the underlying tendency to lust for existence, the underlying tendency to conceit, and the underlying tendency to ignorance?
