Why do you not penetrate and know the wisdom of a disciple's perfection (sāvakapāramīñāṇa) like Sāriputta and Moggallāna, who fulfilled the perfections for one hundred thousand aeons and one incalculable period? Why do you not penetrate and know the wisdom of a Private Buddha (paccekabodhiñāṇa) like the Private Buddhas who fulfilled the perfections for one hundred thousand aeons and two incalculable periods? Ānanda, if this Dependent Origination is shallow to you in every aspect, why do you not realize Omniscience (sabbaññutañāṇa) like the Buddhas who fulfilled the perfections for one hundred thousand aeons and four, eight, or sixteen incalculable periods? That Sāriputta...
85:
"...Why do you not penetrate the knowledge of a disciple's perfection like the Venerable Sāriputta and the Venerable Moggallāna, who fulfilled the perfections for one incalculable and a hundred thousand aeons? Why do you not penetrate the knowledge of a Silent Buddha's enlightenment like the Paccekabuddhas, who fulfilled the perfections for two incalculables and a hundred thousand aeons? If this Dependent Origination appears shallow to you in every way, why do you not realize Omniscience like the Buddhas, who fulfilled the perfections for four, eight, or sixteen incalculables and a hundred thousand aeons? Do you not desire these special attainments? Look at your own fault. You, being a disciple and standing in partial knowledge (padesañāṇa), say of the extremely profound Dependent Origination, 'It appears shallow to me.' This statement of yours is contrary to the words of the Buddhas. It is proper that such a monk should not speak words contrary to the words of the Buddhas."

"Ānanda, have not four incalculables and a hundred thousand aeons passed for me, the Buddha, while striving to penetrate this Dependent Origination? For the sake of penetrating Dependent Origination, there is no gift I have not given, no perfection I have not fulfilled. When I was destroying the army of Māra with the resolve 'I shall penetrate Dependent Origination,' and when I was accomplishing the knowledge of recollection of past lives in the first watch and the divine eye in the middle watch, this great earth did not tremble even as much as two finger-breadths, as if it were devoid of effort. However, in the last watch, at the time of dawn, as soon as I saw that 'Ignorance is a condition for volitional formations in nine ways,' the ten-thousandfold world system released hundreds and thousands of sounds like a bronze gong struck with an iron rod, and it trembled like a drop of water on a lotus leaf struck by the wind. Ānanda, thus this Dependent Origination is both profound and profound in appearance. Ānanda, because of not understanding... they do not transcend this Dhamma."

'Of this Dhamma' means of this causal law of Dependent Origination. 'Because of not understanding' means not understanding through the full understanding of the known (ñātapariññā). 'Because of not penetrating' means not penetrating through the full understanding by investigation (tīraṇapariññā) and the full understanding by abandoning (pahānapariññā). 'Become tangled like a ball of thread' means becoming tangled like the ball of thread spread out by weavers. For example, a ball of thread belonging to weavers that is poorly kept and bitten by mice becomes tangled here and there, making it difficult to match end with end or beginning with beginning. In the same way, beings are stumbled and tangled in this Dependent Origination, and they are unable to make this Dependent Origination straight. In that simile of the weaver's thread, the thread might be straightened by human effort, but setting aside..."
86:
Excluding the two types of Bodhisattas—the Perfectly Enlightened Buddhas and the Paccekabuddhas—other beings are not able to straighten out Dependent Origination (paṭiccasamuppāda) by their own nature. Just as a tangled ball of thread, when treated with starch and struck with a brush, becomes knotted and clumped here and there, even so, these beings, stumbling in the causal conditions which are impermanent by nature, are unable to straighten out the conditions. They become entangled and knotted through the power of the sixty-two types of wrong views. All recluses and brahmins who rely on any of these wrong views are simply unable to straighten out Dependent Origination.

In the term 'kulagaṇṭhikajātā', the thread treated with starch by weavers is called 'kulagaṇṭhika'. Some teachers say that 'kulā' refers to the nest of the weaver bird (mိုးစက်ငှက်). Just as both that weaver's thread and the bird's nest are so tangled that it is difficult to match end to end or root to root, this should be understood in the same way as the previous method.

'Muñjapabbajabhūtā' means they have become like muñja grass and pabbaja grass. When a rope made by pounding these grasses becomes old and falls somewhere, and one picks it up, it is very difficult to match them end to end or root to root, saying 'this is the tip' or 'this is the root' of these grasses. Even such a rope might be straightened through the individual effort of men. However, excluding the two types of Bodhisattas, there are no other beings who are able to straighten out Dependent Origination by their own nature. Thus, this generation of beings, being unable to straighten out Dependent Origination, becomes entangled through the power of wrong views and cannot transcend the round of rebirths (saṃsāra), which consists of the states of deprivation (apāya), the unhappy destinations (duggati), and the abyss (vinipāta).

In that context, 'apāya' refers to the realms of hell, the animal kingdom, the realm of hungry ghosts (petas), and the host of asuras. They are called 'apāya' because of the absence of 'aya', which means growth or happiness. Likewise, they are called 'duggati' because they are the destination of suffering. They are called 'vinipāta' because they are a state of ruin, having fallen away from the accumulation of happiness. Regarding the other term, saṃsāra:
"The uninterrupted occurrence of the succession of aggregates (khandhas), elements (dhātus), and sense bases (āyatanas) is called saṃsāra."
This is how it should be understood.

They cannot transcend all those states of deprivation and the suffering of the round of rebirths. Instead, taking up death and rebirth repeatedly—from death to rebirth, and from rebirth to death—they revolve throughout the three realms of existence, the four modes of birth, the five destinations, the seven stations of consciousness, and the nine abodes of beings, like a boat tossed by the wind in the great ocean, or like an ox yoked to a mill.
87:
...they are merely revolving (like a boat tossed by the wind or like an ox yoked to an oil mill). Thus, it should be understood that the Blessed One said all this with the intention of rebuking the Venerable Ānanda.

## Commentary on Dependent Origination
Now, since this sutta is connected only by these two phrases: "Ānanda, this Dependent Origination is profound" and "it has become like a tangled ball of thread," the Blessed One began the teaching to show the profundity of the causal conditions with this sequence: "Ānanda, this Dependent Origination is profound," and then said, "Is there aging and death because of this condition?" and so forth. The meaning in that text is as follows: The cause of this aging and death is called 'this condition' (idappaccaya). Therefore, "Is there aging and death because of this condition? Is there indeed a cause for aging and death? From what cause would aging and death arise?" When asked thus, Ānanda, a wise person should not act as one does when asked, "Is the soul the same as the body?" where the question must be set aside (ṭhapanīya) and one must remain silent, or where one must say, "This has not been declared (avyākata) by the Tathāgata." Instead, just as when asked, "Is the eye permanent or impermanent?" one must answer categorically (ekaṃsa) as "impermanent," so too should one answer categorically as "It exists."

Again, when asked, "Because of what condition does aging and death occur? What is the name of that condition from which aging and death arise?" one should answer, "Aging and death occur with birth (jāti) as condition." This is the meaning of how it should be stated. This method applies to all terms.

As for the statement, "With name-and-form as condition, contact arises," when it is said "with the sixfold sense base (saḷāyatana) as condition," it refers only to the six types of resultant contact (vipāka-phassa) such as eye-contact. But in this sutta, by the phrase "with the sixfold sense base as condition," the Blessed One intended to show the distinction of the produced states (paccayuppanna)—both the resultant contact already included and the other types of contact (wholesome, unwholesome, and functional) not yet included—and also to show other specific conditions for contact that go beyond the sixfold sense base. Thus, it should be understood that He said this. What did the Blessed One teach by this section? He taught the root cause (nidāna) of the conditions. This sutta is called "Mahānidāna" (The Great Discourse on Causes) because it is taught by making the conditions free from tangles and obstructions.

Now, to show that the causal status of those various conditions is real, not unreal, and not otherwise, He said: "It was said: 'With birth as condition, aging and death come to be'," and so forth. In that context, "pariyāyena" means by way of reason or method. "Sabbena sabbaṃ sabbathā sabbaṃ" are two indeclinables. The meaning is: if every type of birth in every way and in every respect were not to exist. The meaning in the case of 'existence' (bhava) and so forth should be understood in this same way. The word "kassaci" refers to anyone indefinitely (among devas, etc.). The word "katthaci" is also indefinite, meaning in any realm of existence among the nine realms such as the sense-sphere existence. The phrase "seyyathidaṃ" means...
88:
It means, "If there were no birth of any kind, in any way, for anyone." The meaning should be understood in the same way for existence (bhava) and so forth. "Kassaci" (for anyone) is an indefinite term, referring to any individual among devas and so forth. "Kimhici" (in anything) is also an indefinite term, meaning in any of the nine types of existence, such as sense-sphere existence (kāmabhava). "Seyyathidaṃ" (as follows) is a particle used when one wishes to analyze and explain a meaning that has been stated indefinitely. Its meaning is: "I shall analyze for you the meaning of the words 'for anyone, in anything'." Then, wishing to analyze that meaning, he said, "Whether of devas into the state of devas," and so on.

In that phrase, "Whether of devas into the state of devas" refers to the arising of the aggregates (birth/jāti) for the sake of devas becoming devas. It is because of the arising of these aggregates that devas are called "devas." The meaning in all phrases should be understood in this way: "If birth did not occur in any way." Here, "deva" refers to devas by rebirth (upapatti-deva). "Gandhabba" refers to tree deities (rukkha-devatā) residing in roots, trunks, and so forth. "Yakkha" refers to non-human beings (amanussa). "Bhūta" refers to all beings that have been born. "Pakkhi" (birds) refers to those with bony wings, leathery wings, or feathery wings. "Sarīsapa" (reptiles) refers to any creature that moves by crawling on the ground. "Tesaṃ tesaṃ" means of those various devas, gandhabbas, and so forth. "Tadatthāya" means for the sake of attaining the state of devas, gandhabbas, and so forth. "Jātinirodhā" means because of the cessation of birth, or because of the absence of birth.

All words such as "hetu" (cause) are synonyms for "cause." A cause is called "hetu" because it sends forth or activates its own result. It is called "nidāna" (source) because it presents the result as if saying, "Here, take it." It is called "samudaya" (origin) because the result arises well from it, and "paccaya" (condition) because the result occurs depending on it. This method applies in all instances. Furthermore, in the phrase "yadidaṃ jāti," "yadidaṃ" is a particle. Its meaning should be understood in accordance with the gender of all the terms. Here, however, it means "this birth which is such." Birth is a condition for aging and death by way of decisive support (upanissaya).

In the term "bhava" (existence), the word "kimhici" encompasses the location. There, sense-sphere existence (kāmabhava) should be understood as including everything from the Avīci hell below up to the Paranimmita-vasavatti heaven above. This method is suitable for "existence as rebirth" (upapatti-bhava). In this sutta, however, it is suitable for "existence as kamma" (kamma-bhava). That kamma-bhava is a condition for birth only by way of decisive support. In terms like "upādāna" (clinging) and so forth, it should be understood that "kimhici" also serves to encompass the location.
89:
In the term "bhava" (existence), the word "kimhici" encompasses the location. There, sense-sphere existence (kāmabhava) should be understood as including everything from the Avīci hell below up to the Paranimmita-vasavatti heaven above. This method is suitable for "existence as rebirth" (upapatti-bhava). In this sutta, however, it is suitable for "existence as kamma" (kamma-bhava). Indeed, that kamma-bhava is a condition for birth only by way of decisive support. In terms like "upādāna" (clinging) and so forth, it should be understood that "kimhici" also serves to encompass the location. In the phrase "upādānapaccayā bhavo" (existence conditioned by clinging), sense-clinging (kāmupādāna) is a condition for the three types of kamma-existence and the three types of rebirth-existence. Similarly, the remaining types of clinging are also conditions for the three types of kamma-existence and the three types of rebirth-existence. Thus, twenty-four types of existence conditioned by clinging should be understood. Strictly speaking (nippariyāyena), among those twenty-four, twelve types of kamma-existence are obtained. For those kamma-existences, clinging assists by way of conascence (sahajāta) and decisive support (upanissaya). "Rūpa-taṇhā" is craving for visible forms. The same applies to "sadda-taṇhā" (craving for sounds) and so forth. That craving assists clinging by way of conascence and decisive support. In the phrase "vedanāpaccayā taṇhā" (craving conditioned by feeling), resultant feeling (vipāka-vedanā) assists craving by way of decisive support. Other types of feeling (wholesome, unwholesome, functional) assist in other ways (such as conascence).

Having thus shown the prior craving which is the root of the round of rebirths, the Blessed One now, wishing to show the craving in active occurrence (samudācāra-taṇhā) through nine terms—like one who strikes someone on the back or grabs them by the hair to lead them off the path while they are crying out—said: "Thus, Ānanda, craving is conditioned by feeling," and so on. There, craving is of two kinds: craving as seeking (esana-taṇhā) and craving for what has been sought (esita-taṇhā). The craving by which one seeks wealth by traveling along goat-paths, stake-paths, and so forth, is called "esana-taṇhā." The craving for those riches that have been sought and obtained is called "esita-taṇhā." Both are synonyms for craving in active occurrence. Therefore, craving conditioned by feeling is of two types. "Pariyesanā" (seeking) is the search for visible forms and so forth; it occurs only when there is craving. "Lābha" (gain) is the obtaining of visible forms and so forth; it occurs only when there is seeking. "Vinicchaya" (decision) is of four kinds by way of knowledge, craving, views, and thought. Among them, "One should know the decision regarding happiness; having known the decision regarding happiness, one should pursue internal happiness"—this is "ñāṇa-vinicchaya" (decision by knowledge). The 108 mental explorations of craving mentioned as "Decision is of two kinds: decision by craving and decision by views" are "taṇhā-vinicchaya." The sixty-two views are "diṭṭhi-vinicchaya." In this sutta, where it is taught, "O Sakka, Lord of Devas, desire has thought as its source," "vinicchaya" refers to thought (vitakka) itself. After obtaining gain, one decides whether it is desirable or undesirable, good or bad, by means of thought alone.
90:
"This much wealth will be for the purpose of visual objects, this much for the purpose of sounds and so forth, this much will be for me, this much for others, this much I will enjoy, this much I will store away"—thus one specifically decides. Therefore, it is said: "Dependent on gain, there is decision (vinicchaya)."

Desire and lust (chandarāga) refers to the arising of weak lust and strong lust toward an object that has been thought about with unwholesome initial thought; in this context, this itself is craving (taṇhā). Desire (chanda) is a designation for weak lust. Attachment (ajjhosāna) is the strong determination and clinging in the form of "I" and "mine." Possession (pariggaha) is the act of seizing through the power of craving and wrong view. Stinginess (macchariya) is the inability to endure sharing with others. For this reason, the ancient teachers state the definition (vacanattha) that it is called macchariya because it occurs in the sense of "Let this wonderful thing be mine alone, let it not be a wonderful thing for others."

Protection (ārakkha) is the act of guarding well by means of closing doors, storing in boxes, and so forth. Cause (adhikaraṇa) is a name for a reason because it performs excessively. The term ārakkhādhikaraṇa is a neuter abstract noun (bhāvanapuṃsaka), meaning "because of the cause of protection." Among the terms beginning with "taking up the rod" (daṇḍādāna), taking up a rod to restrain others is called daṇḍādāna. Taking up a weapon such as a single-edged sword is called taking up weapons (satthādāna). Quarrel (kalaha) is both physical quarrel and verbal quarrel. The initial opposition is called strife (viggaha). The subsequent opposition is called dispute (vivāda). "Tuvaṃtuvaṃ" is disrespectful speech such as saying "you, you" (in an inferior manner).

Now, in order to show that habitual craving (samudācāra-taṇhā) also by the reverse method, the Buddha resumed the teaching starting with "because of the cause of protection." In that context, craving for sensual pleasures (kāma-taṇhā) is the craving for visual objects and so forth that arises through the power of lust for the five cords of sensual pleasure. Craving for existence (bhava-taṇhā) is lust accompanied by the eternalist view (sassata-diṭṭhi). Craving for non-existence (vibhava-taṇhā) is lust accompanied by the annihilationist view (uccheda-diṭṭhi). These two things refer to the craving that is the root of the round of rebirth (vaṭṭamūla-taṇhā) and the habitual craving (samudācāra-taṇhā). The term "by the dyad" (dvayena) means that although they have reached a single state by the characteristic of craving, they converge together in feeling (vedanā) through two portions by way of the root of the round and the habitual craving; the meaning is that they have a single cause, which is feeling.

There are three types of convergence (samosaraṇa): convergence by resorting (osaraṇa-samosaraṇa), convergence by co-arising (sahajāta-samosaraṇa), and convergence by condition (paccaya-samosaraṇa). Among these three, the statement "Then all those things converge in sensual desire" is called convergence by resorting. The statement "Friends, all these things have desire (craving) as their root, contact as their origin, and they converge in feeling" is called convergence by co-arising. The statement "They have a single convergence in feeling by way of the dyad" should be understood as convergence by condition.
91:
All contacts beginning with eye-contact (cakkhusamphassa) are indeed resultant contacts (vipāka-phassa). Among those resultant contacts, excluding the four supramundane resultant contacts, there are thirty-two types of contact. In this context of "contact," contact is a condition for feeling (vedanā) in many ways.

In the passage beginning with "Ānanda, by whatever modes," the dissimilar natures of feeling and so forth are called "modes" (ākāra). When those very modes are well demonstrated, they are called "signs" (liṅga) because they make known the various hidden meanings. They are called "characteristics" (nimitta) because they are the cause of recognizing each respective nature. They are called "designations" (uddesa) because they are to be pointed out in such and such ways. Therefore, the meaning here is: "Ānanda, by whatever modes... by whatever designations there is a description of the mental body (nāmakāya), which is the group of mental factors. When there is the mode of experiencing of feeling, the sign of experiencing, the characteristic of experiencing, and the designation 'feeling'; when there is the mode of perceiving of perception (saññā), the sign of perceiving, the characteristic of perceiving, and the designation 'perception'; when there is the mode of volition of mental formations (saṅkhāra), the sign of volition, the characteristic of volition, and the designation 'volition'; when there is the mode of cognizing of consciousness (viññāṇa), the sign of cognizing, the characteristic of cognizing, and the designation 'consciousness'—then there is the description of the mental body as 'This is the mental body.' If those feelings and so forth, and those modes and so forth, which are the causes for the description of the mental body, were absent, would designation-contact (adhivacanasamphassa) be evident in the physical body (rūpakāya)? Would that mind-contact (manosamphassa), which is another name for designation-contact that arises in the mind-door depending on the four mental aggregates, be evident in the physical body, or would it arise depending on the five sensitive materialities (pasāda-rūpa)?" Then the Venerable Ānanda, just as one would not accept the arising of a ripe mango from a Jambu tree when no mango tree exists, did not accept the arising of that mind-contact from the physical body and said, "No, venerable sir."

In the second question, the meaning of modes and so forth should be understood by way of the mode of being oppressed (ruppana), the sign of being oppressed, the characteristic of being oppressed, and by way of the designation "matter" (rūpa). Impingement-contact (paṭighasamphassa) is the contact that arises depending on the aggregate of matter which is accompanied by impingement (sappaṭigha). Here too, just as the Elder would not accept the arising of a ripe Jambu fruit from a mango tree when no Jambu tree exists, he did not accept the arising of that impingement-contact from the mental body and said, "No, venerable sir."
92:
The third question is stated only by way of both [types of contact, namely, designation-contact (adhivacanasamphassa) and impingement-contact (paṭighasamphassa), which depend on name-and-form (nāmarūpa)]. In that question, just as the Elder would not admit the arising of ripe mangoes or rose-apples in the sky [without a tree], so he does not wish to admit the arising of the two types of contact without name-and-form, and thus says, "No, venerable sir."

Having thus shown the individual causes of the two types of contact, he now begins the fourth question to show the state of name-and-form as the cause for both of them without distinction: "In whatever ways, Ānanda..." What is called "this name-and-form" means whatever name-and-form arises in the six doors; that name-and-form alone is the cause, that name-and-form alone is the support for those [types of] contact. In the eye-door, etc., the eye-sensitivity (cakkhu-pasāda), etc., and the visible-form object (rūpārammaṇa), etc., are called "form" (rūpa); the mental aggregates such as feeling (vedanā) associated with contact are called "name" (nāma). Thus, that fivefold contact is a contact that has name-and-form as its cause. In the mind-door also, the heart-base (hadaya-vatthu) and the form which is the object are called "form"; the associated states and the non-form (arūpa) which is the object are called "name". Thus, mind-contact (manosamphassa) should also be understood as a contact having name-and-form as its cause. Name-and-form is a cause that benefits that contact in many ways.

"If it were not to descend" means it would not occur by way of rebirth-linking (paṭisandhi) as if entering and proceeding [into the womb]. "Would it congeal?" means if rebirth-linking consciousness (paṭisandhi-viññāṇa) were absent, would the remaining pure name-and-form, without being mixed with rebirth-linking consciousness, congeal and occur in the mother's womb in the form of the embryonic-sludge (kalala), etc.? "Having descended, if it were to depart" means having descended by way of rebirth-linking, it would depart by way of death (cuti); the meaning is that it would cease. That cessation does not occur merely by the cessation of that rebirth-linking consciousness, nor by the cessation of the second or third life-continuum (bhavaṅga) consciousnesses that occur after it. 

For the thirty kamma-born matters (kammaja-rūpa) that arise together with the rebirth-linking consciousness are produced. While those kamma-born matters remain, sixteen life-continuum consciousnesses arise and cease. Within these sixteen mind-moments (cittakkhana), there is no danger of death for the child who has taken rebirth-linking or for the mother of that child. This time is called "the occasion that is not an opportunity [for death]". If the matters that arose together with the rebirth-linking consciousness are able to provide support to the seventeenth life-continuum consciousness, the process of life proceeds and the continuity is joined. If they are not able, the process of life does not proceed, the continuity is not joined, and it is said to "depart". Intending this, it is said: "Having descended, if it were to depart."

"For such a state" means for such a condition, for the state of the complete five aggregates. "While still a young child" means for one who is a tender, young child. "If it were to be cut off..."
93:
If consciousness were cut off, would name-and-form alone arise and reach growth (vuḍḍhi) by way of the first stage of life, increase (virūḷhi) by way of the middle stage, and expansion (vepulla) by way of the last stage? Or would it reach growth, increase, and expansion by reaching ten years, twenty years, a hundred years, or a thousand years?

Therefore, Ānanda, because consciousness is the cause of this name-and-form at the time of taking rebirth-linking in the mother's womb, during the stay in the womb, at the time of exit from the womb, and during the course of life at times such as ten years [of age], etc., this consciousness alone is the root-cause, this consciousness alone is the support for name-and-form. Just as a king, wishing to subdue his retinue, might say: "Who made you the Viceroy? Who made you the General? Was it not I? If I had not done so, would you have become the Viceroy or the General by your own nature? Without me, would I know your power?" In the same way, consciousness is the cause of name-and-form. In terms of meaning, it is as if consciousness says to name-and-form: "Who made you 'name'? Who made you 'form'? Who made you 'name-and-form'? Was it not I? If I were not the precursor and did not take rebirth-linking in the mother's womb, would you have become name, or form, or name-and-form? Without me, would I know your power?" That consciousness is a cause for name-and-form in many ways.

"The origin of the arising of suffering" (dukkhasamudayasambhavo) means the arising of the mass of suffering. In saying "this name-and-form alone is the cause, this name-and-form alone is the support," it refers to this name-and-form. Just as the king's men, wishing to subdue the king, might say: "Who made you the King? Was it not we? If I did not stand in the position of Viceroy, and I did not stand in the position of General, would you alone be the King? Without us, would your state as a King be seen?" In the same way, name-and-form also, in terms of meaning, says to consciousness: "Who made you the rebirth-linking consciousness? Was it not we? If you did not depend on the three [mental] aggregates and the heart-base, would you be called rebirth-linking consciousness? Without us, would your state as rebirth-linking consciousness be seen?" That name-and-form is also a cause for consciousness in many ways.

"By this much only" means when consciousness is the cause of name-and-form, when name-and-form is the cause of consciousness, and when both consciousness and name-and-form proceed by way of being mutual causes...
94:
By this much, beings may be born, or they may age, or they may die, or they may pass away, or they may reappear. In this way, birth and so forth would be known, and the successive rounds of passing away and rebirth would be known.

'Path of designation' (adhivacanapatha) refers to the way of common usage that arises by focusing only on the words themselves, such as "Sirivaḍḍhaka" or "Dhanavaḍḍhaka," without looking at the meaning corresponding to the sound. 'Path of language' (niruttipatha) refers to the way of common usage that arises by pointing out the root cause, such as "one is called 'sata' because one remembers" or "one is called 'sampajāna' because one knows clearly in various ways." 'Path of concept' (paññattipatha) refers to the way of common usage that arises for the purpose of making things known through various methods, such as "he is wise, skilled, sagacious, proficient, and knowledgeable in the doctrines of others." Thus, by these three terms, only the aggregates (khandhā), which are the basis for designations and so forth, are spoken of.

'Sphere of wisdom' (paññāvacara) means the collection of the five aggregates that should be frequented or known by wisdom. "The round turns" (vaṭṭaṃ vattati) means the round of saṃsāra turns. "This state of being" (itthattaṃ) means being in this manner; it is a name for the group of five aggregates. "For the purpose of designation" (paññāpanāya) means for the purpose of designating names. It means for the purpose of designating as "feeling, perception," and so forth. It means that by this much—the mutual conditioning of consciousness and name-and-form—the group of five aggregates can also be known. "That which is name-and-form together with consciousness" (yadidaṃ nāmarūpaṃ saha viññāṇena) refers to how this name-and-form exists in mutual dependence with consciousness. It means it occurs only through this much mutual conditioning of consciousness and name-and-form. This statement is the concluding remark.

## Description of the Designation of Self

Thus, the Blessed One, having shown the connection to the phrase "Deep is this dependent origination, Ānanda, and deep it appears," now wishing to show the connection to the phrase "it has become like a tangled skein," began the teaching starting with "To what extent, Ānanda."

In that teaching, the meaning should be understood thus: In the phrases such as "Ānanda, one designating a self as material and finite," the person who takes an undeveloped kasiṇa sign as the self designates a material and finite self. Furthermore, a person who has attained various kasiṇas designates that self as sometimes having a blue color or sometimes having a yellow color. The person who takes a developed kasiṇa sign as the self designates a material and infinite self. Or again, the person who removes the undeveloped kasiṇa sign and takes either the space touched by the sign, or the four mental aggregates occurring therein, or just the consciousness among them as the self, designates an immaterial and finite self. The person who removes the developed kasiṇa sign and takes either the space touched by the sign, or the four mental aggregates occurring therein, or just the consciousness among them as the self, designates an immaterial and infinite self.
95:
In the phrase "therein, Ānanda" (tatrānanada), "therein" (tatra) means among those four types of individuals holding wrong views. "Or at present" (etarahi vā) means only in this present life, and not beyond this. This is spoken by way of the view of annihilation (uccheda). "Or one that will be there" (tatthabhāviṃ vā) means one that will definitely exist in the next world. This is spoken by way of the view of eternalism (sassata). "Or though it is unreal" (atathaṃ vā pana santaṃ) means while being of an untrue nature. "For the sake of truth" (tathattāya) means to arrive at the state of truth. "I will prepare" (upakappessāmi) means I will accomplish. By this, the conflict of views is shown. For the annihilationist thinks, "I will prepare the eternalist's unreal self to become the true nature of annihilation; I will make him know the eternalist view and then make him accept only the annihilationist view." The eternalist also thinks, "I will prepare the annihilationist's unreal self to become the true nature of eternalism; I will make him know the annihilationist view and then make him accept only the eternalist view."

"When this is so" (evaṃ santaṃ kho) means when one is thus designating a material and finite self. "Material" (rūpiṃ) refers to one who has attained a material kasiṇa meditative absorption. "The underlying tendency of the view of a finite self lies dormant" (parittattānudiṭṭhi anuseti) means this view that "the self is finite" repeatedly dwells within. It should be understood that this view "lies dormant" not by clinging like a creeper or a vine, but because it has not yet been abandoned by the Path. "This is sufficient to say" (iccālaṃ vacanāya) means it is appropriate to say that such a view lies dormant in that person. This method should be understood in all cases.

In the word "immaterial" (arūpiṃ), the meaning should be understood as one who has attained an immaterial kasiṇa absorption or one who takes the mental aggregates as the object. By this much, sixteen types of individuals holding wrong views regarding the self are shown: four who have attained absorptions, four who are their disciples, four who are speculators, and four who are their disciples.

## Description of the Non-designation of Self

Having thus shown those who designate a self, he now spoke the words beginning with "And to what extent, Ānanda" to show those who do not designate a self. Who are those who do not designate a self? First of all, all noble individuals (ariya) do not designate it. Also, learned persons (bahussuta) who bear the Three Baskets, Two Baskets, or One Basket, or even a preacher of the Dhamma who has well-determined and learned at least one Nikāya, or a person who has begun insight meditation (vipassanā)—they do not designate a self at all. For those individuals, in the counterpart sign of a kasiṇa (paṭibhāgakasina), there is only the knowledge "this is a counterpart sign." And in the mental aggregates, there is only the knowledge "these are mental aggregates."
96:
## Explanation of the Contemplation of Self

Having shown those who do not designate a self, the Buddha now wishes to show those who do designate a self. (Those who do not designate a self include all Noble Ones (Ariyas), worldlings (puthujjanas) who have mastered the three Piṭakas, two Piṭakas, or one Piṭaka, Dhamma preachers who have well-decided and learned even a single Nikāya, and those practicing insight meditation (vipassanā). To these persons, knowledge arises regarding the kasina sign as just a kasina sign, and regarding the mental aggregates as just mental aggregates; therefore, they do not designate them as a self.) After showing them, He now wishes to show those who designate a self, who do so by contemplating repeatedly through the power of wrong view (diṭṭhi). Their repeated contemplation occurs because they have not yet abandoned the twenty types of identity view (sakkāyadiṭṭhi). Therefore, to show those twenty types of identity view, He spoke again starting with the words, 'Kittāvatā ca Ānanda'.

In that passage, by the words 'vedanaṃ vā hi', identity view based on the aggregate of feeling (vedanākkhandha) is mentioned. By the words 'appaṭisaṃvedano me attā', identity view based on the aggregate of form (rūpakkhandha) is mentioned. By the words 'attā me vediyati, vedanādhammo hi me attā', identity view based on the aggregates of perception (saññā), mental formations (saṅkhāra), and consciousness (viññāṇa) is mentioned. Indeed, these three aggregates experience because they are associated with feeling. For these three aggregates, the nature of experiencing is inseparable.

Now, wishing to show the faults in those three doctrines, He spoke the words starting with 'tatrānananda'. In that context, 'tatra' means among those three types of holders of wrong views. The words starting with 'yasmiṃ Ānanda samaye' were spoken to show the faults such as the self of such-and-such a person sometimes existing and sometimes not existing, according to whichever feeling they contemplate as the self.

Regarding the terms such as 'anicca' (impermanent): they are called impermanent because they do not exist after having come to be. They are called conditioned (saṅkhata) because they are made by various causes coming together and meeting. They are called dependently arisen (paṭiccasamuppanna) because they arise only due to appropriate causes in dependence on various conditions. All words such as 'khaya' (destruction) are synonyms for dissolution (bhaṅga). Whatever dissolves also gets exhausted, passes away, fades away, and ceases; therefore, He said 'khayadhammā' and so on.

'Byagā me' means 'viagā' (it has gone away). The meaning is 'my self has gone away, has ceased'. How is it? Does it occur to a single person in all three periods of time that 'this is my self'? Why would it not occur? (It does). Indeed, for a holder of wrong view, there is no such thing as stability, just like a stake driven into a heap of chaff; like a forest monkey, they grab one thing and let go of another. 'Aniccasukhadukkhavokiṇṇaṃ' means that one who specifically contemplates such-and-such a feeling as the self contemplates their self as impermanent, pleasant, or painful. One who contemplates feeling as the self without specification contemplates a self that is mixed with feelings that have the nature of arising and passing away.
97:
One repeatedly contemplates oneself as a self that has the nature of arising and passing away. Truly, feeling is of three kinds and also has the nature of arising and passing away. That person contemplates that feeling as the self. Because of such contemplation, not only does that person's self come to be impermanent, but many feelings would also come to arise at the same single moment. That person admits that the self is impermanent, yet there is no such thing as the arising of many feelings at the same single moment. Referring to this meaning that many feelings do not arise simultaneously, He taught: "Therefore, Ānanda, for this reason also, it is not fit to contemplate that 'feeling is my self'."

"Friends, when..." refers to the time when there is no experience of feeling at all in the pure aggregate of form. "In that case... would it occur?" means would the ego-conceit (ahaṃkāra) of clinging to "I" as "I am" arise even in a palm-leaf fan or a window which are devoid of feeling? "Therefore, Ānanda" means that because the pure aggregate of form cannot rise up and say "I am", for this reason also, the wise do not approve of contemplating that feeling as the self. "In that case, would there be the thought 'this person is I'?" means, among the three aggregates of perception, mental formations, and consciousness which have the nature of experiencing, should any single state be spoken of as "this state is I"? Alternatively, it means: would the thought "this state is I" or "I am" arise in those three aggregates which have ceased along with the cessation of feeling? Then, just as one would not accept the sharpness of a rabbit's horn, the Venerable Ānanda did not accept the occurrence of the mode of "I" in that teaching and replied, "No, indeed, Bhante."

By this sequence of teaching, what is being told? The discourse on the round of rebirth (vaṭṭakathā) is being told. Indeed, when the Blessed One teaches the discourse on the round, in some places He teaches it with ignorance (avijjā) as the head, in some places with craving (taṇhā) as the head, and in some places with wrong view (diṭṭhi) as the head. Among those three: "Monks, the first point of ignorance is not apparent, such that 'before this, ignorance did not exist, but afterwards it came to be'. Monks, though this is said, it is apparent that ignorance arises due to this condition." Thus, He taught making ignorance the head. "Monks, the first point of craving for existence (bhavataṇhā) is not apparent... it is apparent that craving for existence arises due to this condition." Thus, He taught making craving the head. "Monks, the first point of the view of existence (bhavadiṭṭhi) is not apparent... it is apparent that the view of existence arises due to this condition." Thus, He taught making wrong view the head. Here also, it is taught specifically making wrong view the head.
98:
A person with wrong view, grasping at feelings such as pleasure as the self, through the power of the conceit 'I', the conceit 'mine', and wrong misapprehension, shifts from this existence to that among all types of becoming (bhava), modes of birth (yoni), destinations (gati), stations of consciousness (viññāṇaṭṭhiti), and abodes of beings (sattāvāsa). Being reborn in various states, they constantly wander like a boat tossed by a storm in the great ocean, unable even to lift their head above the suffering of the cycle (vaṭṭa).

In this way, the Blessed One, having taught the cycle of existence (vaṭṭa) through this sequence of discourse to the person with wrong view who is confused about dependent origination (paṭiccasamuppāda), now wishing to teach the cessation of the cycle (vivaṭṭa), said: "Ānanda, when a monk..." and so forth.

Being skillful in teaching, the Blessed One did not refer to a person whose mind is distracted by new works and has abandoned meditation, but rather, wishing to start with the power of a person who follows the Buddha's instruction and dwells in the foundations of mindfulness (satipaṭṭhāna), He said: "He does not regard feeling as the self," and so forth. A monk of such nature, through the power of the knowledge of comprehension (sammasana-ñāṇa) taught in the manner: "He defines all form (rūpa)—whether past, future, or present; internal or external; gross or subtle; inferior or superior; far or near—as impermanent (anicca), which is one kind of comprehension; he defines it as suffering (dukkha), which is one kind of comprehension; he defines it as non-self (anatta), which is one kind of comprehension," and so forth, because this knowledge occurs in all phenomena, he does not regard feeling as the self, nor does he regard any other phenomenon as such. When it is said that such a person does not cling to anything in the world, it means that among the phenomena such as form in the world consisting of the world of aggregates (khandha-loka) and so forth, he does not cling to even a single phenomenon as 'I' or as 'mine'.

In the phrase "because of non-clinging, he is not agitated," the one who does not cling is not agitated by the agitations of craving (taṇhā), wrong view (diṭṭhi), and conceit (māna). "Because he is not agitated" means being without agitation, "he attains parinibbāna by himself," meaning he attains peace through the extinction of defilements (kilesa-parinibbāna). To show the occurrence of the reviewing knowledge (paccavekkhaṇa-ñāṇa) of such an Arahant whose defilements are extinguished, the Buddha said: "Birth is exhausted," and so forth.

"Thus he has that view" means that the view of the Arahant who is thus liberated from defilements is of such a kind. There is also a variant reading "iti'ssa diṭṭhi." It means that the Arahant who is thus liberated from defilements has such a view. In the phrase "that is not proper," it means that statement is not suitable. Why? Because if it were so, it would amount to saying, "The Arahant does not know anything." To say of an Arahant who is liberated by knowing thus that "he does not know anything"...
99:
...is not proper to say. It is precisely because it is not proper to say so that at the end of the four methods, the Buddha spoke the words beginning with "Taṃ kissa hetu" (For what reason is that?).

In that passage, "yāvatā Ānanda adhivacanaṃ" means as far as there are all designations known as 'adhivacana-paññatti'. "Yāvatā adhivacanapatho" means as far as there are all the aggregates (khandha), bases (āyatana), and elements (dhātu) which are the causes for designation. This method should be understood in all places. "Paññāvacaraṃ" refers to the group of five aggregates which is the sphere to be comprehended by wisdom. "Tadabhiññā" means having known that group of phenomena such as designation with higher knowledge (abhiññā). What did the Blessed One show by this sequence of teaching? He showed the connection (anusandhi) of the passage that was as tangled as a knotted thread.

## Exposition on the Seven Stations of Consciousness

Now, the person described as "he does not designate" (na paññāpeti) becomes one liberated in both ways (ubhatobhāgavimutta) as he proceeds towards Nibbāna through the path of insight (vipassanā-magga), being liberated from both the mental body (nāma-kāya) and the material body (rūpa-kāya). The person described as "he does not regard" (na samanupassati) becomes one liberated by wisdom (paññāvimutta) as he proceeds towards Nibbāna through the path of insight. Therefore, to show the liberation from the cycle and the names of those two types of monks mentioned below, the Buddha said: "Ānanda, there are these seven stations of consciousness," and so forth.

In that passage, the "seven" are spoken of by way of rebirth (paṭisandhi). The four stations of consciousness spoken of by way of object (ārammaṇa) in the Saṅgīti Sutta will come later. It is called a station of consciousness (viññāṇaṭṭhiti) because the rebirth-consciousness (paṭisandhi-viññāṇa) stands therein. This name 'viññāṇaṭṭhiti' is a designation for the aggregates which are the standing-place of the rebirth-consciousness. "Two spheres" (dve āyatanāni) means two places of residence. In this context, the place of residence itself is intended as 'āyatana'. Therefore, the Buddha will say later: "the sphere of unconscious beings (asaññasattāyatana) and the second, the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception (nevasaññānāsaññāyatana)."

Why are all these taken together? They are taken to fully encompass the cycle of existence (vaṭṭa). The cycle does not reach its end merely by way of the stations of consciousness alone, nor merely by way of the spheres alone. It reaches its end only by way of becoming (bhava), modes of birth (yoni), destinations (gati), and abodes of beings (sattāvāsa). Therefore, all of these are included.

Now, wishing to analyze that meaning in order, the Buddha said: "What kind of beings?" and so forth. Therein, "seyyathāpi" is a particle used for the purpose of illustration. "Just as humans" is the meaning. Among the infinite humans in the infinite universes (cakka-vāḷa), there are not even two people who are identical in terms of complexion, shape, and so forth. Even if twin brothers are identical in complexion or shape in some places, there is still a difference among them in terms of looking straight, looking askance, speaking, laughing, walking, standing, and so forth.
100:
Among humans, there is no one identical in appearance; they differ in their gaze, speech, gait, and so forth. Therefore, they are described as 'nānattakāyā' (having diverse bodies). Their perceptions associated with rebirth-linking may be triple-rooted, double-rooted, or rootless. Therefore, they are described as 'nānattasaññino' (having diverse perceptions).

'Ekacce ca devā' refers to the six heavens of the sense sphere (kāmāvacara). Among these devas, some have dark blue bodies, while others have golden-colored bodies, and so on. Their perceptions are either double-rooted or triple-rooted; they do not have rootless rebirth-linking perceptions.

'Ekacce ca vinipātikā' refers to those who are exempt from the four woeful states, such as the female yakkhas Uttaramātā, Piyaṅkaramātā, Phussamittā, Dhammaguttā, and other vimānika-petas (spirits with mansions). The bodies of these vinipātikā vary just like those of humans, in terms of color—such as golden, white, black, or dark green like the back of a bedbug—and in terms of being thin, fat, short, or tall. Their perceptions also vary like those of humans, being double-rooted, triple-rooted, or rootless. These vinipātikā are not as powerful as devas; they have little power, like destitute humans, and live oppressed by suffering due to the difficulty of obtaining food and clothing. Some vinipātikā suffer during the waning moon and are happy during the waxing moon. Because they have fallen away from a state of total happiness, they are called 'vinipātikā'.

Among these vinipātikā, those who possess triple-rooted rebirth-linking can also attain the realization of the Dhamma (dhammābhisamaya). Indeed, the female yakkha who was the mother of Piyaṅkara heard the sound of the Dhamma recited by the Elder Anuruddha at dawn and said:

'Dear Piyaṅkara, do not make a sound; the monk is reciting the words of the Dhamma. Let us understand the Dhamma and practice it; it will be for our benefit. Let us exercise restraint toward living beings and not knowingly speak falsehoods. Let us train ourselves in good virtue; perhaps we may be released from this yakkha birth.'

After making her young son understand in this way, on that very day, she attained the fruit of Stream-entry (sotāpattiphala). Uttaramātā also became a Stream-enterer (sotāpanna) just by hearing the Dhamma of the Blessed One.

'Brahmakāyikā' refers to the Brahmapārisajja Brahmas, Brahmapurohita Brahmas, and Mahābrahmas. 'Paṭhamābhinibbattā' means that all these Brahmas are reborn through the first jhāna. Among these Brahmas, the Brahmapārisajja Brahmas are reborn through a limited degree of the first jhāna and have a lifespan of one-third of an incalculable aeon (asaṅkheyya-kappa). The Brahmapurohita Brahmas are reborn through a medium degree of the first jhāna and have a lifespan of half an incalculable aeon; their bodies are also more expansive. The Mahābrahmas are reborn through a superior degree of the first jhāna and have a lifespan of a full incalculable aeon; their bodies are extremely expansive. Thus, although these Brahmas differ in their physical forms, they are understood as 'nānattakāyā ekattasaññino' (diverse in body, uniform in perception) because their rebirth-linking perceptions are identical by virtue of the first jhāna.
101:
In the same way, beings in the four woeful planes should be understood as having diverse bodies but unified perception (nānatta-kāya ekatta-saññī). Indeed, in the hells, the bodies of some beings are one gāvuta in size, some half a league (yojana), and some one league. However, Devadatta’s body grew to be a hundred leagues. Among animals, some are small and some are large. In the realm of hungry ghosts (peta-visaya), some are sixty cubits tall, some seventy, and some eighty. Some are beautiful, and some are ugly (disfigured). Likewise, there are the Kālakañjika Asuras. Furthermore, among these petas, those called Dīghapiṭṭhika are as large as sixty leagues. Regarding perception, the perceptions of all those in the four woeful planes are only rootless unwholesome resultant perceptions (akusala-vipāka ahetuka-saññā). Therefore, although their bodies differ, beings in the woeful planes are counted as having unified perception (nānatta-kāya ekatta-saññā).

The Ābhassara (Radiant) devas are so called because radiance spreads and flows from their bodies like the flames of a torch, appearing to break off and fall away. Among them, according to the fivefold method, those who arise after developing the second and third jhānas to a limited (paritta) degree are called Parittābha; their lifespan is two aeons (kappa). Those who arise after developing them to a medium (majjhima) degree are called Appamāṇābha; their lifespan is four aeons. Those who arise after developing them to a superior (paṇīta) degree are called Ābhassara; their lifespan is eight aeons. However, in this context of showing the stations of consciousness, all are included under the name Ābhassara based on the highest division. The bodies of all these devas have a similar pervasiveness (eka-vipphāra). Their perception, however, differs: some have perception with only sustained application (vicāra) without initial application (vitakka), while others have perception without both initial and sustained application.

Subhakiṇha (Lustrous) means permeated and strewn with beauty; it means having a body of solid radiance. Unlike the Ābhassaras, their radiance does not appear to break off but remains solid. In the fivefold method, due to the power of developing the fourth jhāna to limited, medium, or superior degrees, they are reborn as Parittasubha, Appamāṇasubha, and Subhakiṇha devas, with lifespans of 16, 32, and 64 aeons respectively. Thus, all of them should be understood as having similar bodies (ekatta-kāya) and similar perception (ekatta-saññā) through the perception of the fourth jhāna. The Vehapphala devas also belong to the fourth station of consciousness. The non-percipient beings (asañña-satta), due to the absence of consciousness, are not included here in the stations of consciousness, but they are included in the nine abodes of beings (sattāvāsa).

The Suddhāvāsa (Pure Abodes) exist on the side of liberation (vivaṭṭa-pakkha) and are not present at all times. They do not appear in a world empty of Buddhas (buddha-suñña) for a hundred thousand aeons or even an incalculable period (asaṅkheyya). They only appear when Buddhas arise within sixteen thousand aeons; they are like the encampment (khandhāvāra-ṭṭhāna) of the Blessed One who turns the Wheel of Dhamma. Therefore, they are usually not included in the stations of consciousness or the abodes of beings. However, Mahāsīva Thera, based on the Sutta passage: "Sāriputta, there is no abode of beings that I have not previously lived in during this long journey, except for the Suddhāvāsa devas," stated that the Suddhāvāsa realms also fall within the fourth station of consciousness and the fourth abode of beings. This statement of Mahāsīva Thera is acceptable as it does not contradict the Pali. The meaning of the words beginning with "Sabbaso rūpasaññānaṃ" should be understood as explained in the Visuddhimagga. Just as in the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception (nevasaññānāsaññāyatana), the rebirth-linking perception occurs, the consciousness is also so subtle that it cannot be called distinct consciousness, nor can it be said there is no consciousness. Therefore, it is not included in the stations of consciousness but is taught among the spheres (āyatana).

In those stations of consciousness, "tañca pajānāti" means one understands that station of consciousness. "Tassā ca samudayaṃ" means one understands the cause of that station of consciousness through the method such as "with the arising of ignorance, there is the arising of form," etc.
102:
"I have lived in almost every place during this long journey, except for the Suddhāvāsa devas" (M. Ni. 1.160). By this Sutta, Mahāsīva Thera states that the Suddhāvāsa realms also belong to the fourth station of consciousness and the fourth abode of beings. This statement is permitted because it is not contradicted by the Sutta Pali.

The meaning of the words beginning with "Sabbaso rūpasaññānaṃ" should be understood as taught in the Visuddhimagga. In the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception, just like perception, consciousness is also subtle; it is neither consciousness nor non-consciousness. Therefore, it is not mentioned among the stations of consciousness but is taught among the spheres (āyatana).

"Tatra" means in those stations of consciousness. "Tañca pajānāti" means one understands that station of consciousness. "Tassā ca samudayaṃ" means one understands the cause of that station of consciousness by the method: "With the arising of ignorance, there is the arising of form" (Paṭi. Ma. 1.49), etc. "Tassā ca atthaṅgamaṃ" means one understands the cessation of that station of consciousness by the method: "With the cessation of ignorance, there is the cessation of form," etc. "Assāda" (gratification) means: "The pleasure and joy that arise dependent on form... dependent on consciousness—this is the gratification of consciousness." In this way, one understands the gratification of that station of consciousness. "Ādīnava" (danger) means: "The fact that form... consciousness is impermanent, suffering, and subject to change—this is the danger of consciousness." In this way, one understands the danger of that station of consciousness. "Nissaraṇa" (escape) means: "The disciplining of desire and lust, the abandoning of desire and lust for form... for consciousness—this is the escape from consciousness" (Saṃ. Ni. 2.26). In this way, one understands the escape from that station of consciousness. "Kallaṃ nu tena" (Is it fit for him?) is a question: Is it fit for that bhikkhu to delight in that station of consciousness through the power of craving, conceit, and views as "I am" or "This is mine"? In this manner, it should be understood in all places. In realms where there is no form, the arising (samudaya) should be applied by way of the four aggregates; in realms where there is no consciousness, it should be applied by way of one aggregate. The phrase "with the arising of nutriment, with the cessation of nutriment" should also be applied here.

"Yato kho Ānanda bhikkhu" means "Ānanda, when a bhikkhu..." "Anupādā vimutto" means liberated without clinging through the four types of grasping. "Paññā-vimutto" means liberated by wisdom. It means one who is liberated by making the non-occurrence of the mental body (nāma-kāya) and the physical body (rūpa-kāya) through the power of wisdom alone, without having realized the eight liberations (vimokkha). That person liberated by wisdom is either a dry-insight practitioner (sukkhavipassaka) or one who attains Arahatship while abiding in one of the jhānas such as the first jhāna...
103:
There are also five types of persons who reach the fruit of Arahantship. It is also stated thus: "What is the person liberated by wisdom (paññāvimutta)? Here, in this Dispensation, a certain person does not dwell having touched the eight liberations with the mental body (nāmakāya), but having seen with wisdom, his taints (āsavas) are exhausted. This person is called one liberated by wisdom."

## Explanation of the Eight Liberations (Aṭṭhavimokkhavaṇṇanā)
Having thus shown the conclusion and the name of one monk, [the Buddha] spoke the words beginning with "These eight" to show the other person. In that context, for what reason is it called "liberation" (vimokkha)? It is called liberation in the sense of "resolving" (adhimuccana). What is this sense of resolving? It is the sense of being well-freed from opposing states and being well-freed through the power of great delight in the object. It means occurring in the object without anxiety and without being oppressed, like the sleeping of a child who has let go of his limbs in his father's lap. This meaning does not exist in the last liberation, but it exists in all the preceding ones.

In the passage "One possessing form sees forms" (rūpī rūpāni passati), the form-sphere jhāna (rūpajjhāna) produced by way of the blue kasiṇa, etc., in one's own internal hair, etc., is called "form" (rūpa); because he has that form-sphere jhāna, he is called "one possessing form" (rūpī). "He sees forms externally" (bahiddhā rūpāni passati) means he sees kasiṇa forms such as the blue kasiṇa, etc., externally with the eye of jhāna. By this passage, the four form-sphere jhānas of a person who has produced jhāna in kasiṇas with internal and external bases are shown. "Perceiving formlessness internally" (ajjhattaṃ arūpasaññī) means not having the perception of form internally; the meaning is not having produced form-sphere jhāna in one's own hair, etc. By this passage, the form-sphere jhānas of a person who has performed the preliminary work externally and produced jhāna only externally are shown.

By the passage "He is resolved only on the beautiful" (subhanteva adhimutto hoti), the jhānas in the color kasiṇas such as the very pure blue, etc., are shown. In that passage, although there is no reflection as "it is beautiful" within the attainment (appanā), because he dwells having made the pure and beautiful kasiṇa his object, it is appropriate to say "he is resolved on the beautiful"; therefore, the teaching was given in this way. In the Paṭisambhidāmagga, however: "How is the liberation 'he is resolved only on the beautiful'? Here, a monk dwells pervading one direction with a mind imbued with loving-kindness... because of the development of loving-kindness, beings become non-repulsive. He dwells pervading one direction with a mind imbued with compassion, appreciative joy, and equanimity... because of the development of equanimity, beings..."
104:
...become non-repulsive. Thus it is the liberation "he is resolved only on the beautiful," as stated in the Paṭisambhidāmagga.

Whatever needs to be said regarding the passages beginning with "completely [surpassing] perceptions of form" (sabbaso rūpasaññānaṃ), all of that has already been stated in the Visuddhimagga. This eighth liberation is called the eighth noble liberation because of the complete purity and liberation of the four mental aggregates.

"In forward order" (anuloma) means from the beginning to the end. "In reverse order" (paṭiloma) means from the end to the beginning. This phrase "in forward and reverse order" is said by way of moving back and forth without stopping in one place because of great mastery in the attainments. "Wherever he wishes" (yatthicchakaṃ) indicates the location, meaning entering [the attainment] in whatever location he wishes. "Whichever he wishes" (yadicchakaṃ) indicates the attainment, meaning entering whichever attainment he wishes. "For as long as he wishes" (yāvaticchakaṃ) indicates the duration, meaning entering for as long a duration as he wishes. "He attains" (samāpajjati) means he enters that particular attainment. "He emerges" (vuṭṭhāti) means he rises from that attainment and stands.

"Liberated in both ways" (ubhatobhāgavimutta) means one who is liberated from two parts: liberated from the material body (rūpakāya) by the formless attainments, and liberated from the mental body (nāmakāya) by the Path. This has also been stated:

"Just as a flame tossed by a gust of wind
Goes out and cannot be designated,
So the sage, liberated from the mental body,
Goes out and cannot be designated."

That person liberated in both ways is of five types: one who reaches Arahantship after emerging from one of the formless attainments such as the base of infinite space, and one who reaches Arahantship after emerging from the attainment of cessation (nirodhasamāpatti) having become a non-returner. Some teachers, however, say: "Since the fourth form-sphere jhāna also has two factors and is accompanied by equanimity, and the formless-sphere jhāna is also like that, therefore, one who reaches Arahantship after emerging from the fourth form-sphere jhāna is also called 'liberated in both ways'."

This question regarding the one liberated in both ways arose beneath the Brazen Palace (Lohapāsāda) and was decided after a long time based on the explanation of the Elder Tipitaka Cūḷasumana...
105: He arrived. It is said that a monk, a disciple of the Elder at Giri Vihāra, heard that question from an alms-collecting monk and said, "Friends, while our teacher was explaining the Dhamma at the lower Bronze Palace (Lohapāsāda), he spoke words that no one had ever heard before." When asked, "Venerable sir, what did the Elder say?" he replied: "Although the fourth jhāna of the fine-material sphere has two factors and is accompanied by equanimity, and although it can temporarily suppress defilements, it still occurs and functions in the vicinity where defilements arise. Indeed, these defilements arise in the realm of five constituents (pañcavokāra bhava) depending on an object such as the color blue and so on, and the fine-material sphere jhāna does not transcend that object. Therefore, only one who has removed all material objects, suppressed defilements by the power of immaterial jhānas (arūpajjhāna), and reached Arahantship is one liberated in both ways (ubhatobhāgavimutta)." This is what the Elder said, friend. Having said this, he cited this sutta: "Ānanda, what kind of person is one liberated in both ways? Here, a certain person dwells having touched the eight liberations (vimokkha) with the body, and having seen with wisdom, his taints (āsava) are exhausted. This person is called one liberated in both ways." The phrase "imāya ca ānanda ubhatobhāgavimuttiyā" means "than this liberation in both ways, Ānanda." The remaining words are clear in meaning in all places. ## The Commentary on the Mahānidāna Sutta is finished.
106:
## 3. Commentary on the Mahāparinibbāna Sutta

This sutta beginning with 'Evaṃ me sutaṃ' is the Mahāparinibbāna Sutta. In this sutta, this is the sequential commentary on the words: 'Gijjhakūṭe' means it is called Gijjhakūṭa (Vulture Peak) because vultures live on the peaks of that mountain, or because its peak resembles a vulture; on that Gijjhakūṭa mountain. 'Abhiyātukāmo' means desiring to go for the purpose of subduing. 'Vajjī' refers to the Vajjian kings. 'Evaṃmahiddhike' means endowed with such great royal power, and by this word, their state of unity is spoken of. 'Evaṃmahānubhāve' means endowed with such great majesty, and by this word, their state of being well-trained in elephant-craft and so on is spoken of. With reference to that, it was said: 'These Licchavi princes are indeed trained, these Licchavi princes are indeed well-trained, in that they can shoot arrows through a fine keyhole one after another without missing.' 'Ucchecchāmī' means I will cut off and destroy the lineage. 'Vināsessāmī' means I will destroy, I will make them disappear. In the phrase 'anayavyasanaṃ', 'anaya' is the name for misfortune (lack of prosperity). 'Vyasana' is the name for the ruin of relatives and so on, because it removes welfare and happiness. 'Āpādessāmī' means I will cause them to reach such ruin.

That King Ajātasattu, whether standing or sitting, would speak only this talk of war and command his army, 'Be prepared to go.' Why? It is said that based on a port village near the Ganges river, half a yojana was under the authority of Ajātasattu, and half a yojana was under the authority of the Licchavis. This was the place where the two authorities met. There, valuable goods would arrive from the foot of the mountain. Hearing of this, while Ajātasattu was still arranging, saying 'I will go today, I will go tomorrow,' the united Licchavis, rejoicing in harmony, would go earlier and take everything. King Ajātasattu would arrive later, and upon learning of that event, would return in anger. They did the same in subsequent years as well. Then, King Ajātasattu, having become extremely resentful, acted in this way at that time.

Then he thought: 'War with a group (a united body) is a heavy matter; there is no such thing as a vain blow. If I act after consulting with a wise man, it will be faultless. And as for a wise man, there is no one equal to the Teacher. The Teacher is residing in a nearby monastery. I will send [someone] and...'
107:
...ask him. If there is any benefit in my going, the Teacher will remain silent. But if there is no benefit, he will say, "What is the use of the King going there?"' He sent the Brahmin Vassakāra. The Brahmin went and informed the Blessed One of this matter. Therefore, it is said: 'Then the King... pe... I will cause them to reach ruin.'

## Commentary on the Conditions for Non-decline of Kings (Rāja-aparihāniya-dhamma)

'Bhagavantaṃ bījayamāno' means the Elder Ānanda was fanning the Blessed One, performing it as a duty. For the Blessed One, however, there is neither cold nor heat. The Blessed One, having heard the words of the Brahmin, desired to discuss not with that Brahmin but with the Elder, and thus said, 'Ānanda, what have you heard?' and so on.

'Abhiṇhaṃ sannipātā' means assembling constantly, whether three times a day or at various intervals. 'Sannipātabahulā' means having many assemblies without falling into weariness, thinking, 'We assembled yesterday, we assembled the day before, why must we assemble again today?'

'Yāvakīvañca' means for as long a period of time. 'Ānanda, only growth is to be expected for the Vajjis, not decline' means: if they do not assemble constantly, they do not hear the news coming from various directions. Consequently, they do not know, 'Such a village boundary or market boundary is being disturbed, or bandits have arisen in such a place.' The bandits, knowing 'The kings are negligent,' attack the villages and markets and destroy the country. In this way, the decline of kings occurs.

But if they assemble constantly, they hear various reports and, by sending troops, they can crush the enemies. The bandits also, knowing 'The kings are vigilant, it is not possible for us to move about in groups,' break up and flee. In this way, the growth of kings occurs. Therefore, it was said: 'Ānanda, only growth is to be expected for the Vajjis, not decline.' In that statement, 'pāṭikaṅkhā' means that which is desirable, that which must certainly happen; it should be understood in this sense.

Regarding the words 'samaggā' and so on, if they do not assemble in unity, making excuses when the assembly drum is sounded, saying 'Today I have work, I have a festive ceremony,' they are not said to assemble in unity. But if, upon hearing the sound of the drum, they assemble even while eating, or while being adorned, or while putting on clothes, leaving those tasks half-finished, they are said to assemble in unity. Having assembled, they deliberate and perform what should be done, and then [depart] only in unity...
108:
If they do not rise from the assembly in harmony, they are not said to rise in harmony. In such rising, those who leave first might think, "We have heard only external talk; only now will the talk of decision-making occur." Only when they rise together at the same time are they said to rise in harmony. Furthermore, upon hearing, "In such a place, the village boundaries or market-town boundaries are in disorder, and robbers have arisen in rebellion," and when it is asked, "Who will go and crush this enemy?" those kings who go saying, "I will go first, I will go first," are also said to rise and act in harmony. When the affairs of one king are declining, if the remaining kings send their sons and brothers to support his affairs; or when a visiting king arrives, if they all welcome him together without distinction, not saying, "Go to this one's house, go to that one's house"; or when a celebration, an illness, or any such happiness or sorrow occurs to one king, if all the kings go there as companions—they are said to perform the duties of the harmonious Vajjīs.

Regarding the words "apannattaṃ" and so forth: Kings who cause to be collected tolls, taxes, or fines that were not previously established are said to enact what was not enacted. Kings who do not cause to be collected the taxes that have come down through ancient tradition are said to abolish what was enacted. Kings who, when someone is caught and presented as a "robber," pass sentences of execution or mutilation without investigation are said not to live according to the ancient Vajjian traditions. In the kingdoms of those who enact what was not enacted, people oppressed by new tolls and so forth, thinking, "We are greatly oppressed; who can live in the realm of these kings?" enter the border forests and, becoming robbers or associates of robbers, attack the countryside. For those who abolish what was enacted and do not accept the tolls and so forth that have come down through tradition, the treasury declines. Because the treasury declines, the elephant and horse forces, the troops, and the harem and others do not receive their regular maintenance and thus decline in strength and power. They become capable neither of fighting in war nor of rendering service. In the kingdoms of those who do not live according to the ancient Vajjian traditions, people, becoming angry and thinking, "They have executed and mutilated our sons, fathers, and brothers, treating them as robbers though they were not robbers," enter the border forests and, becoming robbers or associates of robbers, attack the countryside. Thus, the decline of kings occurs. However, in the kingdoms of those who practice only what was enacted, people, being joyful and satisfied, thinking, "The kings perform only what has come down through tradition," carry out their work such as farming and trade. For those who do not abolish what was enacted and [accept] the tolls and so forth that have come down through tradition...
109:
...for those who accept [the tolls and so forth], the treasury increases. Because the treasury increases, the elephant and horse forces, the troops, the harem, and others receive their regular maintenance and provisions, thus becoming endowed with strength and power, capable of both fighting in war and rendering service.

## Regarding the phrase "porāṇaṃ vajjidhammaṃ" (ancient Vajjian traditions), the details should be understood thus: In ancient times, when the Vajjian kings were presented with someone caught and brought as "This is a robber," they would not immediately command, "Seize this robber," but would hand him over to the Ministers of Justice (vinicchayamahāmatta). Those ministers would investigate, and if he was not a robber, they would release him. If he was a robber, they would say nothing themselves but hand him over to the Legal Experts (vohārika). Those legal experts, too, if he was not a robber, would release him. If he was a robber, they would hand him over to the Reciters of the Law (suttadhara). They, too, would investigate, and if he was not a robber, would release him. If he was a robber, they would hand him over to the Eight Clans (aṭṭhakulika). They would do the same and hand him over to the General (senāpati). The General would hand him over to the Viceroy (uparāja), and the Viceroy to the King. The King would investigate personally, and if he was not a robber, would release him. If, however, he was a robber, the King would have the Book of Precedents (paveṇīpotthaka) read. In that book, it is written: "If such a person has committed such an act, such a punishment shall be given to him." The King, comparing the person's action with that book, would pass a sentence appropriate to the case. When they live according to these ancient Vajjian traditions, the people do not complain. Reflecting, "The kings perform their duties according to ancient tradition; there is no fault in these kings, the fault is only in us," they carry out their work without negligence. In this way, the prosperity of the kings occurs. Therefore, it was said: "Ananda, only growth is to be expected for the Vajjīs, not decline."

"Sakkaroṇti" means that when they perform any act of hospitality or honor toward those [elder] kings, they do it well. "Garum karoṇti" means they act only after establishing a sense of reverence. "Māneṇti" means they cherish them with their minds. "Pūjeṇti" means they show respectful conduct. "Sotabbaṃ maññanti" means they go to attend upon them two or three times a day, considering that the words of those kings should be heard and believed. Those junior kings who do not perform such honors to the elder kings and do not go to attend upon them for the sake of advice, being neglected by the elders and receiving no advice, become devoted to play and decline from their kingship. Those junior kings who practice respectfully in that way are told by the elder kings about the ancient traditions, "This should be done, this should not be done." Even upon reaching the battlefield, they show them the methods and strategies, "In this way one should enter, in this way one should exit." Those junior kings, receiving advice from them and practicing according to that advice, are able to maintain the royal lineage. Therefore, it was said: "Ananda, only growth is to be expected for the Vajjīs, not decline."
110:
"Kulitthiyo" refers to noble housewives of good family. "Kulakumāriyo" refers to the young maiden daughters of those noblewomen who have not yet had relations with men. In the phrase "okkassa pasayha," both the terms "okkassa" and "pasayha" are names for the manner of using force and oppression. It is also read as "ukkassa." Among these terms, "okkassa" means dragging away by force, and "pasayha" means overwhelming or oppressing.

In the kingdom of kings who act in this way, the people become angry, saying, "These kings are forcibly seizing the mothers of our sons in our homes, as well as our young daughters whom we have raised by removing their saliva and mucus with our own mouths, and are making them live in their own houses." They then enter the border forests and, becoming either bandits or associates of bandits, attack and destroy the countryside. However, in the kingdom of kings who do not act in this way, the people perform their own work without anxiety and increase the royal treasury. In this way, the increase and decrease [of prosperity] in this matter should be understood.

"Vajjīnaṃ vajjicetiyāni" refers to the shrines or abodes of spirits (yakkhas) that have received the name "cetiya" because they are places of honor in the Vajjian realm of the Vajjian kings. "Abbhantarāni" refers to those located inside the city. "Bāhirāni" refers to those located outside the city. "Dinnapubbaṃ" means what was previously given. "Katapubbaṃ" means what was previously done. "No parihāpessanti" means they will perform them as they have always been done, without letting them decline. Indeed, for kings who let the righteous offerings (bali) decline, the deities do not provide well-arranged protection. Although they cannot cause suffering that has not yet arisen, they increase existing ailments such as coughs and headaches. When a battle is encountered, they do not provide assistance. However, for kings who do not let the offerings decline, the deities provide well-arranged protection. Although they cannot produce happiness that has not yet arisen, they heal existing ailments such as coughs and headaches. They also provide assistance on the battlefield. In this way, the increase and decrease in this matter should be understood.

In the phrase "dhammikā rakkha-āvaraṇa-gutti," protection itself is called "āvaraṇa" (shelter) because it prevents the arrival of what is undesired. It is called "gutti" (guarding) because it secures the desired welfare so that it is not destroyed. In that context, guarding by surrounding with military forces is not what is called righteous protection, shelter, and guarding (dhammikā rakkha-āvaraṇa-gutti) for monks.
