Rather, it is the practice of not cutting down trees in the groves near the monastery, hunters not killing animals, and not catching fish in the ponds that is called righteous protection. By the passage "kinti anāgatā ca," [the Buddha] asks about the state of the Vajjian kings' minds as they think: "How shall the Arahants who have not yet come, come [to our realm]? How shall the Arahants who have already arrived live in comfort?"
111:
Among those kings, those who do not wish for the arrival of Arahants who have not yet come are without faith and devotion. When monks arrive, they do not go out to welcome them, do not go to see them, do not perform the courtesy of welcoming, do not ask questions, do not listen to the Dhamma, do not give offerings, do not listen to the appreciation (anumodanā), and do not arrange a place to stay. Then, the ill-repute of those kings spreads: "The king named so-and-so is without faith and devotion; when monks arrive, he does not welcome them... he does not arrange a place to stay." Hearing this, monks do not go through the gates of that king's city; even if they go, they do not enter the city. Thus, Arahants who have not yet come simply do not come. Even for those who have already come, if there is no comfortable living, those Arahants who arrived without knowing the kings' behavior think, "We came thinking we would stay, but who can live with such behavior from these kings?" and they depart. In this way, when those who have not come do not arrive, and those who have come live in misery, that place becomes a non-habitation for renunciants. From then on, there is no protection from deities. When there is no protection from deities, non-human beings (amanussa) find an opportunity. As non-human beings increase, they cause diseases that have never occurred before. Meritorious deeds based on seeing virtuous ones and asking questions do not occur. Conversely, the occurrence of the "white side" (sukkapakkha), which is the opposite of the aforementioned "black side" (kaṇhapakkha), takes place. Thus, in this matter, progress and decline should be understood.

"Ekamidāhaṃ"—the Blessed One spoke these words to show that he had previously taught these seven principles of the Vajjis to the Vajjian kings. In that context, "Sārandade cetiye" means in the monastery of that name. It is said that before the Buddha appeared, there was a cetiya (shrine) that was the dwelling place of a yakkha named Sārandada. Later, a monastery was built there for the Blessed One. Because that monastery was built at the site of the Sārandada Cetiya, it came to be known simply as the Sārandada Cetiya.

"Akaraṇīyā" means they should not be done, or they cannot be captured. "Yadidṃ" is merely a particle. The word "yuddhassa" is in the genitive case with the meaning of the instrumental. It means they cannot be captured by direct battle. "Aññatra uplāpanāya" means except for persuasion. "Uplāpanā" means performing hospitality by sending elephants, horses, chariots, gold, silver, etc., saying, "Enough with the dispute, let us now be united." By performing such hospitality, they can be captured only through pure trust. "Aññatra mithubhedāya" means except for mutual dissension. This means that by causing division among one another, those Vajjian kings...
112:
It is shown that the Vajjis cannot be captured [by force of arms]. Having obtained the method from the Blessed One’s discourse [on the conditions of non-decline], Vassakāra the Brahmin spoke this [that they could not be captured except by persuasion or sowing discord] of his own accord.

If it is asked, "Did the Blessed One not know that the Brahmin would obtain a method from these words?" the answer is, "Yes, He knew." If it is asked, "Knowing this, why did He speak?" the answer is, "Out of compassion." For the Blessed One had this thought: "Even if I do not speak, [Vassakāra] will go and capture all the Vajjis within a few days. But if I speak, he will capture them only after three years while sowing discord among the united Vajjis. Living for even this much time is better. While living for this long, the Vajjis will have the opportunity to perform meritorious deeds, which are their true refuge."

'Abhinanditvā' means rejoicing in the mind. 'Anumoditvā' means expressing appreciation through speech, saying, "What has been spoken by the Venerable Gotama is indeed well-spoken." 'Pakkāmi' means he went to King Ajātasattu. Then the King asked him, "Teacher, what did the Blessed One say?" The Brahmin replied, "Great King, according to the words of the Ascetic Gotama, it is impossible for anyone to capture the Vajjis [by force]. However, they can be captured by persuasion or by sowing internal discord."

Then the King asked, "If we use persuasion, our treasures such as elephants and horses will be exhausted. I will capture them only by sowing discord. What should we do?"

The Brahmin then suggested, "Great King, if that is so, you should start a discussion in the midst of the assembly about going to war with the Vajjis. Then I will say, 'Great King, what is the use of those Vajjis? Let those kings live by farming and trading with their own property,' and then I will leave. At that, you should say, 'Why does this Brahmin oppose the talk of war with the Vajjis?' During the day, I will send a gift to those Vajjis. You must seize that gift, blame me, and without binding or beating me, simply have my head shaved and expel me from the city. Then I will say, 'I am the one who built the walls and moats in the King's city. I know the weak points, the shallow places, and the deep places. I will soon make that city straight [vulnerable].' Hearing this, you should say, 'Let him go.'" The King did everything accordingly.

When the Licchavis heard of the Brahmin's departure, they said, "The Brahmin is treacherous; do not let him cross the Ganges." Some among them said, "He was treated this way because he spoke on our behalf," and so they said, "In that case, friends, let him come." When the Brahmin arrived and saw the Licchavis, he was asked, "Why have you come?" and he told them the whole story. The Licchavis remarked, "It is not proper to give such a heavy punishment for a minor offense," and they asked, "Teacher Brahmin, what kind of position do you wish to have in Rājagaha?" When he replied, "I was a judicial minister," they said, "Let that same position be yours here." Vassakāra the Brahmin then judged cases very well. The princes also studied various arts under him. Being established in the status of a teacher, one day he took a Licchavi prince aside...
113:
...and having gone to a secluded place, he asked, "Do the boys plow?" The prince replied, "Yes, sir, they plow." "By yoking two oxen?" he asked again. "Yes, by yoking two oxen," the prince replied. Having said only this much, the Brahmin returned. Then another person asked the prince, "What did the teacher say?" and not believing what the prince told him, he thought, "This person is not telling me the truth," and thus became divided from him.

On another day, the Brahmin took another Licchavi to a secluded place and asked, "With what curry did you eat?" and returned. When another person asked him and did not believe the answer, he likewise became divided. On another day, the Brahmin took another Licchavi to a secluded place and asked, "Is it true that you are very poor?" When asked, "Who said so?" he replied, "A certain Licchavi prince said so." He took another to a secluded place and asked, "Is it true that you are a coward?" When asked, "Who said so?" he replied, "A certain Licchavi prince said so."

In this way, by telling one person what another had not actually said, he sowed discord among those kings over three years, making it so that no two would walk the same path together. Then he had the assembly drum beaten. The Licchavis said, "Let the lords assemble, let the brave ones assemble," but they did not assemble. 

The Brahmin then sent a message to the King, saying, "Now is the time; come quickly." As soon as the King heard this, he had the war drum beaten and set out. When the people of Vesālī heard this, they had the drum beaten, saying, "We will not let the King cross the Ganges." But even hearing that drum, they said, "Let the brave kings go," and did not assemble. Again the drum was beaten, saying, "We will not allow entry into the city; we will stay with the gates closed," but not a single person assembled. The King entered through the gates that remained open as they were, brought everyone to ruin and destruction, and departed.

## Commentary on the Conditions for the Non-decline of Monks

Then, in the passage beginning with "Soon after the Blessed One had departed," the word "sannipātetvā" (having assembled) means that He sent monks with psychic powers to the distant monasteries and went Himself to the nearby monasteries, saying, "Assemble, venerable ones; the Blessed One desires your assembly," and thus caused them to gather.
114:
Aparihāniya means those things that prevent decline and are causes for growth. Regarding the statement 'I will teach the Dhamma,' it means he will teach by making it clear, as if making a thousand moons and a thousand suns shine, or as if lighting a thousand oil lamps inside a house with four walls.

Among those, 'frequent assembly' is just as described in the section on the Vajjī princes. In this Dispensation (Sāsana) as well, if they do not assemble frequently, they do not hear the news arriving from various directions. Because they do not hear, they cannot know that the boundary (sīmā) of such-and-such a monastery is in disorder, that the Uposatha and Pavāraṇā ceremonies have stopped, that in such-and-such a place monks are practicing medicine or acting as messengers, or that they are making a living by many requests such as giving flowers and so on. Bad monks, knowing that the Saṅgha is negligent, gather in groups and cause the Dispensation to decline. However, if they assemble frequently, they hear about various events; then, they send the Saṅgha to rectify the boundary, they cause the Uposatha and Pavāraṇā to proceed, they send those endowed with the fourfold Noble Lineage (Ariyavaṃsa) to places where wrong livelihood is prevalent to preach the Ariyavaṃsa Dhamma, and they have the masters of the Vinaya (Vinayadhara) restrain the bad monks. The bad monks, realizing that the Saṅgha is diligent and that they can no longer wander about in groups, break up their cliques and flee. Thus, in this matter of assembly, decline and growth should be understood.

Regarding 'in harmony' and so on: when the drum or bell is struck for the purpose of repairing shrines (cetiyas), roofing the Bodhi-tree house or the Uposatha hall, making an agreement, or giving an exhortation, saying 'Let the Saṅgha assemble,' those who make excuses such as 'I have robe-work,' 'My bowl needs to be fired,' or 'I have new construction work' are said to assemble disharmoniously. Only when they set aside all such business and assemble simultaneously, each thinking 'I will get there first,' are they said to assemble in harmony. After assembling, they should rise together only after deliberating and completing the necessary tasks; otherwise, rising individually is not called rising in harmony. For if they rise in that way, those who leave first might think, 'We have only heard external talk; the decisive talk will happen only now.' Only when they rise simultaneously is it called rising in harmony. Alternatively, when hearing that a monastery boundary is in disorder, that Uposatha and Pavāraṇā have stopped, or that bad monks practicing medicine etc. are numerous in a certain place, if it is asked 'Who will go and restrain those monks?' those monks who go saying 'I will go first, I will go first' are also said to rise in harmony.
115:
When it is said, 'Who will go and restrain them?' those monks who go saying 'I will go first, I will go first' are indeed called those who rise in harmony.

When seeing a visiting monk, those monks who perform all the major and minor duties without saying 'Go to this precinct (pariveṇa), go to that precinct, who is this person?'; those who, seeing a monk with worn-out bowl and robes, seek a bowl and robes for him through the practice of alms-round; those who seek medicine for a sick monk; those who look after a helpless sick monk in their own precinct without saying 'Go to that precinct, go to this precinct'; and those who, if there is a damaged text, invite a wise monk and have him restore that text—all these are said to perform the duties of the Saṅgha in harmony.

In the phrases beginning with 'Apannattaṃ' (what is not prescribed): prescribing a new unrighteous agreement or training rule is called 'prescribing what was not prescribed.' This is like the monks in the story of the old rug (Purāṇasanthata) in Sāvatthī. Showing the Dispensation in a way that is contrary to the Dhamma and Vinaya is called 'abolishing what was prescribed.' This is like the Vajjiputtaka monks of Vesālī a hundred years after the Blessed One's Parinibbāna. Intentionally transgressing minor and lesser offenses and not conducting oneself by undertaking the training rules as prescribed is like the followers of Assaji and Punabbasu. However, not prescribing new agreements or training rules, showing the Dispensation in accordance with the Dhamma and Vinaya, and not abolishing the minor and lesser training rules is called 'not prescribing what was not prescribed, not abolishing what was prescribed, and conducting oneself by undertaking the training rules as prescribed.' This is like the Venerable Upasena and the Venerable Yasa Kākaṇḍakaputta.

'Venerables, let the Saṅgha listen to me. Our training rules are known to the laity. Even laypeople know: "This is allowable for you Sakyaputtiya ascetics, this is not allowable for you." If we were to abolish the minor and lesser training rules, there will be those who say: "The training rules prescribed by the ascetic Gotama for his disciples lasted only as long as smoke. As long as their teacher remained, they trained in the training rules. Since their teacher has attained Parinibbāna, they no longer train in the training rules." If the time is right for the Saṅgha, let the Saṅgha...'
116:
## 
"One should not prescribe what has not been prescribed, nor abolish what has been prescribed, but should undertake and practice according to the training rules as they have been prescribed" (Cullavagga, 442)—one should practice like the Venerable Mahākassapa who established this tradition. "Only growth will occur" means there is only growth through virtues such as morality (sīla) and no decline.

"Theras" (Elders) are those who have attained stability in the Dispensation and are endowed with the qualities that make one an elder. They are called "Rattaññū" (of long standing) because they have known many nights. They are called "Cirapabbajita" because they have been ordained for a long time. They are called "Saṅghapitara" (Fathers of the Saṅgha) because they stand in the position of a father to the Saṅgha. Because they stand in the position of a father, they lead the Saṅgha and, being forerunners, guide them in the three trainings; thus they are called "Saṅghapariṇāyaka" (Leaders of the Saṅgha).

Those monks who do not show honor and respect to these elders, and do not go to attend upon them two or three times to receive advice—those elders also do not give them advice, do not speak the traditional discourses, and do not teach the essential Dhamma. Being abandoned by those elders, they decline in virtues such as the aggregates of Dhamma (sīla, etc.) and the seven noble treasures.

Those monks who show honor and respect to these elders and go to attend upon them—then those elders give them advice: "In this way you should advance, in this way you should retreat, in this way you should look ahead, in this way you should look aside, in this way you should bend, in this way you should stretch, in this way the double-robe, bowl, and robes should be carried." They speak the traditional discourses, teach the essential Dhamma, and instruct them with the thirteen ascetic practices (dhutaṅga) and the ten subjects of discourse (kathāvatthu). Abiding by the advice of the elders, those monks grow in virtues such as morality and gradually attain the Noble Path, which is the fruit of recluseship. Thus, decline and growth should be understood here.

"Punabbhava" (renewed existence) is so called because it gives rise to renewed existence. "Ponobbhavika" means having the habit of giving renewed existence; it refers to craving (taṇhā) that gives rise to renewed existence. Therefore, in the passage "they do not fall under the power of that craving (ponobbhavika)"—those monks who, for the sake of the four requisites, wander from village to village following in the footsteps of their supporters, are said to fall under the power of that craving. Others are said not to. In this regard, decline and growth are evident.

"Āraññakesu" refers to forest dwellings at a distance of at least five hundred bow-lengths. "Sāpekkhā" refers to those with craving and attachment. Indeed, even if one attains jhāna in a village-monastery, as soon as one emerges from it, one hears the sounds of women, men, children, etc., whereby even the special attainment one has reached declines. In the forest, however, as soon as one wakes from sleep, one hears the sounds of lions, tigers, peacocks, and so on. Obtaining the joy (pīti) found in the forest and reflecting on that very joy, one stands in the fruit of Arahantship. Therefore, the Blessed One praised a monk sleeping in the forest more than a monk dwelling in jhāna in a village-monastery. Thus, based on that special benefit, He taught: "They will have regard for forest dwellings."

"They will establish mindfulness only within themselves" means they will fix mindfulness in their own interior. "Pesalā" refers to those who love morality and are dear. Regarding the seven conditions for non-decline (aparihāniya dhamma) taught to these monks—some monastery-dwelling monks, lacking faith and devotion, do not desire the arrival of fellow monks. They do not perform duties such as welcoming arriving monks, taking their bowl and robes, preparing a seat, or taking a fan. If they do not do so, they are to be blamed: "The monks living in this monastery lack faith and devotion; they do not perform the major and minor duties for monks who enter the monastery."
117:
That monk hears a sound (of a woman, a man, a young girl, etc.), and by doing so, attains forest-born joy. Contemplating that very joy, he is established in the fruit of Arahatship. Thus, the Blessed One praises a monk sleeping in the forest more than a monk sitting in a village-vicinity dwelling having attained jhāna. Therefore, based on that specific benefit, He said: 'They will have regard for forest dwellings.'

'They will establish mindfulness in themselves' means they will establish mindfulness within themselves by their own effort. 'Pesalā' means those who love virtue. In this context (the seven principles of non-decline), resident monks who do not desire the arrival of fellow practitioners are without faith and without devotion. They do not perform duties such as welcoming arriving monks, receiving their bowls and robes, preparing seats, or holding fans. Then, an ill report of them spreads: 'The monks living in such-and-such a monastery are without faith and devotion; they do not perform the duties for monks who enter the monastery.' Hearing this, even when passing by the monastery gate, monks do not enter. Thus, those who have not yet come do not come. As for those who have arrived, because there is no comfortable living, even those who arrived without knowing say, 'We came thinking we would stay, but who can live with such behavior from these resident monks?' and they depart. Thus, that monastery becomes a non-dwelling for other monks. Consequently, the resident monks, not getting the opportunity to see virtuous monks, do not get to dispel their doubts, learn the training of conduct, or hear the sweet Dhamma. For them, there is no learning of the Dhamma not yet learned, nor the recitation of the Dhamma already learned. Thus, for them, there is only decline, not growth.

However, those monks who desire the arrival of fellow practitioners are faithful and devoted. They perform duties such as welcoming the arriving fellow practitioners and providing them with seats. They enter for alms together with them, dispel their doubts, and get to hear the sweet Dhamma. Then, their good reputation spreads: 'The monks of such-and-such a monastery are thus faithful, devoted, accomplished in duties, and hospitable.' Hearing this, monks come even from afar. The resident monks perform duties for them; approaching, they pay homage to a visiting monk who is senior and sit down. They take a seat and sit near a visiting monk who is junior. Having sat, they ask, 'Will you stay in this monastery or will you go?' If the visitor says, 'I will go,' they discourage them from leaving by saying, 'The lodging is suitable, alms are easy to obtain,' and so on. If the visitor is a bearer of the Vinaya, they recite the Vinaya in his presence. If he is a bearer of the Suttantas, etc., they recite those respective teachings in his presence. Abiding by the advice of the visiting elders, they reach Arahatship along with the four analytical insights (paṭisambhidā). The visiting monks, though they came thinking 'We will stay for only a few days,' say that they have lived for ten or twelve years because living with these resident monks is pleasant. Thus, one should understand the decline and growth regarding the desire or lack of desire for the arrival of fellow practitioners who have not yet come and the comfortable living of those who have arrived. Thus should the decision on the second seven principles of non-decline be understood. Those monks have a fondness for activities. Therefore, they are called 'kammarāma' (delighting in work). Because they delight in work, they are called 'kammarata'. 'Kammarāmatā anuyuttā' means excessive application or repeated application. In that phrase, the word 'kamma' refers to the work to be done. Those tasks include preparing robes, sewing robes, making double-robes (dukuṭa) etc., making jackets, preparing bowl-bags, waistbands, water filters, bowl-stands, foot-scrubbing pot-sherds, and performing tasks such as sweeping. Thus it should be understood.
118:
They arrive saying, "We will stay for only one or two days," but because of the pleasantness of living with these resident monks, they end up saying, "We will stay for ten or twelve years." Thus, decline and growth should be understood in this context.

In the second set of seven: "They are called kammārāma because they delight in work." "They are called kammarata because they take pleasure in work." "Devotion to delighting in work" means being intensely devoted and repeatedly devoted. Here, "work" refers to various duties to be performed. These include: arranging robes, making robes, supporting [the fabric], making needle cases, making alms-bowl bags, making unconnected cloths (asambaddhaka), making waistbands, making water filters, making alms-bowl stands, making foot-scrubbing potsherds, and sweeping, etc. Indeed, some monks, while performing these tasks like robe-making, spend the whole day doing only those. It is with reference to doing this all day that such delight is prohibited. However, if a monk performs these tasks only at the appropriate time, and at the time for learning Pali, he learns; at the time for recitation, he recites; at the time for duties at the cetiya courtyard, he performs those duties; at the time for reflection, he reflects—then such a monk cannot be called kammārāma (one who delights in work).

Regarding the term "na bhassārāma": a monk who spends day and night merely engaging in conversation concerning the appearance of women and men, etc., and who does not set a limit to such talk, is called bhassārāma (one who delights in talk). However, if a monk spends the day and night teaching the Dhamma or answering questions, he is one of few words and sets a limit to talk. Why? Because the Blessed One said: "Monks, when you have gathered together, you should do one of two things: either talk on the Dhamma or maintain noble silence."

Regarding the term "na niddārāma": a monk who falls asleep while walking, sitting, or lying down, overcome by sloth and torpor (thīna-middha), is called niddārāma (one who delights in sleep). However, if a monk's mind enters the bhavaṅga (life-continuum) due to physical illness, he is not called niddārāma. Therefore, the Blessed One said: "Aggivessana, I recall that in the last month of the summer, after returning from the alms round after the meal, I would spread out the double-layered outer robe (saṅghāṭi) in four folds and lie down on my right side, mindful and clearly comprehending, and fall asleep."

Regarding the term "na saṅgaṇikārāma": a monk who always lives in company, being a second to one, a third to two, or a fourth to three, and finds no pleasure in being alone, is called saṅgaṇikārāma (one who delights in company). However, if a monk finds pleasure in being alone in all four postures, he should be known as one who is not saṅgaṇikārāma.
119:
Regarding the term "na pāpiccha": monks of immoral conduct who are possessed of evil desires, wishing to make qualities they do not actually possess appear as if they do, are called pāpiccha (those with evil desires).

Regarding the terms beginning with "pāpamitta": monks who have evil friends are called pāpamitta. Because they associate with evil companions in all four postures, they are called pāpasahāya. Because they lean, slope, and incline only toward those evil friends, they are called pāpasampavaṅka.

"Oramattakena" means with a mere trifle of benefit. "Antarā" means in the interval before reaching the fruit of Arahantship. "Vosānaṃ" means settling for less, thinking "this much is enough," or stopping as if the task were finished. This means: "As long as monks do not settle for less with mere purity of virtue, or mere insight, or mere jhāna, or merely becoming a stream-enterer, once-returner, or non-returner, only growth is to be expected for the monks, not decline."

In the third set of seven, "saddhā" means being endowed with faith. That faith is of four kinds: āgamanīya-saddhā, adhigama-saddhā, pasāda-saddhā, and okappana-saddhā. Among these four, āgamanīya-saddhā belongs to the Bodhisattas of Omniscient Buddhas. Adhigama-saddhā belongs to noble persons (ariya-puggala). Devotion when "the Buddha, the Dhamma, the Saṅgha" is mentioned is called pasāda-saddhā. Faith that is established through conviction and decision is called okappana-saddhā. In this context, both of these [latter] types are intended. A person liberated by faith (saddhā-vimutta) who is endowed with such faith is like the Elder Vakkali. For such a person, the duties at the cetiya courtyard or the Bodhi-tree courtyard are as if already done. He also fulfills all duties such as those toward the preceptor (upajjhāya) and the teacher (ācariya). "Hirimana" refers to those whose minds are associated with hiri (moral shame), characterized by loathing evil. "Ottappī" refers to those endowed with ottappa (moral dread), characterized by fear of evil.

Regarding the term "bahussutā": here, there are two kinds of learnedness: pariyatti-bahussuta (learned in the scriptures) and paṭivedha-bahussuta (learned in penetration). Pariyatti refers to the three Piṭakas. Paṭivedha refers to the penetration of the Four Noble Truths. In this context, pariyatti is intended. One who has heard much of that pariyatti is called bahussuta. That pariyatti-bahussuta is of four kinds: one who is free from dependence (nissaya), one who serves the assembly, one who exhorts the bhikkhunīs, and the sabbattha-ka-bahussuta who knows the meaning in all respects. Among these four, the first three should be understood as stated in the Ovāda-vagga of the Samantapāsādikā, the Vinaya Commentary. The sabbattha-ka-bahussuta are like the Elder Ānanda. In this context, those sabbattha-ka-bahussuta are intended.
120:
"Āraddhavīriyā" refers to those who have exerted physical and mental energy. Among these two types, those who dispel physical socializing and remain solitary in the four postures by virtue of the eight grounds for the arousal of effort are said to have exerted physical energy. Those who dispel the socializing of mental defilements and remain solitary by virtue of the eight attainments (samāpatti), not allowing defilements that arise during the posture of walking to reach the posture of standing, not allowing defilements that arise during standing to reach sitting, and not allowing defilements that arise during sitting to reach lying down—suppressing defilements right where they arise—are said to have exerted mental energy.

"Upaṭṭhitassatī" refers to those who remember and repeatedly recollect deeds done long ago, such as the Elder Mahāgatimbaya Abhaya, the Elder Dīghabhāṇaka Abhaya, and the Elder Tipiṭaka Cūḷābhaya. It is said that on the fifth day after his birth, the Elder Mahāgatimbaya Abhaya saw a crow stretching its beak toward the auspicious milk-rice and made the sound "hum hum." Later, when he had become a senior Elder, he was asked by the monks, "Venerable sir, from what time can you remember?" He replied, "Friends, I can remember from the time I made that sound on the fifth day after my birth."

On the ninth day after the birth of the Elder Dīghabhāṇaka Abhaya, while his mother leaned down to kiss him, her hair-knot came undone, and a measure of jasmine flowers fell onto the infant's chest, causing him pain. Later, when he was asked by the monks, "Venerable sir, from what time can you remember?" he replied, "I can remember from the ninth day after my birth."

Regarding the Elder Tipiṭaka Cūḷābhaya, he stated, "If three gates of the city of Anurādhapura were closed and people were made to exit through only one gate, and I were to ask, 'What is your name? What is your name?', I would be able to recite their names again in the evening without asking a second time." Referring to monks of such nature, it is said "upaṭṭhitassatī."

"Paññavanto" refers to those endowed with the wisdom that discerns the arising and passing away of the five aggregates. Furthermore, by these two terms, [the Buddha] is teaching right mindfulness and insight-wisdom, which are the requisites for insight (vipassanā) for monks who practice insight meditation.

In the fourth set of seven, because mindfulness itself is a factor of enlightenment, it is called the mindfulness factor of enlightenment (satisambojjhaṅga). This method applies everywhere. Among those factors of enlightenment, the mindfulness factor of enlightenment has the characteristic of establishing (upaṭṭhāna); the investigation-of-states factor of enlightenment (dhammavicayasambojjhaṅga) has the characteristic of investigation (pavicaya); and the energy factor of enlightenment (vīriyasambojjhaṅga) has the characteristic of upholding or exertion (paggaha).
121:
The Joy Enlightenment Factor has the characteristic of pervasion (pharaṇa); the Tranquility Enlightenment Factor has the characteristic of calming (upasama); the Concentration Enlightenment Factor has the characteristic of non-distraction (avikkhepa); the Equanimity Enlightenment Factor has the characteristic of reflection (paṭisaṅkhāna). 'They will develop' (bhāvessanti) means they will increase the Mindfulness Enlightenment Factor through four causes, the Dhamma-investigation Enlightenment Factor through six causes, the Energy Enlightenment Factor through nine causes, the Joy Enlightenment Factor through ten causes, the Tranquility Enlightenment Factor through seven causes, the Concentration Enlightenment Factor through ten causes, and the Equanimity Enlightenment Factor through five causes. By this, the Buddha taught the enlightenment factors associated with the path and fruit of insight, which are a mixture of mundane and supramundane.

In the fifth heptad, 'anicca-saññā' (perception of impermanence) is the perception that arises together with the contemplation of impermanence. The same method applies to 'anatta-saññā' (perception of non-self) and so forth. These seven factors are mundane insight. It should be understood that two factors here are also supramundane, as stated in the passage: 'This is peaceful, this is sublime, namely the stilling of all formations, the relinquishing of all acquisitions, the destruction of craving, dispassion, cessation, Nibbāna.'

In the sextet, 'mettā-kāyakamma' (bodily action of loving-kindness) is bodily action performed with a mind of loving-kindness. The same method applies to verbal action and mental action. Although these are mentioned in the context of monks, they are also found among laypeople. For monks, fulfilling the duties of minor conduct (ābhisamācārika) with a mind of loving-kindness is called bodily action of loving-kindness. For laypeople, going to worship a shrine, going to worship a Bodhi tree, going to invite the Saṅgha, going out to welcome a monk seen entering the village for alms, taking his bowl, preparing a seat, and following him to see him off—such actions are called bodily action of loving-kindness.

For monks, making known the training rules of conduct, teaching meditation subjects, preaching the Dhamma, and reciting the Word of the Buddha in the Tipiṭaka with a mind of loving-kindness is called verbal action of loving-kindness. For laypeople, saying such things as: 'Let us go to worship the shrine,' 'Let us go to worship the Bodhi tree,' 'Let us listen to the Dhamma,' 'Let us make an offering of lamps and flowers,' 'Let us undertake and practice the three types of good conduct,' 'Let us give alms-food by tickets (salāka-bhatta) and so forth,' 'Let us give rainy-season robes,' 'Today let us offer the four requisites to the Saṅgha,' 'Invite the Saṅgha and prepare the food and so forth,' 'Prepare the seats,' 'Set out drinking water,' 'Go out to welcome the Saṅgha and bring them,' 'Let them sit on the prepared seats,' 'Perform the voluntary service (veyyāvacca) with desire and effort'—speaking such words is called verbal action of loving-kindness. For monks, rising early in the morning and performing bodily ablutions...
122:
"May they sit in the prepared seats; having strong desire and effort, may they perform the various duties (veyyāvacca)"—when spoken in this way, it is called verbal action associated with loving-kindness (mettā vacīkamma).

Monks rising early, attending to bodily needs, performing duties at the shrine terrace (cetiyangaṇa) and so forth, and then sitting in a secluded place thinking, "May the monks in this monastery be happy, free from enmity, and free from suffering"—this is called mental action associated with loving-kindness (mettā manokamma). The thought of laypeople, "May the venerable ones be happy, free from enmity, and free from suffering," is also called mental action associated with loving-kindness.

"Āvi ceva raho ca" means both in presence and in absence. Among these, helping junior monks in tasks such as sewing robes is called bodily action associated with loving-kindness in their presence. All forms of proper service to senior elders, such as washing their feet, paying homage, and fanning them, is also called bodily action associated with loving-kindness in their presence. Storing away wooden items (dārubhaṇḍa) and other belongings left untidily by both junior and senior monks, without looking down on them but as if one had left them untidily oneself, is called bodily action associated with loving-kindness in their absence.

Speaking respectfully as "Venerable Devatthera, Venerable Tissatthera" is called verbal action associated with loving-kindness in their presence. When inquiring about a monk not present in the monastery, saying words of affection such as "Where has our Venerable Devatthera gone? Where has our Venerable Tissatthera gone? When will he return?" is called verbal action associated with loving-kindness in their absence.

Opening eyes softened with the moisture of loving-kindness and looking with a clear, pleasant face is called mental action associated with loving-kindness in their presence. Directing the mind with the thought, "May Venerable Devatthera and Venerable Tissatthera be free from illness and free from affliction," is called mental action associated with loving-kindness in their absence.

"Lābhā" refers to the requisites obtained, such as robes. "Dhammikā" refers to those obtained righteously through the practice of alms-gathering, avoiding wrong livelihoods (micchājīva) like creating false wonders. "Antamaso pattapariyāpannamattampī" means even as little as two or three spoonfuls of alms-food contained within the bowl. In the term "appaṭivibhattabhogī," sharing is of two kinds: sharing of material things (āmisa-paṭivibhatta) and sharing among persons (puggala-paṭivibhatta). Among these, dividing in the mind as "I will give this much, I will not give that much" is called āmisappaṭivibhatta. Dividing in the mind as "I will give to such a person, I will not give to such a person" is called puggalappaṭivibhatta. One who enjoys gains without doing either of these is called an appaṭivibhattabhogī (one who shares gains without discrimination).
123:
In the phrase "sīlavantehi sabrahmacārīhi sādhāraṇabhogī," the characteristic of one who shares in common is as follows: any excellent gains received are not given to laypeople for the sake of seeking further gains, nor are they consumed alone. Instead, accepting them with the thought "May this be shared with the Saṅgha," one views them as property of the Saṅgha to be consumed after striking the bell.

Who fulfills this sāraṇīyadhamma (virtue of fraternal living), and who does not? First, an immoral person (dussīla) cannot fulfill it. This is because virtuous people do not accept his belongings. Only one with pure virtue can fulfill it without breaking the practice. In this fulfillment, the practice is as follows: if a monk gives specifically to his mother, father, teacher, or preceptor, etc., he gives what should be given, but it does not yet become sāraṇīyadhamma; it is merely the clearing of obligations (palibodhajaggana). Sāraṇīyadhamma is suitable only for one who is free from such obligations.

One who gives specifically in this way gives to the sick, the caregivers of the sick, guests, traveling monks, and junior monks who do not yet know how to handle the double-robe and bowl. After giving to them, without failing to give a little starting from the seat of the senior elder, he gives as much as anyone wishes to take. If nothing remains, he should go for alms again and, starting from the seat of the senior elder, give whatever excellent food is obtained before consuming the remainder. Because of the word "sīlavantehi," it is also proper not to give to an immoral person.

This sāraṇīyadhamma is easily fulfilled in a well-trained assembly, but not in an untrained one. In a well-trained assembly, one who receives from elsewhere does not take. Even one who does not receive from elsewhere takes only in moderation, not in excess.

This sāraṇīyadhamma is fulfilled only after twelve years for one who gives whatever is obtained by repeatedly going for alms; it cannot be fulfilled in a shorter time. If, in the twelfth year, the one fulfilling the sāraṇīyadhamma leaves a bowl full of alms-food in the hall and goes to bathe, and the senior elder of the Saṅgha asks, "Whose bowl is this?" and is told, "It belongs to the one fulfilling the sāraṇīyadhamma," and the elder says, "Bring it," and after distributing and eating all the alms-food, leaves the empty bowl—if that monk, seeing the empty bowl, feels displeasure thinking, "They have consumed it without leaving anything for me," the sāraṇīyadhamma is broken and must be fulfilled again for twelve years. This is similar to the parivāsa (probation) of the sectarians; if it is broken once, it must be fulfilled again.

If a monk thinks, "My fellow practitioners have consumed the food in my bowl without asking; I have truly gained! My human life is well-attained!" and feels joy, then he is said to have fulfilled the sāraṇīyadhamma. For a monk who has fulfilled the sāraṇīyadhamma in this way, envy (issā) does not arise, and stinginess (macchariya) does not arise. Such a monk is loved by people and easily obtains the four requisites. The food in his bowl does not run out even if he does not give it. Also, when distributing items like robes, the best...
124:
If a monk generates joy, thinking, 'My fellow practitioners are enjoying the food in my bowl without even asking; indeed, it is a great gain for me, indeed, I have well obtained this human life,' then he is said to be fulfilled in the Sāraṇīyadhamma (virtues of social solidarity).

For a monk who has thus fulfilled the Sāraṇīyadhamma, there is neither envy (issā) nor stinginess (macchariya). He is beloved by people and easily obtains the four requisites. Even when being given away, the food in his bowl does not run out. In the distribution of gifts, he receives the most excellent item. When danger or famine arrives, the deities take care to assist him.

Regarding these benefits, there are these illustrative stories: Elder Tissa, residing at Senagiri, lived depending on the village of Mahāgiri. Once, fifty great elders, traveling to the island of Nāgadīpa to worship the shrine, wandered for alms in the village of Giri but left without receiving anything. Elder Tissa, entering the village, saw them and asked, 'Venerables, did you receive alms?' They replied, 'Friend, we have wandered [but received nothing].' Knowing they had received nothing, he said, 'Venerables, please stay right here until I return.' The elders said, 'Friend, we fifty people did not receive even enough to moisten our bowls.' He replied, 'Venerables, those who reside here are capable; even if they do not receive alms, they know the right path to obtain them,' and he entered the village. At the very first house, a great female lay devotee had prepared milk-rice and stood looking out for the elder. As soon as the elder reached the door, she filled his bowl. Taking that bowl, he went to the elders and said to the Sangha Elder, 'Venerable, please accept this.' The Sangha Elder thought, 'We, so many people, received nothing, yet this monk has returned quickly having received alms. How can this be?' and looked at the faces of the other elders. Elder Tissa, knowing the meaning of that look, said, 'Venerables, this almsfood was obtained righteously and fairly; please accept it without hesitation.' Starting from the most senior elder, he served all the monks as much as they desired, and he himself ate as much as he desired.

After finishing the meal, the elders asked, 'Friend, when did you penetrate the supramundane Dhamma (lokuttara dhamma)?' He replied, 'Venerables, I have no supramundane Dhamma.' They asked again, 'Friend, are you an attainer of jhāna?' He replied, 'Venerables, I do not have that either.' They asked, 'Friend, is this not a miracle, then?' He said, 'Venerables, I have fulfilled the Sāraṇīyadhamma. From the time I fulfilled that Dhamma, even if there were a hundred thousand monks, the food in my bowl does not run out.' Hearing this, the elders said, 'Sadhu, sadhu, virtuous one! This is worthy of you.' This is the story regarding 'the food in the bowl not running out.'

This same elder, having gone to the place of distribution during the Giribhaṇḍa Great Offering at Cetiyapabbata, asked, 'What is the most excellent item in this place?' They replied, 'Venerable, two cloths.' Those [cloths]...
125:
"...will come to me," [he said]. Hearing those words, a minister informed the King, "A certain young monk speaks thus." Although the young monk’s mind was set thus, the King said, "Fine cloths are suitable only for the great elders," and set them aside, intending to give them to the great elders. While the Sangha of monks stood in order, as the King was giving them away, those cloths placed at the top did not come into the hands [of the elders]. Other cloths did. However, at the time of giving to the young monk, they came into his hands. The King, having let the cloths fall into the young monk's hands, looked at the minister's face, had the young monk sit down, gave the offering, and after dismissing the Sangha, sat near the young monk and asked, "Venerable, when did you penetrate this Dhamma?" That elder, not wishing to speak of supramundane Dhamma which he did not possess even by implication, said, "Great King, I have no supramundane Dhamma." The King asked, "Venerable, did you not say earlier [that they would come to you]?" He replied, "Great King, it is true. I am one who fulfills the Sāraṇīyadhamma. From the time I fulfilled that Dhamma, among the goods to be distributed, the most excellent item comes to me." The King said, "Venerable, it is good indeed; this speech is worthy of you," and after paying homage, he departed. This is the story regarding "the most excellent item among distributed goods coming to one."

During the peril of Brāhmaṇatissa, the villagers of Bhātara fled without informing the Elder Nun Nāgā. At dawn, the Elder Nun said to the young nuns, "The village is exceedingly silent; go and investigate the situation." They went and, knowing that everyone had fled, returned and informed the Elder Nun. Hearing this, she said, "Do not worry about their departure; apply yourselves only to your own recitation, questioning, and wise reflection." Having said this, at the time for almsround, she robed herself and, together with twelve nuns including herself, stood at the foot of a banyan tree at the village gate. The deity residing in the tree offered almsfood to all twelve nuns and said, "Ladies, do not go elsewhere; please always come right here."

The Elder Nun had a younger brother named Elder Nāga. He thought, "The danger is very great; it is not possible to survive here. I will go to the other shore." Together with twelve monks including himself, he set out from his residence and came to the village of Bhātara, thinking, "I will go after seeing the Elder Nun." Hearing that "the elders have arrived," the Elder Nun went to them and asked, "Venerables, why have you come?" Elder Nāga told her the reason. The Elder Nun requested, "Please stay in the monastery for just this one day and depart tomorrow," and the elders went to the monastery.
126:
On the following day, the Elder Nun (Therī) wandered for alms at the foot of a tree, approached the Elder (Thera), and said, "Please accept this alms-food." The Elder replied, "It is proper, Sister," and remained silent. She spoke again, "Venerable Sir, this alms-food was obtained righteously; please partake of it without hesitation." He replied, "It is proper, Sister." The Elder Nun then took the bowl and threw it into the air, where it remained suspended. The Elder said, "Sister, even if it stays at a height of seven palm-lengths, it is still the food of a bhikkhunī." He continued, "Danger does not exist at all times. When the danger has subsided and I am preaching the Ariyavaṃsa Dhamma, if I am mentally reproached with the thought, 'O alms-collecting monk, you once spent your time eating the food of a bhikkhunī,' I shall not be able to maintain my composure. Therefore, Sisters, strive with diligence," and he proceeded on his way.

The tree deity (Rukkha-devatā) thought, "If the Elder partakes of the alms-food from the Elder Nun's hand, I shall not intervene. If he does not partake, I shall intervene." Seeing the Elder departing, the deity descended from the tree and said, "Venerable Sir, please give me the bowl." Taking the bowl, the deity invited the Elder back to the foot of the tree, prepared a seat, and offered the alms-food. After obtaining an acknowledgment from the Elder who had finished his meal, the deity supported twelve bhikkhunīs and twelve bhikkhus for seven years. This story illustrates the point that "deities take care (exert effort)." Among them, the Elder Nun was one who fulfilled the Sāraṇīya-dhamma (qualities of courtesy).

Regarding the terms beginning with "Akhaṇḍāni," the decision is as follows: If a monk's training rules (Sikkhāpada) are broken at the beginning or at the end of the seven classes of offenses (Āpattikkhandha), his virtue (Sīla) is called "broken" (Khaṇḍa), like a cloth torn at the hem. If it is broken in the middle, it is called "perforated" (Chidda), like a cloth with a hole in the middle. If two or three rules are broken in succession, it is called "spotted" (Sabala), like a cow with patches of a different color (such as black or red) on its back or belly. If it is broken here and there, it is called "mottled" (Kammāsa), like a cow variegated with spots here and there. If the virtue is entirely unbroken, it is called unbroken (Akhaṇḍa), unperforated (Acchidda), unspotted (Asabala), and unmottled (Akammāsa).

Furthermore, these virtues are called "liberating" (Bhujissa) because they free one from the slavery of craving and make one a free person. They are "praised by the wise" (Viññuppasattha) because they are commended by the Buddha and other wise ones. They are "untarnished" (Aparāmaṭṭha) because they are not wrongly grasped by craving and views, and because no one can reproach the person by saying, "You have previously committed such an offense." They are called "conducive to concentration" (Samādhisamvattanika) because they bring about access concentration (Upacāra-samādhi) or absorption concentration (Appanā-samādhi).
127:
"Sīlasāmaññagatā viharissaṃti" means they will dwell possessing virtue that is equal to that of the monks living in various regions. Indeed, the virtue of Stream-enterers (Sotāpanna) and others living in the midst of the ocean or in the celestial realms is identical to the virtue of other Stream-enterers. There is no difference in the virtue associated with the Path (Magga-sīla). This was said with reference to that Path-virtue.

"Yāyaṃ diṭṭhi" refers to Right View associated with the Path. "Ariyā" means faultless (free from defilements like lust). "Niyyāti" means emancipatory (Niyyānika), leading out from the suffering of the round of rebirths. "Takkarassa" refers to one who acts according to the instructions. "Sabbadukkhakkhayāya" means for the purpose of the destruction of all suffering of the round. "Diṭṭhisāmaññagatā" means they will dwell having reached the state of sharing a common view. "Vuddhiyeva" means that for monks dwelling in this way, only growth is to be expected, not decline.

"Etadeva bahulaṃ" means that because the Buddha was near the time of his Final Nibbāna (Parinibbāna), he repeatedly gave this very Dhamma talk on virtue and so on to instruct the monks. "Iti sīlaṃ" means virtue is of such kinds, or virtue is of this extent. Here, the Fourfold Purification of Virtue (Catupārisuddhisīla) should be understood as virtue (Sīla), one-pointedness of mind (Cittekaggatā) as concentration (Samādhi), and insight-wisdom (Vipassanā-paññā) as wisdom (Paññā). In the passages beginning with "Sīlaparibhāvito," it means that when one abides in that Fourfold Purification of Virtue and brings about Path-concentration and Fruition-concentration, that concentration is fully developed through that virtue and brings great fruit and great benefit. When one abides in that concentration and brings about Path-wisdom and Fruition-wisdom, that wisdom is fully developed through that concentration and brings great fruit and great benefit. When one abides in that insight-wisdom and brings about the Path-mind and Fruition-mind, that mind is fully developed through that wisdom and is rightly liberated from the taints (Āsavas).

"Yathābhirantaṃ" means that although the Buddhas have no such thing as lack of delight or agitation, this was said according to the wishes and dispositions (Ajjhāsaya) of those to be taught. "Āyāma" means "Come, let us go." There is also the reading "Ayāma," which has the same meaning, "Let us go." The Buddha addressed the Elder as "Ānanda" because he was the one attending closely to him. The Elder then informed the monks, saying, "Friends, take your bowls and robes; the Blessed One wishes to go to such-and-such a place."

## 144-145. The Journey to Ambalaṭṭhikā
The account of the journey to Ambalaṭṭhikā is clear. The passage beginning with "Atha kho āyasmā Sāriputto" has been explained in detail in the Sampasādanīya Sutta.
128:
## Explanation of the Disadvantages of Immorality

In the passage concerning the journey to the village of Pāṭali, the term "āvasathāgāra" refers to a house (a rest-house) where guests come to stay temporarily. It is heard that in the village of Pāṭali, the royal officials of the two kings (of Vajjī and Magadha) used to come at all times, evicting the families of householders from their homes and staying there for a month or even half a month. Those people, being constantly oppressed, thought, "This will be a place for these royal officials to stay when they come," and so they built a large hall in the middle of the city. In one part of that hall, they made a place for storing goods, and in another part, a place for living. When those people heard that "The Blessed One has arrived," they thought, "We should have gone to invite the Blessed One, but the Blessed One has arrived at our place of residence on his own accord; today we shall have the Blessed One pronounce a blessing in this rest-house." It was for this purpose alone that they approached him. Therefore, they requested, "Venerable Sir, may the Blessed One accept this rest-house."

The decision regarding the phrase "yena āvasathāgāraṃ" is as follows: Those people, thinking, "The Buddhas are by nature inclined toward the forest and delight in the forest; they may or may not wish to stay within a village," did not know the Blessed One's mind and thus came without having cleaned the rest-house. Now, having known the Blessed One's mind, they thought, "We shall go ahead and clean it," and so they approached the rest-house. "Sabbasanthariṃ" means spreading it in such a way that everything is completely covered with mats.

"Dussīla" refers to one who is immoral or devoid of virtue. "Sīlavipanna" refers to one whose virtue is ruined or whose restraint is broken. "Pamādādhikaraṇaṃ" means on account of negligence.

Although this sutta is taught in terms of householders, it also applies to those who have gone forth. Indeed, if an immoral householder is negligent through such acts as killing living beings while earning a living through various crafts such as farming or trade, he cannot complete those various works in time, and thus even his original capital is destroyed. Furthermore, if he commits killing, stealing, and so on at a time when the kings have issued a decree against killing, he meets with a great loss of wealth due to punishment. An immoral monk, likewise, on account of negligence, meets with loss in terms of virtue, the word of the Buddha, jhāna, and the seven types of noble wealth.

For an immoral householder, a bad reputation spreads among the four assemblies: "This person, born in such-and-such a family, is immoral, of evil nature, has abandoned the welfare of this world and the next, and does not give even a mere ticket-food (salāka-bhatta)." For an immoral monk, a bad reputation also spreads among the four assemblies: "This monk was unable to guard his virtue, unable to learn the word of the Buddha; he lives by practicing medicine and so on, and is possessed of the six kinds of disrespect."

"Avisārada" means: Therein, an immoral householder must approach a gathering of many people with fear, thinking, "Some people will know of my deeds; if they know, they will oppress me." He sits with a dejected face, with drooping shoulders, with his face cast down, scratching the ground with his finger. Being without confidence, he is unable to speak. An immoral monk also must approach a gathering of many monks with fear, thinking, "Some monk will know of my deeds; if he knows, he will exclude me from the Uposatha and Pavāraṇā, cause me to fall from the state of a recluse, and expel me." Being without confidence...
129:
..."He lives by practicing medicine and so on, and is possessed of the six kinds of disrespect." Such an evil reputation spreads and rises in the midst of the four assemblies.

"Avisārado" means: A householder approaches with fear, thinking, "In a place where many people assemble, some will surely know of my misdeeds; if they know, they will punish me or hand me over to the royal family." He sits dejected, with drooping shoulders, with his face cast down, scratching the ground with his finger. He is unable to speak with confidence. A monk also approaches with fear, thinking, "Many monks are assembled; surely someone will know of my misdeeds; if they know, they will prohibit me from the Uposatha and Pavāraṇā, cause me to fall from the state of a recluse, and expel me." He is unable to speak with confidence. Even if some immoral person wanders about as if he were bold, he is nonetheless dejected in his inner disposition.

"Sammuḷho kālaṅkarotīti" means: While that immoral person is lying on his deathbed, the immoral deeds he has undertaken and performed appear in his mind. When he opens his eyes, he sees this world; when he closes his eyes, he sees the next world. The four lower realms appear to him. It is as if he is being struck on the head with a hundred spears. He dies crying out, "Stop it! Stop it!" Therefore, it is said, "He dies confused." The fifth point is quite clear.

Advantageous talk (the benefits of virtue) should be understood by the opposite of the meaning already stated.

"Bahudeva rattiṃ dhammiyā kathāya" means: By means of other Dhamma talks outside of the Pali text and by the talk of appreciation for the rest-house, as if bringing down the celestial Ganges, or as if squeezing a huge honeycomb a league in size to give honey to drink, he showed the Dhamma for much of the night, gladdened them, and then dismissed them. "Abhikkantā" means the night that has passed, ended, or reached destruction. "Suññāgāraṃ" means there is no separate house called a secluded house. However, in that very rest-house, they screened off one side with a curtain and prepared a couch, thinking, "The Teacher will rest here." The Blessed One, reflecting, "The use of these four postures by these people will be of great fruit," took up the lion's posture on that couch. With reference to this, it is said, "He entered the secluded house."
130:
## Explanation Regarding the Construction of Pāṭaliputta City

Sunīdha and Vassakāra refer to the two brahmins, the Brahmin Sunīdha and the Brahmin Vassakāra. Magadhamahāmatta refers to the great ministers of the King of Magadha, or they are called Magadhamahāmatta because they are endowed with great administrative authority in the country of Magadha. Building a city in the village of Pāṭali means making the village of Pāṭali into a city and constructing it. To prevent the Vajjīs means for the purpose of cutting off the entry routes of the Vajjī royals. By thousands means they were constructed in groups of one thousand each. Vatthu refers to house sites. Minds incline to build houses means the minds of those skilled in the science of geomancy (vatthuvijjā) incline toward constructing houses for the king and the great royal ministers. Those skilled in geomancy, by the power of their science, see into the ground at a depth of about thirty cubits: "This place is occupied by nāgas; this place is occupied by yakkhas; this place is occupied by spirits; here there is a stone or a tree stump." At that time, they recite their spells and construct the city as if they were consulting with the deities. Alternatively, deities possess their bodies and incline their minds to build houses in various places. Those deities, having driven stumps into the four corners, depart as soon as the house site is taken. Deities with faith do this for families with faith; only deities without faith do this for families without faith. For what reason? To the deities with faith, this thought occurs: "In this place, people will build houses, and having first invited the Saṅgha of bhikkhus to reside there, they will perform auspicious rites. Then we shall have the opportunity to see the virtuous ones, to hear the Dhamma, to hear the discussion of questions and answers, and to hear the discourse of appreciation (anumodanā); people will give offerings and share the merit with us."

With the Tāvatiṃsa deities means—for example, just as the reputation spreads that "people of that family are wise" or "bhikkhus of that monastery are very learned" based on one wise person in a family or one learned bhikkhu in a monastery—similarly, based on Sakka, the king of gods, and Vissakamma, the son of a god, the reputation spread that "the Tāvatiṃsa deities are wise." Therefore, it is said "with the Tāvatiṃsa deities"; it means they build as if consulting with the Tāvatiṃsa deities.

As far as the gathering place of noble people extends means however much space there is for the gathering of noble people; it refers to that much space. As far as the merchants' route extends means however much space there is for the trading of goods brought by merchants or the residence of merchants; it refers to that much space. This will be the supreme city means this city will be the greatest and the chief among those gathering places of noble people and trading places of merchants. Puṭabhedana means it will be a place where bundles of goods are opened, a place where packages of merchandise are unpacked. To speak extensively—even goods that cannot be obtained elsewhere in the whole of Jambudīpa will be obtained only in this city of Pāṭaliputta. Goods that have not yet arrived for sale in other cities will arrive for sale only in this city of Pāṭaliputta. Therefore, it means that only in this city of Pāṭaliputta will the bundles of goods be opened.
131:
There is a place for trading or a place for merchants to reside by virtue of the heaps of goods brought there. "This is the supreme city" means this city will be the greatest, the eldest, and the chief among those gathering places of noble people and trade routes. "Puṭabhedana" means the place of opening bundles of goods, the place of unpacking merchandise. Indeed, even goods not obtained in the whole of Jambudīpa will be obtained here; and goods not going elsewhere for sale will come here. Therefore, the meaning is that they will break the seals (open the bundles) here. He shows that every day, five hundred thousand [units of] wealth will arise: four hundred thousand at the four gates and one hundred thousand at the assembly hall.

In the phrases beginning with "Aggito vā" (or from fire), the word "vā" has the sense of "ca" (and). It means it will be destroyed by fire, by water, and by internal dissension. One part will be destroyed by fire, and they will not be able to extinguish it. The river Gaṅgā will wash away and take one part. One part will be destroyed only by the mutual dissension of people who are divided due to slanderous words, saying, "This person said this without that person saying it; that person said that without this person saying it." Having spoken thus, the Blessed One went to the bank of the Gaṅgā at dawn, washed his face, and sat down awaiting the time for alms-round.

Sunīdha and Vassakāra also thought: "Our king is a supporter of the ascetic Gotama. That king will ask us, 'I heard the Teacher went to Pāṭaligāma; did you approach that Venerable One or not?' If we say, 'We approached him,' he will ask again, 'Did you invite him or not?' If we say, 'We did not invite him,' he will blame and suppress us. Furthermore, we are building a city in this place where we have arrived; wherever the ascetic Gotama goes, ill-omened beings depart. By inviting that Venerable One, we shall have it said that it is an auspicious omen for the city." Having thought thus, they approached the Teacher and invited him. Therefore, the passage beginning with "Atha kho Sunīdhavassakārā" is stated.

"Pubbaṇhasamayaṃ" means in the morning time. "Nivāsetvā" means dressing in the lower robe in the manner of entering a village and fastening the waistband. "Pattacīvaramādāya" means taking the bowl and the robes and keeping them inseparable from the body.

"Sīlavantettha" should be resolved into "Sīlavante ettha." "Saññatā" refers to those who are well-restrained in body, speech, and mind.
132:
"tāsaṃ dakkhiṇamādiye" means one should dedicate and share the portion of the four requisites offered to the Saṅgha with those house-guarding deities; one should share the merit. "pūjitā pūjayanti" means they provide good protection, saying, "These people are not our relatives, yet they share merit with us in this way; therefore, provide them with good protection." "mānitā mānayanti" means the deities, being honored by the periodic offering of oblations (bali), respect [the humans] in return, thinking, "These people are not our relatives, yet they offer us oblations every four or six months." Being thus respected, they remove the dangers that arise.

"tato naṃ" refers to that wise person who thus honors and respects [the deities]. "orasaṃ" is like a child who is raised by being held to the breast. Just as a mother compassionately protects her own breast-born child to remove any dangers that arise and strives for that child's sake, so too do they [the deities] compassionately protect [the person]. This is the meaning. "bhadrāni passati" means one sees auspicious things.

"uḷumpaṃ" is a wooden raft made by driving nails to cross to the other shore. "kullaṃ" is a bamboo raft made by binding with creepers and such.

In the verse "ye taranti aṇṇavaṃ," "aṇṇavaṃ" is the name for a deep and wide body of water at least one yojana in extent. Here, "saraṃ" refers to a river. The meaning is: those who cross the deep and wide river of craving do so by making a bridge, which is the Noble Path. They cross by abandoning the water-filled hollows and marshes without touching them. However, while these people [ordinary folk] wish to cross even a small amount of water, they must construct a raft. The wise Buddhas and their disciples have crossed over without any raft.

## The Explanation of the First Recitation Section is finished.

## Commentary on the Discourse on the Noble Truths

"Koṭigāma" is a village built at the pinnacle (koṭi) of King Mahāpanāda's palace. "ariyasaccānaṃ" means of the truths that make one an Ariya (Noble One). "ananubodhā" is due to not knowing with mundane knowledge. "appaṭivedhā" is due to not penetrating with Path-knowledge. "sandhāvitaṃ" means hurried from one birth to another. "saṃsaritaṃ" means wandered by way of repeated coming and going.
133:
"mamañceva tumhākañca" means for me and for you. Alternatively, in this passage "sandhāvitaṃ saṃsaritaṃ," it should be understood that there has been a hurrying and wandering from birth to birth for both me and for you. "bhavanetti samūhatā" means the cord of craving, which is capable of leading from one birth to a new birth, has been well cut, severed, and made not to arise again.

## Commentary on the Destination of Enlightenment for One Not Subject to Return

"Nātikā" refers to two villages of the sons of paternal uncles (younger and elder) situated near a single pond. "Nātike" means in one of the villages named Ñāti. "Giñjakāvasathe" means in a dwelling made of bricks.

"orambhāgiyānaṃ" means those that lead to entering the lower realm, the sensual realm, and that cause rebirth only in the sensual realm. Alternatively, they are called "orambhāgiya" because they are to be abandoned by the three lower paths known as "ora" (lower). Among those lower fetters, the two fetters of sensual desire (kāmacchanda) and ill-will (byāpāda), if not yet suppressed by mundane attainments or not yet completely cut off by the Path, do not allow one to go to the higher realms—the fine-material realm and the immaterial realm—by virtue of their arising. The three fetters beginning with self-identity view (sakkāyadiṭṭhi) bring back even a being born in those fine-material or immaterial realms to be reborn again in this very sensual realm. Therefore, all five fetters are indeed called "orambhāgiya." "anāvattidhamမာ" refers to those who, by virtue of rebirth, do not have the nature of returning to this human world.

In the passage "rāgadosamohānaṃ tanuttā," the state of being "thinned" should be understood in two ways: because of occurring only once in a while, and because of the weakness of the outbursts of defilements. Indeed, for a Sakadāgāmī (Once-returner), defilements such as lust do not arise constantly as they do for worldlings (puthujjana); they arise only once in a while. And when they do arise, they do not arise very thickly as they do for worldlings; they arise very thinly, like a fly's wing. However, the Dīgha-bhāṇaka Tipiṭaka Mahāsīva Thera said: "Because a Sakadāgāmī has sons, daughters, and consorts, the defilements are thick; this statement [about thinning] is spoken only in terms of the fewness of births." That statement of Mahāsīva Thera is refuted in the Commentary, which states: "For a Sotāpanna, excluding seven births, there is no 'fewness of births' in the eighth birth. For a Sakadāgāmī, excluding two births, there is no 'fewness of births' in the five births. For an Anāgāmī, excluding the fine-material and immaterial births, there is no 'fewness of births' in the sensual realm. For an Arahant, there is no 'fewness of births' in any realm at all."

"imaṃ lokaṃ" is spoken with reference to this sensual world (kāmāvacaraloka). The meaning here is: if a person who has attained the fruit of Once-returning among humans is born in the celestial realm...
134:
If one attains the fruit of Arahantship after being reborn in the deva realm, that is good. If unable, one will certainly come to the human realm and realize it. Even if one reaches the fruit of Once-returner (Sakadāgāmi) in the deva realm, if one is reborn in the human realm and realizes the fruit of Arahantship, that is good. If unable, one will certainly go to the deva realm and realize it.

Regarding the term "avinipātadhammo", "vinipāta" means falling away or ruin. Since a Stream-enterer does not have the nature of falling away, they are called "avinipātadhamma". It means one who does not have the nature of falling into the four lower realms. "Niyato" means fixed by the "dhammaniyāma" (natural law of Dhamma) known as the higher paths. "Sambodhiparāyaṇo" means "sambodhi", the knowledge of the Four Noble Truths known as the three higher paths, is the destination, the goal, and the refuge of that person. Because they will certainly reach it, they are called "sambodhiparāyaṇo".

## Commentary on the Mirror of Dhamma Discourse (Dhammādāsadhammapariyāyavaṇṇanā)

"Vihesā" refers only to the physical weariness of the Tathāgata, Ānanda, when observing the course of knowledge, the rebirth with knowledge, and the future state with knowledge of various beings. He shows, "Ānanda, for the Buddha, there is only this physical weariness." In reality, Buddhas have no mental weariness. "Dhammādāsaṃ" is a mirror made of Dhamma (the knowledge of the Noble Path). "Yena" refers to the person who is endowed with the Path-dhamma which is like a mirror. "Khīṇāပါယဒုဂ္ဂတိဝိနိပါတော" (khīṇāpāyaduggativinipāto) is spoken by way of synonyms for hell and so on. This is because hell and so on are called "apāya" because they are devoid of the happiness called prosperity ("aya"). They are "duggati" because they are the destination and refuge of suffering. They are "vinipāta" because those who do evil fall into these four lower realms against their will.

"Aveccappasādena" means with unwavering and unshakable confidence because of knowing the qualities of the Buddha as they really are. The same method applies to the next two phrases. The details of "Itipi so bhagavā," etc., are stated in the Visuddhimagga.

"Ariyakantehi" means with (virtues) that are loved, cherished, and pleasing to the Noble Ones. For the five precepts are dear to the noble disciples because they are not abandoned even in another life. This is said with reference to those five precepts. In fact, all forms of restraint (saṃvara) are included here.

"I am a stream-enterer" is just the peak of the teaching. In fact, Once-returners and others also declare their status in the same way, saying "I am a once-returner," etc. For it is permitted for all Noble Ones to declare their special attainment in appropriate places without violating the training rules.
135:
## Commentary on the Story of the Courtesan Ambapālī (Ambapālīgaṇikāvatthuvaṇṇanā)

Regarding "He was staying in Vesālī", the prosperity of Vesālī should be understood in the manner stated in the Khandhaka, such as "At that time, Vesālī was prosperous and flourishing." "In Ambapālī's grove" means in the mango grove which was the garden of the courtesan Ambapālī. "Mindful, O monks"—the Blessed One began the teaching on the foundations of mindfulness (satipaṭṭhāna) specifically here to establish mindfulness when seeing Ambapālī. In that teaching, one is called "sato" because of being mindful. One is called "sampajāno" because of knowing clearly in various ways. It means one should live endowed with both mindfulness and clear comprehension. What should be said regarding "contemplating the body in the body," etc., will be stated in the Mahāsatipaṭṭhāna Sutta.

"Nīlā" (Blue/Dark) is a comprehensive term. "Blue-colored," etc., shows the details of that meaning. Their natural complexion was not blue; this is said because they were anointed with blue ointment. Their white clothes, silk clothes, etc., were also blue. They were adorned with blue gems and blue flowers. Their chariots were also inlaid with blue gems, covered with blue cloth, had blue banners, and were yoked to blue horses with blue armor and blue ornaments. The goads were also blue. In this way, the meaning should be understood in all terms. "Parivaṭṭesī" means "struck against" (collided with). In the phrase "Kiṃ je Ambapāli", "je" is a form of address; it means "O Ambapālī, why (did you collide)?" There is also a reading "kiñcā", but the meaning is the same. "Sāhāraṃ" has the meaning "together with the countryside." "Aṅguliṃ phoṭesuṃ" means they moved their fingers (snapped their fingers). "Ambakā" means "woman".

The genitive case "yesaṃ" is used in the sense of the instrumental; it means "by which monks (she) was not seen." "Oloketha" means "look." "Avaloketha" means "look repeatedly." "Upasaṃharatha" means "bring near." Bring this assembly of Licchavīs near to your mind as being like the Tāvatiṃsa gods. Just as the Tāvatiṃsa gods are very beautiful, inspiring, and have various colors like blue, etc., so too, look at these Licchavī kings as being equal to the Tāvatiṃsa gods.

Why did the Blessed One, after forbidding the taking of signs (nimittaggāha) in the eye and so on regarding forms and so on in hundreds of discourses, now encourage the taking of signs with great effort? It is because he desired their welfare. Among those monks, some were slack in energy...
136:
Tempting those monks with the splendor of the heavenly realms, the Buddha taught them to arouse effort in monastic duties (samaṇadhamma), saying, "For monks who practice monastic duties without negligence, such sovereign splendor is easily attainable." He also spoke thus to clarify the mark of impermanence (anicca-lakkhaṇa). Indeed, all these Licchavī princes would soon meet their destruction at the hands of King Ajātasattu. At that time, the monks standing there, seeing the glorious splendor of those Licchavī princes, would develop the mark of impermanence, thinking, "Even such glorious splendor as this is seen to reach destruction," and would attain Arahantship along with the four analytical insights (paṭisambhidā). Thus, he spoke to clarify the mark of impermanence.

Regarding the word "adhivāsetu" (let him accept), why did the Licchavīs invite the Buddha even though they knew Ambapālī had already invited him? They invited him both because of their disbelief and out of social custom. Indeed, they thought that since Ambapālī was a woman addicted to sensual pleasures, she might say "I have invited him" even without having done so. Furthermore, it is the custom of people to depart after inviting someone at the time of leaving after hearing a sermon.

## Veḷuvagāmavassūpagamanavaṇṇanā

Veḷuvagāmaka refers to Veḷuva village near the city of Vesālī. In the phrases beginning with "yathāmittaṃ," the decision should be understood. "Mittā" refers to friends. "Sandiṭṭha" refers to acquaintances who have merely met and seen each other in various places, not being very firm friends. "Sambhatta" refers to firm and devoted friends who have associated well. The meaning is: "Whichever monks have such friends in whichever places, let those monks enter the rains retreat in those respective places."

Why did the Buddha speak thus? It was for the comfortable living of those monks. Indeed, for those monks, the lodgings in the small village of Veḷuva were insufficient, and alms food was scarce. However, around Vesālī, there were many lodgings and alms food was easily obtainable. Therefore, he spoke thus. If so, why did he not dismiss them by saying, "Go as you please"? It was out of compassion for those monks. For this thought occurred to the Blessed One: "I will attain Parinibbāna in about ten months. If these monks go far away, they will not be able to see me at the time of my Parinibbāna. Then, remorse might arise in them, thinking, 'When the Teacher was about to attain Parinibbāna, he did not even give us a reminder; had we known, we would not have lived so far away.' If they live around Vesālī, they can come eight times a month to hear the Dhamma and receive the advice of the Sugata." Thus, he did not dismiss them.

"Kharo" means harsh. "Ābādho" means a disease caused by an imbalance of the elements. "Bāḷhā" means strong. "Māraṇantikā" means having death as its end, or capable of leading to the presence of the King of Death. "Sato sampajāno adhivāsesi" means that having established mindfulness well and having distinguished with wisdom, he endured it. "Avihaññamāno" means not being oppressed, without tossing and turning according to the influence of the pain...
137:
...without tossing and turning from side to side by following the course of the pain, being neither oppressed nor distressed, he endured it. "Anāmantetvā" means without informing. "Anapaloketvā" means without asking permission, which means without giving the final advice and instruction.

"Vīriyena" refers to both the effort of the preliminary stage and the effort of the attainment of fruition (phalasamāpatti). "Paṭipaṇāmetvā" means having warded off the pain. In the term "jīvitasaṅkhāra," the life-faculty (jīvitindriya) is called jīvitasaṅkhāra. The attainment of fruition by which the life-faculty is conditioned, and which, by joining together the breaking life-faculty, causes it to remain, is also called jīvitasaṅkhāra. Here, that attainment of fruition is intended as jīvitasaṅkhāra. "Adhiṭṭhāya" means having determined and maintained it. The brief meaning here is: "If I were to enter the attainment of fruition that is capable of sustaining the life-faculty."

Did the Blessed One not enter the attainment of fruition before this pain arose? He did. However, that was a momentary attainment (khaṇikasamāpatti). A momentary attainment wards off pain only while one is within the attainment.
