As soon as one emerges from the attainment, the pain overwhelms the body again, just as moss that has been parted by the falling of a stick or a potsherd closes over the water again. However, the attainment entered by means of great insight (mahāvipassanā), having cleared the sevenfold groups of materiality and the sevenfold groups of immateriality of tangles and knots, wards off pain effectively. For example, just as when a man descends into a pond and thoroughly pushes away the moss with his hands and feet, that moss takes a long time to cover the water again; likewise, for one who emerges from such an attainment, pain arises only after a long time.

Therefore, on that day, as if establishing a new insight on the throne of Great Enlightenment, the Blessed One cleared the sevenfold groups of materiality (rūpasattaka) and the sevenfold groups of immateriality (arūpasattaka) of tangles and knots, saturated them by fourteen modes, and having warded off the pain with great insight, he entered the attainment with the determination: "Let this pain not arise for ten months." The pain warded off by the attainment did not arise at all for ten months.

"Gilānā vuṭṭhito" means having been ill and then rising again. "Madhurakajāto viya" means the occurrence of heaviness and stiffness of the body, like a man who has been impaled on a spit. "Na pakkhāyanti" means they are not clear, they do not appear in their various aspects. "Dhammāpi maṃ na patibhanti" indicates that "the teachings such as the foundations of mindfulness (satipaṭṭhāna) do not appear clearly to me." However, those scriptural teachings were well-mastered by the Elder Ānanda. "Na udāharati" means he does not give the final advice. It is said with reference to not giving such advice.
138:
"Anantaraṃ abāhiraṃ" means teaching without making a distinction between internal and external, whether by way of the Dhamma or by way of the person. Indeed, one who thinks, "I will not teach this much of the Dhamma to others," is said to make the Dhamma internal. One who thinks, "I will teach this much of the Dhamma to others," is said to make the Dhamma external. Furthermore, one who thinks, "I will teach this person," is said to make the person internal. One who thinks, "I will not teach this person," is said to make the person external. The meaning is that the Dhamma was taught without making such distinctions.

"Ācariyamuṭṭhi" (the teacher's fist) refers to how teachers outside the Dispensation often have what is called a "teacher's fist." Such teachers do not tell anyone anything during their youth, and only when they are lying on their deathbed do they tell their beloved and dear pupils. Similarly, it is shown that for the Tathāgata, there is nothing held back in a "fist," thinking, "I will teach this in my old age at the final place."

"Ahaṃ bhikkhusaṅghaṃ" refers to the thought, "I alone shall lead the Saṅgha of monks." "Mamuddesiko" means a Saṅgha that has a person designated as "mine" because of the sense of being designated. It refers to one who has the thought, "Let the Saṅgha of monks be dedicated only to me and long for me; let them not exist after my passing, or let it be whatever it may be." "Na evaṃ hoti" means such a thought does not arise because envy and stinginess were already destroyed at the foot of the Bodhi tree. "Sa kiṃ" should be parsed as "Why would that Blessed One speak so?" "Āsītiko" means eighty years old. This was said to show that he had reached the final stage of life. "Veṭhamissakena" refers to the repair and binding of cart parts and wheels to make them firm. Just as an old cart is maintained by being bound together, it shows that for the Tathāgata, the four postures must be maintained by the binding of the attainment of the fruit of Arahantship.

Now, wishing to clarify that meaning, he spoke the words beginning with, "At which time, Ānanda." Therein, "sabbanimittānaṃ" refers to the signs of forms and so forth. "Ekaccānaṃ vedanānaṃ" refers to mundane feelings. "Tasmātihānanda" shows: "Because dwelling in this attainment of fruition (phala-samāpatti) is pleasant, therefore you too should dwell in this way for that purpose." "Attadīpā" means dwell making yourselves an island and a support, like an island in the great ocean. "Attasaraṇā" means be those who have yourselves as a refuge; do not have another as a refuge. The same method applies to the terms "Dhammadīpa" and "Dhammasaraṇa." "Tamatagge" is "tama-agge." The letter "t" in the middle is inserted by way of euphonic combination (sandhi). The meaning is: "These are the most excellent (aggatamā)." Thus, having cut off all unwholesome states associated with the darkness of ignorance, they will become exceedingly supreme.
139:
"These, Ānanda, shall be my monks. Among those monks, those who are desirous of training shall reach the highest state. All those monks who have the four foundations of mindfulness as their resort shall also reach the highest state." Thus, he concludes the teaching by placing the fruit of Arahantship at the summit.

## The Explanation of the Second Recitation Section is finished.

## Explanation of the Talk on the Intimation of Signs

In the phrase "He entered Vesālī for alms," when did he enter? He entered when he had departed from Ukkacela and arrived at Vesālī. It is said that after the rains retreat, the Blessed One departed from Veḷuvagāma, thinking, "I will go to Sāvatthī," and returning by the same path he had come, he eventually reached Sāvatthī and entered the Jeta Grove. The General of the Dhamma (Venerable Sāriputta), after performing his duties to the Blessed One, went to his day-quarters. When his pupils had performed their duties and departed, that Elder swept the day-quarters, spread out his leather mat, washed his feet, sat down cross-legged, and entered the attainment of fruition.

Then, having emerged from the attainment of fruition at the predetermined time, this thought occurred to Venerable Sāriputta: "Do the Buddhas attain Parinibbāna first, or do the Chief Disciples?" Then, knowing that "the Chief Disciples attain Parinibbāna first," he reflected on his own life-span. Knowing that "my life-span will continue for only seven days," he thought, "Where shall I attain Parinibbāna?"

Then he thought again, "Rāhula attained Parinibbāna in the Tāvatiṃsa heaven; the Elder Aññāsi Koṇḍañña at Lake Chaddanta. Where shall I attain Parinibbāna?" As he thought further, mindfulness arose regarding his mother: "My mother, though she is the mother of seven Arahants, is not yet devoted to the Buddha, the Dhamma, and the Saṅgha. Does she have the supporting condition (upanissaya) or not?" Upon reflection, he saw her supporting condition for the path of Stream-entry. He looked to see, "By whose teaching will the realization of the Four Noble Truths (abhisamaya) occur?" and saw, "It will occur only by my teaching, not by another's. If I remain indifferent, there will be those who criticize me, saying, 'Venerable Sāriputta is a refuge even for other people. Indeed, on the day he taught the Samacitta Sutta, one hundred thousand crores of deities attained Arahantship. The deities who attained the three lower paths are beyond counting. In other places, too, many realizations have been seen to occur. Eighty thousand families who were devoted to the Elder were reborn in heaven. Yet now, he is unable to remove his own mother from wrong view.'"

Therefore, he decided, "I will release my mother from wrong view and attain Parinibbāna in the very chamber where I was born." Thinking, "I will ask permission from the Blessed One and depart this very day," he called Venerable Cunda and spoke. How did he speak? He said, "Friend Cunda, come, let us go. Tell our company of five hundred monks, 'Friends, take up your bowls and robes.'" The General of the Dhamma...
140:
They attained the fruit of Arahantship. As for the number of devas who penetrated the three lower paths, it is beyond measure. In other places as well, many realizations (abhisamaya) of the Dhamma were seen. There were eighty thousand families who, by simply having faith in that Elder, were reborn in the celestial realms. There would be those who might criticize, saying, "This Elder is now unable to remove even his own mother's wrong view." Therefore, having made the decision, "I will free my mother from wrong view and attain Parinibbāna in the very chamber where I was born," he thought, "I will ask the Blessed One for permission and depart this very day," and then called for the Elder Cunda and said:

"Friend Cunda, give the signal to our assembly of five hundred monks: 'Friends, take your bowls and robes; the General of the Dhamma wishes to go to Nālaka village.'"

The Elder did as instructed. The monks packed their lodgings, took their bowls and robes, and came to the Elder. The Elder also packed his lodging, swept the day-quarters, and standing at the door of the day-quarters, looked at that place, reflecting, "This is now the last sight for this life; there is no coming back again." Surrounded by five hundred monks, he approached the Blessed One, paid homage, and spoke thus:

"I will now be cut off, O Lord of the World, Great Sage;
There is no more coming and going; this is my final salutation.
My life is very short; after seven days from now,
I shall lay down this body, like laying down a burden.
Permit me, O Blessed One; permit me, O Sugata;
It is the time for my Parinibbāna; my life-force is relinquished."

Because if the Buddhas say, "Attain Parinibbāna," they would be praising death, and if they say, "Do not attain Parinibbāna," they would be speaking of the virtues of the round of rebirth (vaṭṭa), and thus those with wrong views would find fault; therefore, they say neither. Thus, the Blessed One asked him, "Sāriputta, where will you attain Parinibbāna?"

"Venerable Sir, there is the birth chamber in Nālaka village in the Magadha country; I will attain Parinibbāna there," he replied. The Blessed One said, "Sāriputta, do as you think it is now time. However, it will now be difficult for your elder and younger brothers to see such a monk as you; therefore, preach the Dhamma to them."

The Elder, knowing that "The Teacher desires from me a Dhamma teaching preceded by a display of psychic powers," paid homage to the Blessed One, rose into the air to the height of a palm tree, and then descended and paid homage to the Blessed One again.
141:
Standing in the air at the height of seven palm trees, he displayed psychic transformations and preached the Dhamma. The people of the entire city gathered. The Elder descended, paid homage to the Blessed One, and said, "Venerable Sir, it is time for me to go." The Blessed One, thinking, "I will see off the General of the Dhamma," rose from the Dhamma-seat, went towards the Gandhakuṭi, and stood on a jewelled slab.

The Elder circumambulated the Buddha three times, paid homage at four places, and said, "Venerable Sir, one hundred thousand aeons and an incalculable period ago, at the feet of Anomadassī Buddha, I prostrated and aspired to see you. That aspiration of mine has been fulfilled; I have seen you. That was the first sight, and this is the last sight. There will be no more seeing you again."

Having said this, he raised his hands in salutation, radiant with the meeting of his ten fingernails, and backed away facing the Blessed One as long as he remained within sight, saying, "From now on, there is no such thing as coming and going in any place by way of death and rebirth," and having paid homage, he departed.

A great earthquake occurred, reaching as far as the edge of the ocean. The Blessed One said to the monks who stood surrounding Him, "Monks, follow your elder brother." The monks followed as far as the gatehouse. The Elder said, "Stay here, friends; be diligent," and having turned them back, he departed with only his own assembly.

People followed him, lamenting, "In the past, the Venerable One traveled on a journey from which he would return; but now, this journey is not for returning again." He turned those people back as well, saying, "Lay disciples, be diligent; conditioned things (saṅkhāra) are indeed of such a nature."

Then, the Venerable Sāriputta, while providing support to the people along the way for seven days, reached Nālaka village in the evening and stayed under a banyan tree at the village gate. At that time, a nephew of the Elder named Uparevata, who was going outside the village, saw the Elder, approached him, paid homage, and stood there. The Elder said to him, "Is your grandmother at home?" "Yes, Venerable Sir," he replied. "Go and inform her of our arrival here. And if she asks why we have come, say, 'He will stay inside the village for just one day today; prepare the birth chamber, and arrange the place of residence for five hundred monks.'"

He went and said, "Grandmother, my uncle has arrived." "Where is he now?" she asked. "At the village gate," he said. "Is he alone, or is there anyone else?" she asked. "There are five hundred monks," he said. "For what reason has he come?" she asked. He informed her of the matter. The Brahmin woman thought, "Why does he have the place for so many monks cleaned? Having become a monk when young, he probably wishes to disrobe now that he is old," and she had the birth chamber cleaned, the place for the five hundred monks prepared, and the lamps lit, and then to the Elder...
142:
The Brahmin woman thought, "Why does he have the place cleaned? Having ordained when young, does he wish to become a layman in his old age?" She had the birth chamber cleaned, prepared a dwelling place for five hundred monks, lit lamps, and sent word to the Elder.

The Elder ascended the mansion with the monks. Having ascended, he entered the birth chamber and sat down. After sitting, he dismissed the monks, saying, "Go to your own dwelling places." Just as those monks had left, a severe illness arose in the Elder; painful dysentery that could lead to death occurred, with blood entering one vessel and leaving another. The Brahmin woman, thinking, "My son's condition is unpleasant to me," stood leaning against the door of her own living quarters.

The Four Great Kings, looking out and wondering, "Where is the General of the Dhamma residing?" saw him. Realizing, "He is lying on the bed of his final passing (Parinibbāna) in the birth chamber in Nālaka village; we shall go for a final sight," they came, paid homage, and stood there. The Elder asked, "Who are you?" "Venerable Sir, we are the Great Kings," they replied. "Why have you come?" he asked. "We have come to attend to the sick," they replied. "Let it be, there is someone to attend to me. You may go," he dismissed them. After those Great Kings had left, in the same manner, Sakka, the King of the Devas, came; and after Sakka had left, Suyama and others, and Mahābrahmā came. The Elder dismissed them in the same way.

The Brahmin woman, seeing the coming and going of the deities, thought, "Who are these people who pay homage to my son and leave?" She went to the door of the Elder's chamber and asked, "Dear Cunda, what is the situation?" Cunda explained the situation and told the Elder, "Venerable Sir, the Great Lay-Devotee has come." The Elder asked, "Great Lay-Devotee, why have you come at an unseasonable time?" The Brahmin woman said, "Dear son, I have come to see you," and then asked, "Dear son, who were those who came first?" "Great Lay-Devotee, they were the Four Great Kings," he said. "Dear son, are you greater and more eminent than those Four Great Kings?" she asked. "Great Lay-Devotee, they are like temple attendants; from the time our Teacher, the Buddha, took conception, they have stood guard with swords in their hands," he said.

"Dear son, who came after they left?" she asked. "It was Sakka, the King of the Devas," he said. "Dear son, are you even greater and more eminent than Sakka, the King of the Devas?" she asked. "Great Lay-Devotee, this Sakka is like a novice who carries requisites; when our Teacher descended from Tāvatiṃsa, he followed, carrying the bowl and robes," he said. "Dear son, who was it that came shining brightly after Sakka had left?" she asked. "Great Lay-Devotee, this is Mahābrahmā, who is your refuge and teacher," he said. "Dear son, are you even greater and more eminent than my refuge, Mahābrahmā?" she asked. "Yes, Great Lay-Devotee, these are our..."
143:
"On the day our Teacher was born, the four Mahābrahmās received the Great Being with a golden net," he said.

Then, the mother Brahmin woman thought, "If my son's power is this much, how great must be the power of my son's Teacher, the Blessed One?" As she thought this, fivefold joy (pīti) suddenly arose and suffused her entire body. The Elder thought, "Joy and gladness have arisen in my mother; now is the time for a Dhamma discourse." He asked, "Great Lay-Devotee, what are you thinking?" She replied, "Dear son, even my son's virtues are this much; I am thinking about how great the virtues of my son's Teacher, the Buddha, must be." "Great Lay-Devotee, at the moment of my Teacher's birth, at his Great Renunciation, at his Enlightenment, and at the turning of the Wheel of Dhamma, the ten-thousandfold world system trembled. In virtue, concentration, wisdom, liberation, and the knowledge and vision of liberation, there is no one equal to the Buddha," he said, and expanding on "Itipi so Bhagavā..." and so forth, he delivered a Dhamma discourse related to the Buddha's virtues.

At the end of her beloved son's Dhamma discourse, the Brahmin woman was established in the Fruit of Stream-entry (Sotāpatti-phala). She said to her son, "Dear Upatissa, why did you do this? Why did you not give me this Deathless Dhamma for such a long time?" The Elder thought, "Now I have repaid the debt of my upbringing to my mother, the Brahmin woman Rūpasārī; being established in the Fruit of Stream-entry is sufficient." He dismissed her, saying, "Go, Great Lay-Devotee." Then he asked, "Cunda, what time is it?" When Cunda replied, "Venerable Sir, it is the time of early dawn," he said, "If so, assemble the community of monks." When Cunda said, "Venerable Sir, the Saṅgha has assembled," he said, "Cunda, lift me up and make me sit." So he was lifted and seated.

The Elder addressed the monks, "Friends, for forty-four years you have wandered with me. If there is any action of mine, whether of body or speech, that you did not like, friends, forgive me for that fault." They replied, "Venerable Sir, for such a long time we have followed you without leaving, like a shadow; there is nothing that we disliked. Rather, Venerable Sir, you yourself please forgive us for our faults." Then, as the glow of dawn appeared, making the great earth resound, the Elder passed away into the Nibbāna element without remainder (anupādisesa-nibbāna-dhātu). Many devas and humans performed offerings and honors at the Elder's passing.

Then, the Venerable Cunda took the bowl, robes, and water filter of the Venerable Sāriputta and went to Jetavana Monastery. He called the Venerable Ānanda and approached the Buddha. The Buddha took the water filter and, with five hundred verses, preached the virtues of the Venerable Sāriputta. Then, having a stupa built for the relics, He instructed the Venerable Ānanda to prepare to travel to the city of Rājagaha.
144:
The venerable Cunda, taking the bowl, robes, and water filter of the venerable Sāriputta, went to Jetavana Monastery and, accompanied by the venerable Ānanda, approached the Blessed One. The Blessed One took the water filter and, after speaking of the Elder's virtues with five hundred verses, had a reliquary (cetiya) built for the relics and gave a signal to the venerable Ānanda to depart for the city of Rājagaha. The Elder informed the monks. The Blessed One, surrounded by a great assembly of monks, traveled to Rājagaha. While staying there, the venerable Mahāmoggallāna attained Parinibbāna. The Blessed One took his relics, had a cetiya built, and then departing from Rājagaha, traveled gradually toward the Ganges and arrived at the town of Ukkacela. There, on the bank of the Ganges, seated and surrounded by the assembly of monks, he preached the sutta concerning the Parinibbāna of Sāriputta and Moggallāna. Departing from Ukkacela, he traveled to the city of Vesālī. Having arrived there, the Blessed One, in the morning, adjusted his lower robe and, taking his bowl and robes, entered Vesālī for alms. This is the chronological account of the matter.

In the word "nisīdana," a piece of leather (sitting cloth) is intended. "Udenacetiya" refers to the monastery built on the site of the shrine of the yakkha Udena. The same applies to Gotamaka and others. "Bhāvitā" means developed. "Bahulīkatā" means practiced repeatedly. "Yānīkatā" means made like a well-yoked vehicle. "Vatthukatā" means made like a foundation in the sense of a basis. "Anuṭṭhitā" means well-established. "Paricitā" means accumulated from all sides, well-developed. "Susamāraddhā" means well-exerted.

Having preached thus without specific limitation, the Blessed One, wishing to show it with limitation, spoke the words beginning with "Tathāgatassa kho." In that passage, "kappa" refers to the lifespan (āyukappa). Whatever the lifespan of humans is at a particular time, he could remain for the duration of that full lifespan. "Kappāvasesaṃ vā" means for a period exceeding a hundred years, which is expressed as "a little more." However, the Elder Mahāsīva said: "There is no such thing as an empty boast for the Buddhas. Just as he suppressed the deadly pains that arose at Veḷuva village for ten months, so too, by repeatedly entering that attainment and suppressing it for ten months at a time, he could remain for this entire Bhaddakappa. But why did he not remain? The physical body (upādinnaka-rūpa) is oppressed by things such as the breaking of teeth. The Buddhas, before reaching the state of broken teeth and so on, attain Parinibbāna in the fifth part of their lifespan, at a time when they are still beloved and pleasing to the multitude. Alternatively, when the Buddhas and the Great Disciples who followed the Buddha have attained Parinibbāna, the Blessed One would have to remain alone like a stump..."
145:
...(The Blessed One would have to remain alone like a stump), or surrounded by young novices. Furthermore, he might fall into a state of being disparaged, with people saying, 'Oh, look at the Buddha's assembly!' Therefore, he did not remain." Even though this was said, it is not preferred; in the Commentary, the meaning is specifically determined only as "āyukappa" (lifespan).

In the phrase "yathā taṃ mārena pariyuṭṭhitacitto," the word "taṃ" is merely a particle. Just as any other worldling whose mind is obsessed and overwhelmed by Māra would be unable to penetrate the meaning, so too (the venerable Ānanda) was unable to penetrate it. For what reason? Māra obsesses the mind of one in whom the twelve perversions (vipallāsa) have not been abandoned in every way. Since the four perversions had not yet been abandoned by the venerable Ānanda, Māra obsessed his mind. When Māra obsesses the mind, what does he do? He either shows a terrifying visual object or makes a terrifying sound heard. Then, beings, seeing or hearing that, lose their mindfulness and stand with their mouths open. He then thrusts his hand through their mouths and crushes their hearts. Consequently, they remain unconscious. But how could he be able to thrust his hand into the mouth of the venerable Ānanda? Instead, he showed a terrifying object. Because of seeing that, the Elder did not penetrate the hint and sign. Although the Blessed One knew (that Ānanda did not know), why did he call him up to three times? It was so that later, when Ānanda would beg, "Venerable Sir, let the Blessed One remain," he could say, "This is your own fault, this is your own mistake," and by thus laying the blame, he could lessen Ānanda's grief.

## Commentary on the Request of Māra

In the phrase "māro pāpimā," he is called "Māra" because he leads beings to harm and kills them. "Pāpimā" (the Evil One) is a synonym for him. He is called "Pāpimā" because he is possessed of evil states. Kaṇha, Antaka, Namuci, and Pamattabandhu are also his names. In the phrase "bhāsitā kho panesā," this Māra, in the eighth week after the Blessed One's attainment of Enlightenment, came to the foot of the Bodhi tree and said: "Blessed One, the purpose for which you fulfilled the perfections has been attained; the knowledge of omniscience has been penetrated. What is the use of your wandering in the world?" and just as he did today, he then begged: "Venerable Sir, let the Blessed One now attain Parinibbāna." And the Blessed One to that Māra...
146: The Blessed One rejected it, saying words such as "I shall not attain Parinibbāna yet." Referring to that rejection, Māra addressed him, saying, "Venerable sir, you have previously spoken these words," and so on. In that passage, "viyattā" means they are skilled in extraordinary matters by the power of the Noble Path. Similarly, "suvinītā" means well-disciplined; "visāradā" means confident. "Bahussutā" means they are learned because they have much hearing by the power of the Three Pitakas. They are "dhammadharā" because they can bear that scriptural Dhamma. Alternatively, those who possess learning of the scriptures (pariyatti-bāhusacca) and learning of realization (paṭivedha-bāhusacca) are called "learned." Because they bear the Dhamma of scripture and realization, they are "dhammadharā"; thus should the meaning be understood. "Dhammānudhammapaṭipannā" means they practice the Dhamma of insight (vipassanā) which is in accordance with the Noble Dhamma. "Sāmīcippaṭipannā" means they practice the appropriate way. "Anudhammacārino" means they are habituated to practicing in accordance with the Dhamma of insight. "Sakaṃ ācariyakaṃ" means the doctrine of their own teacher, the Buddha. All words such as "ācikkhissanti" are synonyms of one another. "Sahadhammena" means with speech accompanied by reasons and causes. "Sappāṭihāriyaṃ" means "as long as I have not taught the Dhamma making it lead out (from Saṃsāra), I shall not attain Parinibbāna." "Brahmacariyaṃ" means the entire holy life of the Dispensation, which is comprised of the three trainings (sikkhā). "Iddhaṃ" means well-developed by the power of the bliss of jhāna. "Phītaṃ" means reaching growth like a tree in full bloom, by the power of the attainment of higher knowledge (abhiññā). "Vitthārikaṃ" means widespread by the power of being established in various regions. "Bāhujaññaṃ" means known by many people, known by the power of the realization of the great masses. "Puthubhūtaṃ" means reaching expansiveness in every aspect. How is it expanded? "Yāva devamanussehi suppakāsitaṃ" means it has been well-manifested to all wise devas and humans as many as there are. "Appossukko" means "be without concern." "O Evil One, from the eighth week onwards, you have been wandering around crying out, 'Venerable sir, let the Blessed One attain Parinibbāna now; let the Sugata attain Parinibbāna.' From this day forward, be without effort; do not strive for my Parinibbāna," he said. ## Commentary on the Relinquishment of the Life-Principle. "Sato sampajāno āyusaṅkhāraṃ ossajī" means that having established mindfulness well and having delimited with knowledge, he relinquished or gave up the life-principle. In that relinquishing, the Blessed One did not relinquish the life-principle like throwing a stone with his hand. Rather, he resolved in his mind, "I shall enter meditative attainment for only three months; after three months, I shall no longer enter meditative attainment." Referring to such a mental state, it is said, "He relinquished." There is also the Pali reading "ossajji".
147:
After entering meditative attainment, he produced the thought: "From now on, I shall not enter it." Referring to the production of that thought, it is said: "He relinquished (ossaji)." There is also a reading "ussajjī". "Mahābhūmicālo" refers to a great earthquake. At that time, it is said that the ten-thousandfold world system shook. "Bhiṃsanako" means causing terror. "Devadundubhiyo ca phaliṃsu" means the celestial drums thundered; it means the sky thundered without clouds, untimely flashes of lightning emerged, and a momentary rain fell.

Why did he utter this inspired utterance (udāna)? Someone might say: "The Blessed One relinquished the life-formation out of fear, being harassed by Māra who followed him closely, saying, 'Venerable Sir, attain Parinibbāna; Venerable Sir, attain Parinibbāna.'" To prevent such an opportunity for speech and to demonstrate that there is no such thing as an inspired utterance for one who is afraid, he uttered this inspired utterance released by the force of joy (pīti).

In that inspired verse, because it is perceptible even to all dogs, jackals, and so forth, the measurable (tulita/paricchinna) state is called "tula". What is that? It is sense-sphere kamma (kāmāvacara-kamma). It is called "atula" because there is no other mundane kamma equal to it. What is that? It is sublime kamma (mahaggata-kamma). Alternatively, sense-sphere and fine-material sphere kamma are "tula", while immaterial-sphere kamma is "atula". Or, kamma with small fruit is "tula", and kamma with great fruit is "atula". "Sambhava" refers to the heap or accumulation that is the cause of birth. "Bhavasaṅkhāra" refers to the kamma that conditions renewed existence. "Awassaji" means he relinquished. "Muni" refers to the Buddha-sage. "Ajjhattarato" means delighting in his own internal states. "Samāhito" means concentrated by way of access and absorption concentration. "Kavacamiva abhindi" (broke like a coat of mail) means he destroyed the defilements (kilesa) arisen within himself. This is what is meant: He relinquished the mundane kamma, both measurable and immeasurable, which is named "sambhava" in the sense of yielding fruit and "bhavasaṅkhāra" in the sense of conditioning existence. Like a great warrior on the battlefield breaking a coat of mail, being concentrated and delighting in the internal, he broke the defilements arisen within himself.

Alternatively, "tula" means weighing or investigating. "Atula" and "sambhava" refer to Nibbāna and birth. "Bhavasaṅkhāra" refers to kamma leading to existence. The Buddha-sage, weighing in this manner: "The five aggregates are impermanent; Nibbāna, the cessation of the five aggregates, is permanent," and so forth, seeing the danger in existence and the benefit in Nibbāna, relinquished that bhavasaṅkhāra-kamma, which is the root of the aggregates, through the Noble Path that makes an end of kamma, as it is said: "It leads to the exhaustion of kamma." How? Being concentrated and delighting in the internal, like breaking a coat of mail...
148:
Delighting in the states arisen within himself, with a mind well-concentrated by the power of tranquility (samatha), he destroyed the entire net of defilements (kilesa) called 'attasambhava' (arisen in oneself) because it arises within oneself and stands enveloping the individual existence (attabhāva) like armor through the power of tranquility and insight (vipassanā) from the very beginning. Because of the absence of defilements, the kamma performed is also said to be relinquished because it does not cause rebirth (paṭisandhi). Thus, by abandoning defilements, he abandoned kamma; and since there is no such thing as fear for one who has abandoned defilements, he relinquished the life-formation (āyusaṅkhāra) without fear, and it should be understood that he uttered an inspired utterance (udāna) to make known his fearlessness.

## Explanation of the Great Earthquakes (Mahābhūmicālavvaṇṇanā)

'Yaṃ mahāvātā' means at which time the great winds blow. When the great winds blow, winds called 'ukkhepaka' (uplifting winds) arise. These winds cut off the wind that supports the water, which is nine hundred and sixty thousand yojanas thick. Then the water falls in the sky. When the water falls, the earth falls. Again, the wind, by its own power, binds and holds the water as if in a water-strainer (dhamakaraṇa). Then the water rises. When the water rises, the earth rises. In this way, the moving water causes the earth to shake. This shaking occurs even up to the present day, but because of the great thickness of the earth, the sinking and rising are not apparent.

'Mahiddhiko mahānubhāvo': He is called 'mahiddhika' (of great power) because of the greatness of the fulfillment of desired benefits. He is called 'mahānubhāva' (of great majesty) because of the greatness of the enjoyments to be experienced. 'Parittā' refers to those who are weak. 'Appamāṇā' refers to those who are strong. 'So imaṃ pathaviṃ kampeti': That person endowed with such power and majesty causes the earth to shake, like the Elder Mahāmoggallāna who terrified the heedless Sakka by exercising his power, or like the novice Saṅgharakkhita, the nephew of the Elder Mahānāga, who wished to test [his power]. It is said that this venerable one, having reached Arahantship at the very moment his hair was being shaved with a razor, thought: 'Is there any monk who, having reached Arahantship on the very day of his ordination, has ever shaken the Vejayanta Palace?' Then, knowing that 'There is no one,' he thought, 'I will shake it.' Standing on top of the Vejayanta Palace by the power of higher knowledge (abhiññā), he tried to shake it by striking it with his foot, but he was unable to do so. Then Sakka's dancing women said, 'Dear Saṅgharakkhita, do you wish to shake the Vejayanta Palace with a head that smells foul like one just out of the mother's womb? Dear, the palace is very firmly established. How could you possibly shake it?' The novice thought, 'These women are mocking me. I will ask my teacher.' Considering 'Where is my teacher, the Elder Mahānāga, who lives by the ocean?', he realized that the Elder was spending the day in a water-cave he had created in the great ocean. He went there, paid homage to the Elder, and stood.
149:
The novice reflected, 'These goddesses are mocking me; I have not yet met my teacher. Where is my teacher, the Elder Mahānāga, who lives by the ocean?' Realizing that the Elder was dwelling in a water-cave he had created in the great ocean, he went there, paid homage to the Elder, and stood. Then the Elder said, 'Dear Saṅgharakkhita, have you entered the battlefield without learning the tactics?' and asked, 'Dear, were you unable to shake the Vejayanta Palace?' He replied, 'Venerable sir, it is because I had not met my teacher.' Then the Elder said, 'Dear, if someone like you cannot shake it, who else can? Dear, have you ever seen a piece of cow dung floating on the surface of the water? Dear, those who fry cakes in a pan cut them from the edges; understand by this simile.' The novice replied, 'Venerable sir, this simile is sufficient,' and having resolved that the place where the palace stood should become water, he went towards the Vejayanta Palace. The goddesses, seeing the novice, said, 'Having gone away in shame once, the novice comes again; he comes again!' Sakka, the king of gods, said, 'Do not speak thus to my son; now he has found his teacher, he will shake the palace in a moment.' The novice then struck the pinnacle of the palace with his big toe. The palace tilted towards the four directions. The deities cried out, 'Dear Saṅgharakkhita, let the palace stand firm! Dear, let the palace stand firm!' The novice, having placed the palace in its original position, stood on top of the palace and uttered this inspired utterance: 'Only today was I ordained, today I reached the destruction of the taints (āsavakkhaya). Today I shake the palace; oh, how grand is the Buddha! Only today was I ordained... [as before] ... oh, how grand is the Dhamma! Only today was I ordained... [as before] ... oh, how grand is the Saṅgha!'

What should be said regarding the other six earthquakes besides these has already been stated in the Mahāpadāna Sutta. Thus, among these eight earthquakes, the first is due to the disturbance of elements (dhātukopa), the second is due to spiritual power (iddhānubhāva), the third and fourth are due to the power of merit (puññateja), the fifth is due to the power of knowledge (ñāṇateja), the sixth is due to the power of giving applause (sādhukāradāna), the seventh is due to the state of compassion (kāruññabhāva), and the eighth is due to lamentation (ārodana). When the Great Being (Bodhisatta) descends into his mother's womb and when he is born from it, the earth shakes due to the power of his merit. When he attains Enlightenment, it shakes due to the power of his knowledge. When he preaches the Discourse of the Turning of the Wheel of Dhamma (Dhammacakkappavattana Sutta), it shakes along with the sound of applause, being established in the power of giving applause. When he relinquishes the life-formation (āyusaṅkhāra), it shakes as if unable to endure the trembling of the mind, being established in the state of compassion. When he attains Parinibbāna, it shakes as if reaching the force of lamentation. In this context, the meaning stated by 'giving applause' and so on should be understood through the power of the earth-protecting deity. In reality, the earth, being a great primary element (mahābhūta), is insentient and thus cannot give applause and so on. In the text 'Ānanda, these are the eight causes of earthquakes,' the word 'these' refers to the meanings already pointed out. Thus ends the explanation of the causes of earthquakes.
150:
When he realized the Four Noble Truths, the earth shook, struck by the power of his penetrative knowledge (paṭivedha-ñāṇa). When he preached the Discourse on the Turning of the Wheel of Dhamma (Dhammacakkappavattana), the earth shook, established in the state of giving applause and offering praise. When he relinquished the life-force (āyusaṅkhāra), the earth shook, established in a state of compassion, unable to endure the agitation of the mind. When he attained Parinibbāna, the earth shook, being struck by the force of lamentation. This meaning should be understood through the power of the earth deity (pathavī-devatā); for indeed, the great primary element of earth, being inanimate, does not possess such qualities as giving applause.

In the statement, "Ānanda, these are the eight causes," the word "these" refers to the meanings already pointed out. By showing the causes of earthquakes to this extent, the Venerable Ānanda noted, "Today, the Blessed One has surely relinquished the life-force." The Blessed One, though knowing that Ānanda had noted it, did not give the Elder the opportunity to entreat him, but wishing to group together other sets of eight, said: "Monks, these assemblies are eight," and so on.

## Explanation of the Eight Assemblies

In that text, "an assembly of many hundreds of nobles (khattiya)" refers to an assembly of nobles similar to the gatherings of King Bimbisāra, the royal relatives, the Licchavīs, and so forth. Such assemblies can also be found in other world-systems (cakkavāḷa). "Had previously greeted" means having previously engaged in conversation. "Had previously discussed" means having previously engaged in Dhamma discussion. "Whatever their appearance was" means that although those nobles might be fair-skinned, dark-skinned, or of a brownish complexion, the Teacher is always of a golden hue. This statement is made with reference to physical appearance (saṇṭhāna).

To those nobles, only the physical appearance is apparent. In reality, the Blessed One is not like a rustic, nor is he one wearing jeweled earrings; he sits only in the form of a Buddha. However, they see only an appearance similar to their own. "Whatever their voice was" means that although those nobles might have broken voices, hoarse voices, or crow-like voices, the Teacher has only a noble voice like that of Mahābrahmā. This statement is made with reference to different languages.

Indeed, if the Blessed One sits on a royal throne and teaches, those nobles think, "Today the King is teaching with a sweet voice." When the Blessed One has finished teaching and departed, and they see the original King return, the inquiry arises: "Who was that?" In that context of "Who was that?", it means that even when they inquire, "Who was this person who just now taught so sweetly in the Māgadha or Sīhaḷa language and has now disappeared? Was it a deva or a human?", they still do not know. "For what purpose does he teach the Dhamma to those who do not know in this way?" is the question.
151:
(He taught) for the sake of establishing some latent tendencies (vāsanā). Because the Dhamma heard in this way becomes a condition in the future, he taught it with reference to future benefit. In the phrases beginning with 'Anekasataṃ brāhmaṇaparisaṃ' (many hundreds of the assembly of brahmins), the occurrence should be understood through meetings with assemblies headed by the brahmins Soṇadaṇḍa and Kūṭadanta, as well as through other world-systems (cakkavāḷa). For what purpose did the Blessed One bring up these eight assemblies? Only to show his fearlessness. Having brought this up, he said: "Ānanda, for the Tathāgata who approaches these eight assemblies and teaches the Dhamma, there is no fear or trepidation. Indeed, who should entertain the thought that the Tathāgata might be afraid upon seeing Māra alone? Ānanda, the Tathāgata, being fearless, without trembling, mindful and clearly comprehending, has relinquished the life-principle (āyusaṅkhāra)."

## Explanation of the Eight Bases of Overcoming (Abhibhāyatana)

Abhibhāyatana means the causes of overcoming (the jhāna possessing preparatory knowledge that overcomes and is a cause for special happiness). What do they overcome? They overcome opposing unwholesome states as well as objects. They overcome opposing states because of their contrary nature, and they overcome objects because of the person's superior knowledge.

In the phrases beginning with "Ajjhattaṃ rūpasaññī" (perceiving forms internally), it means having the perception of form (access perception in the kasina-form) in one's own internal kasina-form through the power of repeated preparation (parikamma). One who practices the blue kasina internally does so on the hair, bile, or the pupils of the eyes. One who practices the yellow kasina does so on the fat, the skin, the soles of the hands and feet, or the yellow parts of the eyes. One who practices the red kasina does so on the flesh, the blood, the tongue, or the red parts of the eyes. One who practices the white kasina does so on the bones, the teeth, the nails, or the white parts of the eyes. However, the kasina sign produced by the power of internal practice is not very blue, not very yellow, not very red, and not very white, but is impure.

"Alone, he sees forms externally" means that for such a person, the preparation occurs internally, but the counterpart sign (paṭibhāganimitta) occurs externally. Through the power of internal preparation and external absorption (appanā), it is said: "Being one who perceives forms internally, he alone sees forms externally." "Limited" (parittāni) means forms that have not yet been expanded (small). "Beautiful or ugly" means they may be of good color or bad color. It should be understood that this base of overcoming is spoken of only by way of a small kasina sign. In the phrase "having overcome them" (tāni abhibhuyya), for example, a person with a good digestion who receives a mere spoonful of rice and thinks, "Where will the state of having been eaten be?" and being satisfied, in one mouthful...
152:
Just as one might shrink it down and make it into a single mouthful of alms-food, saying, "Where is there anything to be eaten here?" in the same way, a person of superior wisdom and clear wisdom reflects, "What is there to be attained in this limited object? This object is no burden for me." Thus, he attains [the jhāna] by overcoming those limited kasiṇa forms. The meaning is that he reaches absorption (appanā) in this object simultaneously with the arising of the counterpart sign (paṭibhāganimitta). By the words "he knows, he sees," his attention (ābhoga) is described. And that attention occurs for one who has emerged from the attainment, not within the attainment. "He is one who has such a perception" means he has such a perception either through the perception associated with attention or through the perception associated with jhāna. For that practitioner, the perception of overcoming (abhibhavanasaññā) exists even within the attainment, but the perception associated with attention exists only for one who has emerged from the attainment.

"Immeasurable" means those that have been developed and are great. Regarding the word "overcoming," for example, just as a man who eats a lot, upon receiving a single serving of rice, does not regard it as much, saying, "Let there be more, what can this rice do for me?" in the same way, a person of superior wisdom and clear wisdom reflects, "What is there to be attained in this immeasurable object? This is not immeasurable; it is no burden for me in achieving one-pointedness of mind." Thus, he attains [the jhāna] by overcoming those kasiṇa forms. The meaning is that he reaches absorption in this object simultaneously with the arising of the counterpart sign.

"One who is percipient of formlessness internally" means one who is devoid of the preparatory perception (parikamma-saññā) regarding the internal kasiṇa forms such as hair, etc., either because of not having attained it or because of not desiring it.

"Alone, he sees forms externally" means for whom both the preparatory work and the counterpart sign have arisen only in external kasiṇas. Such a person is said to be "one who, being percipient of formlessness internally, alone sees forms externally" by virtue of external preparatory work and absorption. The remaining terms here are to be understood in the same way as explained in the fourth base of mastery (abhibhāyatana). Among these four, the "limited object" comes by way of the temperament of initial thought (vitakka-carita); the "immeasurable object" by way of the temperament of delusion (moha-carita); "beautiful color" by way of the temperament of hatred (dosa-carita); and "unbeautiful color" by way of the temperament of greed (rāga-carita). These objects are suitable for those respective temperaments. Their suitability is explained in detail in the "Description of Temperaments" (Carita-niddesa) in the Visuddhimagga.

In the fifth base of mastery and so on, "blue" (nīlāni) is said by way of encompassing all shades of blue. "Blue-colored" is said by way of the color itself. "Appearing blue" is said by way of their appearance; it means they appear as a solid mass of blue, having indistinct openings and unmixed colors. "Having a blue luster" is said by way of their radiance; it means having a blue glow, possessed of a blue light. By this, the extreme purity of those kasiṇa forms is shown. The four bases of mastery are spoken of only by way of their extremely pure color.
153:
These four bases of mastery are spoken of only by way of the power of color. The Ummā flower (flax flower) is smooth and soft, and when seen, it is purely blue. However, flowers like the Girikannika (butterfly pea), when seen, have a white element. Therefore, only this Ummā flower is taken, not those others. "Vārāṇaseyyaka" refers to cloth produced in the city of Benares. It is said that there, the cotton is soft, the spinners and weavers are skillful, and the water is clean and smooth. Therefore, that cloth is smooth on both sides; it appears smooth, soft, and glossy on both edges.

In the words "yellow" (pītāni) and so on, the meaning should be understood in this same way. Herein, the method of making the kasiṇa, the preparatory work, and the procedure for absorption—such as "one learning the blue kasiṇa grasps the sign in a flower, or a cloth, or a color element"—are all explained in detail in the Visuddhimagga. These eight bases of mastery are also brought in to show the state of fearlessness (of the Buddha). Having spoken of these, it is said: "Ānanda, for the Tathāgata who enters and emerges from such attainments, there is no fear or trepidation. Who could possibly entertain the thought that the Tathāgata would be afraid upon seeing Māra alone? Ānanda, the Tathāgata is fearless, undaunted, and being mindful and clearly comprehending, he has relinquished the life-force (āyusaṅkhāra)."

## Explanation of the Eight Liberations
The discussion on the liberations (vimokkha) has a clear meaning. These eight liberations are also brought in to show the state of fearlessness. Having spoken of these also, it is said: "Ānanda, for the Tathāgata who enters and emerges from these attainments, there is no fear or trepidation... (and so on) ...he has relinquished the life-force."

Now, without giving Venerable Ānanda an opportunity, the Blessed One began another discourse in the manner starting with "Once, Ānanda, I..." (Ekamidāhaṃ). In that discourse, "Newly Awakened" (paṭhamābhisambuddho) means in the first eighth week after becoming a Buddha. "Relinquished" (ossaṭṭho) means released or determined. Having spoken thus, he said: "Because of that relinquishing of the life-force, this ten-thousandfold world system shook."

## The Account of Ānanda’s Request
"Enough" (alaṃ) is a word of refusal. "Bodhi" means the penetration of the knowledge of the four paths. "Do you believe?" (saddahasi tvaṃ) is asking whether he believes the statement that the Tathāgata could remain for an aeon or more than an aeon. Therefore...
154:
"O Ānanda, because you believed this word, this failure to request is indeed your own fault," thus he shows.

The Blessed One began this teaching starting with "Once, I [was staying here]..." (Ekamidāhaṃ) to dispel sorrow and to point out the fault of the Venerable Ānanda in various ways, saying: "I did not call you only here in this city of Vesālī; at other times too, I called you and gave a gross sign, but you did not perceive that sign. This failure to perceive is your own fault."

"From those who are dear and appealing" (Piyehi manāpehi) refers to the separation by birth, the parting by death, and the change by becoming another state from those loved and cherished, such as mother, father, brother, sister, and so on. How can it be obtained here? Since separation from all those who are dear and appealing is a natural occurrence, even after fulfilling the ten perfections, attaining omniscience, turning the Wheel of Dhamma, performing the Twin Miracle, and descending from the Tāvatiṃsa heaven, there is no possibility of preventing the body of the Tathāgata—which is born, come to be, conditioned, and subject to disintegration—from disintegrating. Even by weeping and wailing, one cannot obtain the cause for that body not to disintegrate. "Will return to eat what was vomited" (Puna paccāvamissati) means there is no such thing as eating again what has been discarded or vomited.

"Just as this holy life" (Yathayidaṃ brahmacariyaṃ) means this holy life of the Dispensation, which is comprised of the three trainings, should be long-lasting and endure for a long time. "Addhaniyaṃ" means long-lasting. "Ciraṭṭhitikaṃ" means enduring for a long time. All the teachings beginning with "the four foundations of mindfulness" (cattāro satipaṭṭhānā) were spoken in terms of both the mundane and the supramundane. The analysis of these factors of enlightenment (bodhipakkhiya-dhamma) has been stated in detail in the Visuddhimagga, in the "Description of Purification by Knowledge and Vision of the Way" (Paṭipadā-ñāṇadassana-visuddhi-niddesa). The remaining words are clear.

## The Explanation of the Third Recitation Section is finished.

## Explanation of the Elephant-Look

"The elephant-look" (Nāgāpalokitaṃ): The bones of ordinary people are placed end to end. The bones of Paccekabuddhas are linked like the hooks of a goad. But it is not so for the Buddhas.
155:
The neck bones of the Buddhas are connected as a single unit, like a chain. Therefore, when looking back, it is not possible to turn only the neck. Just as a noble elephant, wishing to look behind, turns with its whole body, so must [the Buddha] turn. However, when the Blessed One stood at the city gate and the thought "I will look at Vesālī" merely arose in his mind—thinking, "You, who have fulfilled the perfections for many hundreds of thousands of crores of aeons, should not perform the act of looking by turning the neck"—this earth turned like a potter's wheel and made the Blessed One face the city of Vesālī. It was with reference to that (the earth turning) that this statement (Nāgāpalokita) was made.

Is it not that not only at Vesālī, but also when departing from Sāvatthī, Rājagaha, Nāḷandā, Pāṭaligāma, Koṭigāma, and Nātika, all those sights were "last looks"? Why was the elephant-look (the earth turning) not performed in those places? Because it would not be extraordinary. Turning and looking by oneself in those places is not extraordinary; therefore, he did not look in that way. Alternatively, the kings of Vesālī were near destruction; they would perish within three years. Those kings would build a shrine named Nāgāpalokita at the city gate and worship it with flowers and perfumes. That worship would lead to their welfare and happiness for a long time. Thus, he looked out of compassion for those kings.

"Ender of suffering" (Dukkhassantakaro) means one who makes an end to the suffering of the round of rebirths. "The one with vision" (Cakkhumā) means one endowed with the five types of eyes. "Attained Nibbāna" (Parinibbuto) means cooled by the extinction of defilements.

## Explanation of the Four Great Authorities

"In the Great Authorities" (Mahāpadesesu) means in the great locations, or in the reasons where great persons are referred to. It means the great reasons spoken by referring to great persons such as the Buddha.

"Should be neither welcomed" (Neva abhinanditabbaṃ) means one should not listen with immediate approval, giving a cry of "Sadhu" in joy. If one accepts it immediately in this way, later when it is said, "This does not agree (with the Sutta or Vinaya)," one might say, "This was Dhamma before, and it is Dhamma now," and thus fail to relinquish one's view. "Nor rejected" (Nappaṭikkositabbaṃ) means one should not immediately revile or reject it, saying, "What is this fool saying?" If one speaks thus, the person might not continue to speak even what is appropriate to be said. Therefore, he said, "Without welcoming and without rejecting." "Words and syllables" (Padabyañjanāni) means the syllables known as words which lead to the understanding of the meaning. "Having learned them well" (Sādhukaṃ uggahetvā) means having properly noted that "in this place the Pali text is spoken, in this place the meaning is spoken, in this place the connection of meaning is spoken, in this place the sequence is spoken"...
156:
In this context, the Pali text is stated, the meaning is stated, the connection (anusandhi) is stated, and the preceding and following (pubbāpara) are stated; having grasped these well. 'Sutte otāretabbāni' means they should be entered into the Sutta (Pali text). 'Vinaye sandassetabbāni' means they should be compared with the Vinaya.

In this context, 'Sutta' refers to the Vinaya. As it is said: 'Where was it prohibited? In the Suttavibhaṅga at Sāvatthī.' 'Vinaya' refers to the Khandhaka. As it is said: 'In the transgression of the Vinaya.' If so, the entire Vinaya Piṭaka is not yet included. If it is said that the two Vibhaṅgas are called Sutta, and the Khandhaka and Parivāra are called Vinaya, then the entire Vinaya Piṭaka is included. Alternatively, if the Suttanta Piṭaka is called Sutta and the Vinaya Piṭaka is called Vinaya, then only these two Piṭakas are entirely included. Or, if the Suttanta and Abhidhamma Piṭakas are called Sutta and the Vinaya Piṭaka is called Vinaya, even then the three Piṭakas are not yet fully included. This is because there are Buddha's words that are not named 'Sutta'. These are: Jātaka, Paṭisambhidāmagga, Niddesa, Suttanipāta, Dhammapada, Udāna, Itivuttaka, Vimānavatthu, Petavatthu, Theragāthā, Therīgāthā, and Apadāna.

However, Sudinnatthera, rejecting all the above, said, 'There is no Buddha's word that is not named Sutta; the three Piṭakas are called Sutta, while the Vinaya is the cause (for removing defilements).' Then, wishing to show that cause, he brought forth this Sutta:

'Gotamī, of whatever teachings you may know: "These teachings lead to passion, not to detachment; they lead to being fettered, not to being unfettered; they lead to accumulation (of rebirth), not to reduction; they lead to great wishes, not to fewness of wishes; they lead to discontent, not to contentment; they lead to socializing, not to seclusion; they lead to laziness, not to the arousal of energy; they lead to being difficult to support, not to being easy to support." Gotamī, you may definitely bear in mind: "This is not the Dhamma, this is not the Vinaya, this is not the Teacher's instruction." Gotamī, of whatever teachings you may know: "These teachings lead to detachment, not to passion; they lead to being unfettered, not to being fettered; they lead to reduction, not to accumulation; they lead to fewness of wishes, not to great wishes; they lead to contentment, not to discontent; they lead to seclusion, (not to socializing)..."'
157:
'(These teachings) lead to socializing and to the arousal of energy; they do not lead to laziness. They lead to being easy to support, not to being difficult to support. Gotamī, you may definitely bear in mind: "This is the Dhamma, this is the Vinaya, this is the Teacher's instruction."' (Aṅguttara Nikāya 8.53).

Therefore, 'Sutte' (in the Sutta) means they should be entered into the Buddha's words known as the three Piṭakas. 'Vinaye' (in the Vinaya) means they should be compared with the cause which is the removal of passion and so forth; this is the meaning here. 'Sutte osaranti' (they enter into the Sutta) refers to words that do not appear anywhere in the order of the Pali text, but appear to have come from one of the Gulha-Vessantara, Gulha-Ummagga, Gulha-Vinaya, or Vedalla-piṭaka, which are like raising the husk (superficial). If such words do not clearly lead to the removal of passion and so forth, they should be discarded. Therefore, He said: 'Bhikkhus, in this way, you should discard that statement.' In this manner, the meaning should be understood in all places.

'Bhikkhus, you should bear in mind this fourth Great Authority' means you should bear in mind this fourth occasion for the establishment of the Dhamma.

In this context, this miscellaneous information should be known: the four Great Authorities in the Sutta, the four Great Authorities in the Khandhaka, the four ways of answering questions, the Sutta, the Suttānuloma (conformity to Sutta), the Ācariyavāda (teacher's tradition), the Attanomati (one's own opinion), and the three Councils (Saṅgīti).

Among those, when deciding the Dhamma and Vinaya as 'This is the Dhamma, this is the Vinaya,' these four Great Authorities (from the Sutta) are the standard. Only the words that agree with these four should be accepted; other words that do not agree should not be accepted, no matter how much they are proclaimed.

When deciding on what is allowable and what is not allowable as 'This is allowable, this is not allowable,' the four Great Authorities taught in the Khandhaka are the standard, in the manner of: 'Bhikkhus, whatever I have not rejected as unallowable, if it conforms to what is unallowable and goes against what is allowable, that is not allowable for you,' and so forth. The explanatory discussion of those Great Authorities is stated in the Vinaya Commentary named Samantapāsādikā. According to the method stated there, whatever conforms to what is allowable, that alone is allowable; other things are unallowable. Thus the conclusion should be made.

A question to be answered categorically, a question to be answered analytically, a question to be answered with a counter-question, and a question to be put aside—these four are called the ways of answering questions (pañhabyākaraṇa). Among those four, if asked 'Is the eye impermanent?', it should be answered categorically as 'Yes, it is impermanent.'
158:
(If asked 'Is the eye impermanent?',) it should be answered: 'Yes, it is impermanent.' The same method should be noted for the ear-sensitivity and so on. This question is called a question to be answered categorically (ekaṃsavyākaraṇīya-pañha).

To one who asks 'Is only the eye called impermanent?', it should be answered by analyzing thus: 'Not only the eye is impermanent; the ear is also called impermanent, and likewise the nose is called impermanent.' This question is called a question to be answered analytically (vibhajja-vyākaraṇīya-pañha).

To one who asks 'Is the ear as the eye is? Is the eye as the ear is?', one should counter-question: 'In what sense do you ask?' If he says, 'I ask in the sense of seeing,' it should be answered: 'No.' If he says, 'I ask in the sense of impermanence,' it should be answered: 'Yes.' This question is called a question to be answered by counter-question (paṭipucchā-vyākaraṇīya-pañha).

However, if one asks 'Is the soul the same as the body?' and so forth, it should be set aside by saying: 'This question has been left unexplained by the Blessed One.' This question should not be answered. This question is called a question to be set aside (ṭhapanīya-pañha). Thus, when such questions are encountered in that manner, these four ways of answering questions are the standard. The question should be answered by means of these ways of answering.

Regarding 'Sutta' and so forth: 'Sutta' refers to the three Piṭakas as recited in the three Councils. 'Suttānuloma' (conformity with the Sutta) means what is suitable and in accordance with the Pāḷi texts. 'Ācariyavāda' (the teachers' tradition) refers to the Commentaries (Aṭṭhakathā). 'Attanomati' (personal opinion) refers to one's own intuition arising from following a method or from understanding the Suttas and so forth in sequence. Among these four, the Sutta should not be rejected; one who rejects the Sutta is said to reject the Buddha himself. As for 'Suttānuloma' (what is suitable and in accordance with the Pāḷi), only that which agrees with the Sutta should be accepted, not otherwise. 'Ācariyavāda' also should only be accepted if it agrees with the Sutta, not otherwise. 'Attanomati' is the weakest of all; it too should only be accepted if it agrees with the Sutta, not otherwise.

The Council of five hundred Arahants, the Council of seven hundred Arahants, and the Council of one thousand Arahants are called the three Councils. Only the Pāḷi text that appears in these three Councils is the standard; other blameworthy texts (gārayha-sutta) should not be accepted. It should be understood that even if certain words and syllables seem to fit into those three Councils, if they do not fit into the Sutta and do not appear in the Vinaya, they are not to be accepted.

## Commentary on the Story of Cunda the Smith's Son
'Kammāraputtassa' means 'to the son of a goldsmith.' That smith's son was a wealthy merchant who became a Stream-enterer (Sotāpanna) upon his first sight of the Blessed One, and he built and offered a monastery in his own mango grove. With reference to his building and offering a monastery in his mango grove, it is said: 'Ambavane' (in the mango grove).

'Sūkaramaddavaṃ' refers to the meat of a single, large pig that is neither too young nor too old, which was naturally available. That meat is both soft and tender. Having had that meat prepared well...
159:
...and cooked—this is the meaning. Some teachers say: 'Sūkaramaddava' is the name of soft rice cooked with the five products of the cow; just as milk-rice is called 'gavapāna,' this is the name of a cooking method. Others say: 'Sūkaramaddava' is a method of preparing a medicinal elixir (rasāyana) found in the Rasāyana texts; Cunda prepared that elixir with the intention that 'the Blessed One might not pass away.' Deities from the four great islands, which are surrounded by two thousand small islands, infused divine essence (ojā) into that meal of rice mixed with pork.

For what purpose did he utter this lion's roar: 'I do not see [anyone else who can eat this]'? It was to free himself from the reproach of others. It should be understood that he uttered this like the roar of a lion to free himself from the reproach of others, so that those who might wish to say that he buried his leftovers in a hole and destroyed them instead of giving them to monks or laypeople would have no opportunity to speak upon hearing these words.

After eating the pork-mixed meal, the sensation (pain) arose; however, it did not arise because of the eating. If he had not eaten it, a very harsh sensation would have arisen. Because he ate the delicate food, the Blessed One's sensation was only slight. Because it was only slight, he was able to travel on foot. 'Virecamāno' means while he was constantly purging blood, he spoke thus for the purpose of attaining Parinibbāna at the place he desired. It should be understood that these verses were established by the Elders who compiled the Dhamma (Dhamma-saṅgāhaka).

## Commentary on Fetching Water
'Ingha' is a particle in the sense of urging. 'Accodakā' means having clear water. 'Sātodakā' means having sweet water. 'Sītodakā' means having cool water. 'Setakā' means having pure water because of the absence of mud. 'Suppatitthā' means having good landing places (banks).

## Commentary on the Story of Pukkusa the Mallan
'Pukkusa' is his name. 'Mallaputto' means the son of a Mallan king. The Mallans, it is said, rule the kingdom in turns. During the time when their turn has not yet arrived, they engage in trade. This Pukkusa also engaged in trade; having yoked five hundred wagons, he would travel in front when the wind blew from the front of the wagons, and when the wind blew from behind, he would send the caravan leader ahead and follow behind himself. At that time, because the wind blew from behind, this Pukkusa sent the caravan leader ahead...
160:
He mounted a vehicle made of all kinds of jewels, departed from the city of Kusinārā, and entered the road, thinking, "I will go to the city of Pāvā." Therefore, it is said, "He was one who had entered the long-distance road from Kusinārā to Pāvā."

Āḷāra is his name. It is said that this ascetic had long, yellowish-brown eyes; therefore, he was named Āḷāra. Kālāma is his clan name. "Yatra hi nāma" means "whoever." "Neva dakkhati" means "did not see." However, because it is associated with the word "yatra," this meaning of "addasa" (did not see) is expressed with a future tense suffix (dakkhati—will see). In such instances, this use of the future tense is a characteristic of grammar.

"Niccharantīsu" means while wandering about. "Asaniyā phalantiyā" means while making a loud sound as if a ninefold thunderbolt were breaking. There are nine types of thunderbolts: Asaññā, Vicakkā, Saterā, Gaggarā, Kapisīsā, Macchavilolikā, Kukkuṭakā, Daṇḍamaṇikā, and Sukkhāsanī. Among these nine, the Asaññā thunderbolt causes loss of consciousness. The Vicakkā thunderbolt creates a circle. The Saterā thunderbolt falls like lightning. The Gaggarā thunderbolt falls with a "gag-gag" sound. The Kapisīsā thunderbolt is like a monkey raising its eyebrows. The Macchavilolikā thunderbolt is like a quivering fish. The Kukkuṭakā thunderbolt falls like a cock with spread wings. The Daṇḍamaṇikā thunderbolt falls like a plow. The Sukkhāsanī thunderbolt utterly destroys the place where it falls.

"Deve vassante" means while it was thundering without rain and then raining intermittently. "Ātumāyaṃ" means residing depending on the city of Ātumā. "Bhusāgāre" means in a straw hut at the threshing floor. "Ettheso" means this multitude of people has gathered because of this reason (the death of beings due to the thunderbolt). "Kva ahosi" means where were you? "So taṃ bhante" means "Venerable Sir, that you..."

"Siṅgīvaṇṇaṃ" means having a color like the color of Siṅgī gold. "Yugamaṭṭhaṃ" means a pair of smooth and fine cloths (a pair of delicate garments). "Dhāraṇīyaṃ" means to be worn by me from time to time. It is said that Pukkusa would wear that cloth only on such festival days and store it away at other times. This refers to such a pair of excellent auspicious garments. "Anukampā upādāya" means out of compassion for me. The word "acchādehi" (clothe) is a figurative expression; it means "give one to me and one to Ānanda."

When asked whether the Elder Ānanda accepted that robe, the answer is: Yes, he accepted it. Why did he accept it? Because his duty of service had reached its conclusion. Even though the Venerable Ānanda had practiced in his role as an attendant by rejecting such gains, he accepted it because that duty of service had reached its end. Furthermore, for twenty-five years of service, the Venerable Ānanda had never received any material gift from the Blessed One. He also accepted it to cut off the opportunity for people to say, "Ānanda, it seems, was unable to please (the Buddha)." One more reason is that the Blessed One thought, "Even if Ānanda accepts it, he will not wear it himself, but only for me..."
161:
Even though the Venerable Ānanda had served the Blessed One for twenty-five years, he had never before received any material gift from the Blessed One. He accepted the robe also to cut off the opportunity for the words of those who might say, "Venerable Ānanda must be someone unable to fulfill the Blessed One's wishes." Furthermore, the Blessed One knew, "Even if Ānanda accepts the robe, he will not wear it himself; he will offer it only to me. By Pukkusa the Mallaputta honoring Ānanda, the Saṅgha will also be honored; thus, there will be a great mass of merit for that prince." Therefore, He had one robe given to the Elder. The Elder also accepted it for that very reason. "Dhammiyā kathāyā" means with a discourse of appreciation for the robes.

"Bhagavato kāyaṃ upanāmitaṃ" means brought close to the Blessed One's body by way of wearing and dressing. The Blessed One then wore one of those two robes as an undergarment and one as an upper garment. "Hataccikaṃ viya" means just as an ember whose flames have gone out glows only on the inside but has no radiance on the outside, so it appeared as having its radiance covered on the outside.

"Ānanda, on these two occasions," when it is said, why does the complexion of the body become so clear on these two occasions? It is because of the excellence of nutriment and because of powerful joy. Indeed, on these two occasions, the deities throughout the entire universe infuse essence (ojā) into the food; when that exquisite food enters the stomach, it produces a clear physical form. Because of the clarity of the form produced by nutriment, the sense faculties, with the mind as the sixth, shine exceedingly. On the day of attaining Enlightenment, powerful joy arose in the Blessed One as He reflected, "Indeed, the mass of defilements I have accumulated for many hundreds of thousands of billions of aeons has been abandoned today"; the mind became clear, and when the mind is clear, the heart-blood becomes clear; when the heart-blood is clear, the sense faculties, with the mind as the sixth, shine exceedingly. On the day of His Parinibbāna also, powerful joy arose in the Blessed One as He reflected, "Today, I shall enter the city called the Great Deathless Nibbāna, which has been entered by many hundreds of thousands of Buddhas"; the mind became clear, and when the mind is clear, the heart-blood becomes clear; when the heart-blood is clear, the sense faculties, with the mind as the sixth, shine exceedingly. Thus, it should be understood that it happens this way on these two occasions due to the excellence of nutriment and powerful joy. "Upavattana" refers to the Sāla grove which is a turning point from the east to the north. "Antarena yamaka-sālānaṃ" means between the twin Sāla trees.

The verse beginning with "Siṅgīvaṇṇaṃ" was placed (in the text) at the time of the Council (Saṅgīti).
162:
Regarding the phrase "Having bathed and drunk" (nahatvā ca pivitvā ca), it is said that at that time, while the Blessed One was bathing in the river, the fish and turtles within the river and the forest thickets on both banks all turned the color of gold. "The Mango Grove" (ambavanaṃ) refers to the mango grove situated on the bank of that same river. Regarding the phrase "to the Venerable Cundaka" (āyasmantaṃ cundakaṃ), the explanation is as follows: at the moment of approaching that mango grove, the Venerable Ānanda Thera remained behind wringing out his water-garment, while the Venerable Cunda Thera was near the Blessed One. Then the Blessed One addressed the Venerable Cunda.

The verses beginning with "The Buddha, having gone to the Kakudhā River" (gantvāna buddho nadikaṃ kakudhaṃ) were also inserted only at the time of the Council. In those verses, "The Blessed One here in the Dhamma" (bhagavā idha dhamme) means that the Blessed One always teaches the scriptures (pariyatti) in this Dispensation (sāsana); it means he teaches the eighty-four thousand aggregates of Dhamma. "He sat" (nisīdi) means he sat in front of the Teacher. During this interval, the Venerable Ānanda Thera followed and arrived. The Blessed One then addressed the Venerable Ānanda who had thus arrived.

"Loss" (alābhā) refers to not obtaining the benefits of giving that others obtain. "Poorly gained" (dulladdhaṃ) means that even the human life gained through special merit is poorly gained. "Of yours" (yassa te) refers to your (alms-food). Who can know whether the rice was undercooked or overcooked? After consuming what kind of final alms-food did the Tathāgata attain Parinibbāna? (One might think) the alms-food you gave might be just any insignificant meal, which could cause distress (therefore, this was said to prevent such thoughts). "Gain" (lābhā) refers to the benefits of giving to be obtained in this life and in the future life. "Well gained" (suladdhaṃ) means that human life is well gained for you. "Equal in fruit" (samasamaphalā) means they have equal results in every respect.

An objection might be raised: Having consumed the alms-food given by Sujātā, the Blessed One realized the Four Noble Truths; that meal was consumed at a time when greed, hatred, and delusion still existed (before becoming a Buddha). However, this meal given by Cunda was consumed at a time when greed, hatred, and delusion had been extinguished. Why, then, do these two meals have equal fruit? They have equal fruit because of equality in attaining Parinibbāna, equality in the entry into attainments (samāpatti), and equality in recollection (anussaraṇa). To elaborate, having consumed the alms-food given by Sujātā, the Blessed One attained Parinibbāna through the element of Nibbāna with residue (sa-upādisesa-nibbānadhātu); having consumed the alms-food given by Cunda, he attained Parinibbāna through the element of Nibbāna without residue (anupādisesa-nibbānadhātu). Thus, they are equal in fruit due to equality in attaining Parinibbāna. Furthermore, just as he entered into two hundred and forty billion (24,000 crore) attainments on the day of his Enlightenment, he also entered into all those same attainments on the day of his Parinibbāna. Thus, they are equal in fruit due to equality in the entry into attainments. Moreover, Sujātā later heard: "This is not a tree deity; this is a Bodhisatta. Having consumed the milk-rice I offered, he attained the unsurpassed Perfect Enlightenment (sammāsambodhi)."
163:
It is said that after the Blessed One had penetrated and realized Omniscience, he subsisted for seven weeks (49 days) solely on the milk-rice I offered. Hearing this, that merchant's daughter named Sujātā felt powerful joy and gladness while recollecting, "Great indeed is my gain!" Later, for Cunda too, hearing that "I have offered the final alms-food; because of my alms-food, the Blessed One attained Nibbāna, the pinnacle of the Dhamma; after partaking of my alms-food, the Blessed One attained parinibbāna in the Nibbāna-element without remainder of the aggregates of resultants and kamma-born matter," powerful gladness arose while recollecting, "Great indeed is my gain!" Thus, because the recollection is similar, it should be understood that they have equal fruits.

"Conducive to fame" (yasasaṃvattanika) means the fruit that brings about a retinue. "Conducive to lordship" (ādhipateyyasaṃvattanika) means the fruit that brings about the state of being a leader.

"From restraint" (saṃyamato) means for one who restrains through moral restraint, established in the restraint of virtue. "Enmity is not accumulated" (veraṃ na cīyati) means the fivefold enmity does not increase. "The skilled one abandons evil" (kusalosa ca jahāti pāpakaṃ) means the person endowed with wisdom abandons unwholesome, low evil without remainder through the Noble Path. "With the destruction of lust, hatred, and delusion, he is extinguished" (rāgadosemohakkhayā sa nibbuto) means that person, having abandoned this evil, is cooled through the extinction of defilements due to the destruction of lust, etc. Thus, the Blessed One, seeing clearly the excellence of Cunda's gift and his own excellence as the recipient, uttered this inspired utterance (udāna).

## The Explanation of the Fourth Recitation Section is finished.

## Explanation of the Twin Sal Trees

In the phrase "with a great Saṅgha of monks" (mahatā bhikkhusaṅghena saddhiṃ), there is no numerical limit to the monks. Because from the time he dispelled the pain at Beluva village, hearing that "the Blessed One will soon attain parinibbāna," among the monks who arrived from various places, not even one departed. Therefore, it was a Saṅgha that exceeded counting. In the phrase "the Mallas' Sal Grove at Upavattana" (upavattanaṃ mallānaṃ sālavanaṃ), just as one must go from the bank of the Kalamba River through the gate of the Rājamatū Monastery to the Thūpārāma, so too one must go from the far bank of the Hiraññavatī River to the Sal Grove garden. Just as the Thūpārāma is in the southwest corner of Anurādhapura, so too that Sal Grove is in the southwest corner of the city of Kusinārā. Just as the road entering the city from the Thūpārāma through the south gate goes eastward and turns back to the north, so too the Sal Grove from the garden goes eastward and turns back to the north. Therefore, that grove is called "Upavattana." Between...
164:
"Yamaka-sālānam uttara-sīsakaṃ" means that there was a row of Sāla trees at the head of that couch and a row of Sāla trees at the foot. Among those rows, one young Sāla tree was close to the head, and one young Sāla tree was close to the foot. Alternatively, "Yamaka-sālā" refers to Sāla trees that stand intertwined with each other by their roots, trunks, branches, and leaves, as stated in the Mahā-aṭṭhakathā. "Prepare the couch" means that in that garden, there was a couch used as a bed for the royalty; he said, "Prepare it," referring to that couch. The Elder Ānanda also prepared and offered that very couch.

"Ānanda, I am weary, I will lie down," he said. To explain in detail—
The Gocarī elephant, the Kaḷāpa elephant, the Gaṅgeyya elephant, the Piṅgala elephant, the Pabbateyya elephant,
The Hemavata elephant, the Tamba elephant, the Mandākinī elephant, the Uposatha elephant,
And the Chaddanta elephant as the tenth;
These ten are the most excellent among elephants.
