In this verse, the strength of ten ordinary elephants, called Gocarī, is equal to the strength of one Kaḷāpa elephant. Calculating by ten-fold increases, the Blessed One's strength, which was equal to the strength of a thousand crores of ordinary elephants, reached exhaustion from the time he partook of Cunda's alms-food, like water poured into a basket. From the city of Pāvā to the city of Kusinārā is a distance of three gāvutas; although he traveled with great effort, sitting and resting at twenty-five places along that journey, the Blessed One entered the Sāla grove only at the time of sunset, at twilight. Thus, the pain of the disease came pressing upon his entire health. As if to show this fact, and as if to cause spiritual urgency (saṃvega) in all the people of the world, he said, "Ānanda, I am weary, I will lie down."

Why did the Blessed One come to this place with such great effort? Was it not possible to attain Parinibbāna elsewhere? Indeed, attaining Parinibbāna is possible anywhere. However, he came here for three reasons. The Blessed One saw thus: "If I attain Parinibbāna elsewhere, the occasion for the Mahāsudassana Sutta will not arise. Only if I attain Parinibbāna in the city of Kusinārā can I preach, adorned in two recitation sections, how I enjoyed in the human world the same kind of prosperity that is enjoyed in the celestial world. Hearing that discourse, many people will take it to heart that wholesome deeds should be performed."
165:
He saw another reason: 'If I attain Parinibbāna elsewhere, Subhadda will not see me. And that Subhadda is one who can be tamed only by a Buddha, not by a disciple; the disciples are not able to tame him. But when I am attaining Parinibbāna in Kusinārā, he will approach me and ask questions. At the conclusion of the answers to his questions, he will be established in the Refuges, receive the lower and higher ordinations in my presence, take up a subject of meditation, and while I am still alive, reach Arahantship and become the last disciple.'

He saw yet another reason: 'If I attain Parinibbāna elsewhere, there will be a great quarrel over the distribution of the relics; blood will flow like a river. If I attain Parinibbāna in Kusinārā, the Brahmin Dona will settle that dispute and divide the relics.' It should be understood that for these three reasons, the Blessed One came here with such great effort.

Regarding the term 'Sīha-seyyā' (Lion's posture), there are four types of lying down: the posture of those who enjoy sensual pleasures, the posture of hungry ghosts, the posture of a lion, and the posture of a Tathāgata.

Among these: 'Monks, for the most part, beings who enjoy sensual pleasures lie on their left side'—this is the Kāmabhogī-seyyā. Among them, there are generally none who lie on their right side.

'Monks, for the most part, hungry ghosts lie on their backs'—this is the Peta-seyyā. Because they have little flesh and blood, hungry ghosts, whose skeletons are intertwined, are unable to lie on one side; they lie only on their backs.

'Monks, the lion, the king of beasts, takes his rest on his right side... he is satisfied'—this is the Sīha-seyyā. The lion, the king of beasts, being of great majesty, places his two front paws in one place and his two hind paws in another place, tucks his tail between his thighs, and having noted the position where the front paws, hind paws, and tail are placed, he lies down with his head on top of his two front paws. Even if he sleeps all day, when he wakes up, he wakes without fear. Lifting his head, he carefully re-examines the position where his front paws and so on were placed. If any part has moved from its original position, he becomes dissatisfied, thinking, 'This is not suitable for your birth and your bravery,' and he lies down again in that very place, not going out for food. If they remain unmoved, he becomes very joyful, thinking, 'This is suitable for your birth and your bravery,' and he gets up...
166:
The king of lions, having performed the stretch called the lion’s yawn (sīhavijambhita), shaking his mane, and roaring the lion’s roar three times, sets out in search of food. “Sleeping with the fourth jhāna is called the Tathāgata’s sleep” (Aṅguttara 4.246). Among those types of sleep, the lion’s posture (sīhaseyyā) is mentioned here. This sleep is called the noble sleep because it is a posture of great power and majesty. “Foot upon foot” (pāde pādaṃ) means placing the right foot over the left foot. “Placing over” (accādhāya) means placing it slightly beyond. If the ankles touch ankles and knees touch knees, pain often arises, the mind cannot be concentrated, and the sleep is uncomfortable. If they are placed slightly beyond so as not to touch, pain does not arise, the mind becomes concentrated, and one can sleep comfortably. Therefore, he lay down in this manner. Since he had reached the sleep from which one does not rise (anuṭṭhānaseyyā), it is not said here, “mindful of the thought of rising.” In this context, “not rising” should be understood in terms of the physical body; as for sleep, there was no opportunity for the life-continuum (bhavaṅga) to occur for the Blessed One that night. This is because in the first watch, he preached the Dhamma to the Mallas; in the middle watch, he preached to Subhadda; in the last watch, he exhorted the Sangha of monks; and at the break of dawn, he attained Parinibbāna.

“All in full bloom” (sabbaphāliphullā) means all the Sāla trees were covered with flowers of a single color from root to tip. Not only the twin Sāla trees, but all trees were in full bloom. Not only in that park, but in the entire ten thousand world systems, flowering plants bloomed and fruit-bearing plants bore fruit. Trunk-lotuses bloomed on the trunks of all trees, branch-lotuses on the branches, vine-lotuses on the vines, sky-lotuses in the sky, and stalk-lotuses bloomed by piercing through the ground. The entire great ocean was covered with lotuses of five colors. Mount Himavā, three thousand yojanas in extent, was extremely delightful, like a dense bundle of peacock feathers, like a continuous network of flower garlands, like a well-fastened floral crest, and like a well-filled flower basket.

“They scatter over the Tathāgata’s body” (te tathāgatassa sarīraṃ okiranti) means the terrestrial deities shook the trunks, branches, and twigs of those twin Sāla trees and showered them down upon the Tathāgata’s body; the meaning is that they scattered flowers over his body. “They cover” (ajjhokiranti) means they scatter as if covering him completely. “They strew” (abhippakiranti) means they scatter repeatedly and continuously.
167:
“Divine Mandārava flowers” (dibbāni mandāravapupphāni) are those that originate in the Nandā lotus pond in the deva world; they are golden in color, have leaves the size of a leaf-umbrella, and carry pollen the size of a large bushel. Not only Mandārava flowers fell from the sky, but other divine flowers such as Pāricchattaka and Kovilāra (coral tree) flowers were also filled into golden baskets and cast down from the sky by deities stationed at the rim of the universe, in the Tāvatiṃsa heaven, and in the Brahma world. When these flowers reached the vicinity of the Tathāgata’s body, they did not scatter haphazardly in between but showered only upon the Tathāgata’s body with fine flower pollen.

“Divine sandalwood powder” (dibbāni candanacuṇṇāni) refers to white sandalwood powder prepared by the deities. Not only the sandalwood powder of the deities, but also that prepared by Nagas, Garudas, and humans showered upon the Tathāgata’s body. Not only white sandalwood powder, but all kinds of divine aromatic powders such as black sandalwood and red sandalwood, as well as orpiment (haritāla), collyrium (añjana), gold powder, silver powder, and various divine perfumes were filled into golden and silver caskets and cast down by deities stationed at the rim of the universe and other places; they did not scatter haphazardly in between but fell and showered extensively only upon the Tathāgata’s body.

“Divine instruments” (dibbāni tūriyāni) refers to musical instruments prepared by the deities. Not only those of the deities, but all instruments—stringed, percussion, solid, and wind—belonging to devas, Nagas, Garudas, and humans within the ten thousand world systems, gathered in this single universe and were played in the sky.

“Divine songs” (dibbāni saṅgītāni) refers to the songs of the deities named Varuṇavāraṇa, who are said to be long-lived deities. Having heard that “A Great Man (Mahāpurisa) has been born in the human world and will become a Buddha,” they began weaving garlands, thinking, “We will take them and go on the day he is conceived.” While they were weaving, they heard, “The Great Man has been conceived in his mother’s womb.” When asked, “For whom are you weaving?” they replied, “It is not finished yet; we will take them and go on the day he is born from the womb.” Again, hearing “He is born,” they said, “We will go on the day of the Great Renunciation.” After he lived in the house for twenty-nine years, hearing “Today he has gone forth in the Great Renunciation,” they said, “We will go on the day of his Enlightenment.” After he practiced austerities for six years, hearing “Today he has attained Enlightenment,” they said, “We will go on the day he sets the Wheel of Dhamma in motion.” Hearing “He spent seven weeks at the Bodhi tree and went to Isipatana to set the Wheel of Dhamma in motion,” they said, “We will go on the day of the Twin Miracle.” Hearing “Today he performed the Twin Miracle,” they said, “We will go on the day he descends from Tāvatiṃsa.” Hearing “Today he has descended from Tāvatiṃsa,” they said, “We will go on the day he relinquishes the life-principle.”
168:
Upon hearing, "He has made his descent from the deva world," they said, "We shall go on the day of his descent from the deva world." Upon hearing, "Today he has made his descent from the deva world," they said, "We shall go on the day he relinquishes the life-force." Upon hearing, "Today he has relinquished the life-force," they said, "It is not over yet; we shall go on the day of his Parinibbāna."

When they heard, "Today, the Blessed One has lain down on his right side between the twin Sāla trees, mindful and clearly comprehending, in the lion's posture; he will attain Parinibbāna in the last watch of the night. For whom are you going?"—they said: "What is this? They say, 'Only today he took conception in his mother's womb, only today he emerged from his mother's womb, only today he went forth in the Great Renunciation, only today he became a Buddha, only today he set in motion the Wheel of Dhamma, only today he performed the Twin Miracle, only today he descended from the deva world, only today he relinquished the life-force, and now, it is said, only today he will attain Parinibbāna.' Surely he should remain at least for the duration of a morning meal on the second day! For him who attained Buddhahood by fulfilling the ten perfections, such an occurrence is indeed unbecoming."

Thus saying, they came carrying flowers that were not yet fully arranged as they desired. Finding no space within the world-system, they clung to the rim of the world-system, running to and fro, holding hand to hand and neck to neck. Focusing on the Triple Gem, they sang praises of the thirty-two marks of a Great Man, the six-colored rays, the ten perfections, the five hundred and fifty Jātakas, and the fourteen types of Buddha-knowledge. At the end of each song, they cried out, "Great is his fame! Great is his fame!" It was with reference to this that it was said: "Divine songs also resounded in the sky in honor of the Tathāgata."

While the Blessed One was lying on his right side between the twin Sāla trees, he saw the great exertion of the assembly gathered from the surface of the earth to the rim of the world-system, and from the rim of the world-system to the Brahma world, and he addressed the Venerable Ānanda. Therefore, it was said: "Then the Blessed One addressed the Venerable Ānanda... in honor of the Tathāgata." Having shown such grand honor, and wishing to show that he was not truly honored by such means, he said: "Not by this much, Ānanda, (is the Tathāgata honored)," and so forth.

This means: "Ānanda, when I lay at the feet of the Buddha Dīpaṅkara, combining the eight factors and making the resolution (abhinīhāra), I did not make that resolution for the sake of flowers, scents, instruments, and songs; nor did I fulfill the perfections for their sake. Therefore, I am not truly honored by such worship."
169:
...seeing this, he addressed the Venerable Ānanda. Therefore, it was said: "Then the Blessed One addressed the Venerable Ānanda... in honor of the Tathāgata." Having displayed such grand honor, and wishing to show that he is not truly revered by such material offerings of many flowers, scents, instruments, and songs, he spoke the words beginning with: "Not by this much, Ānanda."

This means: "Ānanda, when I lay at the feet of the Buddha Dīpaṅkara, combining the eight factors and making the resolution (abhinīhāra), I did not make that resolution for the sake of flowers, scents, songs, and instruments; nor did I fulfill the perfections for their sake. Therefore, I am not truly honored by such material worship (āmisa-pūjā)."

Why did the Blessed One, who elsewhere praised the merit of offering even a single Umma flower while reflecting on the Buddha's virtues—describing its fruit as immeasurable even by a Buddha's knowledge—reject such grand worship here? He rejected it out of compassion for the assembly and out of a desire for the long-lastingness of the Dispensation (Sāsana). For if the Blessed One had not rejected it, in the future, when it is time to practice virtue, they would not fulfill virtue; when it is time to practice concentration, they would not fulfill concentration; when it is time to practice insight, they would not develop the womb of insight. They would live merely urging attendants to perform offerings. Material worship cannot sustain the Dispensation for even a single day, or even for the time it takes to drink a cup of gruel. Even a thousand monasteries like the Mahāvihāra and a thousand stupas like the Mahācetiya cannot sustain the Dispensation. Merit belongs only to the one who performs the deed. Right practice (sammā-paṭipatti) alone is the worship befitting the Tathāgata. That practice alone is what he desired, and only that practice can sustain the Dispensation. Therefore, wishing to show that practice, he spoke the words beginning with: "Whoever, Ānanda..."

In that passage, 'dhammānudhamma-ppaṭipanno' means one who practices the preliminary path (pubbabhāga-paṭipadā) that is in accordance with the ninefold supramundane Dhamma. That very practice, being appropriate, is called 'sāmīci' (proper). One who is established in that proper practice is 'sāmīci-ppaṭipanno'. One who practices and fulfills that 'anudhamma' known as the preliminary path is 'anudhamma-cārī'.

By 'preliminary path' (pubbabhāga-paṭipadā), one should understand the right practice starting from virtue (sīla), the regulations of conduct (ācāra-paññatti), and the undertaking of dhutaṅga practices, up to the stage of Gotrabhū-knowledge. Therefore, if a monk, established in the six kinds of disrespect, transgresses the regulations and leads his life through wrong livelihood, he is not one who 'practices the Dhamma in accordance with the Dhamma'. But if a monk does not transgress even slightly the rules of training, the Buddha's discipline, the Buddha's boundaries, and the Buddha's guidelines, he is truly called 'dhammānudhamma-ppaṭipanno'. The same principle applies to bhikkhunīs. If a layman lives committing the five enmities (breaking the five precepts) and the ten unwholesome paths of action, he is not 'dhammānudhamma-ppaṭipanno'. But if a layman is one who fulfills the three refuges, the five precepts, and the ten precepts; who observes the eight Uposatha precepts eight times a month; who gives alms; who makes offerings of scents and flowers; who cares for his mother and father; and who serves virtuous recluses and brahmins—he is truly called 'dhammānudhamma-ppaṭipanno'. The same principle applies to laywomen.
170:
"Paramāya pūjāya" means with supreme worship. Only this nirāmisa-pūjā (non-material homage) is capable of sustaining my Sāsana. As long as these fourfold assemblies worship me with this homage unmixed with material things, for that long my Sāsana will shine and flourish in the midst of the sky like the full moon. This is what is shown.

## Description of the Elder Upavāṇa

"Apasāresi" means he moved aside. "Apehi" means go away. With just a single word, the Elder put down the palm-leaf fan and stood to one side. The words starting with "Upaṭṭhāko" were spoken referring to the fact that he was not a permanent attendant during the period of the first enlightenment. When Venerable Ānanda said, "Venerable Sir, this venerable one is Upavāṇa," Venerable Ānanda perceived that there might be some fault in Venerable Upavāṇa. At that time, the Blessed One, intending to say, "Now I shall speak of this Elder's faultlessness," spoke the words beginning with "Yebuyyena Ānanda." In those words, "yebuyyena" (mostly) was said referring to the fact that the non-percipient (asaññasatta) and formless (arūpa) deities were left behind. "Apphuṭo" means not touched or not filled. It is said that even in a space the size of a hair-tip near the Blessed One, ten, then ten more, great powerful deities stood, having created subtle forms. Beyond them, they stood in groups of twenty, thirty, forty, fifty, and sixty. These deities did not obstruct one another with hands, feet, or clothing. There was no need to say, "Move aside for me, do not bump into me." As taught in the Samacitta Sutta: "Those deities, being ten, twenty, thirty, forty, or fifty, stood even in a space as small as the point of an awl, yet they did not harm one another." "Ovārento" means obstructing or blocking. The Elder was naturally large in body, like a young elephant. When he wore his pāṃsukūla robes, he appeared extremely large.

"Tathāgataṃ dassanāya" means those deities complained because they could not see the Blessed One's face. If one asks, "Could they not see through the Elder?" Yes, they could not. Deities can see through worldlings (puthujjanas), but they cannot see through those whose taints are destroyed (khīṇāsavas). Moreover, due to the Elder's great majesty and overflowing power, they could not even approach him.
171:
Why is it that only the Elder Upavāṇa has such great majesty and power, and not other Arahants? It is because he had been a guardian deity at the cetiya of Kassapa Buddha.

To elaborate: when Vipassī Buddha attained Parinibbāna, a single cetiya was built for his bodily relics, which were like a solid mass of gold. For Buddhas who have a long life-span, there is only a single cetiya. People built that cetiya to a height of one yojana, using golden bricks one cubit long, one span wide, and two inches thick, using orpiment and realgar for the mortar work, and using only sesame oil for the water work. After that, the earth-dwelling deities (bhumma devas) raised it by one yojana, then the sky-dwelling deities (ākāsa devas) by one yojana, then the heat-cloud deities (uṇhavalāhaka devas) by one yojana, then the cloud deities (abbhavalāhaka devas) by one yojana, then the Cātumahārājikā deities by one yojana, and then the Tāvatiṃsa deities by one yojana. Thus, it became a cetiya seven yojanas high. When people came bringing flowers, scents, clothes, and so on, the guardian deity took them and worshipped the cetiya even while they were watching.

At that time, this Elder Upavāṇa was a wealthy Brahmin (brahmana-mahāsāla) and went there taking a single golden-colored cloth. The deity took the cloth from the hand of that wealthy man and worshipped the cetiya. Seeing that act of worship, the Brahmin was filled with faith and made a wish: "May I also become a guardian deity at the cetiya of such a Buddha in the future." After passing away from that life, he was reborn in the celestial realm. While that future Elder was wandering through the celestial and human realms, Kassapa Buddha appeared in the world and attained Parinibbāna. For that Buddha too, there was only a single bodily relic. Taking that relic, they built a cetiya one yojana high. He became the guardian deity at that cetiya. When the Sāsana disappeared, he was reborn in heaven, and in the time of our Blessed One, he passed away from that heaven, took rebirth in a noble family, went forth into homelessness, and attained Arahantship. Thus, it should be understood that because he came after being a guardian deity at a cetiya, the Elder Upavāṇa possessed great majesty and power.

With the words "Ānanda, the deities are complaining," the Buddha showed: "Ānanda, the deities are complaining; there is no other fault in my son Upavāṇa."

Why did he ask, "Venerable Sir, what are those deities like?" "Venerable Sir, you say 'the deities are complaining'; what are those deities like that you are mindful of?"...
172:
Venerable Ānanda asked, "The Blessed One said, 'The deities are reproaching.' What kind of deities are thinking of the Blessed One? Do they approve of the Blessed One's Parinibbāna?" Then the Blessed One, saying "I do not speak of the cause of approval," and wishing to show the deities' disapproval, spoke the words beginning with "Santānanda."

In that passage, "ākāse pathavīsaññiniyo" means that they created earth in the sky and, being possessed of the perception of earth on that created ground, (they acted thus). "Kandanti" means they weep. "Chinnapātaṃ papatanti" means they fall down in all directions without consideration, as if they were cut in the middle. "Āvaṭṭanti" means they roll about and return to the very place where they fell. "Vivaṭṭanti" means they roll away from the place where they fell to another part. Alternatively, deities who stretch out their two legs and toss and turn repeatedly—once forward, once backward, once to the left, and once to the right—are also described as "āvaṭṭanti vivaṭṭanti."

"Ānanda, the deities who perceive earth on the earth" refers to the saying that the natural earth is unable to support the deities. In that natural earth, the deities sink down like Hatthaka Brahmā. Therefore, the Blessed One said, "Hatthaka, create a coarse physical form." Thus, it was said, "pathaviyaṃ pathavīsaññiniyo" with reference to those deities who created an earth that could support them upon the natural earth.

"Vītarāgā" refers to the Anāgāmī and Arahant deities who have abandoned grief and are like stone pillars.

## Description of the Four Places Stirring Emotion (Catusaṃvejanīyaṭṭhānavannanā)

"Vassaṃvuṭṭhā" means that during the time of the Buddha, monks would assemble at two times: near the time of entering the rains retreat (Vassa) to receive meditation subjects (kammaṭṭhāna), and after the rains retreat to report the special attainments achieved through the practice of the meditation subjects they had taken. Just as in the time of the Buddha, so too in the island of Tambapaṇṇi (Sri Lanka), monks on this side of the river (Ganges/Mahaweli) assembled at the Lohapāsāda (Brazen Palace), and monks on the other side of the river assembled at the Tissamahāvihāra. Among them, the monks on this side of the river, when the time for the rains retreat approached, would bring brooms and bundles for disposing of rubbish, assemble at the Mahāvihāra, and perform plastering work at the Cetiya. Then, having made an appointment saying, "Come and assemble at the Lohapāsāda when the rains retreat is over," they lived in comfortable places. After the rains retreat, they would come and assemble in the circle of monks who were bearers of the five Nikāyas at the Lohapāsāda. Among those monks, those who were proficient in the Pāli recitals would recite the Pāli; those who were proficient in the Commentaries (Atthakathā) would recite the Commentaries.
173:
If any monk should cause a mistake or deviation in either the Pāli or the Commentary, they would investigate by asking, "From whom did you learn this Pāli or Commentary?" and then correct it to be straight and accurate, making him learn it again. The monks living on the other side of the river did exactly the same at the Tissamahāvihāra. When the monks assembled at these two times, those who had previously departed after taking meditation subjects before the rains retreat would return to report their special attainments; it was with reference to such monks that the words beginning with "Venerable Sir, those who have previously completed the rains retreat" were spoken.

"Manobhāvanīya" means those who are developed or esteemed by the mind. Alternatively, it refers to those monks who develop their minds, increase them, and wash away the dust of passion (rāgaraja) and so forth; this is the meaning. It is heard that a certain Elder (Thera) accomplished in duties, upon seeing an elderly monk, would not remain seated out of pride but would go out to meet him, take the umbrella, bowl, and robes from his hands, dust off the bench and offer it, and after he was seated, perform the major and minor duties and prepare the lodgings (senāsana) for him. Upon seeing a junior monk, he would not remain silent but would stand nearby and perform the duties. That Elder, desiring not to fall away from such practices of duty, made this request.

Then the Blessed One thought, "Ānanda is thinking that he will no longer have the opportunity to see the monks who are worthy of esteem. Come now, I will tell him the places for seeing those monks worthy of esteem, where Ānanda, residing without having to wander here and there, will be able to see the monks who are worthy of esteem." Thinking thus, he spoke the words beginning with "Cattārimāni."

In that passage, "saddhassa" refers to one who has a mind of faith in the Triple Gem beginning with the Buddha and who is accomplished in duties; in such a person, all duties such as the duties of the stupa courtyard (cetiyangaṇa) are clearly seen to have been performed from the morning onwards. "Dassanīyāni" means things worthy of seeing, or places that should be visited for the purpose of seeing. "Saṃvejanīya" means things that cause a sense of urgency or emotion (saṃvega). "Ṭhānāni" means causes or geographical locations.

This statement "Ye hi keci" was spoken to show the benefit of wandering to visit shrines (cetiyacārikā). Among those wandering to visit shrines, there is no need to speak of those who wander about sweeping the stupa courtyards in various places, washing the seats, and watering the Bodhi tree. It shows that even those who set out with a faithful heart, saying "We will worship the shrine in such and such a monastery," and pass away during the journey, will certainly be established in heaven without any obstacle.
174:
## Explanation of the Opening Words Regarding the Questions of the Venerable Ānanda

"Not seeing, Ānanda" means not seeing women (mātugāma). This shows that not seeing is the supreme practice in relation to women. Indeed, as long as a monk staying in a dwelling with the door closed does not see a woman who has come and is standing at the door, greed certainly does not arise in him, nor does his mind waver. However, if there is seeing, both might occur. Therefore, He said: "Not seeing, Ānanda (is best)." "But if there is seeing, Lord, how should we act?" This is a question asking how one should act when there is seeing in places such as where one goes to receive alms.

Then the Blessed One said that it is better to speak with a man standing with a sword, saying, "If you speak with me, I will cut off your head right here," or with an ogress (yakkhiṇī) standing and saying, "If you speak with me, I will crunch and eat your flesh right here." This is because, due to such speech, only one's current existence (attabhāva) is destroyed, and it does not lead to the experience of boundless suffering in the lower realms. However, if there is conversation and mutual talk with a woman, intimacy (vissāsa) arises; when there is intimacy, mental involvement (otāra) occurs; and a monk with an involved mind reaches the ruin of virtue (sīlabyasana) and becomes one who fills the lower realms. Therefore, He said: "Not speaking (is best)." It has also been said:

"One may speak with one who holds a sword in hand, one may even speak with a demon;
One may even sit with a venomous snake, whose bite leaves no one alive;
But a monk alone should never speak with a woman alone."

"But if one must speak" means if a woman asks questions all day, or requests the precepts (sīla), or wishes to hear the Dhamma, or asks a problem, or if there is a duty to be performed by the monks for her. At such a time, people would say of a monk who does not speak, "This one is mute, this one is deaf, he sits with his mouth bound after eating." Therefore, one must certainly speak. He asks how a monk who thus speaks should act. Then the Blessed One, referring to this advice: "Monks, come, establish the thought of 'mother' towards women who are of an age to be mothers; establish the thought of 'sister' towards those of an age to be sisters; establish the thought of 'daughter' towards those of an age to be daughters," said: "Mindfulness, Ānanda, should be established."

"Abyāvaṭā" means be unconcerned, without taking up the burden. "Sāratthe ghaṭatha" means strive for the supreme goal, Arahantship. "Anuyuñjatha" means exert effort for the attainment of that goal.
175:
Exert effort. In that context, "appamattā" means being possessed of unremitting mindfulness. "Ātāpino" means having effort that burns away defilements through the application of energy. "Pahitattā" means dwell with a mind directed towards Nibbāna because of being indifferent to the body and life.

By the words "But how, Lord?" he asks how those wise nobles and others should act. "Venerable Ānanda, how should we act regarding the body of the Tathāgata?"—thus those wise nobles and others will certainly ask me; "How shall I give an answer to them?" is the meaning of the question. "Ahatena vatthena" means with new cloth from the Kāsi country. "Vihatena kappāsena" means with well-carded cotton. Because Kāsi cloth is fine, it does not absorb oil, whereas cotton does. Therefore, He said, "with well-carded cotton." "Āyasāya" means made of gold. Here, gold is intended by the word "ayasa."

## Explanation of Persons Worthy of a Stupa

In the words "A Wheel-turning Monarch (Rājā Cakkavatti)," why does the Blessed One allow the worthiness of a stupa only for a Wheel-turning Monarch who died after living in the midst of a household, and not for a virtuous worldling (puthujjana) monk? Because it is not extraordinary. If stupas for worldling monks were allowed, there would be no space left for stupas first in the island of Sri Lanka (Tambapaṇṇidīpa), and similarly in other places. Therefore, considering "They will not be extraordinary," He did not allow it. A Wheel-turning Monarch appears only as a single individual; therefore, his stupa is extraordinary. Nevertheless, for a virtuous worldling person, it is indeed proper to perform great honor and offerings just as for an Arahant monk who has attained Parinibbāna.

## Explanation of the Wonderful Qualities of Ānanda

"Vihāra" here intends a circular pavilion (maṇḍalamāla); having entered it. "Kapisīsa" refers to the door-post or the cross-bar (monkey-head) situated at the edge of the door-frame. "Rodamāno aṭṭhāsi" means that the Venerable Ānanda thought thus: "The Teacher has told me of the dwelling place that causes spiritual urgency (saṃvega); He has told me of the benefit of going on a pilgrimage to the shrines (cetiyas); He has answered the question on how to act towards women; He has declared the practice to be performed on His own body; He has told of the four types of persons worthy of a stupa; surely the Blessed One will attain Parinibbāna today." While he was thinking thus, powerful sorrow arose. Then this thought occurred to him: "Weeping in the presence of the Blessed One is inappropriate; I will go to a suitable place and diminish my grief." Thinking so, he did accordingly. Therefore, it is said, "he stood weeping." The word "ahañca vatāmhi" should be resolved as "ahañca vata amhi." It means, "I am indeed still a trainee (sekha), there is still work to be done for the sake of the higher paths." There is also a variant reading "ahaṃ vata amhi." "Yo mama anukampako" means "The Blessed One who has compassion for me, who has always admonished me, now..."
176:
Thinking, "I will go and diminish my grief," that Venerable Ānanda did so. Therefore, [the Blessed One] said, "He stood weeping."

"Ahañca vatamhī" should be analyzed as "Ahañca vata amhi." There is also a reading "Ahaṃ vatamhī." It means, "I am indeed still a trainee (sekha) (there is still work to be done for the sake of the higher paths)." "Yo mama anukampako" means "The Blessed One who always has compassion for me and always admonishes me." He lamented greatly, saying, "From now on, to whom shall I give water for washing the face tomorrow? Whose feet shall I wash? Whose dwelling place shall I clean? Whose bowl and robes shall I carry as I wander?" "Āmantesi" means that [the Buddha] called for him because he did not see the Elder Ānanda in the midst of the Saṅgha of monks.

"With loving-kindness in bodily action" (mettena kāyakammena) refers to bodily actions such as giving face-washing water, performed through the power of a mind associated with loving-kindness. "Hitena" means bodily action performed out of a desire for welfare and growth. "Sukhena" means performed only with happiness and joy, without a pained or dejected mind. "Advayena" means bodily action not performed in two parts. It means it is performed without distinction between being in one's presence or behind one's back, unlike some who act only in presence and not in absence, or only in absence and not in presence. "Appamāṇena" means bodily action that is immeasurable. It is intended to show that even the universe (Cakkavāḷa) is too narrow, even the highest plane of existence (bhavagga) is too low; the bodily action performed by you is much more than that.

"With loving-kindness in verbal action" (mettena vacīkammena) refers to verbal actions such as announcing the time for washing the face, performed through the power of a mind associated with loving-kindness. Furthermore, saying "It is well, Bhante" after hearing an admonition is also verbal action associated with loving-kindness. "With loving-kindness in mental action" (mettena manokammena) refers to mental action such as sitting in a secluded place after performing personal services early in the morning and thinking, "May the Blessed One be free from illness, free from harm, and be happy." "Katapuññosi" shows that he is one who has fulfilled the aspirations for perfections (pāramī) for a hundred thousand aeons. Alternatively, "Katapuññosi" means "Do not become negligent by being complacent with just this much; rather, exert effort." It shows that "If you exert effort in this way, you will quickly become one free from taints (anāsava); at the time of the Dhamma Recitation (Saṅgīti), you will attain Arhatship. Service performed for a Buddha like me is never without fruit."

Having spoken thus, as if spreading the great earth, as if expanding the sky, as if leveling the Cakkavāḷa mountains, as if lifting Mount Sineru, as if taking hold of and shaking a great Jambu tree, the Blessed One addressed the monks to begin the praise of Venerable Ānanda's virtues. In that [passage beginning with 'Āmantesi']—
177:
Why did he not say, "Monks, even now there are such people"? It is because there is no other Buddha. By this very statement, it should be understood that "there is no other Buddha even in other universes (Cakkavāḷa)." "Paṇḍito" means one who is clever. "Medhāvī" means one who is skilful in the aggregates (khandha), elements (dhātu), bases (āyatana), and so on.

"The assembly of monks approaches to see Ānanda" refers to the monks who approach the Elder Ānanda wishing to see the Blessed One, as well as those who come having heard of the Elder's virtues, thinking, "Venerable Ānanda is said to be inspiring from all sides, very handsome, pleasant to behold, deeply learned, and an ornament to the Saṅgha." This is why it is said, "The assembly of monks approaches to see Ānanda." This method applies everywhere. "Attamanā" means they are delighted in their own minds, thinking, "What we have heard matches what we see." "Dhamma" (Dhamma talk) refers to polite conversation concerning worldly etiquette, such as: "Friends, is it bearable? Is it manageable? Do you perform your work with wise reflection? Do you fulfill the duties toward your teachers and preceptors?" Among the four assemblies, for the nuns, there is this distinction: "Sisters, do you live having undertaken the eight heavy rules (garudhamma)?" When laymen (upāsakas) come, he does not engage in polite conversation like this: "Layman, do you have a headache or pain in your limbs? Are your sons and brothers free from illness?" Instead, he engages in polite conversation thus: "Laymen, how do you observe the three refuges and the five precepts? Do you observe the eight Uposatha precepts eight times a month? Do you fulfill the duty of serving your parents? Do you look after the righteous recluses and brahmins?" The same method applies to laywomen (upāsikās).

Now, wishing to make a comparison of the Elder Ānanda with a Universal Monarch (Cakkavatti), he said the words beginning with "Monks, these four..." In that passage, "Khattiyā" refers to those of the warrior-noble class, both consecrated and unconsecrated. They, having heard the praise of his virtues, thinking, "The Universal Monarch is said to be very handsome, pleasant to behold, inspiring, and he rules the kingdom righteously as a righteous king (Dhammarāja) while traveling through the air," are delighted when "what they see matches what they have heard." When he speaks, he engages in polite conversation: "Dear ones, how do you fulfill the royal duties? Do you preserve the tradition?" For brahmins, he engages in polite conversation: "Teachers, how do you teach the Vedas? How do the students learn the Vedas? Have you received donations, or clothes, or tawny cows?" For householders: "Dear ones, is there no oppression from the royal family through punishment or taxation..."
178:
“Does it rain well? Are the crops abundant?” In this way, he performs the customary greetings. To the monks as well, he performs the customary greetings: “Venerable sirs, are the requisites of a monk easily obtained? Are you not negligent in the practice of a monk?”

## Commentary on the Mahāsudassana Sutta Discourse

“Khuddakanagarake” refers to a small, cramped town that is a mere imitation of a city. “Ujjaṅgalanagarake” refers to a small town on uneven ground. “Sākhānagarake” refers to a small town that is like a branch of other great cities, just as the branches of trees are small. “Khattiyamahāsālā” refers to great nobles of the warrior caste who have attained the essence of great wealth and possessions. This method should be understood in all cases.

Among them, a “Khattiyamahāsāla” is one who has buried and stored wealth of a hundred or a thousand crores, and whose wealth is such that one cartload of coins goes out daily and two cartloads return in the evening. A “Brāhmaṇamahāsāla” is one who has buried eighty crores of wealth, and whose wealth is such that one pot of coins goes out daily and one cartload returns in the evening. A “Gahapatimahāsāla” is one who has buried forty crores of wealth, and whose wealth is such that five ambaṇas of coins go out daily and one pot returns in the evening.

“Ānanda, do not say so. This city should not be called a ‘small town.’ I have come here with great effort and great exertion, standing and sitting many times, to speak of the prosperity of this very city.” Having said this, He preached the words beginning with “Bhūtapubbaṃ.” “Subhikkhā” means being abundant in food and edibles. “Hattisaddena” means not being quiet due to the sound of elephants; when one elephant makes a sound, eighty-four thousand elephants make sounds. Likewise, it was not quiet due to the sound of horses. Meritorious beings traveled on the main streets following one another in chariots yoked with four Sindh horses; thus, it was not quiet due to the sound of chariots. Musical instruments such as drums were always played in this city; thus, it was not quiet due to the sound of drums and so forth. Therein, “Sammasaddo” is the sound of striking bronze gongs and cymbals. “Pāṇitāḷasaddo” is the sound of striking a square drum with the hands. Some also call it the sound of a pot-drum.
179:
“Eat, drink, chew” refers to the very sounds of “Eat, drink, chew.” The summary here is: with this tenth sound, “Eat,” (the city of Kusāvatī) was not quiet, the sound being uninterrupted. In other cities, there are sounds such as “Throw away the rubbish, take the hoe, take the basket, we will go to another place, take the bag of rice, take the bag of cooked rice, prepare the weapons like wooden shields, etc.” He shows that such sounds did not occur in this city.

Having said “with the tenth sound,” He concluded the entire Mahāsudassana Sutta, starting with “Ānanda, the royal capital of Kusāvatī was surrounded by seven walls,” and then said, “Ānanda, you go,” and so forth. In those words, “Abhikkamatha” means “go forward” or “come.” Did those Mallas not know that the Blessed One had arrived? They did know. In the places where Buddhas arrive, there is always a great commotion. However, they did not come because they were sitting engaged in some business. Thinking, “Those Mallas will come and arrange the places for standing and sitting for the community of monks,” the Blessed One sent [Ānanda] to them even at an unseasonable time.

## Commentary on the Veneration by the Mallas

In “Amhākañca no,” “no” is a mere particle. “Aghāvino” means those in whom suffering has arisen. “Dummanā” means those who are displeased. “Cetodukkhasamappitā” means those endowed with mental distress. It means placing the groups of Mallas separately according to each family, following the main streets and side streets.

## Commentary on the Story of Subhadda the Wanderer

“The wanderer named Subhadda” was a wanderer who wore clothes (channa-paribbājaka), having gone forth from a prominent and wealthy brahmin family. “Kaṅkhādhamma” means one who has a nature of doubt and uncertainty. Why did such a thought occur to him today? It was because he possessed such a strong supporting condition (upanissaya) [for the path and fruit]. Formerly, in the time of performing meritorious deeds, there were two brothers. They cultivated crops together. At that time, the elder brother had the thought, “I will give the first-fruits of a single crop nine times.” That elder brother gave the gift called “Bījagga” (first-fruits of the seed) at the time of sowing, and at the time when the crop was pregnant, with the younger brother...
180:
When the two brothers consulted together, the elder brother said, "When the rice is in its 'pregnant' stage, let us split the husk and make an offering." The younger brother replied, "Do you wish to destroy the young crop?" Knowing that the younger brother would not follow his wish, the elder brother divided the field. From his own portion, he split the rice husks, extracted the milky juice, mixed it with the finest ghee and butter, and offered it. At the time suitable for making parched rice (puthuka), he had it prepared and offered it. At the time of harvest, he gave the first-fruit offering of the harvest; at the time of binding the sheaves, the first-fruit of binding; at the time of stacking the sheaves, the first-fruit of stacking; at the threshing floor, the first-fruit of threshing; at the time of piling the winnowed grain, the first-fruit of the grain pile; and at the time of storing in the granary, the first-fruit of the granary. In this way, he gave the first-fruit offerings nine times during a single crop cycle. The younger brother, however, gave the offering only after extracting the grain from his portion.

Among those two brothers, the elder became the Elder Aññāsikoṇḍañña. When the Blessed One looked to see, "To whom should I first preach the Dhamma?", He reflected, "Aññāsikoṇḍañña once gave first-fruit offerings nine times during a single crop cycle; I shall preach this foremost Dhamma to him." Thus, He preached the Dhamma to him before all others. That Elder Aññāsikoṇḍañña, along with eighteen crores of Brahmas, was established in the Fruit of Stream-entry (Sotāpattiphala). The younger brother, because he had been late in giving his offerings, only felt the desire to see the Buddha when the Blessed One was near the time of His Parinibbāna.

"Do not trouble the Tathāgata" means—the Elder Ānanda thought, "These wanderers of other sects (titthiyas) usually cling only to their own views. For the sake of making him relinquish that view, the Blessed One would have to speak much, which would cause physical and vocal fatigue. Moreover, the Blessed One is already naturally exhausted." Thinking thus, he spoke those words. The wanderer Subhadda thought, "This monk does not give me the opportunity; however, one who is in need must persist in requesting." With this thought, he continued to entreat the Elder Ānanda for a second and third time.

"He heard" means that the Buddha heard the words of the Elder Ānanda, who was standing at the curtain-door, with His natural ear. Having heard, and because Subhadda had come with great effort for his own benefit, He said, "Enough, Ānanda," and so forth. In that passage, "Alaṃ" is an indeclinable (nipāta) meaning prohibition. "Aññāpekkho'va" means simply having the desire to know. "Abbhaññiṃsu" means "let them know according to their own claim." The meaning is this: if their claim leads to liberation from the round of suffering (vaṭṭa), then all would know it; if not, they would not know. Therefore, whether their claim leads to liberation or not is the very meaning of that question. At that time, the Blessed One, wishing to show that their views do not lead to liberation, and because it was of no benefit, and because it was not the proper time for an elaborate discourse, prohibited it by saying "Enough" and preached only the Dhamma. The Blessed One preached the Dhamma to the Mallas in the first watch, to Subhadda in the middle watch, and to the assembly of monks in the last watch...
181:
This is the meaning of that question. Then the Blessed One, by showing that the doctrines of teachers such as Pūraṇa Kassapa do not lead to liberation from the round of suffering, and because there was no benefit and no opportunity for elaborate explanation, rejected them with "Enough" and preached only the Dhamma. For the Blessed One had come with the intention: "Having preached the Dhamma to the Mallas in the first watch, to Subhadda in the middle watch, and having exhorted the assembly of monks in the last watch, I shall pass into Parinibbāna at the time of the strong dawn."

"No ascetic is found in those [other sects]" means that in those doctrines, there is no first ascetic who is a Stream-winner (Sotāpanna), no second ascetic who is a Once-returner (Sakadāgāmī), no third ascetic who is a Non-returner (Anāgāmī), and no fourth ascetic who is an Arahant. Having first spoken without specification in the previous discourse to Subhadda, He now spoke specifying His own Dispensation (Sāsana). "Other doctrines are void of ascetics" means that other doctrines are void, empty, and hollow of the twelve types of ascetics: the four who are practicing for the sake of the four paths (magga), the four who are established in the paths, and the four who are established in the fruits (phala). "Subhadda, these monks also" refers to these twelve types of monks.

In the phrase "should they live rightly," a Stream-winner lives rightly when he preaches the attainment he has realized to another and makes that person a Stream-winner. This same method applies to Once-returners and others. One established in the Path of Stream-entry lives rightly when he makes another also established in the Path of Stream-entry. This same method applies to those established in the remaining paths. One who has begun insight (vipassanā) for the sake of the Path of Stream-entry lives rightly when he preaches the meditation subject (kammaṭṭhāna) he has mastered and makes another also a practitioner of insight for the sake of the Path of Stream-entry. This same method applies to those practicing insight for the sake of the remaining paths. Referring to such living, He said, "should they live rightly." "The world would not be void of Arahants" means it would be filled without gaps, like a forest of reeds or a forest of sara grass.

"Twenty-nine years of age" means being twenty-nine years old by age. In the phrase "which [time] I went forth," the word "yaṃ" is merely an indeclinable. "Seeking what is wholesome (kusala)" means searching and seeking for "What is kusala?" In that context, "What is kusala?" refers to Omniscience (Sabbaññutañāṇa); the meaning is that He was searching for that Omniscience. "Since I [went forth]" shows that from the time I became a monk, more than fifty years have passed in this interval. "Of the Ñāya Dhamma" means of the Dhamma of the Noble Path (Ariya Magga). "One who dwells in a portion" refers to a person who dwells in the path of insight (vipassanā-magga) which is the cause for seeing the Noble Path. "Outside of this" means outside of My Dispensation.
182:
“Samaṇopi natthi” means there is no practitioner of insight (vipassaka) who gives rise to the insight path (vipassanāmagga) that leads to the direct realization of the Noble Path (ariyamagga). It also means there is no “first ascetic” (pathamasamaṇa), which refers to a Stream-enterer (sotāpanna).

“Ye ettha” refers to those in this Dispensation (sāsana) who were consecrated as resident disciples (antevāsika) in the presence of the Teacher. It means you have gained the benefit of being commissioned by the Buddha to act in his stead, and you have truly attained a good human life. It is said that in external sects, when a teacher says, “Ordain this person, advise this person, instruct this person,” that disciple is placed in the teacher's position. Therefore, the benefits of being told to “Ordain, advise, and instruct” accrue to that disciple. Subhadda spoke to the Venerable Ānanda based on this very custom of external sects.

Regarding the phrase “Alattha kho” (indeed he obtained), how did he obtain it? It is said that the Elder took Subhadda aside, wetted his head with water from a pitcher, taught him the meditation on the five parts of the body ending in skin (tacapañcaka-kammaṭṭhāna), had his hair and beard shaved, clothed him in saffron robes, gave him the Refuges, and brought him to the Blessed One. The Blessed One granted him ordination and taught him meditation. That monk Subhadda took that meditation, established himself in the walking path in a corner of the garden, and while striving and exerting himself to develop insight, he attained Arahantship along with the four analytical insights (paṭisambhidā). He then returned, paid homage to the Blessed One, and sat down. It was with reference to this that the words “Acirūpasampanno kho pana” and so forth were spoken.

The statement that Subhadda was the last direct witness disciple (sakkhisāvaka) of the Blessed One is the word of the Reciters (Saṅgītikārakas). In this context, anyone who ordained while the Blessed One was still alive and later attained Arahantship, or who received higher ordination while he was alive and later took up meditation and attained Arahantship, or who took up meditation while he was alive and later attained Arahantship—all such persons can be called the “last direct witness disciple.” However, this Subhadda was one who completed everything—novice ordination, higher ordination, taking up meditation, and attaining Arahantship—while the Blessed One was still alive.

## The Explanation of the Fifth Recitation Section is finished.

## Explanation of the Last Words of the Tathāgata

Now, the Blessed One began to give advice to the Saṅgha of monks. To show this, the words “Atha kho bhagavā” and so forth were spoken. In those words, “Desito paññatto” means the Dhamma has been taught...
183:
...and the Vinaya has been prescribed. “Prescribed” (paññatto) means established or laid down in detail. “That Dhamma and Vinaya will be your teacher after I am gone” means that the Dhamma and Vinaya will perform the role of the Teacher for you after I have attained Parinibbāna. Indeed, while I was still present, I taught the Vinaya known as the Twofold Vibhaṅga together with the Khandhaka and Parivāra, based on the seven classes of offenses (sattāpattikkhandha) as cases arose, saying: “This offense is light, this is heavy, this is curable, this is incurable, this is a worldly fault (lokavajja), this is a fault by prescription (paṇṇattivajja); this offense is rehabilitated in the presence of an individual, this in the presence of a group (gaṇa), and this in the presence of the Saṅgha.” That entire Vinaya Piṭaka will fulfill the duties of the Teacher for you after I have attained Parinibbāna.

While I was still present, I taught the Suttanta Piṭaka by analyzing these teachings in various ways, saying: “These are the four foundations of mindfulness (satipaṭṭhāna), the four right efforts (sammappadhāna), the four bases of power (iddhipāda), the five faculties (indriya), the five powers (bala), the seven factors of enlightenment (bojjhaṅga), and the Noble Eightfold Path (ariya aṭṭhaṅgika magga).” That entire Suttanta Piṭaka will fulfill the duties of the Teacher for you after I have attained Parinibbāna. While I was still present, I also taught the Abhidhamma Piṭaka, adorned with the Great Patthana (Mahāpaṭṭhāna) of infinite methods and twenty-four universal conditions, analyzing these teachings, saying: “These are the five aggregates (khandha), the twelve bases (āyatana), the eighteen elements (dhātu), the four truths (sacca), the twenty-two faculties (indriya), the nine causes (hetu), the four nutriments (āhāra), the seven contacts (phassa), the seven feelings (vedanā), the seven perceptions (saññā), the seven volitions (sañcetanā), and the seven consciousnesses (citta).” Furthermore, I analyzed them as: “This many teachings are of the sense-sphere (kāmāvacara), this many are of the fine-material sphere (rūpāvacara), this many are of the immaterial sphere (arūpāvacara), this many are included (pariyāpanna), this many are unincluded (apariyāpanna), this many are mundane (lokiya), and this many are supramundane (lokuttara).” That entire Abhidhamma Piṭaka will fulfill the duties of the Teacher for you after I have attained Parinibbāna.

Thus, all the words spoken and uttered during the forty-five years from the Enlightenment until the Parinibbāna are categorized as the Three Piṭakas, the Five Nikāyas, the Nine Limbs (aṅga), and the 84,000 Dhamma-groups (dhammakkhandha). In this way, these 84,000 Dhamma-groups remain; I alone pass away. Now, I alone advise and instruct you; after I have attained Parinibbāna, these 84,000 Dhamma-groups will advise and instruct you. Thus, the Blessed One, showing many reasons, gave the advice: “That Dhamma and Vinaya will be your teacher after I am gone.” Then, wishing to show the conduct for the future, he spoke the words beginning with “Yathā kho pana.”
184:
In these passages, 'samudācaranti' means they speak or address. 'Nāmena vā gottena vā' (by name or by clan) means that instead of saying "new monk" (navaka), one should address them by name such as 'Tissa' or 'Nāga', or by clan such as 'Kassapa' or 'Gotama', or by the form of address 'Āvuso' as in 'Āvuso Tissa' or 'Āvuso Kassapa'. 'Bhanteti vā āyasmāti vā' means they should be addressed as 'Bhante Tissa' or 'Āyasmā Tissa'. 'Samūhanatu' means "let him abolish if he wishes" or "he may abolish if he desires." Why did the Buddha not give a definitive command 'samūhanatha' (abolish!) but instead left it as an optional statement (vikappa)? It was because he saw the capability of the Venerable Mahākassapa. The Blessed One saw that even if he said "abolish," Venerable Mahākassapa would not do so at the time of the Council. Therefore, he left it as an optional statement.

Regarding that (minor and very minor rules): "Some elders said that, excluding the four Pārājikas, the remaining rules are minor and very minor (khuddānukhuddaka)," and so on. This discussion on minor and very minor rules appeared during the Council of the Five Hundred, and the decision on this is stated in the Samantapāsādikā Commentary. However, some teachers say: King Milinda asked, "Venerable Nāgasena, which is minor and which is very minor?" and because he replied, "Great King, a Dukkaṭa offense is minor, and a Dubbhāsita offense is very minor," the Venerable Nāgasena knew the minor and very minor rules. Venerable Mahākassapa, however, [acting as if] not knowing that point, said:

"Friends, let the Saṅgha listen to me. Our training rules are known to laypeople. Laypeople also know: 'This is allowable for you Sakyaputtian ascetics, this is not allowable.' If we abolish the minor and very minor training rules, there will be those who say: 'The ascetic Gotama prescribed training rules for his disciples that lasted only as long as smoke; as long as their teacher remained, they trained in these rules, but since their teacher has attained Parinibbāna, they no longer train in them.' If it is suitable for the Saṅgha, the Saṅgha should not prescribe what has not been prescribed, nor abolish what has been prescribed, but should undertake and practice the training rules as they have been prescribed. This is the motion (ñatti)."

Thus, they say he recited the Kammavācā. This view should not be taken in that way. Venerable Nāgasena said [what he said] so that "opponents may not have an opportunity." Venerable Mahākassapa recited the Kammavācā with the intention: "I will not abolish the minor and very minor offenses."
185:
The account regarding the Brahma-punishment (Brahmadaṇḍa) was also decided in the Samantapāsādikā Vinaya Commentary, as it appeared in the Saṅgīti (Council) section.

'Kaṅkhā' means doubt. 'Vimati' means the inability to decide: "Is it the Buddha or not? Is it the Dhamma or not? Is it the Saṅgha or not? Is it the Path or not? Is it the Practice or not?" Addressing the monk in whom such doubt might arise, he said to you, dear sons, "Ask, monks." This is the summary of the meaning here. "Do not refrain from asking out of respect for the Teacher" means: "We went forth in the presence of the Blessed One; the four requisites are also the property of the Blessed One; having had no doubt for such a long time, it is not proper for us to have doubt now at this final moment"—if you do not ask out of such respect for the Teacher, he said, "Monks, let a friend inform a friend." Among you, whichever monk is an acquaintance or a close associate of another monk, let him inform that monk; I will explain to that monk, and by hearing that explanation, all will become free of doubt. This is what he intended to show.

"I have confidence thus" means "I believe thus." "Knowledge alone" (ñāṇameva) refers only to the knowledge that directly realizes the state of being free from doubt. Here, it means it is not merely faith in the Tathāgata. "Ānanda, among these monks" refers to these five hundred monks sitting within the pavilion. "The one who is the least" means the one who is the least in terms of spiritual qualities. This was said [by Ven. Anuruddha] referring specifically to the Venerable Ānanda.

"Strive with diligence" (appamādena sampādetha) means you should accomplish all tasks through the non-lapse of mindfulness. In this way, the Blessed One, lying on his parinibbāna bed, condensed all the instructions he had given for forty-five years into this single word "Appamāda" and gave it. "This was the Tathāgata's last word"—this statement, however, is the word of the Council compilers.

## Commentary on the Account of the Passing Away (Parinibbūtakathā-vaṇṇanā)

After this, to show how the Blessed One attained Parinibbāna after performing the preliminary procedures (parikamma) for Parinibbāna, it is said: "Then the Blessed One [entered] the first jhāna..." and so on. In that passage, "Bhante, has the Blessed One attained Parinibbāna?" is asked upon seeing the absence of inhalation and exhalation in the Blessed One who had entered the attainment of cessation (nirodha-samāpatti). "No, friend"—how did the Elder [Anuruddha] know? It is said that the Elder, entering those various attainments along with the Teacher, followed him as far as the emergence from the base of neither-perception-nor-non-perception, and now...
186: The Blessed One entered the attainment of cessation (nirodha-samāpatti). He knew that there is no such thing as passing away (death) within the attainment of cessation. Then the Blessed One, having emerged from the attainment of the cessation of perception and feeling, entered the attainment of the base of neither-perception-nor-non-perception... having emerged from the third jhāna, he entered the fourth jhāna. In this context, the Blessed One entered the first jhāna in twenty-four instances (meditation subjects), the second jhāna in thirteen instances, likewise the third jhāna, and the fourth jhāna in fifteen instances. How? First, he entered the first jhāna in these twenty-four instances: the ten foulnesses (asubha), the thirty-two parts of the body (dvattiṃsākāra), eight kasinas, loving-kindness (mettā), compassion (karuṇā), appreciative joy (muditā), mindfulness of breathing (ānāpāna), and the space-limit (paricchedākāsa). Excluding the thirty-two parts of the body and the ten foulnesses, he entered the second jhāna in the remaining thirteen instances, and likewise the third jhāna in those same instances. He entered the fourth jhāna in these fifteen instances: the eight kasinas, the divine abode of equanimity (upekkhā-brahmavihāra), mindfulness of breathing, the space-limit, and the four immaterial states (arūpa). This is just a brief explanation. The Blessed One, the Lord of Dhamma, entering the city of Nibbāna, entered all the attainments numbering two million four hundred thousand, and having experienced the bliss of all attainments, he entered [Nibbāna], just as a person going to another place might embrace his relatives. In the passage 'Immediately after emerging from the fourth jhāna, the Blessed One attained parinibbāna,' there are two types of 'immediacy': immediacy of jhāna and immediacy of reviewing (paccavekkhaṇā). Among them, the passing away of a person who, having emerged from jhāna, has descended into the life-continuum (bhavaṅga) right after that jhāna, is called 'immediacy of jhāna'. The passing away of a person who, having emerged from jhāna, reviews the jhāna factors and then descends into the life-continuum, is called 'immediacy of reviewing'. These two are indeed the types of immediacy. As for the Blessed One, having entered jhāna, emerged from it, and reviewed the jhāna factors, he attained parinibbāna with the life-continuum consciousness (bhavaṅga-citta), which is indeterminate (abyākata) and the truth of suffering (dukkha-sacca). Indeed, all Buddhas, Paccekabuddhas, or Noble Disciples—down to even the smallest insects like ants—pass away only with the indeterminate life-continuum consciousness, which is the truth of suffering. The great earthquake and so forth are to be understood in the manner already described. 'Bhūtā' means beings. 'Appaṭipuggalo' means one who is devoid of a peer or counterpart. 'Balappatto' means one who has attained the ten powers of knowledge.
187: 'Uppādawayadhammino' means having the nature of arising and passing away. 'Tesaṃ vūpasamo' means the stilling of those formations; the meaning is that only the unconditioned Nibbāna is bliss. 'Nāhu assāsapassāso' means that inhalation and exhalation no longer occurred. 'Anejo' means one who is unshaken because of the absence of the shaking called craving (taṇhā). 'Santimārabbha' means by way of or referring to the Nibbāna element without residue (anupādisesa-nibbāna). 'Yaṃ kālamakari' means that the Blessed One passed away. The meaning is: 'Friends, that Buddha-Sage, my teacher, thinking "I shall go to the state of peace," passed away referring to Nibbāna. For that One of steady mind, the Unshaken One, inhalation and exhalation have now not arisen, do not exist, and do not proceed.' 'Asallīnena' means with a mind that is not shrinking or shriveled, but well-opened. 'Vedanaṃ ajjhavāsayī' means he endured the feeling; it means he did not follow the lead of the feeling and toss about from side to side. 'Vimokkho' means liberation without obstruction by any state; the attainment of the state of being completely unmanifest, like the extinguishing of a lamp. 'Tadāsi' refers to the earthquake mentioned below: 'Simultaneously with the parinibbāna, there was a great earthquake.' That earthquake was hair-raising and terrifying. 'Sabbākārawarūpete' means endowed with all excellent causes. 'Avītarāgā' refers to worldlings as well as Stream-enterers and Once-returners. For them, distress (domanassa) has not been abandoned. Therefore, they too weep with arms outstretched; they weep with both hands placed on their heads—all this should be understood in the manner previously described. 'Ujjhāyanti' means they complain, saying: 'The venerable ones themselves cannot endure it; how can they comfort the rest of the people?' 'Venerable sir, what is the state of the deities' minds?'—this is the question asked for the Venerable Anuruddha to take note of. 'How is it, venerable sir, do those deities endure the Blessed One's parinibbāna?' Then, to show the behavior of those deities, the Elder spoke the words beginning with 'Santāvuso.' The meaning of that is as already stated. 'Rattāvasesaṃ' means the small portion of time remaining in the night, because he attained parinibbāna at the time of late dawn.
188:
“Avasesaṃ cullakaddhānaṃ” refers to the small remaining portion of the night (since the Buddha attained Parinibbāna at dawn). “Dhammiyā kathāyā” means there was no other separate Dhamma talk; they spent the time only with talk related to death, such as: “Friends, in this world with its devas, even this King of Death (Maccu-rāja) does not feel shame before the Teacher, the peerless person; why then would he feel shame before the worldly masses?” While those venerable ones were speaking these words, dawn broke in an instant.

“Atha kho” means that as soon as he saw the dawn, the Venerable Anuruddha said these words to the Venerable Ānanda. “Teneva karaṇīyena” refers to the duties to be performed upon hearing that the Blessed One has attained Parinibbāna, such as: what kind of flowers, scents, and so on should be used for worship; what kind of seating area should be prepared for the community of bhikkhus; and what kind of food and offerings should be provided.

## Description of the Worship of the Buddha’s Body

“Sabbañca tāḷāvacaraṃ” refers to all various kinds of musical instruments. “Sannipātetha” means to assemble the people by beating the great drum. They did exactly as instructed. “Maṇḍalamāḷe” refers to circular pavilions made of cloth. “Paṭiyādentā” means preparing and arranging.

“Dakkhiṇena dakkhiṇaṃ” means from the southern part of the city to the southern part itself. “Bāhirena bāhiraṃ” means carrying the body along the outer route of the city without entering inside. “Dakkhiṇato nagarassa” means placing the body in a location similar to the south gate of Anurādhapura, performing acts of worship and honor, with the intention: “We shall cremate the body in a place similar to the Jetavana monastery.”

“Aṭṭha mallapāmokkhā” refers to eight Malla chiefs who were middle-aged and endowed with great strength. “Sīsaṃ nhātā” means those who had bathed, including washing their heads. “Āyasmantaṃ anuruddhaṃ”: the Venerable Anuruddha was well-known for being endowed with the divine eye (dibba-cakkhu); therefore, even though other great elders were present, they asked that Elder, thinking, “This venerable one will explain it clearly to us.” When they asked, “Venerable sir, what is the intention of the devas?”, it meant, “Venerable sir, we already know our own intention; but what is the intention of the devas?” The Elder, wishing first to show the intention of those Malla kings, spoke the words beginning with “Tumhākaṃ kho.” “Makuṭabandhanaṃ nāma mallānaṃ cetiyaṃ” is the name of the auspicious hall where the Malla kings were adorned during their coronation. It is called a “Cetiya” in the sense of being a place of respect.
189:
In the phrase “up to the alleys, sewage drains, and refuse heaps,” “sandhi” refers to the alleys (gaps between houses). “Samala” refers to the drains through which piles of excrement are discharged. “Saṅkaṭīra” refers to the places where rubbish is heaped. “With the dancing of devas and the dancing of humans” means that the dancing of devas took place above, and the dancing of humans took place below. This same principle applies to singing and other performances. Furthermore, they proceeded while worshipping and paying respect with devas interspersed among humans, and humans interspersed among devas.

As it is said, “carrying it through the very center of the city,” while the Blessed One’s body was being carried, Mallikā, the wife of the Malla general Bandhula, heard that “the Blessed One’s body is being brought.” She had the Mahālatā ornament—which was similar to Visākhā’s and which she had kept without wearing since the time of her husband’s death—brought out. Thinking, “I shall worship the Teacher with this ornament,” she had it polished, washed it with scented water, and stood at the doorway.

It is said that such an ornament had existed in only three places: in the houses of those two women (Mallikā and Visākhā) and in the house of the thief Devadāniya. When the Blessed One’s body reached the doorway, she said, “O princes, please set the Teacher’s body down for a moment,” and she placed the Mahālatā ornament upon the Blessed One’s body. Once placed, starting from the head, it reached down to the soles of the feet. The golden-hued body of the Blessed One, when adorned with that noble ornament made of the seven gems, shone exceedingly bright. Seeing that beauty, Mallikā, with a heart full of faith, made a wish: “Blessed One, for as long as I wander in the round of rebirth (saṃsāra), may I have no need for separate adornment; may my body always be as if naturally adorned.”

Then, having honored the Blessed One with the noble ornament made of the seven gems, they carried the body out through the east gate and placed the Blessed One’s body at the Malla kings’ shrine called Makuṭabandhana, located to the east of the city.

## Description of the Story of the Venerable Mahākassapa

“From Pāvā to Kusinārā” means that after wandering for alms in the city of Pāvā, he set out on the long journey thinking, “I will go to Kusinārā.” In the phrase “he sat at the foot of a tree,” why is it not called a “day-rest” (divāvihāra)? It is not so called because he did not sit for the purpose of a day-rest. All the bhikkhus who were followers of the Elder were of great merit and had been raised in comfort. Those monks became exhausted walking on foot at midday on the ground which was like hot stone slabs. The Elder saw them and thought: “The monks are exhausted, and the destination is not far. After resting a while to allay the fatigue, I will go to Kusinārā in the evening and see the One of Ten Powers (Dasabala).”
190: Leaving the road, he spread his double-robe (saṅghāṭi) at the foot of a certain tree, cooled his hands and feet with water from a water-pot, and sat down. The accompanying monks also sat at the foot of trees, practicing wise reflection (yoniso manasikāra) and reciting the virtues of the Triple Gem. Because they sat there to dispel fatigue, it is not called "day-rest" (divāvihāra). ## "Having taken a mandārava flower" means he came holding a flower the size of a large bowl, fixed to a temporary staff like an umbrella. "He saw" means he saw him coming from afar. Having seen him, he thought: ## "This mandārava flower is visible in the hand of this Ājīvaka. This flower does not appear in the human world at all times. It appears only when someone with psychic power performs a feat of psychic power, or when the Omniscient Bodhisatta descends into his mother's womb, and so on. However, today no one has performed a feat of psychic power. My Teacher, the Blessed One, did not descend into his mother's womb today, nor was he born, nor did he attain Enlightenment, nor did he set the Wheel of Dhamma in motion, nor did he perform the Twin Miracle, nor did he descend from Tāvatiṃsa, nor did he relinquish the life-principle. Indeed, my Teacher is aged; he must surely have attained parinibbāna." ## Then, the thought arose, "I will ask him." Thinking, "If I ask while sitting, it would be disrespectful to the Teacher," he rose from his seat. Moving slightly from where he stood—just as the Chaddanta elephant king wraps himself in a jewel-like dark hide—he donned the cloud-colored rag-robe (pāṃsukūla) given by the Blessed One. Placing his hands, bright with the meeting of ten fingernails, in anjali on his head, out of respect for the Teacher, he went before the Ājīvaka and asked, "Friend, do you know our Teacher?" ## Why did he ask, knowing the Teacher had attained parinibbāna, or did he ask not knowing? The knowledge of Arahants is connected to reflection (āvajjana). Some teachers say that because the Elder Mahākassapa did not reflect, he asked without knowing. The Elder frequently entered meditative attainments (samāpatti). In his night quarters, day quarters, caves, and pavilions, he always spent his time by the power of samāpatti. Even when entering the village of his supporters, he would enter samāpatti at every door and only accept alms after emerging from it. It is said the Elder thought, "I will favor the people in this last existence; may the alms given to me or the offerings of scents and flowers be of great fruit for them." Thus, they say he did not know because of his frequent samāpatti and therefore asked without knowing. ## That view should not be accepted. In truth, there is no moment of not knowing regarding this parinibbāna. The parinibbāna of the Blessed One was very clear through omens such as the shaking of the ten thousand world systems. However, among the Elder's retinue, some monks had seen the Blessed One before, while others had not. All of them desired to see him. Among them, those who had not seen him before, out of a great desire to see him, would go and ask, "Where is the Blessed One?" Upon hearing "He has attained parinibbāna," they would be unable to control themselves, would discard their robes and bowls, and, being improperly dressed or wearing only one garment, would beat their breasts...
191: ...and act in this way. Therefore, some say he did not know because of his frequent samāpatti and asked without knowing; that should not be accepted. ## There is no reason for not knowing here. The parinibbāna of the Teacher was very well-marked by omens such as the shaking of the ten thousand world systems. In the retinue of the Elder Mahākassapa, some monks had seen the Blessed One before, and some had not. Among them, both those who had seen him and those who had not desired to see him. Among them, those who had not seen him before, out of a great desire to see him, would go and ask, "Where is the Blessed One?" and upon hearing "He has attained parinibbāna," they would be unable to control themselves. They would discard their robes and bowls, and wearing only one garment, or being poorly dressed or poorly covered, they would beat their breasts and weep. Then people would say, "The rag-robe-wearing monks who came with the Elder Mahākassapa are weeping like women themselves; how can these venerable ones comfort us?" and they would see fault in me. But this is a lonely great forest; here, there is no fault if they weep in whatever way. By hearing it beforehand, their grief will also be lessened. Thus, thinking to alert the monks, he asked even though he knew. ## "Today it is seven days since the ascetic Gotama attained parinibbāna" means today is the seventh day since the ascetic Gotama attained parinibbāna. "From there to me this" means from the place where the ascetic Gotama attained parinibbāna. ## "One named Subhadda who was ordained in old age" means "Subhadda" was his name. Because he was ordained when he was old, he is called "one ordained in old age" (vuḍḍhapabbajita). Why did he speak thus? Because of a grudge against the Blessed One. It is said that he was the former barber mentioned in the Ātumā incident in the Khandhaka. When he heard that the Blessed One had left Kusinārā and was coming to Ātumā with two hundred and fifty monks, he thought, "When he arrives, I will make an offering of rice gruel (yāgu)." He said to his two sons, who were in the stage of novices (sāmaṇera): "Dears, the Blessed One is coming to Ātumā with a large Saṅgha of monks, with two hundred and fifty monks. Go, dears, take the shaving kits and wander from house to house with a measuring vessel to collect salt, oil, rice, and food..."
192:
## 
"Let us make an offering of rice gruel to the Blessed One who has arrived; collect [salt, oil, rice, and snacks]." Those novices did accordingly.

When people saw those young novices, who had pleasant voices and were wise, they made offerings, whether they had intended to or not. After making the offerings, they asked, "Dear ones, what will you take?" The novices replied, "We do not need anything else; our father wishes to offer rice gruel when the Blessed One arrives." Hearing this, the people gave everything the young novices could carry, without limit. What they could not carry, the people sent along with them.

Then, when the Blessed One arrived at the city of Atumā and entered the Threshing-floor Hut (Bhūsāgāra), the old monk Subhadda went to the village gate in the evening, called the people, and said, "Lay followers, I do not expect anything else from you. The rice and other items brought by my young novices are sufficient for the Saṅgha. Just give me your manual labor." Saying, "Take this and that," he had them take all the necessary equipment and set up stoves in the monastery. Wearing a dark-dyed robe and wrapping himself in a similar one, he went about all night directing them, saying, "Do this, do that." Having spent a hundred thousand [units of currency], he had the rice gruel with snacks and honey-balls prepared. What is called bojjha-yāgu is rice gruel that is both eaten and drunk. Into that gruel, he put everything that is called edible, such as ghee, honey, molasses, fish, meat, flower-syrup, and fruit-syrup. It was so fragrant that it was fit even for those who wished to play to anoint their heads.

Then, the Blessed One, having attended to his physical needs early in the morning, set out towards the city of Atumā to wander for alms, surrounded by the community of monks. The people informed the old monk Subhadda, "The Blessed One has entered the village for alms; for whom have you prepared the rice gruel?"
