That old monk Subhadda, still wearing those dark-dyed robes, holding a ladle in one hand, knelt with his right knee on the ground like a Brahmā, paid homage, and said, "Venerable Sir, may the Blessed One accept my rice gruel."

Thereupon, following the method found in the Khandhaka that "Even though they know, the Tathāgatas ask," the Blessed One inquired and, having heard the facts, rebuked Subhadda, who had gone forth in old age. Regarding this matter, He laid down two training rules: the training rule concerning the undertaking of what is improper and the training rule concerning the carrying of barber’s tools. [He said,] "Monks, for many millions of aeons, food..."
193:
## 
"...you have spent time seeking food. But this food is improper for you, obtained through unrighteous means. For those who consume this food, they will be reborn only in the states of deprivation (apāya) for many thousands of existences. Go away, do not take it!" Having said this, He proceeded towards the alms-round. Not even a single monk took any of that food.

The old monk Subhadda, being displeased, thought, "This person wanders about saying, 'I know everything.' If he did not wish to take it, he should have sent word to inform me. This prepared food, at most, would last for seven days. This would have been sufficient for me for the rest of my life. He has destroyed everything; this person wishes me harm." Thus, he harbored a grudge against the Blessed One, but while the One of Ten Powers (Dasabala) was alive, he was unable to say anything. It is said that he thought: "This Great Man went forth from a high-born family; if I say anything, he will surely threaten and intimidate me." Now, hearing that "The Blessed One has attained Parinibbāna," he spoke thus, as if relieved and greatly delighted.

The Elder Mahākassapa, when he heard those words, felt as if his heart had been struck, or as if a dry thunderbolt had fallen upon his head, and spiritual urgency (dhamma-saṃvega) arose in him: "The Blessed One has been attained Parinibbāna for only seven days; even now His golden-hued body still remains. In this Dispensation (Sāsana) which the Blessed One accomplished with great difficulty, such a great and evil stain, a thorn, has appeared so quickly. If this evil person prospers and gains similar companions, he will be able to cause the decline of the Dispensation." Then the Elder thought:

"If I were to make this old monk wear rags, sprinkle him with ashes, and expel him right here, people would blame us, saying, 'While the body of the recluse Gotama still remains, his disciples are quarreling.' Therefore, I shall endure it for now.

Indeed, the Dhamma taught by the Blessed One is like a heap of unstrung flowers. Just as flowers struck by the wind scatter here and there, so too, as time passes under the influence of such evil persons, one or two training rules in the Vinaya will perish, one or two sets of questions (pucchā-vāra) in the Sutta will perish, and one or two levels (bhūmantara) in the Abhidhamma will perish. In this way, when the root is gradually destroyed, we shall become like demons. Therefore, let us perform a rehearsal (Saṅgāyana) of the Dhamma and Vinaya. If we do so, like flowers strung together with a firm thread, this Dhamma of the Sutta, Abhidhamma, and Vinaya will remain unshaken. Indeed, for the sake of this rehearsal, the Blessed One came out to meet me for a distance of three gāvutas. He granted me the higher ordination with three kinds of admonitions. He had me exchange His own robes with mine. While He was washing His feet in the open air and teaching the practice similar to the moon, He taught it placing me as a 'body-witness' (kāyasakkhi). Three times He made me the heir to the entire Dispensation. While a monk like me exists, let not this evil person achieve prosperity in the Dispensation. As long as the unrighteous teachings do not yet shine, as long as the righteous teachings are not yet obstructed, as long as the non-Vinaya does not yet shine, as long as the Vinaya is not yet obstructed, as long as those who speak what is not Dhamma are not yet powerful, and those who speak what is Dhamma..."
194:
Like flowers well-strung together with a firm thread, this Dhamma-Vinaya will remain stable and unshaken. For the purpose of this recitation (Saṅgāyanā) of the Dhamma-Vinaya, the Blessed One came to meet me for a distance of three gāvutas; he granted me ordination (upasampadā) with three exhortations; he had me exchange robes with him, taking his robe and giving me mine; while waving his hand in the sky and teaching the practice comparable to the moon, he taught me by making me a body-witness (kāyasakkhī); three times he made me the heir to the entire Sāsana. As long as a monk like me exists, let this wicked person not gain growth in the Sāsana. Before unrighteousness shines forth and righteousness is obstructed; before non-discipline shines forth and discipline is obstructed; before those who speak unrighteousness become powerful and those who speak righteousness become weak; before those who speak non-discipline become powerful and those who speak discipline become weak—within that time, I shall recite the Dhamma and the Vinaya. After that recitation, the monks will learn the word of the Buddha to the best of their ability and will explain what is allowable and what is not. Then this wicked person will be subdued of his own accord and will not be able to raise his head again; the Sāsana will become prosperous, flourishing, and radiant.

Ven. Mahākassapa did not reveal to anyone that such a thought had arisen in him, but he comforted the Saṅgha of monks. Therefore, it is said: "Then Ven. Mahākassapa... there is no possibility of this."

'Citaka' refers to a large sandalwood pyre twenty cubits high. "Let us ignite it" means let us cause the fire to catch. "They could not ignite it" means that although eight, sixteen, or thirty-two Malla kings, in pairs, held torches to make it burn, fanning it with palm-leaf fans and blowing with bellows, and trying various means, they were unable to make the fire catch. 'The intention of the devas' means that those devas were indeed the attendant devas of the Elder. In fact, eighty thousand families who had become attendants to the eighty Great Disciples (Mahāsāvaka) by having faith in them were reborn in heaven. Among them, the devas who were reborn in heaven due to their faith in Ven. Mahākassapa, not seeing the Elder at that assembly, wondered, "Where is our venerable teacher?" Seeing him on the road, they resolved: "Let the pyre not burn as long as our venerable teacher has not yet paid his respects."
195:
When the people heard those words—"It is said that the monk named Mahākassapa is coming with five hundred monks, saying 'I will worship the feet of the Ten-Powered One (Dasabala).' It is said that as long as that Elder has not arrived, the pyre (citaka) will not burn. Friends, what is that monk like? Is he dark or fair, tall or short? While such a monk exists, why did the Ten-Powered One attain Parinibbāna?"—some went to meet him with flowers, perfumes, and so on in their hands. Some decorated the streets and stood watching the road by which he would come.

Then Ven. Mahākassapa arrived at Kusinārā... (and so on) and worshipped with his head. The Elder circumambulated the pyre to the right and reflected, noting: "In this place is the head, in this place are the feet." Then, standing near the feet, he entered the fourth jhāna, which is the basis for direct knowledge (abhiññā), and upon emerging, he resolved (adhiṭṭhāsi): "May the feet of the Ten-Powered One, which are the site of the wheel-marks adorned with a thousand spokes, together with the layers of cotton and the five hundred pairs of cloth, split the golden sarcophagus and the sandalwood pyre in two, and rest upon my noble head."

Simultaneously with his thought of resolution, those five hundred pairs of cloth split in two, and the feet emerged like the full moon from between the clouds. The Elder stretched out his hands, which were like blooming red lotuses, and firmly grasping the golden-colored feet of the Teacher as far as the ankles, he placed them upon his noble head. With reference to this placement, it is said: "He worshipped the feet of the Blessed One with his head."

The great multitude, seeing that miracle, shouted out with a great sound all at once; they worshipped as they pleased, honoring with perfumes, flowers, and so on. Thus, as soon as the Elder, the multitude, and those five hundred monks had finished worshipping, there was no need for another resolution; by the power of the original resolution, the soles of the Blessed One's feet, which were the color of lac-dye, were released from the Elder's hands and returned to their original place without moving the sandalwood logs or anything else. Indeed, while the feet of the Blessed One were emerging or returning, not a single fiber of cotton, a thread of the fringe, a drop of oil, or a log of wood was displaced from its position; everything remained exactly as it was. When the feet of the Tathāgata disappeared, like the moon or the sun that has risen and then set, the great multitude lamented loudly. The compassion and sorrow were even more intense than at the time of the Parinibbāna.
196:
The statement "The Blessed One's funeral pyre ignited of its own accord" was made because no one was seen attempting to light the fire. In truth, this pyre ignited simultaneously from all sides through the supernatural power of the devas.

"Only the bodily remains (sarīra) were left behind" means that while it was previously called "sarīra" (singular) because it existed as a single mass, it is now called "sarīrāni" (plural) because it has become dispersed. This means that relics resembling jasmine buds (sumana-makuḷa), relics resembling washed pearls (dhota-mutta), and relics resembling gold (suvaṇṇa) remained. Indeed, the bodies of long-lived Buddhas remain as a single mass like a block of gold. However, the Blessed One, thinking, "I shall not remain for long before attaining Parinibbāna, and my Dispensation (Sāsana) has not yet spread everywhere; therefore, even after I have attained Parinibbāna, let the great multitude of people take my relics, even those as small as mustard seeds, and by enshrining them in stupas (cetiyas) in their respective places of residence and honoring them, let them be destined for heaven," made a resolution for the dispersal of the relics. How many of the Blessed One's relics were dispersed and how many were not? These seven relics—the four canine teeth (dāṭhā), the two collarbones (akkhaka), and the frontal bone (uṇhīsa)—were not dispersed; the rest were dispersed. Among those dispersed relics, the smallest was the size of a mustard seed (sāsapa-bīja), the middle-sized one was the size of a broken grain of rice (bhinna-taṇḍula), and the largest was the size of a broken mung bean (bhinna-mugga).

As for the "streams of water," streams of water as thick as arms, as thick as horse-heads, and as thick as palm trunks fell from the sky and extinguished the fire. The phrase "water from the Sal trees" refers to the surrounding Sal trees. Indeed, streams of water emerged from the gaps between the trunks and branches of those trees and extinguished the fire. The Blessed One's funeral pyre was very large. Water columns as thick as the end of a plowshare also rose from the earth all around, resembling crystal ornaments, and enveloped the pyre itself. "With scented water" means extinguishing it with various kinds of scented water brought in gold and silver jars. They extinguished the sandalwood pyre by sprinkling it with water-dippers made of gold and silver that had eight handles.

While the pyre was burning, flames rose from between the branches, forks, and leaves of the surrounding Sal trees. However, not a single leaf, branch, or flower was burnt. Even ants and spiders moved about right in the midst of the flames...
197:
...spiders moved about right in the midst of the flames. Regarding the streams of water falling from the sky, the streams of water emerging from the Sal trees, and the streams of water emerging from the earth, the accounts preached by the Dhamma-preachers according to their own wisdom are the standard. After extinguishing the pyre in this manner, the Malla kings had the Santhāgāra (Assembly Hall) smeared with four kinds of perfumes, scattered flowers with parched grain (lāja) as the fifth kind, and hung cloth canopies above, decorated with gold stars and the like, from which hung strings of perfumes, garlands, and jewels. From the Santhāgāra to the Makuṭabandhana auspicious hall, where the coronation regalia are kept, they had screens and mats set up on both sides of the road, hung cloth canopies above decorated with gold stars and the like, and there too, they hung strings of perfumes, garlands, and jewels. They raised five-colored banners on bamboo poles the color of rubies, surrounded them with wind-banners, and placed banana trees and full water pots along the well-swept streets, lighting torches. Placing the golden casket (suvaṇṇa-doṇi) containing the relics on the back of a decorated elephant, they made offerings of flowers, perfumes, and so on. Celebrating with great festivities, they entered the city and placed the casket on a throne made of heartwood (sarabha-maya-pallaṅka) in the Santhāgāra, shading it with a white parasol. Having done this—"Then the Mallas of Kusinārā, having made a cage of spears for the Blessed One's relics in the Santhāgāra for seven days"—all should be understood accordingly.

In that context, "having made a cage of spears" (satti-pañjaraṃ karitvā) means having men with spears in their hands surround the area. "A wall of bows" (dhanu-pākāraṃ) means that first, they had elephants surround the area, with their frontal globes touching. Then horses, with their necks touching; then chariots, with the ends of their axles touching; then warriors, with their arms touching. At the outer edge of those warriors, they had bows surround the area, with their ends touching. Thus, they arranged a guard for seven days over an area one yojana in circumference, making it like an unbroken net. Referring to this arrangement, it was said, "having surrounded it with a wall of bows."

Why did the Mallas do this? During the two weeks prior to this relic festival, they did not have the opportunity to celebrate because they were busy preparing seating and standing space for the community of monks (Bhikkhu-saṅgha) and providing food and snacks. Then they thought, "We shall celebrate for these seven days. However, it is possible that someone, knowing we are negligent, might come and take the relics. Therefore, we shall celebrate after setting up a guard." Thus, they acted accordingly.
198:
## Commentary on the Distribution of the Bodily Relics

Regarding the phrase "The King heard" (Assosi kho rājā): How did he hear? According to the account, King Ajātasattu’s ministers, having heard [of the Buddha's passing], thought: "The Teacher has attained Parinibbāna; it is impossible to bring him back. In terms of the faith of a worldling, there is no one like our King. If he hears [this news] in the usual way, his heart will break. We must certainly protect the King." They brought three golden troughs, filled them with the four sweet substances (catumadhura), went to the King, and said: "Your Majesty, we have seen a bad dream. To ward off its ill effects, it is proper for you to wear two layers of fine white cloth and lie in a trough of catumadhura, with only your nostrils showing." Hearing the words of the ministers who sought his welfare, the King agreed, saying, "So be it, friends," and did as they suggested.

Then, one minister removed his ornaments, disheveled his hair, and facing the direction where the Teacher had attained Parinibbāna, raised his hands in salutation and said to the King: "Your Majesty, there is no being who is free from death. That Blessed One, the Teacher—who increased our lifespan, who was the object of our veneration, who was like a fertile field for planting the seeds of merit, and who performed the auspicious consecration—has attained Parinibbāna in the city of Kusinārā." As soon as the King heard this, he lost consciousness and released heat into the catumadhura trough. Then, they lifted him up and placed him in the second trough. When he regained consciousness, he asked, "Friends, what did you say?" "Great King, the Teacher has attained Parinibbāna," they replied. The King fainted again and released heat into the catumadhura trough. Then, they lifted him from there and placed him in the third trough. When he regained consciousness, he asked again, "Friends, what did you say?" "Great King, the Teacher has attained Parinibbāna," they replied. The King fainted once more. Then, they lifted him up, bathed him, and poured water from jars over his head.

When the King regained consciousness, he rose from his seat, disheveled his hair which was scented with perfumes and had the luster of gems, spreading it over his back which was like a golden slab. Beating his breast with his hands, and clutching his chest—which was like a golden statue—with his well-rounded fingers that resembled coral sprouts, he descended into the middle of the street wailing like a madman. Surrounded by a troupe of decorated dancers, King Ajātasattu left the city and went to Jīvaka’s Mango Grove, looking at the place where the Blessed One had sat and taught the Dhamma...
199:
...holding [it], he descended to the main road in the guise of a madman. King Ajātasattu, surrounded by a troupe of adorned dancers, left the city and went to Jīvaka’s mango grove. Looking at the place where the Blessed One used to stay and teach the Dhamma, he lamented repeatedly: “O Great Blessed One, All-Knowing One, did You not sit in this place and preach the Dhamma? Did You not remove the thorn of my grief? You have indeed extracted the thorn of my sorrow. I have taken refuge in You. But now, O Blessed One, You do not even give me a word in response!”

“O Blessed One... at other times, at such a moment, I used to hear that ‘You are wandering through the land of Jambudīpa, surrounded by a great assembly of monks.’ But now, I hear news that is unsuitable and improper for You.” After speaking such words and recollecting the virtues of the Blessed One with about sixty verses, he thought: “My purpose will not be achieved merely by weeping. I shall have the relics of the One of Ten Powers (Dasabala) brought [to me].” Having heard [the news] and after recovering from his state of fainting and confusion, he dispatched a messenger. Referring to this dispatching of a messenger, it is said [in the Pali text]: “Atha kho rājā” and so forth.

In that passage, “dispatched a messenger” means he sent both a messenger and gifts. After sending them, he thought: “If they give [the relics], it is well. If they do not, I shall bring them by means of force.” He then prepared his fourfold army and set out himself. Just like King Ajātasattu, the Licchavī kings and others also dispatched messengers and set out themselves with their fourfold armies. Among those kings, the people of Pāvā lived closest to Kusinārā, at a distance of about three gāvutas. The Blessed One had entered Pāvā before proceeding to Kusinārā. If it is asked why they did not arrive first, it is because these kings had large retinues, and since they had to prepare such large retinues, they arrived later.

“Te saṅghe gaṇe etadavocuṃ” means all those kings who had arrived from the seven cities surrounded the city of Kusinārā and said: “Give us the relics, or give us battle!” The Mallas of Kusinārā replied: “This Blessed One [attained Parinibbāna] in our village territory.” Those Mallas reportedly said: “We did not send a message to the Teacher, nor did we go and invite Him. The Teacher came here of His own accord, sent word, and summoned us. You also do not give us the treasures that arise in your own village territories. In the world including the devas, there is no treasure equal to the Buddha-treasure. Having obtained such a supreme treasure, we shall not give it up. It is not only you who have drunk milk from a mother’s breast; we too have drunk milk from a mother’s breast. It is not only you who are men; we too are men.” Thus, with mutual pride, they exchanged messages and roared with arrogant defiance. If a war had broken out, only the people of Kusinārā would have been victorious. Why? Because the devas and Brahmas who had arrived to guard the relics were on the side of the people of Kusinārā.

In the Pali text, however, it only says: “The Blessed One attained Parinibbāna in our village territory; we will not give up a portion of the Blessed One’s bodily relics.” Then, the Brahmin Dona heard the words of those kings disputing with one another and thought: “These kings are quarreling at the place where the Blessed One attained Parinibbāna. This quarreling is most improper; there is no benefit in quarreling. I shall appease this dispute.” He then went to the assembly of kings and, standing on a high place, spoke the words known as the “Dona-gajjita” (Dona’s Roar), which is about two recitations (bhāṇavāra) in length.
200:
The devas and brahmas who arrived to guard the relics became the factions of those kings. In the Pali text, however, only this much is mentioned: "The Blessed One attained Parinibbāna in our village territory; we will not give a share of the Blessed One's bodily relics."

When this was said, the brahmin Doṇa, hearing the dispute of those kings, thought: "These kings are quarreling at the place where the Blessed One attained Parinibbāna; this is indeed not fitting. This strife is of no use; I shall appease them." Thus thinking, he went to the assembly of kings and spoke these words. How did he speak? Standing on high ground, he uttered the roar known as the 'Doṇa-gajjita' (Doṇa's Thunder), which was the length of two bhāṇavāras. Among those words, during the first bhāṇavāra, the kings did not understand even a single word. At the conclusion of the second bhāṇavāra, all the kings became silent, saying, "Friends, this voice is like that of our teacher the brahmin; it is like the voice of our teacher."

It is said that on the surface of Jambudīpa, there was almost no one born in a noble family who had not been a pupil of that brahmin Doṇa. Then, Doṇa the brahmin, perceiving that the kings had become silent upon hearing his words, spoke these two verses once more: "Listen, sirs."

In those verses, 'asmākaṃ buddho' means our Buddha. 'ahu khantivādo' means that even before reaching Buddhahood, while fulfilling the perfections, as the ascetic Khantivādī, as Prince Dhammapāla, as the Chaddanta elephant king, as the Bhūridatta naga king, as the Campeyya naga king, as the Saṅkhapāla naga king, as the Mahākapi monkey king, and in many other Jātaka births, he did not show anger toward others but practiced only patience. He praised only patience. What need is there to speak of now, when he has attained the state of a Perfectly Enlightened Buddha and is endowed with the quality of equanimity (tādi) regarding the desired and the undesired? In every way, our Buddha was a teacher of patience. Of such a Blessed One...

In the words 'na hi sādhu yaṃ uttamapuggalassa, sarīrabhāge siyā sampahāro', 'na hi sādhu' means that this striking with weapons is indeed not good. 'sarīrabhāge' means for the sake of dividing the bodily relics, for the reason of the portions of the relics. 'siyā sampahāro' means that the clash of weapons should not occur (it is not good).

'sabbeva bhonto sahitā' means may all you noble princes be of one mind; do not be divided. 'samaggā' means be united, assembling together in body and speech, and speaking with one voice. 'sammodamānā' means be mutually rejoicing in heart as well. 'karomaṭṭhabhāge' means let us make eight portions of the Blessed One's bodily relics...
201:
...we shall do. 'cakkhumato' refers to the Buddha who is endowed with the five eyes: the Buddha-eye, the Dhamma-eye, the divine-eye, the fleshly-eye, and the universal-eye. Not only you are devoted, but many people are also devoted; among those people, there is not even one who is unworthy of receiving the relics. Thus, he convinced them by stating many reasons.

'tesaṃ saṅghānaṃ gaṇānaṃ paṭissutvā' means having accepted the words of the assemblies and groups of kings who had gathered from various places. Regarding the phrase 'bhagavato sarīrāni aṭṭhadhā samaṃ suvibhattaṃ vibhajitvā', the sequence is as follows: Doṇa, having accepted the kings' words, ordered the golden vessel (suvaṇṇa-doṇi) to be opened. When the kings came and saw the gold-colored relics remaining in the vessel, they lamented, saying: "O Blessed One, O All-Knowing One, formerly we beheld your gold-colored body adorned with the thirty-two marks of a Great Man, embellished with the six-colored Buddha-rays, and radiant with the eighty minor marks. But now, only these gold-colored relics remain; O Blessed One, this is not fitting for us."

At that time, Doṇa the brahmin, noticing the kings' negligence, took the right tooth relic and hid it within the folds of his turban. Thereafter, he divided the relics into eight equal portions. All the relics amounted to sixteen nāḷis by standard measurement; each city received two nāḷis. While the brahmin was dividing the relics, Sakka, the king of devas, looked to see: "Who has taken the Blessed One's right tooth relic, which is the basis for the discourse on the Four Noble Truths to cut off the doubts of the world of devas and humans?" Seeing that the brahmin had taken it, he thought: "This brahmin will not be able to perform the honor and worship worthy of the tooth relic; I shall take it." He took it from the folds of the turban, placed it in a golden casket, and having conveyed it to the deva realm, enshrined it in the Cūḷāmaṇi Cetiya.

After dividing the relics, the brahmin did not see the tooth relic, but because he himself had taken it stealthily, he did not dare to ask, "Who took my tooth relic?" Foreseeing that they might blame him, saying, "Did you not divide the relics yourself? Why did you not know from the beginning whether your own portion of the relic existed or not?", he did not dare to say, "Give me a share too." Then, thinking, "This golden vessel is also connected to the relics; with it, the relics of the Tathāgata were measured. I will build a stupa for this vessel," he said, "Sirs, please give this vessel to me."
202:
The Moriya kings living in the Pipphali forest also sent messengers like King Ajātasattu and others, and came out prepared for battle.

## Commentary on the Worship of the Relic Stupa

Regarding the statement, "In Rājagaha, he made a stupa and a great festival for the relics of the Blessed One," how was it done? From Kusinārā to Rājagaha, there is a distance of twenty-five yojanas. Between these two, a level road eight usabhas wide was constructed, and a worship was arranged similar to that which the Malla kings performed between the place of coronation and the assembly hall (Santhāgāra). Having arranged such worship along the twenty-five yojana road, shops were set up everywhere so that the people would not grow weary. The relics, placed in a golden casket, were surrounded by a lattice of spears, and people within a five-hundred yojana radius of his kingdom were gathered. Taking those relics, they departed from Kusinārā while performing sacred festivities. Wherever they saw golden-colored flowers, they placed the relics within the spears and performed worship. Only when those flowers were exhausted did they proceed. When the front of the chariot reached the position of the rear, they performed sacred festivities for seven days. In this manner, for those who were bringing the relics, seven years, seven months, and seven days passed.

Those with wrong view complained, saying, "Since the time the ascetic Gotama attained Parinibbāna, we have been oppressed by these forced festivities and worship; all our work has been ruined." Because they corrupted their minds with such resentment, about eighty-six thousand of them were reborn in the states of deprivation (apāya). The Arahants, having reflected and seen that "the great multitude of people are corrupting their minds and being reborn in the states of deprivation," thought, "We shall have Sakka, the king of devas, arrange a means for bringing the relics." They went to Sakka, informed him of the matter, and said, "Great King, please arrange a means for bringing the relics."

Sakka replied, "Venerable sirs, there is no worldling (puthujjana) with faith equal to King Ajātasattu. That king will not listen to my words. However, I will display terrifying sights similar to the threats of Māra, I will cause a great sound to be heard, and I will cause spirit possession, sneezing, and loss of appetite. You should then say, 'Great King, the non-humans (amanussa) are angry; have the relics brought in.' If you say this, he will have them brought in." Then Sakka performed all of those things.

The Elders also approached the King and said, "Great King, the non-humans are angry; have the relics brought in." The King replied, "Venerable sirs, my..."
203:
"...mind is not yet satisfied; nevertheless, let them bring the relics." On the seventh day, they brought the relics. Having taken the relics brought in this manner, he made a stupa and a great festival in Rājagaha. The other kings also brought the relics according to their own power and made stupas and festivals in their respective places.

'Evametaṃ bhūtapubbaṃ' means that this distribution of relics and the establishment of the ten stupas in Jambudīpa happened in the past, as stated later by the Reciters of the Council (Saṅgītikārakas). After the stupas had been established in this way, the Elder Mahākassapa, seeing danger to the relics, approached King Ajātasattu and said, "Great King, it is proper to make a single enshrinement for the relics."

"Very well, bhante, let the work of enshrinement be my task. But how shall I bring the remaining relics?" the King asked. "Great King, bringing the relics is not your burden; it is our burden," the Elder replied. "Very well, bhante, you bring the relics, and I will perform the enshrinement," the King said.

The Elder brought the remaining relics, leaving only a small amount for the worship of those respective royal families. At Rāma village (Rāmagāma), however, the Nagas took possession of the relics; there was no danger to those relics. Thinking, "In the future, they will be enshrined in the Mahācetiya at the Mahāvihāra in the island of Laṅkā," he did not bring those, but brought them from the other seven cities. Standing at the southeast corner of Rājagaha, he resolved: "Let the rock that is in this place disappear, let the soil be very pure, and let water not rise."

The King had that place excavated, and with the soil removed from there, he had bricks made and built stupas for the eighty Great Disciples. To those who asked, "What is the King building here?" they replied, "Stupas for the Great Disciples." No one knew about the enshrinement of the relics. In that place, which was eighty cubits deep, he had an iron floor laid at the bottom. Upon that iron floor, he had a house made of copper, the size of the shrine-house at Thūpārāma, and he had caskets and stupas made of yellow sandalwood (haricandana) and gold, eight of each.

Then, he placed the relics of the Blessed One in a yellow sandalwood casket, and placed that yellow sandalwood casket inside another yellow sandalwood casket, and that one inside another. In this way, having put eight yellow sandalwood caskets one inside another, he placed those eight caskets into eight yellow sandalwood stupas by the same method. Then he placed the eight yellow sandalwood stupas into eight red sandalwood (lohitacandana) caskets, the eight red sandalwood caskets into eight red sandalwood stupas, the eight red sandalwood stupas into eight ivory caskets, and the eight ivory caskets into...
204:
He placed eight ivory caskets into eight ivory stupas; those eight ivory stupas into eight caskets made of all kinds of jewels; those eight jewel caskets into eight stupas made of all kinds of jewels; those eight jewel stupas into eight gold caskets; those eight gold caskets into eight gold stupas; those eight gold stupas into eight silver caskets; those eight silver caskets into eight silver stupas; those eight silver stupas into eight ruby caskets; those eight ruby caskets into eight ruby stupas; those eight ruby stupas into eight red ruby caskets; those eight red ruby caskets into eight red ruby stupas; those eight red ruby stupas into eight variegated ruby caskets; those eight variegated ruby caskets into eight variegated ruby stupas; those eight variegated ruby stupas into eight crystal caskets; and those eight crystal caskets into eight stupas made of crystal.

Above all these stupas, the crystal stupa was the size of the Thūpārāma Stupa. Above that crystal stupa, he had a house made of all kinds of jewels constructed. Above that house, a house made of gold; above that, a house made of silver; and above that, a house made of copper. In that copper house, he scattered sand made of all kinds of jewels and spread thousands of flowers that grow in water and on land. Then, he had images of the five hundred and fifty Jātakas, the eighty Great Elders, King Suddhodana, Queen Mahāmāyā, and the seven co-born ones all made of gold. He had five hundred gold pots and five hundred silver pots placed there. He had five hundred gold banners raised. He had five hundred gold lamps and five hundred silver lamps made, filled them with scented oil, and placed wicks made of fine cloth in those lamps.

Then the Venerable Mahā Kassapa made a resolution: "May the flowers not wither, may the scents not perish, and may the lamps not go out." He then had an inscription carved on a gold plate: "In the future, a prince named Piyadāsa will raise the parasol and become the Righteous King named Asoka. That king will cause these relics to be widely distributed."

King Ajātasattu made offerings with all kinds of requisites and, starting from the beginning, came out while closing the doors. He closed the copper door and, on the door-rope, the bolt...
205:
King Ajātasattu closed the door and placed a large block of ruby right at that door, having an inscription carved: "In the future, may a poor king take this ruby and use it to make offerings to the relics." Sakka, the king of devas, summoned Vissakamma and sent him, saying, "Dear Vissakamma, King Ajātasattu has performed an enshrinement of relics; establish protection there." Vissakamma came and fashioned a mechanical device of wooden predator-figures joined together. In that relic chamber, he made the wooden figures hold crystal-colored swords and set up a machine that rotated continuously with a speed like the wind, fastened by a single pin. Then, he constructed a stone enclosure in the shape of a brick house all around, covered it with a single stone slab from above, heaped soil over it, leveled the ground, and established a stone stupa upon it. When the enshrinement of the relics was thus completed, the Elder Mahā Kassapa, having lived out his life span, attained Parinibbāna; King Ajātasattu also passed away according to his kamma; and the people of that time also passed away.

Later, a prince named Piyadāsa raised the white parasol and became the Righteous King named Asoka. He took those relics and distributed them throughout the island of Jambudīpa. How did he do it? Relying on the novice Nigrodha, he gained faith in the Dispensation and had eighty-four thousand monasteries built. He then asked the Saṅgha of bhikkhus, "Venerable sirs, I have built eighty-four thousand monasteries; from where shall I obtain the relics?" The Saṅgha replied, "Great King, we have heard that there is an enshrinement of relics, but it is not clearly known that it is in such and such a place." The King had the stupa in Rājagaha broken open, but not seeing the relics, he had it restored to its original state. Taking the fourfold assembly—bhikkhus, bhikkhunīs, laymen, and laywomen—he went to Vesālī. Not finding them there either, he went to Kapilavatthu. From there he went to Rāmagāma, but in Rāmagāma, the Nāgas did not allow the stupa to be broken; the hoes that fell upon the stupa broke into pieces. Thus, not finding them there, he went to Allakappa, Veṭhadīpa, Pāvā, and Kusinārā. Having broken open the stupas in all these places and not finding the relics, he restored them to their original state and returned to Rājagaha. He convened the fourfold assembly and asked, "Has anyone ever heard that there is a relic enshrinement in such and such a place?"

Then an Elder one hundred and twenty years old said, "I do not know that the relic enshrinement is in such and such a place. However, when I was seven years old, my father, a Great Elder, made me hold a flower basket and said, 'Come, novice, there is a stone stupa in the midst of such and such a thicket; let us go there,' and he went and made offerings." He also said, "Novice, you should remember this place." "Great King, I only know this much," he said. The King said, "This must be the place where the relics are enshrined," and had the thicket cleared. When the stone stupa and the soil were removed, a plaster floor was found below. Then, after removing the plaster and bricks, he descended into the precinct in order and found sand made of the seven kinds of jewels.
206: "There is a stone stupa; let us go there," he said. After going and making offerings, he said, "Novice, you should mark this place." The novice replied, "Great King, I only know this much." The King said, "This is indeed the place where the relics are enshrined." He had the bushes cleared away, and upon removing the stone stupa and the earth, he saw the plaster ground beneath. Then, having the plaster and bricks removed, he descended into the courtyard in due order and saw sand made of the seven jewels and wooden mechanical figures holding swords that were revolving back and forth. The King summoned the spirit-servants and offered sacrificial food, but since he could not see the beginning or the end, he paid homage to the deities and said, "I will take these relics and enshrine them in eighty-four thousand monasteries to perform offerings. May the deities not create obstacles for me." Sakka, the king of gods, saw this while traveling and addressed Vissakamma, "Dear, King Asoka the Righteous has descended into the courtyard to take the relics. Go and remove the wooden mechanical figures." Vissakamma went in the guise of a village boy with five topknots, stood before the King holding a bow, and said, "Great King, I shall remove them." When the King said, "Dear, remove them," he took an arrow and shot it exactly at the joint, and all the mechanical figures were scattered. Then the King took the iron bolt tied to the door-pull and saw a mass of rubies. Seeing the inscription again, "In the future, may a poor king take this ruby and make offerings to the relics," he became angry and said, "It is not fitting to call a king like me a poor king." He repeatedly joined the parts, had the door opened, and entered the inner chamber. The lamps that had been lit for over two hundred years (218 years) were still burning just as they were. The blue lotuses appeared as if they had just been brought and placed there; the flower spreads appeared as if they had just been laid out; the perfumes appeared as if they had just been ground and placed there at that very moment. The King took the gold plate and read, "In the future, a prince named Piyadāsa will raise the white parasol and become the righteous king named Asoka. That king will distribute these relics far and wide." He then said, "The Venerable Elder Mahākassapa has indeed seen me!" He bent his left arm and struck it with his right hand in a gesture of triumph. The King left only a small portion of relics for worship at that place, took the remaining relics, closed the relic chamber in the same manner as before, restored everything to its original state, established a stone stupa on top, and in the eighty-four thousand monasteries...
225:
He served the elder for the rest of his life. The elder, residing right there, attained Arahatship and entered Parinibbāna.

The Bodhisatta, having performed meritorious deeds throughout his lifespan, was reborn in the celestial realm. Passing away from there, he came to the human world and was reborn in the royal city of Kusāvatī as King Mahāsudassana.

"Even if not very great, merit performed in the right place (āyatana) yields great results; therefore, the wise person should perform such merit."

'Mahāviyūha' refers to a great palace made of silver. Desiring to reside in that palace, he went there and halted the three types of thoughts at the very door of the palace, saying: "Sensual thoughts (kāmavitakka) are only this much. O sensual thought, you must turn back from here. Beyond this is not your ground; this is called the abode of Jhana (absorption). This is not a place for residing with you."

In the first Jhana and so forth, there is no separate task of kasiṇa preliminary work (parikamma). When there is a need for the blue kasiṇa (nīlakasiṇa), a blue gem (nīlamaṇi) appears; for the yellow kasiṇa (pītakasiṇa), gold; for the red kasiṇa (lohitakasiṇa), a red gem; and for the white kasiṇa (odātakasiṇa), silver. Wherever he looks, the kasiṇa itself becomes manifest.

Everything that should be said regarding 'accompanied by loving-kindness' (metta-sahagata) and so forth has already been stated in the Visuddhimagga. Thus, in the Pali text, only the four Jhanas and the four Boundless States (appamaññā) are mentioned. However, the Great Being (Mahāpurisa), having attained all eight meditative attainments (samāpatti) and the five superknowledges (abhiññā), enters the attainments in fourteen ways, such as in forward and reverse order (anuloma-paṭiloma). Just as a bee entering a honeycomb sustains itself with the taste of honey, he lives sustaining himself solely with the bliss of the meditative attainments.

## Description of the Eighty-four Thousand Cities and So Forth

'Kusāvatīrāja-dhānippamukhāni' means with the royal city of Kusāvatī as the chief, the most excellent among those cities. 'Bhattābhihāro' refers to the food (alms) that is to be brought.
237: Regarding 'oḷārika' (gross): in this context, let bodily formations (kāya-saṅkhāra) and verbal formations (vacī-saṅkhāra) be considered gross first; but why are mental formations (citta-saṅkhāra) considered gross? It is because they have not yet been abandoned. Indeed, bodily formations are abandoned by the fourth jhana, verbal formations by the second jhana, and mental formations by the attainment of cessation (nirodha-samāpatti). Thus, even when bodily and verbal formations have been abandoned, those mental formations still persist; therefore, in comparison to the abandoned states, they are called 'gross' because they are not yet abandoned. 'Sukha' (bliss) refers to the bliss of the attainment of fruition (phala-samāpatti) associated with the fourth jhana that arises for one emerging from the attainment of cessation. 'Somanassa' (joy) that is superior to bliss refers to the joy that occurs repeatedly after emerging from the attainment of fruition. The 'second attainment of opportunity' (okāsādhigama) means that the fourth jhana, having set aside pleasure and pain, takes its own opportunity and stands; therefore, it is called the 'second attainment of opportunity.' In this context, when the fourth jhana is taken, the second and third jhanas are already included, so they are not mentioned separately.## This is wholesome, etc. In these words, 'wholesome' (kusala) refers to the ten wholesome courses of action (kusala-kammapatha). 'Unwholesome' (akusala) refers to the ten unwholesome courses of action. The dyads such as 'blameworthy' (sāvazza-duka) and so on should also be understood by the power of these states. All these states are called 'kaṇha-sukka-sappaṭibhāga' because they are dark (kaṇha), bright (sukka), and have counterparts (sappaṭibhāga). Nibbāna alone is 'appaṭibhāga' (incomparable/without counterpart). 'Avijjā pahīyati' (ignorance is abandoned) means the ignorance that veils the round of rebirth is abandoned. 'Vijjā uppajjati' (knowledge arises) means the knowledge of the path of Arahantship arises. 'Sukha' refers to both the bliss of the path of Arahantship and the bliss of fruition. 'Somanassa' superior to bliss refers to the joy that occurs repeatedly for one who has emerged from the attainment of fruition. The 'third attainment of opportunity' means that the path of Arahantship, having set aside all defilements, takes its own opportunity and stands; therefore, it is called the 'third attainment of opportunity.' The remaining paths are already included within that path of Arahantship, so they are not mentioned separately. These three attainments of opportunity should be explained in detail by way of the thirty-eight meditation objects. How? By defining all meditation objects according to the method stated in the Visuddhimagga, by way of access (upacāra) and absorption (appanā), the first jhana in twenty-four places should be called the 'first attainment of opportunity.' The second and third jhanas in thirteen places, and the fourth jhana and the attainment of cessation in fifteen places, should be called the 'second attainment of opportunity.' The ten access jhanas, which are the proximate cause (padaṭṭhāna) of the path, belong to the third attainment of opportunity. Furthermore, among the three trainings, the training in higher virtue (adhisīla-sikkhā) belongs to the first attainment of opportunity, the training in higher mind (adhicitta-sikkhā) to the second, and the training in higher wisdom (adhipaññā-sikkhā) to the third; thus it should also be explained by way of the trainings. Also in the Sāmaññaphala Sutta, from the minor section on virtue (cūḷa-sīla) up to the first jhana is the first...
243: The seat for the King of Gods is prepared. Then for the thirty-three gods, and then for other powerful deities. For other deities, however, only the pericarp of a flower serves as a seat. The gods enter the divine assembly hall and sit down. Then, clusters of pollen rise from the flowers, hit the canopy above, and fall down, making the bodies of the deities—which are three gāvutas in size—appear as if they were decorated with lacquer resin. Their play comes to an end only after four months. In this way, they assemble to enjoy the play at the Pāricchattaka tree. On the eighth day of the month, the announcement for the great listening of the Dhamma resounds in the deva world. Then, in the Sudhammā divine assembly hall, either Sanatkumāra Mahābrahmā, or Sakka the King of Gods, or a Dhamma-preaching monk, or some other Dhamma-preaching deity preaches the Dhamma. On the eighth day of the fortnight, the ministers of the Four Great Kings; on the fourteenth day, their sons; and on the fifteenth day, the Four Great Kings themselves go out, taking golden scrolls and vermilion, and wander through villages, market towns, and royal capitals. Those kings record with vermilion on the golden scrolls: 'Such a woman or such a man has gone to the Buddha for refuge, has gone to the Dhamma for refuge, has gone to the Saṅgha for refuge. They observe the five precepts. They observe the uposatha eight days a month. They fulfill the duty of serving their mother. They fulfill the duty of serving their father. In such a place, an offering was made with a hundred handfuls of lotuses and flower-pots. A thousand lamps were lit. They listened to the Dhamma at an unusual time. They built tiered shrines, thrones, and staircases. They fulfill the three types of good conduct. They undertake and practice the ten wholesome courses of action.' Having recorded this, they bring it and place it in the hands of the deity Pañcasikha. Pañcasikha places it in the hands of the deity Mātali. Mātali the charioteer gives it to Sakka, the King of Gods. When there are not many people performing meritorious deeds, the book is small; seeing that, the gods become displeased, saying: 'Alas, sirs, the great multitude of people live in negligence; the four woeful states will be filled, and the six deva worlds will be empty.' But if the book is large, seeing it, the gods are pleased, saying: 'Alas, sirs, the great multitude of people live without negligence; the four woeful states will be empty...'
244:
(The six celestial realms) will be filled; they rejoiced, thinking, 'We shall have the opportunity to celebrate the festival of the stars, placing at the forefront the many meritorious ones who have come after performing meritorious deeds in the Buddha's Dispensation.' Sakka, the King of Devas, took that book and read it. When he read in his natural voice, the sound spread for twelve yojanas. When he read with a loud voice, it remained pervading the entire ten thousand celestial cities. Thus, they gathered to hear the Dhamma. However, it should be understood that here they gathered to support the performance of the Pavāraṇā.

'Tathāgataṃ namassantā' means worshipping and honoring the Tathāgata through nine reasons. 'Dhammassa ca sudhammataṃ' refers to the excellent nature of the Dhamma, characterized by being well-proclaimed (svākkhāta) and so forth. 'Saṅghassa ca suppaṭipattiṃ' refers to the good practice of the Saṅgha, characterized by practicing rightly (ujuppaṭipanna) and so forth.

## Commentary on the Eightfold Truthful Praise
'Yathābhucce' means according to the truth, according to nature. 'Vaṇṇe' means virtues or qualities. 'Payirudāhāsī' means he uttered or spoke. 'Bahujanahitāya paṭipanno'—how did he practice? Even while he was striving toward Buddhahood by combining the eight factors at the feet of the Buddha Dīpaṅkara, he was said to be practicing for the benefit of many.

While he was fulfilling these ten perfections (pāramīs)—the perfection of generosity (dāna), virtue (sīla), renunciation (nekkhamma), wisdom (paññā), energy (vīriya), patience (khanti), truthfulness (sacca), determination (adhiṭṭhāna), loving-kindness (mettā), and equanimity (upekkhā)—for four asankheyyas and a hundred thousand aeons, he was also said to be practicing for the benefit of many.

When he performed such difficult deeds as the ascetic Khantivādī, Prince Cūḷadhammapāla, the elephant king Chaddanta, the naga kings Bhūridatta, Campeyya, and Saṅkhapāla, and the monkey king Mahākapi, he was also said to be practicing for the benefit of many. While existing in the life of King Vessantara, giving the great gift of seven hundreds and causing the earth to shake in seven places, reaching the pinnacle of the perfections, he was also said to be practicing for the benefit of many. In the existence immediately following that, while staying in the Tusita heaven for his full lifespan, he was also said to be practicing for the benefit of many.

Having seen the five omens in that celestial realm and being requested by the devas and brahmas of the ten thousand world systems, he looked at the five great investigations and gave his word to support the devas.
259:
'Sikkhamāno' means one who trains and practices in these teachings. This is just a summary; the details have already been spoken above by Mahāgovinda and the Brahmā.

In that context, 'ete avidvā' means 'I do not know, I do not understand these āmagandha (taints/impurities).' 'Idha brūhi dhīra' means 'O wise one, tell me, speak to me about those taints here.' 'Kenāvaṭā vā' means 'By what hindrance of defilements are the multitude of beings obstructed so that they smell with a putrid odor?' 'Āpāyikā' means leading to the states of deprivation (apāya). 'Nivutabrahmalokā' means those for whom the Brahma world is closed. He asks, 'By what defilement is the path of beings leading to the Brahma world obstructed, closed, and hidden?'

Anger (kodha) characterized by irritation; lying (musāvāda) characterized by deceiving others; deception (nikati) characterized by trickery by showing something similar; treachery (dubbha) characterized by betraying friends; stinginess (kadariyatā) characterized by rigid miserliness; arrogance (atimāna) characterized by thinking oneself superior; envy (usūyā) characterized by resentment of others' success; desire (icchā) characterized by craving; meanness (vivicchā) characterized by selfishness; harassing others (paraheṭhanā) characterized by violence; greed (lobha) characterized by attachment to anything; hatred (dosa) characterized by malice; pride (mada) characterized by intoxication; and delusion (moha) characterized by confusion. The multitude of beings associated with these fourteen defilements are not free from āmagandha; they possess āmagandha, they smell like a rotting carcass, and they have a putrid odor. 'Āpāyikā nivutabrahmalokā' means that such a person both goes to the states of deprivation and has the path to the Brahma world obstructed. The one who teaches this sutta should explain it using the Āmagandha Sutta; the Āmagandha Sutta should also be explained using this sutta.

'Te na sunimmadayā' means those taints are not easily subdued or abandoned; they are difficult to give up and difficult to conquer. 'Yassa dāni bhavaṃ govindo kālaṃ maññati' means 'Whatever time Lord Govinda considers right for this renunciation, let it be so; if it is so, my coming to you will be a good coming, and the Dhamma talk spoken will be well-spoken. O dear son, you...'
262:
## Commentary on the Invitation of the Six Khattiyas

"He approached where those six kings were" means that he approached King Reṇu after encouraging him and strengthening his resolve, saying, "Excellent, Great King! While in this world beings even kill their mothers, fathers, brothers, sisters, and so forth to seize royal power, it is truly noble of the Great King to desire to renounce such great royal glory and go forth into the homeless life."

"Thus they thought together" means they thought in the same manner as the King had thought, considering that perhaps at some time the Brahmin's wealth and possessions might decline.

"We shall win them over with wealth" means to entice, win over, or support them.

"Let that much wealth be brought" means let as much as is desired be brought or taken; it means, "Take as much as you wish."

"It is only because of you, sirs" means that it is because of you as the cause, and because of your generosity, that such abundant wealth has arisen.

"If you renounce sensual pleasures" means if you abandon both objective sensuality (vatthukāma) and subjective sensuality (kilesakāma).

"In which sensual pleasures the worldling is attached" means the attachment and clinging of the worldling (puthujjana) to those sensual pleasures.

"Exert effort, be firm" means in such a case, exert energy and be steadfast by resolving on unshakable perseverance.

"Be endowed with the strength of patience" means be possessed of the strength of patience; thus he inspires effort in the kings.

"This path is the straight path" means this path of the meditation on compassion (karuṇājhāna) is called the straight path.

"This path is the unsurpassed path" means this very path is the incomparable and supreme path for rebirth in the Brahma-world.

"The Dhamma of the good, protected by the virtuous" means this is the Dhamma protected by the virtuous ones, namely the Buddhas, Paccekabuddhas, and disciples (sāvakas). Thus, by praising the qualities of the meditation on compassion, he strengthens their resolve so they do not turn back.

"Sirs, who can know [the end of] life?" means, sirs, life is like a water bubble, like a drop of dew on the tip of a blade of grass, having the nature of perishing in an instant; who can know its destination, or at what moment it will break?

"One must surely go to the next world" means the next world must certainly be gone to; a wise man of good family should understand this with wisdom. "Mantā" refers to wisdom (paññā); the meaning is that one should reflect, know, investigate, and understand with that wisdom. Alternatively, the locative case is used in the sense of the instrumental (karaṇattha). "Mantāyaṃ boddhabbaṃ" means it should be understood through wisdom, it should be known through knowledge. What should be understood? The fact that life is difficult to know,
263:
and the certainty of having to go to the next world; and having understood this, one should cut off all impediments (palibodha), perform the merit that should be performed, and practice the holy life (brahmacariya) that should be practiced. Why? Because for a being who is born, there is no such thing as not dying.

## Commentary on the Invitation of the Great Brahmin Halls and Others

"Few followers and few gains" means, sirs, the life of a monk is of little fame; from the time of going forth, people speak of one who has renounced royal glory to become a monk by harassing and troubling him, treating him as a lowly, helpless person. Gains are also very few; even after wandering through an entire village, it is difficult to obtain food to eat. But this Brahmin life is of great fame because of its high status, and gains are abundant because it is endowed with offerings and honor. It means that you, sir, are now the chief chaplain (purohita) in the entire Jambudīpa, receiving the best seat, the best water, the best food, the best scent, and the best flowers in all places.

"Like a king among kings" means, "I am now like a universal monarch (cakkavatti) in the midst of ordinary kings."

"Like a Brahmā among Brahmās" means like a Great Brahma (Mahābrahmā) in the midst of ordinary Brahmas.

"Like a deity among householders" means, "I am like Sakka, the king of devas, in the midst of the remaining householders."

## Commentary on the Invitation of the Wives

"Forty similar wives" means there were forty wives of equal status; however, there were also many other dancing women of the three ages.

## Commentary on the Renunciation of Mahāgovinda

"Wandering on tour" means he wandered through villages and market towns in succession; wherever he went, there was a great stir like the 'Buddha-uproar' (Buddha-kolāhala). When people heard that "the wise Mahāgovinda is coming," they would build pavilions in advance, decorate the roads, go out to meet him, and escort him; great offerings and honors arose, overwhelming like a powerful torrent of water.

"To the chaplain of the seven kings" means because he was the chaplain to seven kings. Thus, just as nowadays in such places or when some suffering arises, people say "Namo Buddhassa," so at that time they said, "Homage to the Brahmin Mahāgovinda, homage to the chaplain of the seven kings."
269:
Thinking, "I shall dispel [the dissatisfaction of the monks]," the Blessed One described the beauty of Lake Kunāla. Those monks desired to see it. "Monks, do you wish to see Lake Kunāla?" he asked. "Yes, Venerable Sir," they replied. "If so, come, let us go," he said. When they asked, "How shall we go to the place where the Blessed One, possessed of psychic power, goes?" he said, "Just have the desire to go; I shall take you by my own psychic power." "Very well, Venerable Sir," they replied. Then the Blessed One, taking the five hundred monks, rose into the air and, alighting at Lake Kunāla, said to those monks: "Monks, in this Lake Kunāla, ask the names of those fishes whose names you do not know."

The monks asked, and the Blessed One answered everything they asked. He had them ask and then explained not only the names of the fishes but also the names of the trees in that forest grove, and the names of the bipeds, quadrupeds, and birds at the foot of the mountain. Then, the Kunāla bird-king came, sitting on a stick held in the beaks of two birds, surrounded by a flock of birds in front, behind, and on both sides. Seeing him, the monks thought, "Venerable Sir, this must be the king of these birds; these must be his retinue." "So it is, monks; this is my lineage, my ancestry," the Blessed One said. "Venerable Sir, now we see these birds. But we wish to hear the words the Blessed One spoke: 'This is my lineage, my ancestry'." "Do you wish to hear, monks?" he asked. "Yes, Venerable Sir," they replied. "Then listen," he said, and dispelled their dissatisfaction by telling the Kunāla Jātaka, adorned with three hundred verses. At the conclusion of the teaching, all the monks were established in the fruit of Stream-entry, and psychic powers also came to them along with the Path. Thinking, "Let this much benefit be for these monks for now," the Blessed One rose into the air and went to the Mahāvana forest. While those monks had gone by the power of the Ten-Powered One, upon returning, they descended to the Mahāvana forest surrounding the Blessed One by their own psychic power.

The Blessed One sat on the prepared seat and addressed those monks: "Come, monks, sit down. I shall teach you the meditation subject for the abandoning of your defilements that are to be destroyed by the three higher paths." He then taught the meditation subject. The monks thought, "The Blessed One, knowing our state of dissatisfaction, took us to Lake Kunāla and dispelled that dissatisfaction. To us who attained the fruit of Stream-entry there, he has now given the meditation subject for the three paths here. It is not proper for us to waste time thinking, 'We are Stream-enterers'; we should strive to be like noble men." Having paid homage at the feet of the Ten-Powered One, they rose, shook out their sitting mats, and sat down individually in mountain caves and at the feet of trees.
275:
Then the Blessed One, reflecting, "What are these deities thinking?" perceived their mental activity as if catching a thief with the stolen goods, or as if squeezing the flesh of the heart by putting a hand into the mouth. He thought, "I shall announce the names and clans of all the deities, both of minor and major influence, who have come from the ten thousand world systems."

Those called Buddhas are extraordinary and great beings. In the world with its devas, whatever is seen, heard, sensed, cognized, attained, sought after, and pondered over by the mind—there is nothing at all, whether among the objects of sight classified by colors like blue and so on, or among the objects of sound classified by drum sounds and so on, that does not come into the range of their knowledge. Regarding this, it is said:
"Monks, whatever in the world with its devas... [pe]... is seen, heard, sensed, cognized, attained, sought after, and pondered over by the mind by devas and humans, that I know, that I see, that I have fully realized with higher knowledge." (A.N. 4.24)

Thus, the Blessed One, whose knowledge is unimpeded in all things, divided all those deities into two groups: the capable (bhabba) and the incapable (abhabba). Those beings described by such methods as "possessed of karmic obstructions" are called incapable. Even if they live in the same monastery, the Buddhas do not look at them. Conversely, those called capable are those whom the Buddhas go to and assist even if they live far away. Therefore, in that assembly of deities as well, he set aside the incapable and took up the capable. Having taken them up, he divided them into six groups according to their temperaments: "This many here are of greedy temperament, this many are of hateful temperament, this many are of deluded temperament."

Then, considering the Dhamma teaching suitable for them, he determined the teaching: "I shall preach the Sammāparibbājanīya Sutta to the deities of greedy temperament, the Kalahavivāda Sutta to those of hateful temperament, the Mahābyūha Sutta to those of deluded temperament, the Cūḷabyūha Sutta to those of speculative temperament, the Tuvaṭṭaka-paṭipadā to those of faithful temperament, and the Purābheda Sutta to those of wise temperament." Having thus determined the teaching, he again reflected on that assembly: "Should I make it known by my own inclination, or by the power of questions arising from the inclination of others?" Then, knowing "It should be known by the power of questions," he looked to see, "Is there anyone capable of taking up the inclination of the deities and asking questions according to their temperaments?" He saw that "Among those five hundred monks, not even one is capable." Then, he turned his attention to the eighty great disciples and the two chief disciples...
291:
Looking at all these splendors—the Cittalatā Grove, the Missaka Grove, and the Phārusaka Grove—he was overwhelmed by fear, thinking, "Indeed, this prosperity of mine will surely perish."

Then, searching for someone, he thought, "Is there any recluse (samaṇa) or brahmin, or even Mahābrahmā, the Grandfather of the World (Lokapitāmaha), who can pluck out this arrow of sorrow (sokasal-la) lodged in my heart and make this prosperity stable?" Seeing no one, he realized again, "Only the Fully Enlightened Buddha is capable of plucking out the arrow of sorrow that has arisen in hundreds of thousands of beings like me." At that moment, as he was reflecting thus, Sakka, the King of Gods, felt a keen desire to see the Blessed One.

He reflected: "Where is the Blessed One staying now? In which district, depending on which city, using whose four requisites, and to whom is he preaching the Deathless Dhamma (Amata Dhamma)?" The phrase "Addasā kho" means he saw or penetrated with knowledge. "Mārisa" is a term of endearment, a specific mode of address among devas. It also means "one who is free from suffering." Why did Sakka call the devas? It was to have them as companions. It is said that previously, when the Blessed One was staying at the Saḷala house, Sakka went to see him alone. The Teacher, thinking, "His wisdom is not yet mature; after a few days, while I am staying in the Indasāla Cave, he will see the five portents (pubbanimitta) and, fearing death, will approach me with the devas of the two heavens, ask fourteen questions, and at the end of the explanation of the questions on equanimity, he will be established in the Fruit of Stream-entry (Sotāpattiphala) along with eighty thousand devas," did not grant him the opportunity. Sakka thought, "Because I went alone before, the Teacher did not grant me an opportunity. Perhaps I do not yet have the supporting condition (upanissaya) for the Path and Fruit. However, if even one person has the supporting condition, the Blessed One will surely preach the Dhamma to the assembly as far as the limits of the world-system. Surely, some deva in the two heavens will have the supporting condition, and the Teacher will preach the Dhamma on account of that deva. By hearing that Dhamma, I too shall appease my own distress." Thinking thus, he called the devas to accompany him.

"May it be a blessing to you, O Great King," the Tāvatiṃsa devas said. "Great King, let it be so. Let us go to see the Blessed One. The arising of a Buddha is rare indeed. It is a blessing to you that you did not say, 'Let us go to play in the mountains or the rivers,' but instead urged us toward such a goal." The word "Passassosuṃ" means they accepted the words of Sakka with the highest respect.
292:
Regarding the statement "He called the Gandhabba deva Pañcasikha"—after calling the other devas, why did he call this deva separately? It was for the purpose of obtaining an opportunity. It is said that Sakka thought, "It is not appropriate to approach the Teacher by leading the devas of the two heavens as if striking him head-on. This Pañcasikha, however, is a beloved attendant of the One of Ten Powers (Dasabala); he goes at any desired moment to ask questions and listen to the Dhamma. I will send him ahead to request an opportunity, and only after he has secured it will I approach and ask my questions." Thus, he called him for the purpose of obtaining an opportunity.

"May it be a blessing to you," said the deva. "Great King, let it be so. May it be a blessing to you, for you did not say to me, 'Come, friend, let us go to see the play in the gardens or to witness the performances of actors and dancers,' but instead said, 'We shall see the Buddha, we shall hear the Dhamma.'" Supporting Sakka's words very firmly, he accepted the command and joined him in going together.

In that context, "Beluvapaṇḍu" refers to a lute with a pale yellow color like a ripe wood-apple. It is said that the lute's soundboard (pokkhara) was made of gold, the neck (daṇḍa) of sapphire, the strings of silver, and the tuning pegs (veṭhaka) of coral. The arm of the lute (vīṇāpattaka) was one gāvuta in length, the area where the strings are tied was one gāvuta, and the upper neck was one gāvuta, making the lute three gāvutas in size. Thus, taking that lute, he tuned it to the fifty musical scales, struck it with his fingertips, and produced a sweet melodic sound. He stood to one side, letting the other devas know it was time for Sakka's departure. When the host of devas had assembled at the signal of his singing and playing, Sakka, the King of Gods... [and so on]... appeared at Mount Vediyaka.

"Atiriva obhāsajāto" means that on other days, the place would be radiant with the light of a single deva, or Māra, or a Brahmā. But on that day, it was exceedingly radiant with the light of the devas from the two heavens, becoming a single blaze of light, like the time when a thousand suns and moons have risen. "Parito gāmesu manussā" means the people in the surrounding villages. It is said that Sakka went to that place exactly at the time of the regular evening meal, while children were playing in the middle of the village. Therefore, the people saw it and said: "Is it not at the middle watch of the night that devas usually approach the Blessed One? This..."
297:
The word 'upanaccantiyā' means while dancing. That goddess, at one time, went with the devas of the Four Great Kings (Cātumahārājika) to watch a dance for Sakka, the king of devas. At that moment, Sakka spoke the eight true qualities of the Tathāgata. Thus, while going and dancing on that day, she heard those qualities.

## Description of Sakka's Approach (Sakkūpasaṅkamavaṇṇanā)

'Paṭisammodatī' means the Blessed One rejoiced, saying, "These things of yours agree with mine," and so on; Pañcasikha also rejoiced in return. When reciting the verses, Pañcasikha rejoiced, and the Blessed One rejoiced in return. 'Āmantesī' means he made it known. It is said that Sakka had this thought: "I sent this Pañcasikha on my business, but he is doing his own business. Standing in the presence of such a Teacher, he speaks inappropriate words connected with sensual pleasures. Those who are dancers are indeed shameless; while speaking, he might even show improper gestures. Let me make my business known to him." Thinking thus, he addressed him.

'Evañca pana tathāgatā' and so forth are the words placed by the Elders who were Dhamma-reciters (Dhammasaṅgāhakas). 'Abhivadantī' means they spoke with words of greeting by way of accepting the salutation. 'Abhivadito' means spoken to with words of greeting.

'Urundā samapādi' means it became large and open; the darkness in the cave vanished. 'Āloko udapādi' means the natural darkness that was in the cave vanished, and light arose. All these are the words of the Dhamma-reciters.

'Bhante, cirapaṭikāhaṃ' means "Venerable Sir, I have desired to see you for a long time," or "since a long time ago."

'Kehici kehici kiccakaraṇīyehī' refers to the fact that the daughters and sons of devas are born on the laps [of devas]; the women who serve at the feet are born on the beds; the devas who perform the tasks of decorating and adorning them are born surrounding the beds; those who perform services are born inside the celestial mansions (vimānas). For these, there is no such thing as a legal dispute. However, those who are born in the boundary between two mansions, being unable to decide "This is yours" or "This is mine," create a dispute and ask Sakka, the king of devas. He says, "To whomsoever's mansion it is closer, it belongs to that person."
298:
If the distance is equal to both sides, he says, "To whomsoever's mansion she stands looking at, it belongs to that person." If she does not look at either one, he takes her as his own property for the sake of cutting off the quarrel between the two. Activities such as playing are also tasks that must be done. Referring to such duties to be performed, he said, "due to some business or other."

'Salalāgārake' means in the scented hut made of Salala wood. 'Aññatarena samādhinā' means at that time, the Blessed One, knowing that Sakka's knowledge had not yet reached maturity and wishing to create an opportunity, sat in the dwelling of the attainment of fruition (phalasamāpatti). Not knowing this, Sakka said, "by a certain concentration."

'Bhūjati' is the name of that goddess. 'Paricārikā' refers to the goddess who serves at the feet. It is said that she had attained two fruits (of the path), and therefore she had no delight at all in the deva world. She would constantly come to serve the Blessed One, and standing with her hands joined in reverence on her head, she would remain worshiping the Blessed One.

Regarding 'nemisaddena tamhā samādhimhā vuṭṭhito' (emerged from that concentration due to the sound of the chariot rim), it should not be said that "one who has entered an attainment hears sound." Did the Blessed One not say to Sakka, the lord of devas, "I have indeed emerged from that concentration due to the sound of the rim of your honor's chariot"? Let alone the sound of the chariot rim, one who has entered an attainment does not hear even the sound of a pair of conch shells being blown near the ear, nor even the sound of a thunderbolt while within the attainment. However, the Blessed One, having determined, "I will not give an opportunity to Sakka for this much time," entered the attainment of fruition according to that time. Sakka, thinking, "Now the Teacher does not yet give me an opportunity," circumambulated the scented hut to the right, turned the chariot, and sent it toward the deva world. The courtyard of the scented hut became as if filled with the sound of the five-fold musical instruments due to the sound of the chariot. When the Blessed One emerged from the attainment according to the predetermined time, the first reflection (āvajjanā) arose precisely because of the sound of the chariot; therefore, he spoke thus.

## Description of the Story of Gopaka (Gopakavatthuvaṇṇanā)

'Sīlesu paripūrakārinī' means one who fulfills the five precepts. 'Itthittaṃ virājetvā' means having become weary of womanhood. Indeed, while remaining in womanhood, it is not possible to experience the glory of a Cakkavatti (Universal Monarch), nor the glories of Sakka, Māra, or Brahma, nor is it possible to reach Paccekabodhi or Sammāsambodhi; thus, one is said to be weary of womanhood. Thinking, "This state of manhood is great, noble, and supreme; staying in this state, it is possible to attain these successes,"...
381:
Knowing, "Today my son has reached the pinnacle of the monk's task," he said, "Mother, my elder brother delights in the Buddha's Dispensation; he is not dissatisfied."

Indeed, this heritage of the Teacher, known as the seven noble wealths, is very great; it is not possible for a lazy person to acquire it. Just as parents might cast out a wayward son, saying, "This person is not our son," and that son does not receive the inheritance upon their passing; in the same way, a lazy person cannot obtain this heritage of noble wealth. Only one who has aroused energy can obtain it. Thus, energy also arises in one who reflects on the greatness of the heritage.

The Teacher is also truly great. At the time of the Teacher's conception in his mother's womb, at his Great Renunciation, at his Enlightenment, at the Turning of the Wheel of Dhamma, at the performance of the Twin Miracle, at the descent from the Tāvatiṃsa heaven, at the relinquishing of the formations of life, and at the time of his Parinibbāna, the ten-thousandfold world system trembled. Is it proper for you to remain lazy after having gone forth in the Dispensation of such a Teacher? Thus, energy also arises in one who reflects on the greatness of the Teacher.

By birth also, you are not of low birth now; you are born in the royal lineage of Okkāka, descended from the unbroken line of Mahāsammata. You are the grandson of King Suddhodana and Queen Mahāmāyā, and the younger brother of Venerable Rāhula. Being a son of the Conqueror (Jinaputta) such as yourself, it is not proper to live lazily. Thus, energy also arises in one who reflects on the greatness of birth.

Venerable Sāriputta, Venerable Mahāmoggallāna, and the eighty great disciples realized the supramundane Dhamma only through energy. Will you follow the path of these fellow practitioners of the holy life, or will you not? Thus, energy also arises in one who reflects on the greatness of one's fellow practitioners.

Energy also arises in one who avoids lazy persons who, like a python lying with a full belly, have lax physical and mental energy; in one who associates with persons of aroused energy who are devoted to the goal; and in one whose mind is inclined, sloped, and bent toward arousing energy in postures such as standing and sitting. He knows that for one in whom energy has thus arisen, the fulfillment of its development is reached through the Path of Arahantship.

Regarding the enlightenment factor of rapture (pītisambojjhaṅga): "Bhikkhus, there are things that are the basis for the enlightenment factor of rapture; frequently giving wise attention to them is the nutriment for the arising of the unarisen enlightenment factor of rapture, or for the growth, increase, and fulfillment of the development of the arisen enlightenment factor of rapture." Thus is its arising.
384:
...causes urgency. The eight grounds for urgency (saṃvegavatthu) are: birth, aging, sickness, and death—these four; the suffering of the states of deprivation is the fifth; the suffering rooted in the round of rebirth in the past; the suffering rooted in the round of rebirth in the future; and the suffering rooted in the search for food in the present. Also, by recollecting the virtues of the Triple Gem, one inspires confidence; this is called "gladdening at the proper time."

Equanimity at the proper time means: at the time when the mind has reached right practice and is not shrinking, not restless, without attachment, proceeding evenly toward the object, and has entered the path of serenity (samatha), then one no longer exerts effort in encouraging, restraining, or gladdening that mind, just like a charioteer when the horses are running evenly. This is called "equanimity at the proper time." Avoiding uncomposed persons means keeping far away from persons who have not attained access concentration (upacāra) or absorption (appanā) and whose minds are distracted. Associating with composed persons means associating with, frequenting, and attending upon persons whose minds are composed through access or absorption concentration. Inclination toward that concentration means having a mind that is inclined, sloped, and bent only toward the arising of concentration in postures such as standing and sitting. For one practicing in this way, this concentration arises. He knows that for one in whom concentration has thus arisen, the fulfillment of its development is reached through the Path of Arahantship.
