Regarding the enlightenment factor of equanimity (upekkhāsambojjhaṅga): "Bhikkhus, there are things that are the basis for the enlightenment factor of equanimity; frequently giving wise attention to them is the nutriment for the arising of the unarisen enlightenment factor of equanimity, or for the growth, increase, and fulfillment of the development of the arisen enlightenment factor of equanimity." Thus is its arising. Therein, equanimity itself is the thing that is the basis for the enlightenment factor of equanimity.

Furthermore, five things lead to the arising of the enlightenment factor of equanimity: neutrality towards beings, neutrality towards formations, avoiding persons who are attached to beings and formations, associating with persons who are neutral towards beings and formations, and having a mind inclined toward that equanimity. Therein, one establishes neutrality towards beings in two ways: through the reflection on ownership of kamma, "You have come by your own kamma and will depart by your own kamma; this person also has come by his own kamma and will depart by his own kamma—whom are you attached to?"; and through the reflection on the absence of a being, "In the ultimate sense, there is no being at all—whom are you attached to?" One establishes neutrality towards formations also in two ways: "This robe, gradually reaching discoloration and wear, will become a foot-wiping cloth and be discarded with the tip of a stick; if it..."
398:
The Blessed One had preached the Sudhābhojanīya Jātaka not long before that. In that Jātaka, it is mentioned: "The deity Canda in the moon, the deity Suriya in the sun." Whether it be a Jātaka or a Sutta preached by the Blessed One, it spreads throughout the whole of Jambudīpa. Thinking, "It cannot be said that there are no deities residing here," he said that they are deities and not humans.

"Rājañña, is there another way?" he asks for the reason. Ābādhikā refers to those possessed of affliction known as disagreeable sensation. Dukkhitā refers to those who have reached suffering. Bāḷhagilānā refers to those who are extremely ill. Saddhāyikā means "I believe you; you are those whose words are to be believed." Paccayikā means "I trust you; you are those who are to be trusted."

## Explanation of the Simile of the Thief and Others
Uddisitvā means pointing out their bodies and the property they have kept, meaning to hand them over. Vippalapantassa refers to one who is lamenting in various ways, saying, "My son, my daughter, my wealth." Nirayapālesu refers to the beings who carry out punishments in hell. Those who say, "Only kamma itself performs the punishment, there are no hell-wardens," contradict the Devadūta Sutta which says, "Monks, the hell-wardens [take] this person..." Indeed, just as there are executioners in the royal courts of the human world, there are hell-wardens in hell.

Veḷupesikāhi means with bamboo splints. Sunimmajjathā means to clean well, meaning to clean so that it is thoroughly cleansed, to remove.

Asuci means unpleasant. Asucisaṅkhāto means a mass of impurity, or one known as impure. Duggandho means having the smell of a corpse. Jeguccho means associated with loathsomeness. Paṭikūlo means bringing about aversion just by being seen. Ubbādhati means that even the scent of humans such as Universal Monarchs, who bathe twice a day, change clothes three times, and are well-adorned, disturbs deities staying a hundred leagues away, like a rotting corpse fastened to the neck.
399:
Again, he speaks by virtue of those who undertake and practice the five precepts such as abstaining from taking life. Tāvatiṃsānaṃ means "Those deities are far away; let them not come for that long; why do these [people] not come?"

Jaccandhūpamo maññe paṭibhāsī means he appeared like one born blind. Araññavanapatthāni: they are called arañña (forests) because they possess the factors of a forest, and vanapattha (forest-haunts) because they are large forest thickets. Pāntāni means remote places.

Kalyāṇadhamme refers to one who has good qualities through that very virtue. Dukkhapaṭikūle refers to one who does not desire suffering. Seyyo bhavissati means the happiness of a good destination will occur in the next life; this is the meaning.

Upavijanyā means one whose time for giving birth is near, who is heavily pregnant, meaning she will give birth before long. Opabhoggā bhavissati means she will be a handmaid. Anayavyasanaṃ means great suffering. Aya means happiness; that which is not aya is anaya (suffering). That suffering is called vyasana (ruin) because it destroys all happiness. Thus, anaya itself is vyasana, hence anayavyasana, meaning great suffering. Ayoniso means by inappropriate means. Apakkaṃ na paripācenti means they do not prematurely cut off the life that is not yet mature or exhausted. Paripākaṃ āgamenti means they wait for the time of the maturity of life. This was also said by the General of the Dhamma (Venerable Sāriputta):
"I do not delight in death, I do not delight in life;
I await the time, as a hireling awaits his wages."

Ubbhinditvā means having broken the coating of fine clay.

Rāmaṇeyyakaṃ means the state of being delightful. Velāsikā refers to those who are excessive in playing. Komārikā refers to young girls. "Do they see the life (soul) that goes out or enters during the time you are dreaming?" Here, the movement of the mind (cittācāra) is taken as "jīva" (soul/life). This is because that person has the perception of a soul in that regard.

Jiyāyā means with a bowstring. Gīvaṃ veṭhetvā means wrapping it around the neck. Patthinnataro means one who is firmer or stiffer. By this, what is shown? At the time when you are alive, the [soul] of a being...
